intro.title: Introduction
paras: The Fifth Thirumurai is the largest of the early books of the Thiru Arutpa. It holds 83 garlands of song, 889 verses in all. Most are sung to Murugan, the Lord who stands on the hill of Thanigai. Others go to Vinayakar at the start, to Siva as the dancer of the golden hall, to the Goddess, to Rama and to the teachers he honored.

Read them for the voice. Vallalar doesn't describe God from a distance. He pleads, he argues with his own heart, he counts the days, he weeps that his hands have fed no one. He calls himself a dog at a miser's gate and a tree that bears only poison. Then, in the next garland, the Lord comes in procession, and a young woman sings of the one who stole her heart.

Under all of it runs one question. How can a life spent on the body and its wants become a life of grace? His answer? Love for God that shows itself as pity for every living being. Where compassion is missing, he says, worship is empty.
Each verse is printed in Tamil, in transliteration, in translation and with a short commentary. A glossary at the end explains the Tamil terms the translation keeps.

intro.title: A Note on Context
paras: These are among Vallalar's early songs. They come from the years when he worshipped God through the forms of the Saiva tradition. Most of them are sung to Murugan on the hill of Thanigai, with others to Vinayakar, to Siva and the Goddess, and even to Rama. Again and again he tells his mind to chant the six letters of Murugan and to wear the holy ash: “If one chants your six letters with a focused mind and applies the exalted holy white ash here, they will attain the realms of earth and heaven.”

He did not stay there. In the Great Teaching (Perupadesam) of 1873 he told those gathered to place no aim in the religions, Saivism among them, and he named himself as the witness. His hold on the Saiva religion had once been beyond measure. For proof he pointed to this very collection: “The hymns I have sung, gathered in the Thiru Arutpa, are enough.” Why had he held to it so firmly? He answered:
அப்போது எனக்கு அவ்வளவு கொஞ்சம் அற்ப அறிவாக இருந்தது.
“Because at that time I had only so little, such petty knowledge.”

In that same teaching he gave one mantra to all: Arutperunjothi Arutperunjothi, Thanipperunkarunai Arutperunjothi (Vast Grace-Light, Vast Grace-Light, Unique Vast Compassion, Vast Grace-Light). From then on he taught the worship of Arutperunjothi, the Vast Grace-Light, alone. His late songs in the Sixth Thirumurai sing of that Light.

So these poems are an early stage of one journey, and a sincere one. The longing in them is real, and so is the shame. In one verse he calls himself “a hunter who associates with killers,” as if no fault could weigh more. Read them as the first steps of the man who later expanded and evolved even further up until the full realization of the Vast Grace-Light.

translit: añcumukat tāṉmakaṉmāl añcumukat tāṉaruḷvāṉ añcumukat tāṉañ caṇikarattāṉ - añcumuka vañcaraiyāṉ kāṇā vakaivataittāṉ ōraraiyō ṭañcaraiyāṉ kaṇkaḷ avai.
translation: He is the son of the five-faced Lord. He whom the great illusion fears grants his grace. He has five beautiful hands. He destroyed the five deceitful senses so that I do not see them. His eyes are three.
commentary: The poet praises Vinayakar as the five-handed son of Siva, the five-faced Lord. Most people think of the five senses as natural tools for experiencing the world, but here they are called deceitful because they distract the mind with worldly illusions. By seeking this deity's grace, the poet asks to be freed from the trap of sensory desires so his vision remains entirely fixed on the divine.

translit: vātākā vaṇṇa maṇiyē-em vallapaitaṉ nātākā vaṇṇa nalaṅkoḷvāṉ - pōtār vaṉaṅkāttu nīraḷitta vaḷḷalē aṉpāl iṉaṅkāt taruḷāy eṉai.
translation: O gem of unfading brilliance, O Lord of our Vallabai. You are the generous one who protected the flower-filled forest and brought forth water. Please protect me and my kin with your love and grant your grace.
commentary: This verse addresses the deity as a brilliant gem and the lord of Vallabai, a goddess representing divine power and grace. The poet recalls a traditional story where Vinayakar protected a sacred forest and brought forth a life-giving spring of water. He asks for this same generous protective love to surround him and all his companions.

tamil: உலகெலாம் தழைப்ப அருள்மத அருவி ஒழுகுமா முகமும்ஐங் கரமும்
இலகுசெம் மேனிக் காட்சியும் இரண்டோ டிரண்டென ஓங்குதிண் தோளும்
திலகவாள் நுதலார் சித்திபுத் திகளைச் சேர்த்தணைத் திடும்இரு மருங்கும்
விலகுறா தெளியேன் விழைந்தனன் சித்தி விநாயக விக்கினேச் சுரனே.
translit: ulakelām taḻaippa aruḷmata aruvi oḻukumā mukamumaiṅ karamum ilakucem mēṉik kāṭciyum iraṇṭō ṭiraṇṭeṉa ōṅkutiṇ tōḷum tilakavāḷ nutalār cittiput tikaḷaic cērttaṇait tiṭumiru maruṅkum vilakuṟā teḷiyēṉ viḻaintaṉaṉ citti vināyaka vikkiṉēc curaṉē.
translation: O Siddhi Vinayakar, Lord of Obstacles. For all the worlds to flourish, a waterfall of grace flows from your great face. You have five hands. Your shining red body is a beautiful sight. Your strong shoulders rise as four. On both your sides you embrace Siddhi and Buddhi, who have radiant foreheads bearing the tilaka. I, a humble soul, constantly yearn for this vision of you without ever turning away.
commentary: The poet describes the traditional form of the elephant-headed deity, transforming physical details into symbols of compassion. The fluid that naturally flows from an elephant's face is seen here as a continuous waterfall of divine grace meant to make all the worlds flourish. The deity embraces his two consorts, Siddhi (spiritual attainment) and Buddhi (intellect or wisdom), showing that true grace brings both perfect knowledge and deep spiritual power.

tamil: உள்ளமும் உயிரும் உணர்ச்சியும் உடம்பும் உறுபொருள் யாவும்நின் தனக்கே
கள்ளமும் கரிசும் நினைந்திடா துதவிக் கழல்இணை நினைந்துநின் கருணை
வெள்ளம்உண் டிரவுபகல்அறி யாத வீட்டினில் இருந்துநின் னோடும்
விள்ளல்இல் லாமல் கலப்பனோ சித்தி விநாயக விக்கினேச் சுரனே.
translit: uḷḷamum uyirum uṇarcciyum uṭampum uṟuporuḷ yāvumniṉ taṉakkē kaḷḷamum karicum niṉaintiṭā tutavik kaḻaliṇai niṉaintuniṉ karuṇai veḷḷamuṇ ṭiravupakalaṟi yāta vīṭṭiṉil iruntuniṉ ṉōṭum viḷḷalil lāmal kalappaṉō citti vināyaka vikkiṉēc curaṉē.
translation: O Siddhi Vinayakar, Lord of Obstacles. I offer my mind, my life, my feeling, my body, and all my possessions to you alone, giving them without deceit or impurity. Meditating on your two feet, I drink the flood of your grace. Dwelling in the home of liberation that knows neither night nor day, will I merge with you without any separation?
commentary: True devotion requires total surrender of the mind, the body, all feelings, and all worldly possessions. The poet offers these without any hidden motives or impurities, asking only to drink deeply of divine compassion. He longs to enter a state of liberation that has no day or night, meaning a realm entirely beyond time and ordinary earthly dualities, to merge with the divine forever.

tamil: நாதமும் கடந்து நிறைந்துநின் மயமே நான்என அறிந்துநான் தானாம்
பேதமும் கடந்த மௌனராச் சியத்தைப் பேதையேன் பிடிப்பதெந் நாளோ
ஏதமும் சமய வாதமும் விடுத்தோர் இதயமும் ஏழையேன் சிரமும்
வேதமும் தாங்கும் பாதனே சித்தி விநாயக விக்கினேச் சுரனே.
translit: nātamum kaṭantu niṟaintuniṉ mayamē nāṉeṉa aṟintunāṉ tāṉām pētamum kaṭanta mauṉarāc ciyattaip pētaiyēṉ piṭippaten nāḷō ētamum camaya vātamum viṭuttōr itayamum ēḻaiyēṉ ciramum vētamum tāṅkum pātaṉē citti vināyaka vikkiṉēc curaṉē.
translation: O Siddhi Vinayakar, Lord of Obstacles. Your feet are borne by the Vedas, by the hearts of those who have cast off faults and religious disputes, and by the head of this poor soul. Pervading beyond the primal sound, realizing that I am truly of your nature, when will I, an ignorant one, grasp that kingdom of silence which transcends the duality of myself and yourself?
commentary: The highest spiritual state is a kingdom of pure silence that exists far beyond all primal sound and any sense of separate identity. To reach this truth, one must completely abandon all religious arguments and sectarian disputes, which Vallalar teaches are false and only obscure reality. The divine presence rests on the ancient scriptures, on the humble head of the poet, and in the pure hearts of those who have given up the falsehood of religious quarrels.

tamil: சச்சிதானந்த வடிவம்நம் வடிவம் தகும்அதிட் டானம்மற் றிரண்டும்
பொய்ச்சிதா பாசக் கற்பனை இவற்றைப் போக்கியாங் கவ்வடி வாகி
அச்சிதா கார போதமும் அதன்மேல் ஆனந்த போதமும் விடுத்தல்
மெய்ச்சிதாம் வீடென் றுரைத்தனை சித்தி விநாயக விக்கினேச் சுரனே.
translit: caccitāṉanta vaṭivamnam vaṭivam takumatiṭ ṭāṉammaṟ ṟiraṇṭum poyccitā pācak kaṟpaṉai ivaṟṟaip pōkkiyāṅ kavvaṭi vāki accitā kāra pōtamum ataṉmēl āṉanta pōtamum viṭuttal meyccitām vīṭeṉ ṟuraittaṉai citti vināyaka vikkiṉēc curaṉē.
translation: You taught that our true form is the form of existence, consciousness, and bliss. This is the fitting foundation. The other two are false imaginations of reflected consciousness. You declared that dispelling these, becoming that very form, and then letting go of the awareness of that conscious form and the subsequent awareness of bliss is the true state of liberation, O Siddhi Vinayakar, Lord of Obstacles.
commentary: True liberation means going beyond even the awareness of our own spiritual joy. Our real nature is a foundation of pure existence, consciousness, and bliss, which we reach by clearing away the false identities created by the mind. Once we rest in that true form, we must let go of even the conscious thought of it to be truly free.

tamil: ஒன்றல இரண்டும் அலஇரண் டொன்றோ டுருஅல அருஅல உவட்ட
நன்றல நன்றல் லாதல விந்து நாதமும் அலஇவை அனைத்தும்
பொன்றல்என் றறிந்துட் புறத்தினும் அகண்ட பூரண மாம்சிவம் ஒன்றே
வென்றல்என் றறிநீ என்றனை சித்தி விநாயக விக்கினேச் சுரனே.
translit: oṉṟala iraṇṭum ala-iraṇ ṭoṉṟō ṭuru-ala aru-ala uvaṭṭa naṉṟala naṉṟal lātala vintu nātamum ala-ivai aṉaittum poṉṟaleṉ ṟaṟintuṭ puṟattiṉum akaṇṭa pūraṇa māmcivam oṉṟē veṉṟaleṉ ṟaṟinī eṉṟaṉai citti vināyaka vikkiṉēc curaṉē.
translation: It is not one, nor two, nor a combination of both. It is neither form nor formless. It is neither abundantly good nor bad. It is neither primal light nor primal sound. Realizing that all these perish, know that both inside and outside, only the undivided, perfect Sivam reigns supreme. You instructed me thus, O Siddhi Vinayakar, Lord of Obstacles.
commentary: The ultimate reality defies all human categories and boundaries. It cannot be counted as one or two, described as form or formless, or defined as vintu (primal light) and nātam (primal sound). All these dualities and concepts eventually perish, leaving only the undivided, perfect divine presence shining supreme everywhere.

tamil: சத்தசத் தியல்மற் றறிந்துமெய்ப் போதத் தத்துவ நிலைபெற விழைவோர்
சித்தமுற் றகலா தொளித்தநின் கமலச் சேவடி தொழஎனக் கருள்வாய்
சுத்தசற் குணத்தெள் ளமுதெழு கடலே சுகபரி பூரணப் பொருளே
வித்தக முக்கண் அத்தனே சித்தி விநாயக விக்கினேச் சுரனே.
translit: cattacat tiyalmaṟ ṟaṟintumeyp pōtat tattuva nilaipeṟa viḻaivōr cittamuṟ ṟakalā toḷittaniṉ kamalac cēvaṭi toḻa-eṉak karuḷvāy cuttacaṟ kuṇatteḷ ḷamuteḻu kaṭalē cukapari pūraṇap poruḷē vittaka mukkaṇ attaṉē citti vināyaka vikkiṉēc curaṉē.
translation: Grant me the grace to worship your red lotus feet, which remain hidden yet inseparable within the minds of those who have known the nature of the real and the unreal and who desire to attain the steadfast state of true wisdom. O ocean welling with the clear nectar of pure and excellent qualities! O reality of perfect bliss! O wise Lord with three eyes, O Siddhi Vinayakar, Lord of Obstacles!
commentary: The divine presence rests quietly within the minds of those who seek true wisdom. This verse is a plea for the grace to recognize and worship that inner presence. The first step on this path is learning to distinguish what is real and eternal from what is unreal and passing.

tamil: மருள்உறு மனமும் கொடியவெங் குணமும் மதித்தறி யாததுன் மதியும்
இருள்உறு நிலையும் நீங்கிநின் அடியை எந்தநாள் அடைகுவன் எளியேன்
அருள்உறும் ஒளியாய் அவ்வொளிக் குள்ளே அமர்ந்தசிற் பரஒளி நிறைவே
வெருள்உறு சமயத் தறியொணாச் சித்தி விநாயக விக்கினேச் சுரனே.
translit: maruḷuṟu maṉamum koṭiyaveṅ kuṇamum matittaṟi yātatuṉ matiyum iruḷuṟu nilaiyum nīṅkiniṉ aṭiyai entanāḷ aṭaikuvaṉ eḷiyēṉ aruḷuṟum oḷiyāy avvoḷik kuḷḷē amarntaciṟ para-oḷi niṟaivē veruḷuṟu camayat taṟiyoṇāc citti vināyaka vikkiṉēc curaṉē.
translation: When will I, a poor wretch, shed this deluded mind, these cruel and harsh qualities, this thoughtless wicked intellect, and this state of darkness to reach your feet? You manifest as the light of grace and dwell as the fullness of supreme conscious light within that light. You remain unknowable to bewildering religions, O Siddhi Vinayakar, Lord of Obstacles.
commentary: The divine reality is a supreme conscious light of grace, completely unknowable to bewildering religions. Vallalar states plainly that organized religions fail to grasp this truth. To reach the divine, a seeker must instead shed their harsh qualities, cruel intellect, and mental delusions.

tamil: கேவலசகல வாதனை அதனால் கீழ்ப்படும் அவக்கடல் மூழ்கி
ஓவற மயங்கி உழலும்இச் சிறியேன் உன்அருள் அடையும்நாள் உளதோ
பாவலர் உளத்தில் பரவிய நிறைவே பரமசிற் சுகபரம் பரனே
மேவுறும் அடியார்க் கருளிய சித்தி விநாயக விக்கினேச் சுரனே.
translit: kēvalacakala vātaṉai ataṉāl kīḻppaṭum avakkaṭal mūḻki ōvaṟa mayaṅki uḻalumic ciṟiyēṉ uṉaruḷ aṭaiyumnāḷ uḷatō pāvalar uḷattil paraviya niṟaivē paramaciṟ cukaparam paraṉē mēvuṟum aṭiyārk karuḷiya citti vināyaka vikkiṉēc curaṉē.
translation: I am sinking in the degrading ocean of vanity, dragged down by the latent tendencies of the isolated and active states of the soul. I wander in ceaseless delusion. Will a day ever come for this lowly one to attain your grace? You are the fullness pervading the hearts of poets. You are the supreme Lord of ultimate conscious bliss. You bestow grace upon the devotees who draw near you, O Siddhi Vinayakar, Lord of Obstacles.
commentary: The soul struggles constantly between kēvala (a dormant, isolated state) and cakala (a state of active worldly entanglement). These deep-seated habits drag us down into an ocean of vanity and ceaseless delusion. The only escape from this exhausting cycle is the direct grace of the divine, which fills the hearts of true seekers with ultimate conscious bliss.

tamil: கானல்நீர் விழைந்த மான்என உலகக் கட்டினை நட்டுழன் றலையும்
ஈனவஞ் சகநெஞ் சகப்புலை யேனை ஏன்றுகொண் டருளும்நாள் உளதோ
ஊனம்ஓன் றில்லா உத்தமர் உளத்தே ஓங்குசீர்ப் பிரணவ ஒளியே
வேல்நவில் கரத்தோர்க் கினியவா சித்தி விநாயக விக்கினேச் சுரனே.
translit: kāṉalnīr viḻainta māṉeṉa ulakak kaṭṭiṉai naṭṭuḻaṉ ṟalaiyum īṉavañ cakaneñ cakappulai yēṉai ēṉṟukoṇ ṭaruḷumnāḷ uḷatō ūṉamōṉ ṟillā uttamar uḷattē ōṅkucīrp piraṇava oḷiyē vēlnavil karattōrk kiṉiyavā citti vināyaka vikkiṉēc curaṉē.
translation: Like a deer thirsting for a mirage, I seek worldly bonds and wander aimlessly. I am a base and deceitful wretch. Is there a day when you will accept me and bestow your grace? O majestic light of the primal sound rising in the hearts of the flawless noble ones! O sweet brother to the Lord wielding the spear! O Siddhi Vinayakar, Lord of Obstacles!
commentary: Vallalar compares the human pursuit of worldly attachments to a thirsty deer chasing a desert mirage. Confessing his own wandering mind, he asks when he will finally be worthy to receive divine grace. He envisions the deity Vinayakar as the shining light of the primal sound (Pranava, the sacred syllable Om) that awakens naturally in pure hearts.

tamil: பெரும்பொருட் கிடனாம் பிரணவ வடிவில் பிறங்கிய ஒருதனிப் பேறே
அரும்பொருள் ஆகி மறைமுடிக் கண்ணே அமர்ந்தபே ரானந்த நிறைவே
தரும்பர போக சித்தியும் சுத்த தருமமும் முத்தியும் சார்ந்து
விரும்பினோர்க் களிக்கும் வள்ளலே சித்தி விநாயக விக்கினேச் சுரனே.
translit: perumporuṭ kiṭaṉām piraṇava vaṭivil piṟaṅkiya orutaṉip pēṟē arumporuḷ āki maṟaimuṭik kaṇṇē amarntapē rāṉanta niṟaivē tarumpara pōka cittiyum cutta tarumamum muttiyum cārntu virumpiṉōrk kaḷikkum vaḷḷalē citti vināyaka vikkiṉēc curaṉē.
translation: O unparalleled supreme boon shining in the form of the primal sound, the seat of the great reality! O supreme bliss seated as the rare truth at the crown of the Vedas! O bountiful Lord who grants heavenly enjoyment, spiritual powers, pure righteousness, and liberation to those who approach and desire them! O Siddhi Vinayakar, Lord of Obstacles!
commentary: The divine presence takes the shape of the primal sound (Pranava) and stands as the ultimate truth above all scriptures. Vallalar praises Vinayakar as a deeply generous giver. The deity grants heavenly joys, spiritual powers, pure righteousness, and final liberation to anyone who approaches with genuine desire.

sections.title: The Garland of Grace for Vallabai Ganesha

tamil: திருநெடு மால்அன் றால்இடை நினது சேவடித் துணைமலர்த் துகளான்
பெருநெடு மேனி தனிற்படப்பாம்பின் பேருரு அகன்றமை மறவேன்
கருநெடுங் கடலைக் கடத்துநற் றுணையே கண்கள்மூன் றுடையசெங் கரும்பே
வருநெடு மருப்பொன் றிலகுவா ரணமே வல்லபைக் கணேசமா மணியே.
translit: tiruneṭu mālaṉ ṟāliṭai niṉatu cēvaṭit tuṇaimalart tukaḷāṉ peruneṭu mēṉi taṉiṟpaṭappāmpiṉ pēruru akaṉṟamai maṟavēṉ karuneṭuṅ kaṭalaik kaṭattunaṟ ṟuṇaiyē kaṇkaḷmūṉ ṟuṭaiyaceṅ karumpē varuneṭu maruppoṉ ṟilakuvā raṇamē vallapaik kaṇēcamā maṇiyē.
translation: I will not forget how the huge serpent form departed from the immense body of the great Vishnu on that day under the banyan tree, when the dust of your paired, lotus-like, red feet touched him. O good companion who helps us cross the dark vast ocean of birth! O red sugarcane with three eyes! O elephant shining with one long tusk! O great gem, Vallabai Ganesha!
commentary: The dust of God's feet has the power to free even the greatest divinities from bondage. A traditional story tells of Vishnu, cursed to take the form of a serpent, who was restored to his true self simply by the dust falling from Ganesha's feet. The divine acts here as a deeply personal companion who helps the soul cross the dark ocean of continuous birth and death.

tamil: நளினமா மலர்வாழ் நான்முகத் தொருவன் நண்ணிநின் துணையடிவழுத்திக்
அளிநலன் உறுபே ரானந்தக் கடலே அருமருந் தேஅருள் அமுதே
வளிநிறை உலகுக் கொருபெருந் துணையே வல்லபைக் கணேசமா மணியே.
translit: naḷiṉamā malarvāḻ nāṉmukat toruvaṉ naṇṇiniṉ tuṇaiyaṭivaḻuttik kaḷinalaṉ uṭaṉ ivvulakelāmpaṭaikkakkaṭaikkaṇittatai-uḷammaṟavēṉ aḷinalaṉ uṟupē rāṉantak kaṭalē arumarun tē-aruḷ amutē vaḷiniṟai ulakuk koruperun tuṇaiyē vallapaik kaṇēcamā maṇiyē.
translation: I will not forget in my heart how you cast your gracious glance on the four-faced Brahma, who dwells on the great lotus flower, when he approached and praised your paired feet so he could create all these worlds with joyful goodness. O ocean of great bliss filled with the goodness of grace! O rare medicine! O ambrosia of grace! O singular great companion for this wind-filled world! O great gem, Vallabai Ganesha!
commentary: Divine grace is the foundation of all creation. Even Brahma, the creator god in Hindu tradition, relies entirely on a higher divine glance to perform his cosmic duties. This supreme grace serves as a rare medicine and an ocean of bliss that sustains the physical world.

tamil: சீர்உருத் திரமூர்த் திகட்குமுத் தொழிலும் செய்தருள் இறைமைதந் தருளில்
பேர்உருத் திரங்கொண் டிடச்செயும் நினது பெருமையை நாள்தொறும் மறவேன்
ஆர்உருத் திடினும் அஞ்சுதல் செய்யா ஆண்மைஎற் கருளிய அரசே
வார்உருத் திடுபூண் மணிமுகக் கொங்கை வல்லபைக் கணேசமா மணியே.
translit: cīrurut tiramūrt tikaṭkumut toḻilum ceytaruḷ iṟaimaitan taruḷil pērurut tiraṅkoṇ ṭiṭacceyum niṉatu perumaiyai nāḷtoṟum maṟavēṉ ārurut tiṭiṉum añcutal ceyyā āṇmai-eṟ karuḷiya aracē vārurut tiṭupūṇ maṇimukak koṅkai vallapaik kaṇēcamā maṇiyē.
translation: Every day I will not forget your greatness in granting sovereign power to the glorious Rudras to perform the three cosmic functions, making them assume great and fierce forms. O king who granted me the courage to fear no one, whoever might threaten! O great gem, Vallabai Ganesha, accompanied by Vallabai whose beautiful jewel-adorned breasts are bound by a band!
commentary: True spiritual refuge brings absolute fearlessness. The same supreme power that grants the fierce Rudras (deities of destruction and transformation) their authority over cosmic functions also gives the humble devotee the courage to stand unthreatened by anyone. Remembering this divine strength daily creates an unshakable inner security.

tamil: விண்ணவர் புகழும் மெய்கண்ட நாதன் வித்தகக் கபிலன்ஆ தியர்க்கே
கண்அருள் செயும்நின் பெருமையை அடியேன் கனவிலும் நனவிலும் மறவேன்
தண்அருட் கடலே அருட்சிவ போக சாரமே சராசர நிறைவே
வண்ணமா மேனிப் பரசிவ களிறே வல்லபைக் கணேசமா மணியே.
translit: viṇṇavar pukaḻum meykaṇṭa nātaṉ vittakak kapilaṉā tiyarkkē kaṇaruḷ ceyumniṉ perumaiyai aṭiyēṉ kaṉavilum naṉavilum maṟavēṉ taṇaruṭ kaṭalē aruṭciva pōka cāramē carācara niṟaivē vaṇṇamā mēṉip paraciva kaḷiṟē vallapaik kaṇēcamā maṇiyē.
translation: I, your servant, will never forget your greatness, in dream or in waking life, in granting your gracious glance to Meykanda Natha praised by the celestials, to the wise Kapila, and to others. O ocean of cool grace! O essence of the blissful experience of Siva's grace! O fullness pervading all moving and unmoving things! O supreme Siva elephant with a beautiful grand body! O great gem, Vallabai Ganesha!
commentary: The supreme divine is the ultimate teacher of all sages. Meykanda Natha, a foundational saint of Tamil spiritual philosophy, and Kapila, an ancient sage, both received their deep wisdom through this same divine grace. This power is the very essence of spiritual experience, and it fills every moving and unmoving thing in the universe.

tamil: நாரையூர் நம்பி அமுதுகொண் டூட்ட நற்றிரு வாய்மலர்ந் தருளிச்
சீரைமே வுறச்செய் தளித்திடும் நினது திருவருள் நாள்தொறும் மறவேன்
தேரைஊர் வாழ்வும் திரம்அல எனும்நற் றிடம்எனக் கருளிய வாழ்வே
வாரைஊர் முலையாள் மங்கைநா யகிஎம் வல்லபைக் கணேசமா மணியே.
translit: nāraiyūr nampi amutukoṇ ṭūṭṭa naṟṟiru vāymalarn taruḷic cīraimē vuṟaccey taḷittiṭum niṉatu tiruvaruḷ nāḷtoṟum maṟavēṉ tērai-ūr vāḻvum tiramala eṉumnaṟ ṟiṭameṉak karuḷiya vāḻvē vārai-ūr mulaiyāḷ maṅkainā yaki-em vallapaik kaṇēcamā maṇiyē.
translation: Every day I will not forget your divine grace in graciously opening your sacred mouth to eat when Nambi of Naraiyur brought food to feed you, blessing him with greatness. O life who granted me the firm conviction that even a life riding in a royal chariot is impermanent! O great gem, our Vallabai Ganesha, beside the goddess lady whose breasts are bound by a band!
commentary: God responds directly to simple and pure devotion. A legendary story tells of Nambi, a young boy who innocently offered food to a stone statue of Ganesha until the deity physically accepted it. This intimate connection brings the deep realization that all worldly power and royal wealth are entirely fleeting.

tamil: கும்பமா முனியின் கரகநீர் கவிழ்த்துக் குளிர்மலர் நந்தனம் காத்துச்
செம்பொன்நாட் டிறைவற் கருளிய நினது திருவருட் பெருமையை மறவேன்
நம்பனார்க் கினிய அருள்மகப் பேறே நற்குணத் தோர்பெரு வாழ்வே
வம்பறா மலர்த்தார் மழைமுகில் கூந்தல் வல்லபைக் கணேசமா மணியே.
translit: kumpamā muṉiyiṉ karakanīr kaviḻttuk kuḷirmalar nantaṉam kāttuc cempoṉnāṭ ṭiṟaivaṟ karuḷiya niṉatu tiruvaruṭ perumaiyai maṟavēṉ nampaṉārk kiṉiya aruḷmakap pēṟē naṟkuṇat tōrperu vāḻvē vampaṟā malarttār maḻaimukil kūntal vallapaik kaṇēcamā maṇiyē.
translation: You overturned the water-pot of the great pot-born sage to protect the cool flower garden. I will not forget the greatness of your divine grace that you bestowed upon the lord of the red-gold realm. O sweet and gracious son of the trusted Lord! O great life of those with good qualities! O great gem, Vallabai Ganesha, beside Vallabai whose hair is like rain clouds adorned with garlands of fresh and fragrant flowers!
commentary: Divine grace playfully intervenes to protect living things. Vallalar recalls a famous story where the deity Ganesha took the form of a bird to tip over a great sage's water pot. This act released a river to save a dying flower garden. Ganesha is praised here alongside Vallabai, his divine consort.

tamil: அயன்தவத் தீன்ற சித்திபுத் திகள்ஆம் அம்மையர் இருவரை மணந்தே
இயன்றஅண் டங்கள் வாழ்வுறச் செயும்நின் எழில்மணக் கோலத்தை மறவேன்
பயன்தரும் கருணைக் கற்பகத் தருவே பரசிவத் தெழுபரம் பரமே
வயன்தரு நிமல நித்தியப் பொருளே வல்லபைக் கணேசமா மணியே.
translit: ayaṉtavat tīṉṟa cittiput tikaḷām ammaiyar iruvarai maṇantē iyaṉṟa-aṇ ṭaṅkaḷ vāḻvuṟac ceyumniṉ eḻilmaṇak kōlattai maṟavēṉ payaṉtarum karuṇaik kaṟpakat taruvē paracivat teḻuparam paramē vayaṉtaru nimala nittiyap poruḷē vallapaik kaṇēcamā maṇiyē.
translation: Marrying the two mothers, Siddhi and Buddhi, who were born of Brahma's penance, you make the created universes flourish. I will not forget your beautiful wedding form. O wish-fulfilling tree of grace yielding fruit! O supreme reality arising from Parasiva! O pure and eternal substance granting strength! O great gem, Vallabai Ganesha!
commentary: The divine brings wisdom and spiritual power into the physical world. Siddhi (spiritual attainment) and Buddhi (intellectual wisdom) are represented here as Ganesha's two divine brides. Vallalar sees this holy union as the cosmic force that keeps the entire universe alive and thriving.

tamil: முன்அருந் தவத்தோன் முற்கலன் முதலா முனிவர்கள் இனிதுவீ டடைய
இன்னருள் புரியும் நின்அருட் பெருமை இரவினும் பகலினும் மறவேன்
என்அரும் பொருளே என்உயிர்க் குயிரே என்அர சேஎன துறவே
மன்அரு நெறியில் மன்னிய அறிவே வல்லபைக் கணேசமா மணியே.
translit: muṉarun tavattōṉ muṟkalaṉ mutalā muṉivarkaḷ iṉituvī ṭaṭaiya iṉṉaruḷ puriyum niṉaruṭ perumai iraviṉum pakaliṉum maṟavēṉ eṉarum poruḷē eṉuyirk kuyirē eṉara cē-eṉa tuṟavē maṉaru neṟiyil maṉṉiya aṟivē vallapaik kaṇēcamā maṇiyē.
translation: You bestowed sweet grace so that ancient sages of rare penance, such as Mudgala, could easily attain liberation. I will not forget the greatness of your grace by day or by night. O my precious treasure! O life of my life! O my king and my kin! O knowledge abiding in the established and rare path! O great gem, Vallabai Ganesha!
commentary: True knowledge leads directly to spiritual liberation. Vallalar recalls how ancient sages reached this freedom through divine grace. He addresses the divine with deep personal intimacy, calling God his king, his kin, and the very life within his own life.

tamil: துதிபெறும் காசி நகரிடத் தனந்தம் தூயநல் உருவுகொண் டாங்கண்
விதிபெறும் மனைகள் தொறும்விருந் தினனாய் மேவிய கருணையை மறவேன்
நதிபெறும் சடிலப் பவளநற் குன்றே நான்மறை நாடரு நலமே
மதிபெறும் உளத்தில் பதிபெறும் சிவமே வல்லபைக் கணேசமா மணியே.
translit: tutipeṟum kāci nakariṭat taṉantam tūyanal uruvukoṇ ṭāṅkaṇ vitipeṟum maṉaikaḷ toṟumvirun tiṉaṉāy mēviya karuṇaiyai maṟavēṉ natipeṟum caṭilap pavaḷanaṟ kuṉṟē nāṉmaṟai nāṭaru nalamē matipeṟum uḷattil patipeṟum civamē vallapaik kaṇēcamā maṇiyē.
translation: You took countless pure and good forms in the praised city of Kashi. I will not forget your grace of appearing as a guest in every proper home there. O fine coral mountain with a river in your matted locks! O goodness sought by the four Vedas! O Sivam established in the discerning heart! O great gem, Vallabai Ganesha!
commentary: God can take countless forms at once to bless receptive souls. Vallalar recounts a traditional story where the deity appeared simultaneously as a sacred guest in every pure home in the holy city of Kashi. He reveals that this exact same supreme presence is permanently established inside every discerning human heart.

tamil: தடக்கைமா முகமும் முக்கணும் பவளச் சடிலமும் சதுர்ப்புயங் களும்கை
இடக்கைஅங் குசமும் பாசமும் பதமும் இறைப்பொழு தேனும்யான் மறவேன்
விடக்களம் உடைய வித்தகப் பெருமான் மிகமகிழ்ந் திடஅருட் பேறே
மடக்கொடி நங்கை மங்கைநா யகிஎம் வல்லபைக் கணேசமா மணியே.
translit: taṭakkaimā mukamum mukkaṇum pavaḷac caṭilamum caturppuyaṅ kaḷumkai iṭakkai-aṅ kucamum pācamum patamum iṟaippoḻu tēṉumyāṉ maṟavēṉ viṭakkaḷam uṭaiya vittakap perumāṉ mikamakiḻn tiṭa-aruṭ pēṟē maṭakkoṭi naṅkai maṅkainā yaki-em vallapaik kaṇēcamā maṇiyē.
translation: I will not forget even for a moment your broad elephant face, your three eyes, your coral-red matted locks, your four arms, the goad and noose in your hands, and your sacred feet. O gracious son who brings great joy to the wise Lord with the poison-stained throat! O great gem, Vallabai Ganesha, beside the tender vine-like queen among women!
commentary: Visualizing the exact features of a deity is a powerful way to anchor the mind in devotion. Vallalar carefully lists the traditional details of Ganesha, describing his elephant face, his four arms holding sacred tools, and his three eyes. Remembering this form constantly prevents the seeker from forgetting the divine even for a single moment.

tamil: பெருவயல் ஆறு முகன்நகல் அமர்ந்துன் பெருமைகள் பேசிடத் தினமும்
திருவளர் மேன்மைத் திறமுறச் சூழும் திருவருட் பெருமையை மறவேன்
மருவளர் தெய்வக் கற்பக மலரே மனமொழி கடந்தவான் பொருளே
வருமலை வல்லிக் கொருமுதற் பேறே வல்லபைக் கணேசமா மணியே.
translit: peruvayal āṟu mukaṉnakal amarntuṉ perumaikaḷ pēciṭat tiṉamum tiruvaḷar mēṉmait tiṟamuṟac cūḻum tiruvaruṭ perumaiyai maṟavēṉ maruvaḷar teyvak kaṟpaka malarē maṉamoḻi kaṭantavāṉ poruḷē varumalai vallik korumutaṟ pēṟē vallapaik kaṇēcamā maṇiyē.
translation: O great gem, Vallabai Ganesha. O fragrant divine wish-fulfilling flower. O supreme reality transcending mind and speech. O unparalleled first treasure of the mountain-creeper Goddess. Every day, as Arumugan of Peruvayal sits joyfully to speak of your glories, I will never forget the greatness of your holy grace that encompasses me with flourishing divine excellence.
commentary: The poet vows to always remember the encompassing grace of Ganesha, addressed here as Vallabai Ganesha. He calls this deity the supreme reality that exists far beyond the reach of human thoughts and words. Ganesha is praised as the first treasure of the goddess Parvati, who is poetically described as a mountain creeper. The verse captures a shared moment of devotion involving Arumugan of Peruvayal, a fellow devotee who joyfully recites the deity's glories every day. Listening to these daily praises, the poet feels entirely surrounded by divine grace.

sections.title: The Garland of Ganesha's Divine Grace

tamil: திருவும் கல்வியும் சீரும்சி றப்பும்உன் திருவ டிப்புகழ் பாடுந்தி றமும்நல்
உருவும் சீலமும் ஊக்கமும் தாழ்வுறா உணர்வும் தந்தென துள்ளத்த மர்ந்தவா
வெருவும் சிந்தைவி லகக்க ஜானனம் விளங்கும் சித்தி விநாயக வள்ளலே.
translit: tiruvum kalviyum cīrumci ṟappumuṉ tiruva ṭippukaḻ pāṭunti ṟamumnal uruvum cīlamum ūkkamum tāḻvuṟā uṇarvum tanteṉa tuḷḷatta marntavā kuruvumteyvamum āki-aṉ pāḷartam kuṟaitavirkkumkuṇapperuṅkuṉṟamē veruvum cintaivi lakakka jāṉaṉam viḷaṅkum citti vināyaka vaḷḷalē.
translation: You gave me wealth, learning, eminence, excellence, the skill to sing the glory of your divine feet, a good form, virtue, zeal, and unfailing awareness, and then took your seat within my heart. You became both Guru and God. You are the great mountain of virtues who dispels the wants of your loving devotees. O elephant-faced one who banishes fearful thoughts, O shining and benevolent Siddhi Vinayakar!
commentary: Every good thing in life, from worldly learning and success to inner virtue, is a direct gift from the divine. Ganesha provides these gifts to prepare the human heart to become his own dwelling place. He acts as both the supreme God and the guiding teacher (Guru), clearing away all anxious thoughts so that clear, fearless awareness can take root.

tamil: சீத நாள்மலர்ச் செல்வனும் மாமலர்ச் செல்வி மார்பகச் செல்வனும் காண்கிலாப்
பாதம் நாடொறும் பற்றறப் பற்றுவோர் பாதம் நாடப் பரிந்தருள் பாலிப்பாய்
நாதம் நாடிய அந்தத்தில் ஓங்கும்மெய்ஞ் ஞான நாடக நாயக நான்கெனும்
வேதம் நாடிய மெய்பொரு ளேஅருள் விளங்கும் சித்தி விநாயக வள்ளலே.
translit: cīta nāḷmalarc celvaṉum māmalarc celvi mārpakac celvaṉum kāṇkilāp pātam nāṭoṟum paṟṟaṟap paṟṟuvōr pātam nāṭap parintaruḷ pālippāy nātam nāṭiya antattil ōṅkummeyñ ñāṉa nāṭaka nāyaka nāṉkeṉum vētam nāṭiya meyporu ḷē-aruḷ viḷaṅkum citti vināyaka vaḷḷalē.
translation: The lord of the cool, fresh lotus and the lord who holds the goddess of the great lotus on his chest could not see your feet. You lovingly bestow your grace upon those who seek the feet of your devotees, who daily cling to your feet devoid of worldly attachments. You are the hero of the drama of true wisdom that rises at the culmination of the primal sound. You are the true reality sought by the four Vedas. O shining and benevolent Siddhi Vinayakar!
commentary: The ultimate divine reality is beyond the reach of even the greatest traditional deities, such as Brahma who sits on a lotus and Vishnu who holds the goddess of wealth on his chest. Yet this supreme truth makes itself readily available to those who let go of worldly attachments and seek the company of humble devotees. Ganesha is praised as the very source of reality itself, awakening deep within the soul when the primordial cosmic sound (nada) reaches its absolute stillness.

tamil: என்னை வேண்டிஎ னக்கருள் செய்தியேல் இன்னல் நீங்கும்நல் இன்பமும் ஓங்கும்நின்
தன்னை வேண்டிச்ச ரண்புகுந் தேன்என்னைத் தாங்கிக் கொள்ளும்சரன்பிறி தில்லைகாண்
அன்னைவேண்டிஅ ழும்மகப் போல்கின்றேன் அறிகி லேன்நின்தி ருவுளம் ஐயனே
மின்னை வேண்டிய செஞ்சடையாளனே விளங்கும் சித்தி விநாயக வள்ளலே.
translit: eṉṉai vēṇṭi-e ṉakkaruḷ ceytiyēl iṉṉal nīṅkumnal iṉpamum ōṅkumniṉ taṉṉai vēṇṭicca raṇpukun tēṉeṉṉait tāṅkik koḷḷumcaraṉpiṟi tillaikāṇ aṉṉaivēṇṭi-a ḻummakap pōlkiṉṟēṉ aṟiki lēṉniṉti ruvuḷam aiyaṉē miṉṉai vēṇṭiya ceñcaṭaiyāḷaṉē viḷaṅkum citti vināyaka vaḷḷalē.
translation: If you desire me and grant me your grace, my afflictions will vanish and true joy will flourish. Desiring you, I have taken refuge. Behold, I have no other refuge to sustain me. I am like a child crying for its mother. I do not know your divine will, O Lord. O Lord with red matted hair that flashes like lightning, O shining and benevolent Siddhi Vinayakar!
commentary: Total surrender is the only path forward for a soul seeking true refuge. The speaker strips away all spiritual pride, coming to God not as a scholar or ascetic but as a helpless child crying for its mother. Without the divine reaching out first with grace, the human mind cannot possibly guess God's will or find its way out of suffering.

tamil: நீண்ட மால்அர வாகிக்கி டந்துநின் நேயத் தால்கலி நீங்கிய வாறுகேட்
டாண்ட வாநின்அ டைக்கலம் ஆயினேன் அடியனேன்பிழை ஆயிர மும்பொறுத்
வேண்டு வாழ்வுத ரும்பெருந் தெய்வமே விளங்கும் சித்தி விநாயக வள்ளலே.
translit: nīṇṭa mālara vākikki ṭantuniṉ nēyat tālkali nīṅkiya vāṟukēṭ ṭāṇṭa vāniṉa ṭaikkalam āyiṉēṉ aṭiyaṉēṉpiḻai āyira mumpoṟut tīṇṭa vāviṉpa ṭikoṭutteṉṉainī-ēṉṟukoḷvataṟkeṇṇu tiyāvarum vēṇṭu vāḻvuta rumperun teyvamē viḷaṅkum citti vināyaka vaḷḷalē.
translation: I heard how the great long serpent lay down and was freed from affliction through its love for you. O Lord, I have come to you for refuge. Forgive the thousands of faults of this lowly devotee. Bring me near, grant me a place of bliss, and resolve to accept me. O great God who grants the life everyone desires, O shining and benevolent Siddhi Vinayakar!
commentary: Hearing how divine love once freed a mythical suffering serpent, a seeker steps forward to ask for the very same mercy. A sincere heart does not hide its flaws, but openly begs for thousands of past mistakes to be forgiven and washed away. The ultimate request is not merely an escape from pain, but an entry into a state of lasting bliss that only God can grant.

tamil: தஞ்சம் என்றுனைச் சார்ந்தனன் எந்தைநீ தானும் இந்தச்ச கத்தவர் போலவே
வஞ்சம் எண்ணி இருந்திடில் என் செய்வேன் வஞ்சம் அற்றம னத்துறை அண்ணலே
பஞ்ச பாதகம் தீர்த்தனை என்றுநின் பாத பங்கயம் பற்றினன் பாவியேன்
விஞ்ச நல்லருள் வேண்டித்த ருதியோ விளங்கும் சித்தி விநாயக வள்ளலே.
translit: tañcam eṉṟuṉaic cārntaṉaṉ entainī tāṉum intacca kattavar pōlavē vañcam eṇṇi iruntiṭil eṉ ceyvēṉ vañcam aṟṟama ṉattuṟai aṇṇalē pañca pātakam tīrttaṉai eṉṟuniṉ pāta paṅkayam paṟṟiṉaṉ pāviyēṉ viñca nallaruḷ vēṇṭitta rutiyō viḷaṅkum citti vināyaka vaḷḷalē.
translation: I approached you, declaring you my refuge. O my Father, if you too harbor deceit like the people of this world, what shall I do? O Lord who dwells in hearts free of deceit! Learning that you eradicate the five great sins, I, a sinner, held tightly to your lotus feet. Will you yearn for me and grant me your supreme, excellent grace? O shining and benevolent Siddhi Vinayakar!
commentary: The human mind naturally projects its own anxieties onto God, wondering if the divine might prove as deceitful as worldly people. Bringing this very fear directly to God is a mark of deep intimacy, showing a relationship built on absolute honesty rather than formal, rigid distance. Trusting that God alone can wipe away the five great sins (pancha patakam, the most severe moral offenses in classical tradition), the seeker clings desperately to the promise of supreme grace.

tamil: கள்ள நெஞ்சகன் ஆயினும் ஐயநான் கள்ளம் இன்றிக்க ழறுகின் றேன்என
துள்ளம் நின்திரு வுள்ளம்அ றியுமே ஓது கின்றதென் போதுக ழித்திடேல்
வள்ள மாமலர்ப் பாதப்பெ ரும்புகழ் வாழ்த்தி நாத்தழும் பேறவ ழங்குவாய்
வெள்ள வேணிப்பெ ருந்தகை யேஅருள் விளங்கும் சித்தி விநாயக வள்ளலே.
translit: kaḷḷa neñcakaṉ āyiṉum aiyanāṉ kaḷḷam iṉṟikka ḻaṟukiṉ ṟēṉeṉa tuḷḷam niṉtiru vuḷḷama ṟiyumē ōtu kiṉṟateṉ pōtuka ḻittiṭēl vaḷḷa māmalarp pātappe rumpukaḻ vāḻtti nāttaḻum pēṟava ḻaṅkuvāy veḷḷa vēṇippe runtakai yē-aruḷ viḷaṅkum citti vināyaka vaḷḷalē.
translation: O Lord, though my heart is deceitful, I speak now without deceit. Your divine heart knows my inner mind. Why do I say this? Do not let my time waste away. Grant me the boon of praising the great glory of your vast lotus feet until my tongue grows calluses. great son of the Lord with flooded matted hair, O shining and benevolent Siddhi Vinayakar.
commentary: Even a deceitful mind can offer a sincere prayer. The speaker confesses his own hypocrisy but begs for the strength to sing God's praises so constantly that his tongue develops calluses. He directs this plea to Siddhi Vinayakar, the elephant-headed god who removes obstacles, asking him not to let a single moment go to waste.

tamil: மண்ணில் ஆசைம யக்கற வேண்டிய மாத வர்க்கும்ம திப்பரி யாய்உனை
எண்ணி லாச்சிறி யேனையும் முன்நின்றே ஏன்று கொண்டனை இன்றுவி டுத்தியோ
உண்ணி லாவிய நின்திரு வுள்ளமும் உவகையோடுவர்ப் பும்கொள ஒண்ணுமோ
வெண்ணி லாமுடிப் புண்ணியமூர்த்தியே விளங்கும் சித்தி விநாயக வள்ளலே.
translit: maṇṇil ācaima yakkaṟa vēṇṭiya māta varkkumma tippari yāyuṉai eṇṇi lācciṟi yēṉaiyum muṉniṉṟē ēṉṟu koṇṭaṉai iṉṟuvi ṭuttiyō uṇṇi lāviya niṉtiru vuḷḷamum uvakaiyōṭuvarp pumkoḷa oṇṇumō veṇṇi lāmuṭip puṇṇiyamūrttiyē viḷaṅkum citti vināyaka vaḷḷalē.
translation: You are beyond the comprehension of even great ascetics who seek to sever the delusion of earthly desire. Yet you stood before me, a lowly one who did not even think of you, and accepted me in the past. Will you forsake me today? Is it fitting for your divine inner heart to harbor both joy and aversion? O holy Lord wearing the white crescent moon on your crown, O shining and benevolent Siddhi Vinayakar.
commentary: God's grace reaches even those who do not seek it. The speaker marvels that God, who remains a mystery even to disciplined ascetics, came to him freely when he was completely ignorant. Since the divine heart accepted him in the past, he asks how it could possibly reject him now.

tamil: ஆணி லேஅன்றி ஆருயிர்ப் பெண்ணிலே அலியி லேஇவ்வ டியனைப் போலவே
காணி லேன்ஒரு பாவியை இப்பெருங் கள்ள நெஞ்சக்க டையனை மாயையாம்
ஏணி லேஇடர் எய்தவி டுத்தியேல் என்செய் கேன்இனி இவ்வுல கத்திலே
வீணி லே உழைப் பேன்அருள் ஐயனே விளங்கும் சித்தி விநாயக வள்ளலே.
translit: āṇi lē-aṉṟi āruyirp peṇṇilē aliyi lē-ivva ṭiyaṉaip pōlavē kāṇi lēṉoru pāviyai ipperuṅ kaḷḷa neñcakka ṭaiyaṉai māyaiyām ēṇi lē-iṭar eytavi ṭuttiyēl eṉcey kēṉiṉi ivvula kattilē vīṇi lē uḻaip pēṉaruḷ aiyaṉē viḷaṅkum citti vināyaka vaḷḷalē.
translation: Among men, women with precious lives, or the genderless, I have not seen another sinner like this devotee. If you abandon this lowest one with a deceitful heart to suffer hardship on the ladder of illusion, what will I do now in this world? I will only toil in vain, O Lord of grace, O shining and benevolent Siddhi Vinayakar.
commentary: A deep sense of unworthiness often accompanies spiritual longing. The speaker feels completely alone in his flaws, believing himself to be the worst sinner among all living beings. He fears being abandoned to the painful ladder of illusion, where worldly attachments lead only to empty and endless struggle.

tamil: வாளி லேவிழி மங்கையர் கொங்கையாம் மலையி லேமுக மாயத்தி லேஅவர்
தோளி லே இடைச் சூழலி லேஉந்திச் சுழியி லேநிதம் சுற்றும்என் நெஞ்சம்நின்
தாளி லேநின்த னித்தபு கழிலே தங்கும் வண்ணம் தரஉளம் செய்தியோ
வேளி லேஅழ கானசெவ் வேளின்முன் விளங்கும் சித்தி விநாயக வள்ளலே.
translit: vāḷi lēviḻi maṅkaiyar koṅkaiyām malaiyi lēmuka māyatti lē-avar tōḷi lē iṭaic cūḻali lē-untic cuḻiyi lēnitam cuṟṟumeṉ neñcamniṉ tāḷi lēniṉta ṉittapu kaḻilē taṅkum vaṇṇam tara-uḷam ceytiyō vēḷi lē-aḻa kāṉacev vēḷiṉmuṉ viḷaṅkum citti vināyaka vaḷḷalē.
translation: My heart constantly circles around women with sword-like eyes, their mountain-like breasts, their enchanting faces, their shoulders, their curving waists, and their whirlpool navels. Will your heart grant that my mind rests instead upon your feet and your supreme glory? who shines before the beautiful spear-wielding Murugan, O shining and benevolent Siddhi Vinayakar.
commentary: Physical desires constantly pull the mind away from spiritual focus. The speaker describes how his attention spins endlessly around lust and the beauty of women. He pleads with God to steady his wandering heart and anchor it firmly in divine glory instead.

tamil: நாவி னால்உனை நாள்தொறும் பாடுவார் நாடு வார் தமை நண்ணிப்பு கழவும்
ஓவி லாதுனைப் பாடவும் துன்பெலாம் ஓடவும்மகிழ் ஓங்கவும் செய்குவாய்
காவி நேர்களத் தான்மகிழ் ஐங்கரக் கடவுளேநற்க ருங்குழி என்னும்ஊர்
மேவி அன்பர்க்க ருள்கண நாதனே விளங்கும் சித்தி விநாயக வள்ளலே.
translit: nāvi ṉāluṉai nāḷtoṟum pāṭuvār nāṭu vār tamai naṇṇippu kaḻavum ōvi lātuṉaip pāṭavum tuṉpelām ōṭavummakiḻ ōṅkavum ceykuvāy kāvi nērkaḷat tāṉmakiḻ aiṅkarak kaṭavuḷēnaṟka ruṅkuḻi eṉṉumūr mēvi aṉparkka ruḷkaṇa nātaṉē viḷaṅkum citti vināyaka vaḷḷalē.
translation: Guide me to approach and praise those who seek you and sing of you daily with their tongues. Make me sing of you ceaselessly so that all sorrow flees and joy swells. O five-armed God who brings delight to the Lord with the dark throat. O Lord of the Ganas who dwells in the good town of Karunguzhi and bestows grace upon devotees, O shining and benevolent Siddhi Vinayakar.
commentary: True joy grows in the company of others who love God. The speaker asks for the blessing to seek out sincere devotees and to sing of God without stopping. He prays to the Lord of the Ganas (the leader of the divine attendants) who dwells in Karunguzhi, a town where Vallalar lived for many years, asking him to drive away all sorrow and bring lasting delight.

tamil: திங்கள்அம் கொழுந்து வேய்ந்த செஞ்சடைக் கொழுந்தே போற்றி
மங்கைவல் லபைக்கு வாய்த்த மகிழ்நநின் மலர்த்தாள் போற்றி
ஐங்கர நால்வாய் முக்கண் அருட்சிவ களிறே போற்றி
கங்கையை மகிழும் செல்வக் கணேசநின் கழல்கள் போற்றி.
translit: tiṅkaḷam koḻuntu vēynta ceñcaṭaik koḻuntē pōṟṟi maṅkaival lapaikku vāytta makiḻnaniṉ malarttāḷ pōṟṟi aiṅkara nālvāy mukkaṇ aruṭciva kaḷiṟē pōṟṟi kaṅkaiyai makiḻum celvak kaṇēcaniṉ kaḻalkaḷ pōṟṟi.
translation: Praise to the tender shoot on the red matted hair adorned with the beautiful crescent moon. Praise to your lotus feet, O joyful beloved of the maiden Vallabai. Praise to the gracious Siva-elephant with five arms, a sweeping trunk, and three eyes. Praise to your ankleted feet, O wealthy Ganesha who rejoices in Ganga.
commentary: This opening verse offers direct praise to Ganesha, the elephant-faced god. He is celebrated here as a gracious manifestation of Siva, sharing his father's divine attributes like the three eyes and the crescent moon.

translit: ulakam paravum poruḷeṉ kō-eṉ uṟaveṉkō kalakam peṟumaim pulaṉveṉ ṟuyarum kati-eṉkō tilakam peṟuney eṉaniṉ ṟilakum civameṉkō ilakaiṅ kara-am paraniṉ taṉai-eṉ eṉkēṉē.
translation: Shall I call you the reality praised by the world, or my own kin? Shall I call you the exalted state attained by conquering the turbulent five senses? Shall I call you the Siva who shines like ghee hidden within sesame seeds? O shining five-armed Lord, what shall I call you?
commentary: The divine reality is so vast that no single name can contain it. The poet wonders whether to call this presence his own family, the quiet state reached by mastering the turbulent five senses, or the pure reality of Siva. The image of ghee hidden inside a sesame seed illustrates how the divine is always present within everything, even when unseen to the naked eye.

translit: aṭiyār uḷḷam tittit tūṟum amuteṉkō kaṭiyār koṉṟaic ceñcaṭai yāṉaik kaṉṟeṉkō poṭiyār mēṉip puṇṇiyar pukaḻum poruḷeṉkō aṭikēḷ citti vināyaka eṉeṉ ṟaṟaikēṉē.
translation: Shall I call you the nectar that wells up sweetly in the hearts of devotees? Shall I call you the elephant child of the red-matted-haired Lord who wears fragrant cassia flowers? Shall I call you the reality praised by the holy ones with ash-smeared bodies? O Lord Siddhi Vinayakar, what shall I say?
commentary: Spiritual experience is deeply personal and sweet to those who open themselves to it. The poet describes this divine presence as a wellspring of nectar rising in the heart. The holy figures smeared with sacred ash recognize this same inner sweetness as the highest truth to be praised.

tamil: கமலமலர் அயன்நயனன் முதல்அமரர் இதயம்உறு கரிசகல அருள்செய்பசு பதியாம்
நிமலநிறை மதியின்ஒளிர் நிரதிசய பரமசுக நிலையைஅருள் புரியும்அதிபதியாம்
விமலபிர ணவவடிவ விகடதட கடகரட விபுலகய முகசுகுண பதியாம்
அமலபர சிவஒளியின் உதயசய விசயசய அபயஎனும் எமதுகண பதியே.
translit: kamalamalar ayaṉnayaṉaṉ mutalamarar itayamuṟu karicakala aruḷceypacu patiyām nimalaniṟai matiyiṉoḷir niraticaya paramacuka nilaiyai-aruḷ puriyumatipatiyām vimalapira ṇavavaṭiva vikaṭataṭa kaṭakaraṭa vipulakaya mukacukuṇa patiyām amalapara civa-oḷiyiṉ utayacaya vicayacaya apaya-eṉum ematukaṇa patiyē.
translation: He is the supreme Lord of souls who graciously removes the blemishes from the hearts of the celestials, beginning with Brahma on the lotus flower and Vishnu. He is the sovereign who bestows the state of unsurpassed supreme bliss shining in the pure full moon. He is the virtuous Lord with a vast elephant face and broad temples exuding rut, embodying the pure primal sound. He is our Ganapati, the rising of the pure supreme Siva light, who grants victory and refuge.
commentary: Ganesha is described here as the embodiment of the pure primal sound (praṇava), the original vibration from which everything begins. He acts as the supreme sovereign who clears impurities from the minds of even the highest celestial beings. Ultimately, this divine figure is recognized as the rising dawn of the pure, supreme light of Siva.

translit: ampoṉṟu ceñcaṭai apparaip pōltaṉ aṭiyartamtuk kampoṉṟum vaṇṇam karuṇaicey tāḷum karutumiṉō vampoṉṟu pūṅkuḻal vallapai yōṭu vayaṅkiyaveṇ kompoṉṟu koṇṭemai āṭkoṇ ṭaruḷiya kuñcaramē.
translation: Just like the Father with red matted hair holding the beautiful waters, He rules with grace to dispel the sorrows of His devotees. Meditate upon Him. He is the elephant who shines alongside Vallabai with her fragrant flower-adorned hair, holding a single white tusk and graciously claiming us as His own.
commentary: The relationship between the divine and the devotee is one of pure grace and protection. Just as a father shields his children, this divine presence clears away sorrow and offers safe refuge. The poet invites the reader to steady their mind on this protective grace, which graciously claims the soul as its own.

translit: tirumāl vaṇaṅkat ticaimukaṉ pōṟṟac civamuṇarnta irumā tavartoḻa maṉṟakat tāṭu miṟaivaṭivāk kurumā malarppiṟai vēṇiyu mukkaṇuṅ kūṟumaintu varumā mukamuṅkoḷ vallapai pākaṉai vāḻttutumē.
translation: We praise the consort of Vallabai. He assumes the form of the Lord who dances in the Hall, bowed to by Thirumal, praised by Brahma, and worshipped by the great ascetics who have realized Sivam. He bears matted hair adorned with beautiful large flowers and the crescent moon, three eyes, and the renowned five great faces.
commentary: The verse praises Ganesha alongside his divine consort Vallabai. Here, Ganesha takes on the exact majestic appearance of Siva, the Lord who dances in the sacred Hall. He wears a crescent moon in his matted hair and possesses three eyes and five faces. The greatest gods, Thirumal (Vishnu) and Brahma, along with wise ascetics who have realized Sivam (the ultimate divine truth), bow to this unified form. The vision blends the features of father and son into a single, undivided divine presence.

translit: cīrkoṇṭa teyva vataṉaṅkaḷ āṟum tikaḻkaṭappan tārkoṇṭa paṉṉiru tōḷkaḷum tāmarait tāḷkaḷumōr kūrkoṇṭa vēlum mayilumnaṟ kōḻik koṭiyumaruṭ kārkoṇṭa vaṇmait taṇikā calamumeṉ kaṇṇuṟṟatē
translation: The six glorious divine faces, the twelve shoulders wearing shining kadambu garlands, the lotus feet, the sharp spear, the peacock, the beautiful rooster flag, and the bounteous hill of Thanigai rich with the dark rainclouds of grace have appeared before my eyes.
commentary: The poem records a direct vision of the divine in the form of Lord Murugan. It lists the familiar symbols of this deity: the six faces, twelve shoulders, spear, peacock, and rooster flag. The vision includes the sacred hill of Thanigai itself, seen here as a place overflowing with the rainclouds of grace.

translit: kaṇmūṉ ṟuṟuceṅ karumpiṉmut tēpatam kaṇṭiṭuvāṉ maṇmūṉ ṟulakum vaḻuttum pavaḷa maṇikkuṉṟamē tiṇmūṉṟu nāṉku puyaṅkoṇ ṭoḷirvac ciramaṇiyē vaṇmūṉ ṟalarmalai vāḻmayil ēṟiya māṇikkamē.
translation: O pearl of the red sugarcane that is the three-eyed Lord. O coral mountain praised by the earth and the three worlds seeking to see your feet. O shining diamond possessing twelve strong shoulders. O ruby who mounts the peacock and dwells on the bounteous blooming mountain.
commentary: The divine is praised here as a collection of precious gems: a pearl, a coral mountain, a diamond, and a ruby. The "pearl of the red sugarcane" refers to Murugan as the sweet essence and child of Siva, the three-eyed Lord. The imagery conveys the supreme value and radiant beauty of the spiritual experience.

translit: māṇitta ñāṉa maruntē-eṉ kaṇṇiṉuḷ māmaṇiyē āṇippoṉ ṉē-eṉa tāruyi rētaṇi kācalaṉē tāṇiṟki lēṉniṉait tāḻāta vañcar tamatiṭampōyp pēṇit tirintaṉaṉ antō-eṉ ceyvaṉip pētaiyaṉē.
translation: O exalted medicine of wisdom. O great pupil within my eye. O pure gold. O my precious life. O Lord of Thanigai. I do not stand firmly at your feet. I wandered, seeking the company of deceitful people who never bow to you. Alas, what will this ignorant one do?
commentary: The divine is addressed as the "exalted medicine of wisdom," a cure for inner ignorance. The speaker confesses a sense of spiritual failure, lamenting time wasted in the company of worldly, deceitful people. This deep expression of personal unworthiness is a traditional way to ask for unconditional mercy.

translit: aṉṉē eṉaittanta appā-eṉ ṟēṅki alaṟukiṉṟēṉ eṉṉē-iv vēḻaik kiraṅkātu nīṭṭit tiruttalentāy poṉṉē cukuṇap poruppē taṇikaip poruppamartta maṉṉē kalapa mayilmēl aḻakiya māmaṇiyē.
translation: I cry out in longing, calling "O Mother, O Father who begot me." My Father, why do you delay without showing mercy to this poor one? O gold. O mountain of virtues. O King who rests upon the mountain of Thanigai. O beautiful great jewel seated upon the plumed peacock.
commentary: The speaker cries out to the divine as both mother and father, the source of his very existence. He asks why grace is being delayed when he is in such desperate need. Viewing God as a perfectly loving parent makes this plea for immediate compassion deeply personal.

translit: maṇiyē tiṉaippuṉa valliyai vēṇṭi vaḷarmaṟaivāṉ kaṇiyē eṉaniṉṟa kaṇṇē eṉuḷḷak kaḷinaṟavē paṇiyēṉ eṉiṉum eṉaivalin tāṇṭuṉ patantaravē naṇiyē taṇikaikku vā-eṉa ōrmoḻi nalkuvaiyē.
translation: O jewel. O eye who came as a celestial astrologer of the lofty Vedas, desiring Valli of the millet field. O nectar of joy in my heart. Even if I do not serve you, you must forcefully rule me and grant me your feet. You must grant me this one word, bidding me "Come near to Thanigai."
commentary: The poem recalls the ancient story where Lord Murugan disguised himself as an astrologer to win the love of Valli, a young woman guarding a millet field. It uses this story of divine pursuit to ask God to pursue the human soul in the same way. The prayer asks the Lord to take control by force, even if the devotee fails to serve willingly, and to simply call him near.

translit: nalkāta īṉartam pāṟceṉ ṟirantu navaippaṭutal malkāta vaṇṇam aruḷceykaṇ ṭāymayil vākaṉaṉē palkātal nīkkiya nallōrk karuḷum parañcuṭarē alkāta vaṇmait taṇikā calattil amarntavaṉē.
translation: O rider of the peacock, grant your grace so that I do not suffer the degradation of going to beg from base people who refuse to give. O Supreme Light who grants grace to the good who have discarded manifold desires. O Lord seated in Thanigachalam of unfailing bounty.
commentary: Begging for help from cruel or miserly people destroys a person's dignity. Vallalar asks the divine to spare him from this humiliation by granting grace directly. He sees God, seated in the bountiful shrine of Thanigachalam (Thanigai), as the only reliable provider for those who have let go of worldly desires.

translit: amarā vati-iṟaik kāruyir īnta aruṭkuṉṟamē camarā purikkara cētaṇi kācalat taṟparaṉē kumarā parama kuruvē kukā-eṉak kūviniṟpēṉ emarājaṉ vantiṭuṅ kālaiya ṉē-eṉai ēṉṟukoḷḷē.
translation: O mountain of grace who gave precious life to the lord of Amaravati. O king of Samarapuri. O Supreme Being of Thanigachalam. I will stand calling out to you: O Kumara, O supreme Guru, O Guha. When the king of death arrives, O Lord, please accept me.
commentary: The fear of death drives this plea for divine rescue. Vallalar promises to call out the many names of the Lord, such as Kumara (the youthful god) and Guha (the hidden one), asking to be taken into God's care when the end finally arrives. He appeals to a supreme being who holds absolute power over life, having once restored the breath of the celestial king of Amaravati.

translit: koḷuṇṭa vañcartam kūṭṭuṇṭu vāḻkkaiyil kuṭṭuṇṭumēl tuḷuṇṭa nōyiṉil cūṭuṇṭu maṅkaiyar tōyveṉumōr kaḷuṇṭa nāykkuṉ karuṇai-uṇ ṭōnaṟ kaṭalamutat teḷuṇṭa tēvar pukaḻtaṇi kācalac ciṟparaṉē.
translation: I joined the company of deceitful people who exploit others, suffered blows in life, burned in the heat of spreading diseases, and became a dog drunk on the toddy of uniting with women. Is there any grace for this dog? O Supreme Being of Thanigachalam praised by the celestials who drank the clear nectar of the good ocean.
commentary: A deep sense of self-reproach runs through this verse. Vallalar compares worldly lust and bad company to cheap liquor, saying it has left him diseased and acting like a drunken dog. He wonders if there is any grace left for someone so degraded, contrasting his own toxic state with the pure nectar enjoyed by heavenly beings.

translit: ciṟpakal mēvumit tēkattai ompit tiru-aṉaiyār taṟpaka mēvilain tāḻntēṉ taṇikai taṉilamarnta kaṟpaka mēniṉ kaḻalkaru tēṉik kaṭaippaṭumeṉ poṟpakam mēviya niṉaruḷ eṉeṉṟu pōṟṟuvatē.
translation: I nurtured this body that lasts only a few days and fell into degradation by wandering after women beautiful as the goddess of wealth. O wish-fulfilling tree seated in Thanigai, I do not contemplate your feet. How can I ever praise your grace that has chosen to dwell in the golden heart of a lowly person like me?
commentary: The physical body is temporary, yet people waste their lives indulging it instead of seeking the divine. Despite confessing his own failures and worldly distractions, Vallalar marvels at a deep mystery. He asks how he can ever adequately praise a God whose grace chooses to dwell right inside the heart of someone so deeply flawed.

translit: pōṟṟēṉ eṉiṉum poṟuttiṭal vēṇṭum puvinaṭaiyām cēṟṟē viḻuntu tiyaṅkukiṉ ṟēṉaic ciṟitumiṉi āṟṟēṉ eṉatara cē-amu tē-eṉ aruṭcelvamē mēṟṟēṉ peruku poḻiltaṇi kācala vēlavaṉē.
translation: Even if I fail to praise you, you must forgive me. I suffer having fallen into the mud of worldly conduct. I cannot bear it even a little longer. O my king, O my nectar, O my wealth of grace. O wielder of the spear in Thanigachalam, a place surrounded by groves overflowing with supreme honey.
commentary: The struggle of living in the material world feels like being trapped in deep mud. Exhausted by worldly conduct, Vallalar begs for unconditional forgiveness even when he forgets to pray. He throws himself entirely on the mercy of God, declaring that he cannot endure this spiritual struggle a moment longer.

translit: vēlkoṇṭa kaiyum viṟalkoṇṭa tōḷum viḷaṅkumayil mēlkoṇṭa vīṟum malarmukam āṟum viraikkamalak kālkoṇṭa vīrak kaḻalumkaṇ ṭālaṉṟik kāmaṉeyyum kōlkoṇṭa vaṉmai aṟumō taṇikaik kuruparaṉē.
translation: O supreme Guru of Thanigai. Unless I see your hand holding the spear, your victorious shoulders, your majesty seated upon the shining peacock, your six flower-like faces, and the heroic anklets on your fragrant lotus feet, will the cruel force of the arrows shot by Kama ever cease?
commentary: Only a direct vision of the divine can defeat worldly desire. The speaker says the cruel arrows of Kama, the god of lust and desire, will only stop when he sees the majestic form of the Lord. The deep beauty of God, with his spear, peacock, and six faces, is the only cure for the pull of the senses.

translit: kuruvē ayaṉari ātiyar pōṟṟak kuṟaitavirppāṉ varuvēl piṭittu makiḻvaḷḷa lēkuṇa māmalaiyē taruvē taṇikait tayāniti yētuṉpac cākaramām karuvēr aṟuttik kaṭaiyaṉaik kākkak kaṭaṉuṉakkē.
translation: O Guru. O benevolent Lord who joyfully wields the advancing spear to remove the grievances of those like Brahma and Vishnu who praise you. O great mountain of virtues, O wish-fulfilling tree, O treasure of compassion in Thanigai. It is your duty to cut the root of birth, this ocean of sorrow, and protect this lowly one.
commentary: The cycle of birth is an ocean of sorrow, and ending it requires a supreme teacher. The speaker calls upon the Lord as the ultimate Guru, appealing to his divine duty to protect the helpless. He asks the Lord to use his spear to cut away the very root of physical birth.

translit: uṉakkē viḻaivukoṇ ṭōlamiṭ ṭōṅki ulaṟukiṉṟēṉ eṉakkē aruḷit tamiyēṉ piḻai-uḷat teṇṇiyiṭēl puṉakkēḻ maṇivalli yaippuṇarn tāṇṭaruḷ puṇṇiyaṉē maṉakkēta māṟṟum taṇikā calattamar vāṉavaṉē.
translation: Desiring you alone, I cry aloud and wither. Grant your grace to me. Do not keep the faults of this lonely one in your heart. O virtuous Lord who embraces and rules the beautiful gem-like Valli of the millet field. O celestial Lord seated on the Thanigai hill, you remove the sorrows of the mind.
commentary: Pure longing for God is the only way forward, even when the soul is full of faults. The speaker confesses his total dependence on the Lord, begging him to overlook his human flaws and heal his mind. He points to the Lord's loving embrace of Valli, the maiden of the fields, asking for that same intimate acceptance.

translit: vāṉōr kuṭikaḷai vāḻvitta teyva maṇiccuṭarē nāṉōreḷiyaṉeṉ tuṉpaṟut tāḷeṉa naṇṇiniṉṟēṉ ēṉōniṉ neñcam iraṅkāta vaṇṇam iruṅkaṇippūn tēṉō ṭaruvi payilum taṇikaic civakuruvē.
translation: O divine, radiant flame who gave life to the clans of the celestials. I approached you and stood declaring that I am a poor soul, asking you to sever my sorrows and rule me. Why does your heart not take pity on me? O Siva-Guru of Thanigai, where great fruits and the honey of flowers mingle with the waterfalls.
commentary: The speaker wonders why divine compassion has not yet reached him. He contrasts the Lord's great cosmic acts, like saving the celestial beings, with his own small, unanswered plea. By describing the rich, honey-filled landscape of the Thanigai hill, he contrasts the sweetness of nature with the agonizing silence of the divine.

translit: kaiyāta tuṉpak kaṭalmūḻki neñcam kalaṅki-eṉṟaṉ aiyāniṉ poṉaṭik kōlamiṭ ṭēṉeṉṉai āṇṭukoḷāy maiyār taṭaṅkaṇ malaimakaḷ kaṇṭu makiḻcelvamē. ceyyār taṇikai malai-ara cē-ayiṟ ceṅkaiyaṉē.
translation: Sinking into the unceasing ocean of sorrow, my heart troubled, I cried out to your golden feet, my Lord. Take me into your fold. O wealth who brings joy to the wide, dark eyes of the mountain goddess. O king of the fertile Thanigai hill, O Lord holding the spear in your red hand.
commentary: Total surrender is the only response to overwhelming worldly suffering. Sinking in the ocean of sorrow, the speaker throws himself completely at the golden feet of the Lord. He invokes the Lord as the cherished child who brings joy to the mountain goddess, Parvati, appealing to his innate gentleness and capacity for love.

translit: ceṅkai-am kāntaṉ aṉaiyamiṉ ṉārtam tiṟattuḻaṉṟē veṅkayam uṇṭa viḷavāyi ṉēṉviṟal vēliṉai-ōr aṅkaiyil ēntiya aiyā kuṟavar aritilpeṟṟa maṅkai makiḻum taṇikēca ṉē-aruḷ vanteṉakkē.
translation: I wandered after lightning-like women with lovely hands like red lilies, and I have become like a wood apple hollowed out by a fierce elephant. O Lord, you hold the victorious spear in your beautiful palm! O Lord of Thanigai, you bring joy to the young woman born so rarely to the hill tribes! Come and bestow your grace upon me.
commentary: Chasing physical desire leaves a person completely hollow. Vallalar compares himself to a wood apple that an elephant has swallowed whole and passed out: the outer shell looks perfectly intact, but the inside has been entirely emptied out. He asks Lord Murugan, the spear-wielding deity of Thanigai hill who loves the tribal girl Valli, to fill this inner emptiness with grace.

translit: kēḷātu pōliruk kiṉṟaṉai ēḻai-ik kīḻnaṭaiyil vāḷā iṭarkoṇ ṭalaṟiṭum ōlattai māmaruntē tōḷā maṇiccuṭa rētaṇi kācalat tūypporuḷē nāḷāyiṉ eṉceyku vēṉiṟap pāya navaivarumē.
translation: You remain as though you do not hear the wailing of this poor wretch, crying out in useless suffering on this lowly path. O great medicine! O unpierced, radiant gem! O pure reality of Thanigai hill! If days pass by, what will I do? The disaster of death will come upon me.
commentary: The fear of dying before receiving divine grace causes intense panic. The poet feels as though God is deaf to his cries of suffering on the earthly path. Calling the divine a healing medicine and a flawless gem, he worries that if too much time passes, the absolute disaster of death will overtake him before he can be saved.

translit: navaiyē taruvañca neñcakam māyavum nāṉuṉaṉpar avaiyē aṇukavum āṉanta vāriyil āṭiṭavum cuvaiyē amutaṉṉa niṉtiru nāmam tutikkavumām ivaiyē-eṉ eṇṇam taṇikā calattuḷ iruppavaṉē.
translation: O Lord residing on Thanigai hill! My only desires are these: let this deceitful heart that breeds evil perish, let me approach the assembly of your devotees, let me bathe in the ocean of bliss, and let me praise your holy name that tastes of sweet nectar.
commentary: True spiritual longing asks only for the death of the deceitful ego and the joy of divine fellowship. Vallalar prays to lose his tricky, evil-breeding mind so he can finally join the assembly of true devotees. Once that false heart is gone, he says he will be free to bathe in an ocean of spiritual bliss and taste the pure sweetness of the divine name.

translit: iruppāya māya maṉattāl varunti iḷaittuniṉṟēṉ poruppāya kaṉmap putuvāḻvil āḻntatu pōtumiṉṟē karuppāḻ ceyumuṉ cuḻalaṭik kē-ik kaṭaiyavaṉait tiruppāy eṉileṉcey kēṉtaṇi kācalat teḷḷamutē.
translation: I stand weary, suffering through this iron-hard, illusory mind. Sinking in this strange life of mountain-like karma is enough for today. O clear nectar of Thanigai hill! If you do not turn this lowest wretch toward your anklet-wearing feet that destroy the cycle of rebirth, what will I do?
commentary: The stubborn, illusion-filled mind makes life exhausting. Vallalar compares karma (the accumulated weight of past actions) to a massive mountain that pulls a person down into endless suffering. He begs the divine to turn his attention toward God's feet, stating that this is the only way to break the brutal cycle of earthly rebirth.

translit: teḷakat tōṅkiya ceñcuṭa rēciva tēcikaṉē kaḷakat tēmalark kā-ār taṇikai-eṅ kaṇmaṇiyē eṉakat tē-uḻaṉ ṟeṉniṉ ṟalaitteḻun tiṅkumaṅkum tuḷakat tēṉciram cērumko lōniṉ tuṇai-aṭiyē.
translation: O red flame rising in the clear heart! O supreme teacher! O our precious gem of Thanigai, filled with honey-brimming flower groves! Will your holy feet ever reach the head of this one whose leaping mind wanders within, stands shaken, and jumps here and there?
commentary: A restless, jumping mind makes a person wonder if they will ever be worthy of divine grace. Vallalar calls God a bright red flame that appears only in a clear, still heart. Looking at his own scattered, wandering thoughts, he questions whether the holy feet of the supreme teacher will ever rest upon his head to bless him.

translit: aṭiyēṉ eṉaccolva tallāmal tāḷaṭain tāraikkaṇṭē tuṭiyēṉ aruṇa kiripāṭum niṉaruḷ tōypukaḻaip paṭiyēṉ pataitturu kēṉpaṇi yēṉmaṉap pantamelām kaṭiyēṉ taṇikaiyaik kāṇēṉeṉ ceyvēṉem kātalaṉē.
translation: I merely say that I am your servant. I do not thrill with joy when I see those who have reached your feet. I do not recite your grace-steeped praises sung by Arunagiri. I do not tremble and melt. I do not bow down. I do not sever all the attachments of my mind. I do not behold Thanigai. What shall I do, our Beloved?
commentary: Calling oneself a servant of God means very little without the inner transformation to match it. True devotion requires a physical and emotional response, such as melting in love, cutting away mental attachments, and reciting the hymns of the medieval poet-saint Arunagiri. Feeling completely empty of these qualities, the speaker asks the divine what to do next.

translit: talaṉē aṭiyar taṉimaṉa māmpukaḻ cārtaṇikā calaṉē ayaṉari ātiyar vāḻntiṭat tāṅkayilvēl valaṉēniṉ poṉaruḷ vāriyiṉ mūḻka maṉōlayamvāyn tilaṉēl caṉaṉa maraṇameṉ ṉumkaṭaṟ keṉceyvaṉē.
translation: O Sacred Abode! O Lord of Thanigai hill whose glory fills the singular minds of devotees! O mighty one holding the sharp spear in your right hand so that Brahma, Vishnu, and the primordial gods may live on! If my mind does not achieve stillness to plunge into the ocean of your golden grace, what shall I do about this ocean of birth and death?
commentary: Stilling the mind is the only way to receive divine grace and escape the endless cycle of birth and death. The verse addresses the lord of Thanigai hill, who wields a spear to protect the major Hindu creator and preserver gods, Brahma and Vishnu. Without finding total mental silence in that grace, the soul remains helplessly adrift in mortality.

translit: eṉceykai eṉceykai entāyniṉ poṉaṭik kē-alaṅkal vaṉceykai nīṅka makiḻntaṇi yēṉtuti vāyuraikka meṉceykai kūppa viḻinīr tuḷittiṭa meycilirkkat taṉceykai eṉpataṟ ṟētaṇi kācalam cārntilaṉē.
translation: What are my actions, what are my actions? O my Mother, leaving behind cruel deeds, I do not joyfully adorn your golden feet with garlands. My mouth does not chant your praise. My soft hands do not fold in prayer. Tears do not drop from my eyes. My body does not thrill. I have not shed the sense of my own agency to reach Thanigai hill.
commentary: The greatest obstacle to reaching God is the illusion of personal control. True spiritual life requires giving up the ego and the sense of being the independent doer of one's own actions. Without this surrender, spontaneous physical acts of worship, like folding hands or shedding tears of joy, remain entirely out of reach.

translit: cārum taṇikaiyil cārntōyniṉ tāmarait tāḷtuṇaiyaic cērum toḻumpā tiruppatam aṉṟi-ic ciṟṟaṭiyēṉ ūrum taṉamum uṟavum pukaḻum uraimaṭavār vārun taṇimulaip pōkamum vēṇṭilaṉ maṇviṇṇilē.
translation: O Lord dwelling in reachable Thanigai! Other than the holy state of servitude that reaches your twin lotus feet, this lowly servant desires nothing on earth or in heaven. I do not want towns, wealth, kinship, fame, or the pleasure of the bound breasts of celebrated young women.
commentary: Pure devotion asks for nothing except the opportunity to serve God. Worldly success, family ties, fame, and physical pleasure lose all their appeal when the soul's single desire is to remain at the feet of the divine. This total surrender leaves no room for personal ambitions in this life or in any heavenly afterlife.

translit: maṇnīr aṉalvaḷi vāṉāki niṉṟaruḷ vattu-eṉṟē teṇnīrmai yālpukaḻ mālaya ṉēmutal tēvarkaḷtam kaṇnīr tuṭaittaruḷ kaṟpaka mē-uṉaik kaṇṭukoṇṭēṉ taṇnīr poḻiṟkaṇ mativan tulāvum taṇikaiyilē.
translation: Vishnu, Brahma, and the primordial gods praise you with pure devotion, realizing you are the gracious Supreme Reality standing as earth, water, fire, wind, and space. O wish-fulfilling tree who wipes away their tears and bestows grace! I have beheld you in Thanigai, where the moon wanders among cool, well-watered groves.
commentary: The divine is the supreme reality that takes form as the five elements of earth, water, fire, wind, and space. Even the highest gods of the traditional Hindu pantheon must pray to this ultimate grace to wipe away their sorrows. The verse compares this absolute compassion to a legendary wish-fulfilling tree that grants all desires to those who approach it.

translit: taṇiyāta tuṉpat taṭṅkaṭal nīṅkaniṉ taṉmalarttāḷ paṇiyāta pāvik karuḷumuṇ ṭōpacu pācamaṟṟōrk kaṇiyāka niṉṟa aruṭcelva mētaṇi kācalaṉē aṇi-ā tavaṉmuta lāmaṭṭa mūrttam aṭaintavaṉē.
translation: O wealth of grace standing as an ornament for those freed from the soul's bonds! O Lord of Thanigai hill! O Lord who assumes the eight beautiful forms beginning with the sun! Is there grace for this sinner who refuses to bow to your flower-feet to cross the unyielding vast ocean of sorrow?
commentary: The poet wonders if divine grace can reach someone entirely unwilling to seek it. He calls himself a sinner who refuses to bow, comparing his state to an endless ocean of sorrow. He contrasts his own stubbornness with the vastness of the Lord, who stands as an ornament for those freed from the soul's worldly attachments and manifests in the eight elemental forms of the universe.

translit: aṭaiyāta vañcakar pālceṉ ṟirantiṅ kalaintalaintē kaṭaiyāṉa nāykkuḷ karuṇai-uṇ ṭōtaṇi kaikkuḷniṉṟē uṭaiyāta nalneñcark kuṇmaiyaik kāṇpikkum uttamaṉē paṭaiyāta tēvar ciṟaimīṭ ṭaḷittaruḷ paṇṇavaṉē.
translation: O supreme one standing in Thanigai, who reveals the truth to those with unbroken good hearts! O Lord who graciously rescued the helpless devas from their prison! Is there compassion for this lowest dog, wandering endlessly and begging from unapproachable deceivers?
commentary: Seeking worldly favors from selfish people only leads to endless wandering and humiliation. The poet calls himself a stray dog for begging from deceivers instead of turning to the divine. He asks if there is any compassion left for him, knowing that the Lord freely reveals the truth to pure hearts and once rescued the celestial beings (devas) when they were entirely helpless.

translit: paṇṇava ṉēniṉ patamalar ēttum payaṉuṭaiyōr kaṇṇava ṉētaṇi kācala ṉē-ayil kaiyavaṉē viṇṇavar ēttiya mēlava ṉēmayal mēvumaṉam puṇṇava ṉēṉaiyum cērntāyeṉ ṉē-uṉṟaṉ poṉaruḷē.
translation: O Supreme Lord! O eye of those who reap the reward of praising your flower-feet! O Lord of Thanigai hill! O wielder of the spear! O supreme one praised by the celestials! You accepted even me, whose illusion-filled mind is a bleeding wound. How great is your golden grace!
commentary: Divine grace accepts us even when our minds are deeply damaged by worldly illusions. The poet describes his own mind as a bleeding wound of confusion. He marvels that the supreme Lord, who wields the spear of wisdom and is praised by the celestials, would still reach out and embrace him.

translit: poṉār puyattaṉum pū-uṭai yōṉum pukaḻmaṇiyē eṉāvi yiṉtuṇai yētaṇi kācalat tē-amarnta maṉṉāniṉ poṉaṭi vāḻttātu vīṇil varuntuṟuvēṉ iṉṉā iyaṟṟum iyamaṉvan tālavaṟ keṉcolvaṉē.
translation: O gem praised by golden-shouldered Vishnu and lotus-seated Brahma! O companion of my soul! O king seated on Thanigai hill! I suffer in vain without praising your golden feet. If the tormenting Yama arrives, what will I say to him?
commentary: Wasting a human lifetime without spiritual focus leaves a person entirely defenseless at the end. The poet laments that he suffers in vain by neglecting his soul's true companion, who is revered even by great creator and preserver deities like Brahma and Vishnu. He asks what excuse he could possibly give when Yama, the god of death, arrives to claim him.

translit: collār malarpuṉai aṉpakat tōrkkaruḷ collumellām vallāyeṉ ṟētta aṟintēṉ iṉi-eṉṟaṉ valviṉaikaḷ ellām viṭaikoṇ ṭiriyumeṉ mēliya maṉciṉamum cellātu kāṇaiya ṉētaṇi kācalac cīraraicē.
translation: I learned to praise you as the omnipotent Lord who grants grace to those with loving hearts who weave floral garlands of sacred words. Henceforth all my cruel karmas will take their leave and flee. Yama's wrath will hold no sway over me. Behold this, O Master, O glorious king of Thanigai hill!
commentary: Sincere devotion completely banishes the fear of death and the weight of past actions (karma). By learning to praise the Lord with a heart full of love, the poet realizes that all his cruel past deeds will simply flee. He declares with absolute certainty that Yama's wrath no longer holds any power over him.

tamil: அணிகொள் வேல்உடை அண்ணலே நின்திரு அடிகளை அன்போடும்
பணிகி லேன்அகம் உருகிநின் றாடிலேன் பாடிலேன் மனமாயைத்
தணிகி லேன்திருத் தணிகையை நினைகிலேன் சாமிநின் வழிபோகத்
துணிகி லேன்இருந் தென்செய்தேன் பாவியேன் துன்பமும் எஞ்சேனே.
translit: aṇikoḷ vēluṭai aṇṇalē niṉtiru aṭikaḷai aṉpōṭum paṇiki lēṉakam urukiniṉ ṟāṭilēṉ pāṭilēṉ maṉamāyait taṇiki lēṉtirut taṇikaiyai niṉaikilēṉ cāminiṉ vaḻipōkat tuṇiki lēṉirun teṉceytēṉ pāviyēṉ tuṉpamum eñcēṉē.
translation: O Lord wielding the beautiful spear! I do not bow to your holy feet with love. My heart does not melt. I do not stand and dance. I do not sing. I do not diminish the illusion of my mind. I do not think of holy Thanigai. O God, I do not dare to walk your path. What have I done with my life, sinner that I am? I cannot escape my suffering.
commentary: A life spent without love for the divine is a life wasted in suffering. The speaker looks back with regret, confessing to a hard heart that never sang, danced, or tried to overcome the mind's illusions.

tamil: சேல்பி டித்தவன் தந்தைஆ தியர்தொழும் தெய்வமே சிவப்பேறே
மால்பி டித்தவர் அறியொணாத் தணிகைமா மலைஅமர்ந் திடுவாழ்வே
வேல்பி டித்தருள் வள்ளலே யான்சதுர் வேதமும் காணாநின்
கால்பி டிக்கவும் கருணைநீ செய்யவும் கண்டுகண் களிப்பேனோ.
translit: cēlpi ṭittavaṉ tantai-ā tiyartoḻum teyvamē civappēṟē mālpi ṭittavar aṟiyoṇāt taṇikaimā malai-amarn tiṭuvāḻvē vēlpi ṭittaruḷ vaḷḷalē yāṉcatur vētamum kāṇāniṉ kālpi ṭikkavum karuṇainī ceyyavum kaṇṭukaṇ kaḷippēṉō.
translation: O God worshipped by primal deities like the father of the fish-bannered god! O supreme reward of Sivam! O living presence dwelling on the great mountain of Thanigai, unknowable to those gripped by delusion! O generous Lord who holds the spear to grant grace! Will I ever see myself grasping your feet, which even the four Vedas cannot perceive, and you granting me your grace, so my eyes may rejoice?
commentary: Divine grace is a direct, personal encounter that even the ancient sacred scriptures, the Vedas, cannot fully capture. The speaker longs for nothing more than to hold the feet of God and personally witness the gift of this grace.

tamil: களித்து நின்திருக் கழலிணை ஏழையேன் காண்பனோ அலதன்பை
ஒளித்து வன்துயர் உழப்பனோ இன்னதென் றுணர்ந்திலேன் அருட்போதம்
தெளித்து நின்றிடும் தேசிக வடிவமே தேவர்கள் பணிதேவே
தளிர்த்த தண்பொழில் தணிகையில் வளர்சிவ தாருவே மயிலோனே.
translit: kaḷittu niṉtiruk kaḻaliṇai ēḻaiyēṉ kāṇpaṉō alataṉpai oḷittu vaṉtuyar uḻappaṉō iṉṉateṉ ṟuṇarntilēṉ aruṭpōtam teḷittu niṉṟiṭum tēcika vaṭivamē tēvarkaḷ paṇitēvē taḷirtta taṇpoḻil taṇikaiyil vaḷarciva tāruvē mayilōṉē.
translation: Will I, a poor soul, rejoice and see your two holy feet? Or will I conceal my love and suffer fierce sorrow? I do not know which of these it will be. O form of the Guru standing to clarify the wisdom of grace! O God bowed to by the celestials! O wish-fulfilling tree of Sivam growing in Thanigai with its flourishing cool groves! O Lord who rides the peacock!
commentary: The spiritual seeker stands in deep uncertainty, caught between the joy of divine vision and the sorrow of a closed heart. In this state of doubt, the speaker looks to God as the ultimate Guru, the only teacher who can grant the clarity of true wisdom.

tamil: மயிலின் மீதுவந் தருள்தரும் நின்திரு வரவினுக் கெதிர்பார்க்கும்
செயலி னேன்கருத் தெவ்வணம் முடியுமோ தெரிகிலேன் என்செய்கேன்
அயிலின் மாமுதல் தடிந்திடும் ஐயனே ஆறுமா முகத்தேவே
கயிலை நேர்திருத் தணிகைஅம் பதிதனில் கந்தன்என் றிருப்போனே.
translit: mayiliṉ mītuvan taruḷtarum niṉtiru varaviṉuk ketirpārkkum ceyali ṉēṉkarut tevvaṇam muṭiyumō terikilēṉ eṉceykēṉ ayiliṉ māmutal taṭintiṭum aiyaṉē āṟumā mukattēvē kayilai nērtirut taṇikai-am patitaṉil kantaṉeṉ ṟiruppōṉē.
translation: My only action is to wait in expectation of your holy arrival, coming upon the peacock to grant your grace. I do not know how my intention will conclude. What shall I do? O Lord who struck down the great root of the mango tree with your spear! O God with six great faces! O you who reside as Skanda in the beautiful town of holy Thanigai, which equals Mount Kailash!
commentary: True devotion often means waiting in complete helplessness for the divine to act. The verse recalls the mythology of Murugan using his spear to split a massive magical mango tree, a symbol for destroying the deep root of the ego, and asks for that same decisive arrival to resolve the speaker's spiritual suspense.

tamil: இருப்பு நெஞ்சகக் கொடியனேன் பிழைதனை எண்ணுறேல் இனிவஞ்சக்
கருப்பு காவணம் காத்தருள் ஐயனே கருணைஅம் கடலேஎன்
விருப்புள் ஊறிநின் றோங்கிய அமுதமே வேல்உடை எம்மானே
தருப்பு காஇனன் விலகுறும் தணிகைவாழ் சாந்தசற் குணக்குன்றே.
translit: iruppu neñcakak koṭiyaṉēṉ piḻaitaṉai eṇṇuṟēl iṉivañcak karuppu kāvaṇam kāttaruḷ aiyaṉē karuṇai-am kaṭalē-eṉ viruppuḷ ūṟiniṉ ṟōṅkiya amutamē vēluṭai emmāṉē taruppu kā-iṉaṉ vilakuṟum taṇikaivāḻ cāntacaṟ kuṇakkuṉṟē.
translation: Do not count the faults of this cruel person with an iron heart. Protect me now, O Lord, from entering the deceptive womb. O beautiful ocean of grace! O nectar that swells and rises within my desire! O our Lord holding the spear! O mountain of peaceful and noble qualities dwelling in Thanigai, where the sun turns away, unable to penetrate the dense trees!
commentary: The ultimate plea of the devotee is to be saved from the suffering of physical rebirth. Acknowledging his own flaws and iron heart, the speaker begs to be absorbed into the ocean of God's grace rather than returning to a worldly womb.

tamil: குன்று நேர்பிணித் துயரினால் வருந்திநின் குரைகழல் கருதாத
துன்று வஞ்சகக் கள்ளனேன் நெஞ்சகத் துயர்அறுத் தருள்செய்வான்
இன்று மாமயில் மீதினில் ஏறிஇவ் வேழைமுன் வருவாயேல்
நன்று நன்றதற் கென்சொல்வார் தணிகைவாழ் நாதநின் அடியாரே.
translit: kuṉṟu nērpiṇit tuyariṉāl varuntiniṉ kuraikaḻal karutāta tuṉṟu vañcakak kaḷḷaṉēṉ neñcakat tuyaraṟut taruḷceyvāṉ iṉṟu māmayil mītiṉil ēṟi-iv vēḻaimuṉ varuvāyēl naṉṟu naṉṟataṟ keṉcolvār taṇikaivāḻ nātaniṉ aṭiyārē.
translation: Suffering the sorrow of a mountain-like illness, I failed to think of your resounding anklets. I am a deeply deceitful thief. If you mount your great peacock and appear before this poor one today to destroy the sorrow in my heart and grant your grace, what will your devotees say? They will say, "Good, very good." O Lord who dwells in Thanigai!
commentary: The speaker feels utterly unworthy, distracted from God by an illness that weighs on him like a mountain.
