translation: I do not approach the good Thanigai hill in truth and lovingly praise your supreme glory. Will I not be saved? I walk a cruel path, like an unusable odhi tree, like a bitter etti tree. Rejecting the begging bowl of the devotees, I desired the pleasures of foolish women. I am base. I have not the slightest purity. Alas, O Lord! Without shame, sinner that I am, to whom can I tell my shortcomings?
commentary: The speaker compares his current state to useless or toxic trees: the ōti (a soft, unusable wood) and the eṭṭi (a tree with bitter, poisonous seeds). By choosing worldly pleasures over the simple, detached life of a devotee, he feels he has made his life completely barren. He confesses his total lack of purity directly to God, offering no excuses for his behavior.

translit: vāṭcellā neṭuṅkaṇṇār mayalil vīḻntu maṉampōṉa vaḻiceṉṟu varuntā niṉṟēṉ cēṭcellār varaittaṇikait tēva tēvē civaperumāṉ peṟṟaperuñ celva mēnāṉ nāṭcellā niṉṟatiṉi eṉcey kēṉō nāyiṉēṉ piḻaitaṉṉai nāṭi niṉpāl kōṭcollā niṟpareṉil eṉṉā mō-eṉ kuṟaiyai-eṭut tevarkkeḷiyēṉ kūṟu kēṉē.
translation: Falling into the delusion of women whose long eyes surpass swords, I went the way my mind went, and I stand suffering. O God of gods on Thanigai hill, untouched by distance! O great wealth born to Lord Siva! My days have passed. What will I do now? If they seek out the faults of this dog-like one and report them to you, what will become of me? To whom can I, a poor wretch, tell my shortcomings?
commentary: Time is running out, and the speaker worries about the consequences of his misguided choices. He fears that others might notice his constant mistakes and report them to the divine. Instead of hiding, he brings his faults to God first, treating the Lord of Thanigai as the only confidant who might truly listen to a struggling soul.

translit: pollāta maṅkaiyartam mayaṟkuḷ ākum pulaiyamaṉat tālvāṭip pulampu kiṉṟēṉ kallāta pāvi-eṉṟu kaiviṭ ṭāyō karuṇai-uru vākiyaceṅ karummē mēru villāṉtaṉ celvamē taṇikai mēvum meyññāṉa oḷiyē-iv viṉaiyēṉ tuṉpam ellāmnī aṟivāyē aṟintum vārā tiruntāleṉ kuṟaiyai-evark kiyampu kēṉē.
translation: With a base mind trapped in the delusion of wicked women, I wither and lament. Did you abandon me thinking I am an unlettered sinner? O red sugarcane whose form is grace! O wealth of the Lord holding the Meru bow! O light of true wisdom residing in Thanigai! You know all the sorrows of this karma-bound one. If you know them and yet do not come, to whom can I express my shortcomings?
commentary: Even feeling deeply unworthy and ignorant, the speaker questions why divine grace is delayed. He reminds the Lord that God is made of grace itself and already knows every sorrow tied to his past actions. If the divine sees all this pain and still stays away, the soul has nowhere left to seek help.

translit: muṉaṟiyēṉ piṉaṟiyēṉ mātar pāleṉ mūṭamaṉam iḻuttōṭap piṉceṉ ṟeyttēṉ puṉṉeṟiyēṉ poyyaroṭum payiṉṟēṉ niṉṟaṉ puṉita-aruṭ kaṭalāṭēṉ puḷakam mūṭēṉ poṉaraiyaṉ toḻumcaṭilap puṉitaṉ īṉṟa puṇṇiyamē taṇikaivaḷar pōta vāḻvē eṉaraicē eṉamutē niṉpāl aṉṟi evarkkeṭutteṉ kuṟaitaṉṉai iyampu kēṉē.
translation: I do not know the past. I do not know the future. My foolish mind dragged me toward women, and I followed it and grew exhausted. I walk a mean path. I associate with liars. I do not bathe in the sacred ocean of your grace. I do not feel the thrill of devotion. O merit born of the holy One with matted locks, worshipped by the golden king! O life of wisdom flourishing in Thanigai! O my king! O my nectar! Except to you, to whom can I express my shortcomings?
commentary: Blind to where he came from and where he is going, the speaker admits he is exhausted by his own foolish choices. He has surrounded himself with false people and missed the joyful thrill of true devotion. Yet, by calling the Lord his king and his nectar, he turns his confession into an act of deep love, showing that his faith remains intact beneath all his confessed flaws.

translit: viṭumāṭṭil tirintumaṭa māta rārtam veyyanīrk kuḻivīḻntu mīḷā neñcat taṭumāṟṟat toṭumpulaiya uṭalai ōmpic cārntavarkkōr aṇu-aḷavum tāṉī yātu paṭukāṭṭil palaṉutavāp paṉaipōl niṉṟēṉ pāviyēṉ uṭaṟcumaiyaip palarum kūṭi iṭukāṭṭil vaikkuṅkāl eṉcey vēṉō eṉkuṟaiyai evarkkeṭuttiṅ kiyampu kēṉē.
translation: Wandering like a stray ox, I fell into the hot watery pit of foolish women. With a wavering heart that never turns back, I nurtured this base body. I gave not even an atom to those who approached me. I stood like a useless palmyra tree in a barren wasteland. What will I do when people gather and place the burden of this sinner's body in the cremation ground? To whom can I express my flaws here?
commentary: The poet compares his life to a barren tree in a wasteland, offering no fruit or shade to anyone. He laments wasting his vital energy on worldly pleasures and physical comfort while giving absolutely nothing to those in need. Without compassion (jīvakāruṇyam, love for all living beings), the physical body becomes nothing but a useless burden waiting for the cremation ground.

translit: miṉṉainēr iṭaimaṭavār mayalcey kiṉṟa veṅkuḻiyil vīḻntaḻunti veṟuttēṉ pōlap piṉṉaiyē eḻunteḻuntu mīṭṭum mīṭṭum pēypōla vīḻntāṭi mayaṟkuḷ mūḻkip poṉṉaiyē otta-uṉa taruḷai vēṇṭip pōṟṟātu vīṇēnāḷ pōkku kiṉṟa eṉṉaiyē yāṉcirippēṉ ākil antō eṉkuṟaiyai evarkkeṭuttiṅ kiyampu kēṉē.
translation: I fell and sank into the cruel, deluding pit of women with waists like lightning. Though I seemed to despise it, I rose up again and again, only to fall and dance like a ghost, drowning in that delusion. I did not seek and praise your golden grace. I waste my days in vain. If I laugh at my own self, alas, to whom can I express my flaws here?
commentary: Sensual delusion functions here as an inescapable trap of repetition. Even after recognizing the emptiness of physical obsession and despising it, the poet confesses to falling back into the same delusions again and again. Driven by compulsion rather than devotion, he wastes the time he could have spent seeking divine grace. He is left with nothing but bitter laughter at his own foolishness.

translit: mulai-orupāl mukamorupāl kāṭṭum pollā mūṭamaṭa vārkaḷtamai muyaṅki niṉṟēṉ ilai-orupāl aṉamorupāl malañcērt tuṇṇum ēḻaimati yēṉtaṇikai ēnta lēpoṉ malai-orupāl vāṅkiyacev vaṇṇa mēṉi vaḷḷaltaru maruntēniṉ malarttāḷ ēttēṉ pulai-oruvā vañcakaneñ cuṭaiyēṉ eṉṟaṉ puṉmaitaṉai evarkkeṭuttup pukalu vēṉē.
translation: I embraced wicked, foolish women who display a breast on one side and a face on the other. I am a feeble-minded fool who eats a leaf on one side and rice mixed with filth on the other. O Lord of Thanigai! O medicine given by the benevolent Lord of red form who bent the golden mountain! I do not praise your lotus feet. I have a deceitful heart that never abandons baseness. To whom can I speak of my wretchedness?
commentary: The poet expresses deep revulsion at his own desires, comparing his obsession with the physical body to a fool eating filth. He contrasts this spiritual sickness with the divine medicine of Murugan, the presiding deity of the shrine at Thanigai. This healing presence is praised as the gift of the supreme Lord who once bent the golden mountain into a bow. Instead of holding onto this grace, the poet remains trapped in his own deceitful mind.

translit: vēyppālmeṉ tōḷmaṭavār maṟaikkum māya vempuḻuccēr veṭippiṉiṭai vīḻntu niṉṟēṉ tāyppālai uṇṇātu nāyppāl uṇṇum takaiyaṉēṉ tiruttaṇikai taṉṉaic cārntu āyppālai orumaruṅkāṉ īṉṟa celvat tāramutē niṉaruḷai aṭaiyēṉ kaṇṭāy ēyppālai naṭuṅkaruṅkal pōlniṉ ṟeyttēṉ eṉkuṟaiyai evarkkeṭuttiṅ kiyampu kēṉē.
translation: I fell into the illusory, hot, worm-filled crevice hidden by women with soft bamboo-like shoulders. I am like one who rejects mother's milk to drink dog's milk. O precious nectar residing in holy Thanigai, begotten by the Lord who keeps the Mother on one side! I do not attain your grace. I stand exhausted like a hard black stone in a deceptive desert. To whom can I express my flaws here?
commentary: Choosing physical lust over divine grace is like a child refusing its mother's milk to drink from a stray dog. The grace he needs is available right before him as the sweet nectar of Thanigai, born of the supreme Lord who shares his form with the Divine Mother. By turning away from this nourishing truth, he has drained his own life force. He stands completely exhausted, as lifeless and isolated as a scorched rock in a desert.

translit: vañcamaṭa mātarār pōkam eṉṉum malattiṉiṭaik kirumi-eṉa vāḷā vīḻntēṉ kañcamalar maṉaiyāṉum mālum tēṭak kāṇāta ceṅkaṉiyil kaṉinta tēṉē tañcam eṉpōrk karuḷpuriyum vaḷḷalēnal taṇikai-arai cē-uṉatu tāḷaip pōṟṟēṉ eñcalilā viṉaiccēma iṭamāy uṟṟēṉ eṉkuṟaiyai evarkkeṭuttiṅ kiyampu kēṉē.
translation: I fell uselessly like a worm into the filth known as the pleasure of deceitful, foolish women. O honey ripened in the red fruit that Brahma on his lotus and Vishnu could not find when they searched! O benevolent Lord who grants grace to those who seek refuge! O King of good Thanigai, I do not praise your feet. I have become a secure storehouse for endless karma. To whom can I express my flaws here?
commentary: Living only for sensual pleasure turns a person into a worm feeding on filth and creates a vast stockpile of karma. By contrast, the divine truth is pure, ripened honey. The poet describes this supreme grace as a reality that even the great creator god Brahma and the preserver god Vishnu failed to comprehend when they searched for its limits. He laments that he has ignored this limitless refuge to build a prison out of his own past actions.

tamil: பொன்னைப் பொருளா நினைப்போர்பால் போந்து மிடியால் இரந்தலுத்தேன்
நின்னைப் பொருள்என் றுணராத நீசன் இனிஓர் நிலைகாணேன்
மின்னைப் பொருவும் சடைப்பவள வெற்பில் விளைந்த வியன்கரும்பே
முன்னைப் பொருளே தணிகையனே முறையோ முறையோ முறையேயோ.
translit: poṉṉaip poruḷā niṉaippōrpāl pōntu miṭiyāl irantaluttēṉ niṉṉaip poruḷeṉ ṟuṇarāta nīcaṉ iṉi-ōr nilaikāṇēṉ miṉṉaip poruvum caṭaippavaḷa veṟpil viḷainta viyaṉkarumpē muṉṉaip poruḷē taṇikaiyaṉē muṟaiyō muṟaiyō muṟaiyēyō.
translation: I went to those who consider gold the only wealth, begged them out of poverty, and grew weary. I am a base person who did not realize You are the true wealth, and now I see no other refuge. O great sugarcane grown on the coral mountain of Siva whose matted locks flash like lightning! O primal reality! O Lord of Thanigai! Hear my appeal! Hear my appeal! Hear my appeal!
commentary: The speaker admits the foolishness of treating money as the only security in life. He chased after wealthy people and begged for their help to escape poverty, only to find himself exhausted and empty-handed. True wealth, he now sees, is the divine presence. He calls upon Murugan, the Lord of Thanigai, comparing the god to sweet sugarcane growing on the red coral mountain of Lord Siva.

tamil: மக்கட் பிறவி எடுத்தும்உனை வழுத்தாக் கொடிய மரம்அனையேன்
துக்கக் கடலில் வீழ்ந்துமனம் சோர்கின் றேன்ஓர் துணைகாணேன்
செக்கர்ப் பொருவு வடிவேற்கைத் தேவே தெவிட்டாத் தெள்ளமுதே
முக்கட் கரும்பின் முழுமுத்தே முறையோ முறையோ முறையேயோ.
translit: makkaṭ piṟavi eṭuttumuṉai vaḻuttāk koṭiya maramaṉaiyēṉ tukkak kaṭalil vīḻntumaṉam cōrkiṉ ṟēṉōr tuṇaikāṇēṉ cekkarp poruvu vaṭivēṟkait tēvē teviṭṭāt teḷḷamutē mukkaṭ karumpiṉ muḻumuttē muṟaiyō muṟaiyō muṟaiyēyō.
translation: Even after taking a human birth, I am like a cruel tree that fails to praise You. I have fallen into the sea of sorrow and my heart faints. I see no other support. O God holding the sharp spear the color of red twilight! O clear nectar that never cloys! O perfect pearl of the three-eyed sugarcane! Hear my appeal! Hear my appeal! Hear my appeal!
commentary: Human birth is meant for spiritual awakening, yet the speaker feels he has stood as senseless and numb as a block of wood. Drowning in worldly sorrow, he finds his only hope in the divine. He addresses God as the essence of sweetness and clarity, calling him a perfect pearl born from the three-eyed Lord Siva.

tamil: அன்பின் உனது திருஅடிக்கே ஆளாய்த் தொண்டொன் றாற்றாதே
துன்பின் உடையோர் பால்அணுகிச் சோர்ந்தேன் இனிஓர் துணைகாணேன்
என்பில் மலிந்த மாலைபுனை எம்மான் தந்த பெம்மானே
முன்பின் நடுவாய் முளைத்தோனே முறையோ முறையோ முறையேயோ.
translit: aṉpiṉ uṉatu tiru-aṭikkē āḷāyt toṇṭoṉ ṟāṟṟātē tuṉpiṉ uṭaiyōr pālaṇukic cōrntēṉ iṉi-ōr tuṇaikāṇēṉ eṉpil malinta mālaipuṉai emmāṉ tanta pemmāṉē muṉpiṉ naṭuvāy muḷaittōṉē muṟaiyō muṟaiyō muṟaiyēyō.
translation: Without serving Your holy feet with love or performing a single act of service, I approached people afflicted by sorrow and grew weary. Now I see no other support. O great Lord given by our Lord who wears a garland of bones! O You who arose as the beginning, the middle, and the end! Hear my appeal! Hear my appeal! Hear my appeal!
commentary: Spiritual life requires active devotion and service. Instead of offering his love to God, the speaker wasted his energy mingling with people trapped in their own miseries. Realizing he can expect no real help from those as lost as he is, he cries out to the supreme reality that exists as the beginning, middle, and end of all things.

tamil: அருகா மலத்தின் அலைந்திரக்கம் அறியா வஞ்ச நெஞ்சகர்பால்
உருகா வருந்தி உழன்றலைந்தேன் உன்தாள் அன்றித் துணைகாணேன்
பெருகா தரவில் சிவன்பெறும்நற் பேறே தணிகைப் பெருவாழ்வே
முருகா முகம்மூ விரண்டுடையாய் முறையோ முறையோ முறையேயோ.
translit: arukā malattiṉ alaintirakkam aṟiyā vañca neñcakarpāl urukā varunti uḻaṉṟalaintēṉ uṉtāḷ aṉṟit tuṇaikāṇēṉ perukā taravil civaṉpeṟumnaṟ pēṟē taṇikaip peruvāḻvē murukā mukammū viraṇṭuṭaiyāy muṟaiyō muṟaiyō muṟaiyēyō.
translation: Wandering in undiminishing impurity, I approached deceitful hearts that know no compassion. I suffered, wandered, and roamed with an unmelting heart. I see no support other than Your feet. O great treasure obtained by Siva in surging love! O great life of Thanigai! O Murugan! O You with six faces! Hear my appeal! Hear my appeal! Hear my appeal!
commentary: The deepest failure of the worldly life is its lack of compassion. The speaker regrets seeking help from deceitful people whose hearts cannot melt for others. He now turns his appeal to Murugan, the six-faced god, describing him as the great treasure that Lord Siva obtained through boundless love.

tamil: பொன்னின் றொளிரும் மார்பன்அயன் போற்றும் உன்தாள் புகழ்மறந்தே
கன்னின் றணங்கும் மனத்தார்பால் கனிந்தேன் இனிஓர் துணைகாணேன்
மின்னின் றிலங்கு சடைக்கனியுள் விளைந்த நறவே மெய்அடியார்
முன்னின் றருளும் தணிகையனே முறையோ முறையோ முறையேயோ.
translit: poṉṉiṉ ṟoḷirum mārpaṉayaṉ pōṟṟum uṉtāḷ pukaḻmaṟantē kaṉṉiṉ ṟaṇaṅkum maṉattārpāl kaṉintēṉ iṉi-ōr tuṇaikāṇēṉ miṉṉiṉ ṟilaṅku caṭaikkaṉiyuḷ viḷainta naṟavē meyaṭiyār muṉṉiṉ ṟaruḷum taṇikaiyaṉē muṟaiyō muṟaiyō muṟaiyēyō.
translation: I forgot to praise Your feet worshipped by Brahma and by Vishnu whose chest shines with gold. I gave my devotion to those with hearts like stone. Now I see no other support. O honey formed inside the fruit of Siva whose matted locks flash like lightning! O Lord of Thanigai who stands before true devotees and bestows grace! Hear my appeal! Hear my appeal! Hear my appeal!
commentary: Even the highest gods in the traditional pantheon, Brahma and Vishnu, worship the supreme reality. The speaker regrets forgetting this ultimate truth and giving his loyalty to cruel, stone-hearted people who offered nothing in return. He asks for the grace of the Lord who always reveals himself to true devotees, calling him the sweet honey formed within the divine nature of Siva.

tamil: வெதிர்உள் ளவரின் மொழிகேளா வீண ரிடம்போய் மிகமெலிந்தே
அதிரும் கழற்சே வடிமறந்தேன் அந்தோ இனிஓர் துணைகாணேன்
எதிரும் குயில்மேல் தவழ்தணிகை இறையே முக்கண் இயற்கனியின்
முதிரும் சுவையே முதற்பொருளே முறையோ முறையோ முறையேயோ.
translit: vetiruḷ ḷavariṉ moḻikēḷā vīṇa riṭampōy mikamelintē atirum kaḻaṟcē vaṭimaṟantēṉ antō iṉi-ōr tuṇaikāṇēṉ etirum kuyilmēl tavaḻtaṇikai iṟaiyē mukkaṇ iyaṟkaṉiyiṉ mutirum cuvaiyē mutaṟporuḷē muṟaiyō muṟaiyō muṟaiyēyō.
translation: Refusing to listen to the words of those with reverent hearts, I went to vain people and grew utterly frail. I forgot your red feet adorned with resounding anklets. Alas, I see no other companion now! O Lord of Thanigai where approaching clouds drift over the peaks! O ripening sweetness of the natural fruit of the three-eyed Lord! O Primal Reality! Hear my appeal! Hear my appeal! Hear my appeal!
commentary: Seeking worldly help from vain people leads only to exhaustion and frailty. The poet laments ignoring wise counsel and forgetting the divine, crying out to the Lord of Thanigai (a sacred hill shrine) to ask if this deep spiritual suffering is fair.

tamil: ஈனத் திவறும் மனக்கொடியோர் இடம்போய் மெலிந்து நாள்தோறும்
ஞானத் திருத்தாள் துணைசிறிதும் நாடேன் இனிஓர் துணைகாணேன்
தானத் தறுகண் மலைஉரியின் சட்டை புனைந்தோன் தரும்பேறே
மோனத் தவர்த்ம் அகவிளக்கே முறையோ முறையோ முறையேயோ.
translit: īṉat tivaṟum maṉakkoṭiyōr iṭampōy melintu nāḷtōṟum ñāṉat tiruttāḷ tuṇaiciṟitum nāṭēṉ iṉi-ōr tuṇaikāṇēṉ tāṉat taṟukaṇ malai-uriyiṉ caṭṭai puṉaintōṉ tarumpēṟē mōṉat tavartm akaviḷakkē muṟaiyō muṟaiyō muṟaiyēyō.
translation: Going to cruel-hearted people who cling to base things, I grew weak every day. I do not seek the support of your holy feet of wisdom even a little. Now I see no other support! O treasure bestowed by the Lord who wears the skin of the fierce mountain elephant shedding rut! O inner lamp of those in silent penance! Hear my appeal! Hear my appeal! Hear my appeal!
commentary: Relying on cruel and greedy individuals saps the soul's strength day by day. True support comes only from divine wisdom, which shines like an inner lamp for those who quiet their minds in silent meditation.

tamil: தேவே எனநிற் போற்றாத சிறிய ரிடம்போய்த் தியங்கிஎன்றன்
கோவே நின்றன் திருத்தாளைக் குறிக்க மறந்தேன் துணைகாணேன்
மாவே ழத்தின் உரிபுனைந்த வள்ளற் கினிய மகப்பேறே
மூவே தனையை அறுத்தருள்வோய் முறையோ முறையோ முறையேயோ.
translit: tēvē eṉaniṟ pōṟṟāta ciṟiya riṭampōyt tiyaṅki-eṉṟaṉ kōvē niṉṟaṉ tiruttāḷaik kuṟikka maṟantēṉ tuṇaikāṇēṉ māvē ḻattiṉ uripuṉainta vaḷḷaṟ kiṉiya makappēṟē mūvē taṉaiyai aṟuttaruḷvōy muṟaiyō muṟaiyō muṟaiyēyō.
translation: Going to petty people who do not praise you as God, I grew bewildered. O my King, I forgot to meditate on your holy feet. I see no support! O sweet son bestowed by the generous Lord who wears the skin of the great elephant! O Lord who cuts away the three afflictions and grants grace! Hear my appeal! Hear my appeal! Hear my appeal!
commentary: Turning to petty people who lack devotion brings confusion and distances the mind from God. The divine alone has the power to cut away the three afflictions (the fundamental spiritual impurities or sufferings that bind the soul) and grant lasting grace.

tamil: வேதா நந்த னொடுபோற்றி மேவப் படும்நின் பதம்மறந்தே
ஈதா னம்தந் திடுவீர்என் றீன ரிடம்போய் இரந்தலைந்தேன்
போதா னந்தப் பரசிவத்தில் போந்த பொருளே பூரணமே.
மூதா னந்த வாரிதியே முறையோ முறையோ முறையேயோ.
translit: vētā nanta ṉoṭupōṟṟi mēvap paṭumniṉ patammaṟantē ītā ṉamtan tiṭuvīreṉ ṟīṉa riṭampōy irantalaintēṉ pōtā ṉantap paracivattil pōnta poruḷē pūraṇamē. mūtā ṉanta vāritiyē muṟaiyō muṟaiyō muṟaiyēyō.
translation: Forgetting your feet that are praised and reached by Brahma and Vishnu, I wandered and begged from base people, asking them to give me their gifts. O Reality that emerged from the supreme Siva of blissful wisdom! O Perfection! O ancient ocean of bliss! Hear my appeal! Hear my appeal! Hear my appeal!
commentary: Even Brahma and Vishnu (the Hindu deities of creation and preservation) look up to this supreme divine state. Begging for worldly gifts from base people is a foolish trade when the true reward is the ancient ocean of bliss that flows from supreme Siva.

tamil: வடியாக் கருணை வாரிதியாம் வள்ளல் உன்தாள் மலர்மறந்தே
அடியார்க் கெளிய முக்கணுடை அம்மான் அளித்த அருமருந்தே
முடியா முதன்மைப் பெரும்பொருளே முறையோ முறையோ முறையேயோ.
translit: vaṭiyāk karuṇai vāritiyām vaḷḷal uṉtāḷ malarmaṟantē koṭiyā riṭampōykkuṟaiyirantēṉ koṭiyēṉ iṉi-ōr tuṇaikāṇēṉ aṭiyārk keḷiya mukkaṇuṭai ammāṉ aḷitta arumaruntē muṭiyā mutaṉmaip perumporuḷē muṟaiyō muṟaiyō muṟaiyēyō.
translation: Forgetting the lotus feet of you, the generous Lord who is an ocean of pure compassion, I went to cruel people and begged them to resolve my lack. I am a cruel person, and now I see no other support! O rare medicine bestowed by the three-eyed Father who is easy for his devotees to reach! O endless, primal, supreme Reality! Hear my appeal! Hear my appeal! Hear my appeal!
commentary: God is an ocean of pure compassion and a healing medicine for the soul. The poet confesses his own error: by forgetting this supreme compassion and begging from cruel people, he allowed his own heart to become cruel and lost his only true support.

sections.title: Expressing the Anguish of the Heart

translit: iḻutai neñciṉēṉ eṉceyvāṉ piṟantēṉ ēḻai mārmulaik kēviḻain tuḻaṉṟēṉ paḻutai pāmpeṉa mayaṅkiṉaṉ koṭiyēṉ pāvi yēṉentap paricukoṇ ṭaṭaivēṉ aḻutu kaṇkaḷnīr ārntiṭum aṭiyar akattuḷ ūṟiya āṉanta amutē toḻutu mālpukaḻ taṇikai-eṉ aracē tōṉṟa lēparañ cuṭartarum oḷiyē.
translation: I have a foolish heart. For what purpose was I born? I wandered in desire for the breasts of young women. Deluded like one mistaking a rope for a snake, I am a cruel person. I am a sinner. By what means will I reach you? O blissful nectar welling up in the hearts of devotees who cry until their eyes brim with tears! O my King of Thanigai, worshipped and praised by Vishnu! O noble one! O light that yields the supreme flame!
commentary: Mistaking a rope for a snake is a traditional way to describe spiritual blindness. A person caught in this illusion chases the temporary physical desires of the body while remaining completely blind to the lasting reality of grace. This foolishness stands in sharp contrast to the pure joy of true devotees, whose hearts overflow with nectar and whose eyes fill with tears of devotion.

translit: vañca neñciṉēṉ valvilaṅ kaṉaiyēṉ maṅkai mārmulai malaitaṉil uruḷvēṉ pañca pātakam ōruru eṭuttēṉ pāvi yēṉentap paricukoṇ ṭaṭaivēṉ kañcaṉ mālpukaḻ karuṇaiyaṅ kaṭalē kaṇkaḷ mūṉṟuṭaik karumpoḷir muttē añcal añcaleṉ ṟaṉparaik kākkum aṇṇa lētaṇi kācalat taracē
translation: I have a deceitful heart. I am like a cruel beast. I roll upon the breast-mountains of young women. I took the very form of the five great sins. I am a sinner. By what means will I reach you? O beautiful ocean of grace praised by Brahma and Vishnu! O sweet sugarcane and radiant pearl of the three-eyed Lord! O noble Lord who protects your devotees by telling them not to fear! O King of Thanigachalam!
commentary: A person consumed by worldly attachments can feel entirely made of sin. Here, the sorrow of a deceitful heart is weighed against a divine presence known as a boundless ocean of grace. The deity raises a hand to tell devotees not to fear, showing that no matter how deep the worldly entanglement feels, grace remains open as a refuge.

translit: maiyal neñciṉēṉ matiþyilēṉ koṭiya vāṭka ṇārmulai malaikkupa carittēṉ paiya pāmpiṉai nikarttaveṅ koṭiya pāvi yēṉentap paricukoṇ ṭaṭaivēṉ meyyar uḷḷakam viḷaṅkoḷi viḷakkē mēlai yōrkaḷum viḷamparum poruḷē ceyya mēṉi-em civapirāṉ aḷitta celva mētirut taṇikaiyan tēvē.
translation: I have a deluded heart. I possess no intelligence. I tended to the breast-mountains of women with cruel, sword-like eyes. Resembling a hooded snake, I am an extremely cruel sinner. By what means will I reach you? O luminous lamp shining in the inner hearts of the truthful! O reality that even the highest celestials find hard to describe! O treasure given by our Lord Siva of ruddy form! O beautiful God of great Thanigai!
commentary: A hooded snake is defensive, venomous, and quick to strike. This image captures a heart hardened by selfish desires and physical distractions. Such a rigid and deluded mind struggles to approach the divine, which is described here as a luminous lamp shining only in the inner hearts of the truthful.

translit: matiyil neñciṉēṉ ōtiyiṉai aṉaiyēṉ mātar kaṇeṉum valaiyiṭaip paṭṭēṉ patiyil ēḻaiyēṉ paṭiṟṟuvañ cakaṉēṉ pāvi yēṉentap paricukoṇ ṭaṭaivēṉ potiyil āṭiya civapirāṉ aḷitta puṇṇi yā-aruṭ pōtaka nātā tuti-i rāmaṉuk karuḷceyum taṇikait tūya ṉēpacun tōkaivā kaṉaṉē.
translation: I have a mindless heart. I am like a chameleon. I was caught in the net of women's eyes. I am a destitute man in this town and a deceitful rogue. I am a sinner. By what means will I reach you? O virtuous one given by Lord Siva who dances in the public hall! O Lord of the teachings of grace! O pure one of Thanigai who granted grace to Rama as he praised you! O one whose mount is the green-plumaged peacock!
commentary: A chameleon constantly changes its colors to match its surroundings. This represents an unstable mind, shifting with every passing temptation and easily caught in the traps of physical attraction. Deliverance from this shifting deceit must come from the steadfast purity of the divine, the son of Lord Siva who dances in the open public hall of creation.

translit: tuṭṭa neñciṉēṉ eṭṭiyai aṉaiyēṉ tuyarcey mātarkaḷ cūḻaluḷ tiṉamum paṭṭa vañcaṉēṉ eṉceya utittēṉ pāvi yēṉentap paricukoṇ ṭaṭaivēṉ naṭṭam āṭiya nāyakaṉ aḷitta nalla māṇikka nāyaka maṇiyē maṭṭa ṟāppoḻil cūḻtirut taṇikai vaḷḷa lēmayil vākaṉat tēvē
translation: I have a wicked heart. I am like the poisonous Etti tree. Caught daily in the snare of sorrow-causing women, I became deceitful. Why was I born? I am a sinner. By what means will I reach you? O fine, principal ruby jewel given by the dancing Lord! O benevolent Lord of Thanigai surrounded by groves full of unending nectar! O God whose mount is the peacock!
commentary: The Etti tree bears fruit that looks appealing but is entirely toxic. A life spent chasing passing pleasures becomes just as bitter and poisonous on the inside. Facing this inner emptiness, a person questions the very purpose of their birth and begs for rescue from the divine, seen here as a flawless, shining ruby.

translit: kāyum neñciṉēṉ pēyiṉai aṉaiyēṉ kaṭikoḷ kōtaiyar kaṇvalaip paṭṭēṉ pāyum vempuli nikarttaveñ ciṉattēṉ pāvi yēṉentap paricukoṇ ṭaṭaivēṉ tāyum tantaiyum cāmiyum eṉatu cārpum ākiya taṇikaiyaṅ kukaṉē āyum koṉṟaiceñ caṭaikkaṇin tāṭum aiyar tantaruḷ āṉantap pēṟē.
translation: I have a burning heart. I am like a demon. I am caught in the net of the eyes of women wearing fragrant garlands. I have cruel anger like a pouncing fierce tiger. I am a sinner. With what merit can I reach you? O beautiful Guha of Thanigai, who is my mother, father, Lord, and refuge! O blissful treasure graciously bestowed by the Lord who dances wearing select konrai flowers on his red matted hair!
commentary: Human beings cannot earn divine grace through their own perfection. Taking on the voice of a deeply flawed person, Vallalar confesses to fierce anger and worldly distractions to show that God remains his only true refuge, acting as mother, father, and Lord all at once.

translit: tīṅku neñciṉēṉ vēṅkaiyai aṉaiyēṉ tīya mātartam tiṟattuḻal kiṉṟēṉ pāṅki lāroṭum paḻakiya veṟiyēṉ pāvi yēṉentap paricukoṇ ṭaṭaivēṉ tēṅku kaṅkaiyaic ceñcaṭai iruttum civapi rāṉcelvat tiru-aruṭ pēṟē ōṅku naltaṇi kācalat tamarnta uṇmai yē-eṉak kuṟṟiṭum tuṇaiyē.
translation: I have an evil heart. I am like a leopard. I wander after wicked women. I am a madman who associates with the ignoble. I am a sinner. With what merit can I reach you? O precious treasure of divine grace from Lord Siva who holds the brimming river Ganga in his red matted hair! O Truth seated on the tall and excellent Thanigai mountain! O my closest companion!
commentary: The divine remains an absolute anchor even when a person is lost to bad influences and destructive desires. Calling this ultimate Truth his closest companion, Vallalar shows that God stands by us even when we feel entirely unworthy.

translit: kaḷḷa neñciṉēṉ nañciṉai aṉaiyēṉ kaṭiya mātartam karukkuḻi eṉumōr paḷḷam āḻntiṭu pulaiyaṉēṉ kolaiyēṉ pāvi yēṉentap paricukoṇ ṭaṭaivēṉ veḷḷa vārcaṭai vittakap perumāṉ vēṇṭa naṟporuḷ viritturait tōṉē puḷa lamputaṇ vāvicūḻ taṇikaip poruppa marntiṭum puṉitapū raṇaṉē.
translation: I have a deceitful heart. I am like poison. I am a base one who sinks into the pit that is the womb of cruel women. I am a murderer. I am a sinner. With what merit can I reach you? O you who expounded the great truth when the wise Lord with long matted hair holding the flood requested it! O pure and perfect one seated on the Thanigai mountain surrounded by cool ponds where birds chirp!
commentary: Spiritual ignorance and worldly obsession can deeply corrupt the human heart. Vallalar contrasts this dark human confusion with the absolute wisdom of Murugan, recalling the traditional story where the young deity became the teacher of his own father, Lord Siva, to explain the highest spiritual truth.

translit: matta neñciṉēṉ pittaril tirivēṉ mātar kaṇkaḷiṉ mayaṅkiniṉ ṟalaintēṉ patti eṉpatōr aṇuvumuṟ ṟillēṉ pāvi yēṉentap paricukoṇ ṭaṭaivēṉ pitta nāyakaṉ aruḷtirup pēṟē piramaṉ mālukkum pēcarum poruḷē tattai pāṭuṟum poḻiṟceṟi taṇikā calattiṉ mēviya taṟpara oḷiyē.
translation: I have an intoxicated heart. I wander like a madman. I roamed about, bewildered by the eyes of women. I do not possess even an atom of devotion. I am a sinner. With what merit can I reach you? O divine treasure of grace from the mad Lord! O reality hard to be described even by Brahma and Vishnu! O supreme Light dwelling on the Thanigai mountain full of groves where parrots sing!
commentary: Recognizing one's own spiritual emptiness is often the first true act of surrender. By admitting he lacks even an atom of devotion, Vallalar yields completely to the supreme light of God, a reality so vast that even the great creator gods cannot describe it.

translit: aḻukku neñciṉēṉ poyyala taṟiyēṉ aṇaṅka ṉārmayal āḻattil viḻuntēṉ paḻukkum mūṭaruḷ cērntiṭuṅ koṭiyēṉ pāvi yēṉentap paricukoṇ ṭaṭaivēṉ maḻukkai ēntiya mācilā maṇikkuḷ maṉṉi ōṅkiya vaḷaroḷip piḻampē vaḻukki lārpukaḻ taṇikai-eṉ aracē vaḷḷa lē-eṉṉai vāḻvikkum poruḷē.
translation: I have an impure heart. I know nothing but lies. I fell into the deep delusion of beautiful women. I am a cruel man who associates with absolute fools. I am a sinner. With what merit can I reach you? O expanding mass of light that rises and endures within the flawless jewel who holds the battle-axe! O my King of Thanigai praised by the faultless! O benevolent Lord! O reality that sustains my life!
commentary: Human weakness and lies fall away before the sustaining power of grace. Vallalar describes this divine reality as an expanding mass of light, one that rises up to clear away all delusion and sustain life itself.

translit: aṇṇāvō eṉ arumai aiyāvō paṉṉiraṇṭu kaṇṇāvō vēlpiṭitta kaiyāvō cempavaḷa vaṇṇāvō naṟṟaṇikai maṉṉāvō-eṉṟeṉṟē eṇṇāvō tuṉpat tiruṅkaṭaṟkuḷ maṉṉiṉaṉē.
translation: Crying out, "O Lord, O my precious master, O twelve-eyed one, O one whose hands hold the spear, O one with the color of red coral, O king of good Thanigai," alas, I am fixed in the great dark sea of sorrow.
commentary: The speaker calls out to Murugan by his traditional attributes: his twelve eyes, the spear in his hand, and his glowing red color. Despite chanting the Lord's names and remembering him constantly, the devotee feels utterly stranded in a dark ocean of worldly suffering.

translit: maṉṉappār pōṟṟu maṇiyēniṉ poṉṉaruḷait tuṉṉappā rātu cuḻaṉṟēṉ aruṇaikiri taṉṉappā naṟṟaṇikai taṉṉil amarntaruḷum eṉṉappā iṉṉum inta ēḻaik kiraṅkāyō.
translation: O gem praised by the kings of the world, I wandered without seeking your golden grace. O father of Arunagiri, O my father who sits and bestows grace in good Thanigai, will you still not take pity on this poor soul?
commentary: The poet confesses that he wasted time wandering in the world instead of seeking divine grace. He appeals to Murugan as the spiritual father of Arunagiri, a famous Tamil saint, asking if the Lord will not show that same mercy to him.

translit: kāyniṉṟa neñcak kaṭaiyēṉ tiruttaṇikai vāyniṉ ṟuṉatupukaḻ vāypāṭak kaikuvittut tūyniṉṟē tāḷaittoḻutāṭit tuṉpamelām pōyniṉ ṟaṭaivēṉō puṇṇiyaniṉ poṉṉaruḷē.
translation: I am the lowest wretch with a burning heart. Will I stand in holy Thanigai, sing your praise with my mouth, fold my hands, stand in purity, worship your feet, and dance? Will all my sorrow vanish so I may attain your golden grace, O virtuous one?
commentary: A deep yearning for physical and spiritual transformation drives this verse. The speaker longs to be cleansed of his inner turmoil so he can stand pure at the temple in Thanigai, dancing in ecstatic worship until his sorrows vanish and he attains grace.

translit: poṉpiṇikkum neñcap pulaiyēṉai ivvulakil vaṉpiṇikkō peṟṟu vaḷarttāy aṟiyēṉē eṉpiṇaittār vaḷḷaṟ kiṉimai peṟummaṇiyē aṉpiṇaittōr pōṟṟum aruṭṭaṇikai maṉṉavaṉē.
translation: I am a base wretch whose heart is shackled to gold. Did you bear and raise me in this world only to suffer severe disease? I do not know. O gem who brings sweetness to the benevolent Lord who wears a garland of bones, O king of gracious Thanigai praised by those united in love.
commentary: Worldly attachments, especially the greed for wealth, keep the mind imprisoned. The speaker questions whether he was brought into this world merely to suffer the sickness of these material attachments, pleading for release from the Lord who is infinitely dear to Siva.

translit: vaṉnōyum vañcakartam vaṉcārpum vaṉtuyarum eṉṉōyuṅ koṇṭataṉai eṇṇi iṭivēṉō aṉṉō muṟaipōki aiyā muṟaiyēyō maṉṉō muṟaitaṇikai vāḻvē muṟaiyēyō.
translation: Severe disease, the cruel company of deceitful people, and severe sorrow: thinking of all these afflictions I have contracted, will I shatter? Alas, is this justice? O master, is this justice? O king, is this justice? O life of Thanigai, is this justice?
commentary: Surrounded by illness, grief, and the toxic company of deceitful people, the poet feels on the verge of shattering. He repeatedly questions the justice of this suffering, demanding an answer from the divine in a deeply personal and desperate plea.

tamil: தாணு ஈன்றருள் செல்வமே தணிகையில் சாமியே நினைஏத்திக்
காணு வேன்இலை அருள்இவண் புன்மையில் காலங்கள் கழிக்கின்றேன்
மாணும் அன்பர்கள் என்சொலார் ஐயநீ வந்தெனக் கருள்வாயேல்
நாணு வேன்அலன் நடுங்கலன் ஒடுங்கலன் நாயினும் கடையேனே.
translit: tāṇu īṉṟaruḷ celvamē taṇikaiyil cāmiyē niṉai-ēttik kāṇu vēṉilai aruḷivaṇ puṉmaiyil kālaṅkaḷ kaḻikkiṉṟēṉ māṇum aṉparkaḷ eṉcolār aiyanī vanteṉak karuḷvāyēl nāṇu vēṉalaṉ naṭuṅkalaṉ oṭuṅkalaṉ nāyiṉum kaṭaiyēṉē.
translation: O wealth graciously begotten by Lord Siva! O Lord of Thanigai! I do not praise you to behold your grace. I waste my days here in baseness. What will your glorious devotees say? O Lord, if you come and bestow grace upon me, I will not feel ashamed, I will not tremble, and I will not shrink away, though I am lower than a dog.
commentary: The poet confesses that he has wasted his life in base pursuits and feels entirely unworthy of divine grace. He wonders how pure devotees will judge his unworthiness. Yet, he tells the Lord of Thanigai (Lord Murugan, the son of Siva) that if grace is offered, he will set aside all shame and fear to accept it, even though he feels lower than a street dog.

tamil: கடைப்பட் டேங்கும்இந் நாயினுக் கருள்தரக் கடவுள்நீ வருவாயேல்
மடைப்பட் டோங்கிய அன்பகத் தொண்டர்கள் வந்துனைத் தடுப்பாரேல்
தடைப்பட் டாய்எனில் என்செய்வேன் என்செய்வேன் தளர்வது தவிரேனே
அடைப்பட் டோங்கிய வயல்திருத் தணிகையம் பதிஅமர்ந் திடுதேவே.
translit: kaṭaippaṭ ṭēṅkumin nāyiṉuk karuḷtarak kaṭavuḷnī varuvāyēl maṭaippaṭ ṭōṅkiya aṉpakat toṇṭarkaḷ vantuṉait taṭuppārēl taṭaippaṭ ṭāyeṉil eṉceyvēṉ eṉceyvēṉ taḷarvatu tavirēṉē aṭaippaṭ ṭōṅkiya vayaltirut taṇikaiyam pati-amarn tiṭutēvē.
translation: O God seated in the city of beautiful Thanigai, surrounded by flourishing and banked fields! If you come to bestow grace upon this dog languishing at the lowest level, and if your devotees with hearts overflowing with surging love come and stop you, what will I do if you are hindered? What will I do? I will not escape despair.
commentary: The speaker's feeling of unworthiness runs so deep that he imagines the Lord's perfect devotees might step in to stop God from blessing him. He asks God what he is supposed to do if these great devotees succeed in blocking the grace he desperately needs. Without that divine grace, he says, he will be trapped in inescapable despair.

tamil: தேவ ரேமுதல் உலகங்கள் யாவையும் சிருட்டிஆ தியசெய்யும்
மூவ ரேஎதிர் வருகினும் மதித்திடேன் முருகநின் பெயர்சொல்வோர்
யாவ ரேனும்என் குடிமுழு தாண்டெனை அளித்தவர் அவரேகாண்
தாவ நாடொணாத் தணிகையம் பதியில்வாழ் சண்முகப் பெருமானே.
translit: tēva rēmutal ulakaṅkaḷ yāvaiyum ciruṭṭi-ā tiyaceyyum mūva rē-etir varukiṉum matittiṭēṉ murukaniṉ peyarcolvōr yāva rēṉumeṉ kuṭimuḻu tāṇṭeṉai aḷittavar avarēkāṇ tāva nāṭoṇāt taṇikaiyam patiyilvāḻ caṇmukap perumāṉē.
translation: O Lord Shanmuga living in the city of Thanigai, a place unapproachable by afflictions! Even if the three primary gods who perform creation and the other divine acts for all the worlds and the celestials come before me, I will not regard them. Whoever speaks your name, O Murugan, they are the very ones who rule my entire lineage and protect me.
commentary: Supreme devotion is presented here as fierce, exclusive loyalty. The poet declares that even if the three primary gods of creation, preservation, and destruction appeared before him, he would pay them no attention. His devotion to Lord Murugan is so complete that he considers any person who merely speaks Murugan's name to be the absolute master and protector of his entire family line.

sections.title: The Glory of the Holy Ash

translit: tivacaṅkaḷ toṟumkoṇṭiṭu tīmaippiṇi tīrum pavacaṅkaṭam aṟumivvika paramumpukaḻ paravum kavacaṅkaḷe ṉaccūḻntuṟu kaṇṇēṟatu tavirum civacaṇmuka eṉavē-aruḷ tirunīṟaṇin tiṭilē.
translation: If you wear the graceful holy ash reciting, "Siva Shanmuga," evil diseases caught day after day are cured. The sorrow of worldly existence is severed. Fame spreads in this world and the next. The evil eye that surrounds you like armor is cast off.
commentary: The sacred white ash (tirunīṟu) is a symbol of purity and divine protection. Vallalar says that applying it while chanting the name of Lord Murugan clears away physical illnesses and the heavy sorrows of worldly life. It acts as a shield, deflecting negativity and the evil eye while bringing lasting honor.

translit: mālēntiya kuḻalārtaru mayalpōmiṭar ayalpōm kōlēntiya aracāṭciyum kūṭumpukaḻ nīṭum mēlēntiya vāṉāṭarkaḷ meliyāvitam orucev vēlēntiya murukā-eṉa veṇṇīṟaṇin tiṭilē.
translation: If you wear the white ash reciting, "O Murugan wielding the singular red spear so the high celestials do not weaken," the delusion caused by women with garlanded hair vanishes. Afflictions depart. Scepter-wielding sovereignty is attained. Fame endures.
commentary: The red spear (vēl) is Murugan's signature weapon, representing the power of divine wisdom to pierce through ignorance. Holding this image in mind while wearing the holy ash breaks the spell of worldly distractions and lust. With a clear mind, a person gains strength and overcomes afflictions to achieve enduring success.

translit: tavamuṇmaiyo ṭuṟumvañcakar tamcārvatu tavirum navamaṇmiya aṭiyāriṭam nalkumtiṟaṉ malkum pavaṉaṉpuṉal kaṉalmaṇveḷi palavākiya poruḷām civacaṇmuka eṉavē-aruḷ tirunīṟaṉin tiṭilē.
translation: If you wear the graceful holy ash reciting, "Siva Shanmuga, who becomes the manifold elements of wind, beautiful water, fire, earth, and space," you attain true penance. Association with the deceitful is avoided. The capacity to give to the new devotees who approach multiplies.
commentary: Murugan is not just a personal deity but the underlying reality of the five physical elements: earth, water, fire, wind, and space. Recognizing God in all things while applying the ash guides a person into true spiritual discipline. This sincerity naturally repels deceitful people and increases a person's capacity to care for true spiritual seekers.

translit: tuyilēṟiya cōrvumkeṭum tuyaramkeṭum naṭuvaṉ kaiyilēṟiya pācamtuṇi kaṇṭēmuṟit tiṭumāl kuyilēṟiya poḻilcūḻtiruk kuṉṟēṟi naṭakkum mayilēṟiya maṇiyē-eṉa vaḷarnīṟaṇin tiṭilē.
translation: If you wear the prospering holy ash reciting, "O Gem riding the peacock that paces the holy hill surrounded by cuckoo-filled groves," the fatigue born of sleep perishes. Sorrow perishes. The noose held in the hands of the God of Death breaks into pieces upon seeing this.
commentary: The image of Murugan riding his peacock is a source of vitality that cures physical exhaustion and spiritual fatigue. Vallalar says the protective power of the holy ash is so complete that it shatters the fear of mortality entirely, breaking the noose of death. It replaces sorrow with a bright, wakeful presence.

translit: tēṟāpperu maṉamāṉatu tēṟuntuyar māṟum māṟāppiṇi māyumtiru maruvumkaru oruvum vīṟāppoṭu varucūrmuṭi vēṟākkiṭa varumōr āṟākkarapporuḷē-eṉa aruḷnīṟaṇin tiṭilē.
translation: If you wear the graceful holy ash reciting, "O Reality of the six syllables who came to sever the heads of Surapadman who advanced with fierce arrogance," the deeply confused mind gains clarity. Sorrow departs. Incurable diseases perish. Wealth embraces you. The cycle of birth ends.
commentary: The six syllables refer to Murugan's fundamental mantra, typically "Sa Ra Va Na Ba Va." The demon Surapadman represents the fierce arrogance of the human ego, which the divine cuts down. Chanting this truth while wearing the ash clears away deep mental confusion, cures incurable ailments, and frees the soul from the cycle of birth and death.

translit: amarāvati iṟaiyōṭunal ayaṉuntiru mālum tamarākuvar civañāṉamun taḻaikkuṅkati cārum emarājaṉai velluntiṟal eytumpukaḻ eytum kumarāciva kuruvē-eṉak kuḷirnīṟaṇin tiṭilē.
translation: If one wears the cooling sacred ash chanting "O Kumara, O Siva Guru", the lord of Amaravati, good Brahma, and Vishnu will become their kin. The wisdom of Siva will flourish and they will reach the highest state. They will attain the power to conquer the lord of death and achieve great fame.
commentary: Calling on Murugan as the youthful god (Kumara) and the one who taught his own father (Siva Guru) while wearing sacred ash brings immense spiritual power. Vallalar says this act of devotion wins the friendship of the highest gods and grants the ability to conquer death itself.

translit: mēlākiya ulakattavar mēvittoḻum vaṇṇam mālākiya iruḷnīṅkinal vāḻvaippeṟu vārkāṇ cīlāciva līlāpara tēvā-umai yavaḷtaṉ pālākatir vēlā-eṉap patinīṟaṇin tiṭilē.
translation: If one wears the sacred ash of the Lord chanting "O virtuous one, O supreme god of Siva's divine play, O son of goddess Uma, O wielder of the radiant spear", the beings of the higher worlds will gather and worship them. The darkness of illusion will vanish and they will attain a good life.
commentary: Devotion to Murugan clears away the deep darkness of illusion. By remembering his divine mother, the goddess Uma, and his radiant spear, the seeker is elevated to a state so pure that even the beings of the heavenly worlds gather to honor them.

translit: akamāṟiya neṟicārkuvar aṟivāmuru aṭaivār mikamāṟiya poṟiyiṉvaḻi mēvānala mikuvār cakamāṟiṉum uyarvāṉilai tāmāṟiṉum aḻiyār mukamāṟuṭai mutalvā-eṉa mutirnīṟaṇin tiṭilē.
translation: If one wears the ancient sacred ash chanting "O supreme Lord with six faces", they will reach the inward path. They will attain a form of pure intelligence. They will avoid the path of the greatly wandering senses and will abound in goodness. Even if the world perishes or their high state shifts, they will remain indestructible.
commentary: Calling upon the six-faced Lord turns the mind inward, drawing it away from the wandering distractions of the senses. The worshipper achieves a form made entirely of pure intelligence, remaining untouched and indestructible even if the physical universe falls apart.

translit: cintāmaṇi niti-aintaru ceḻikkumpuva ṉamumōr nantā-eḻil uruvumperu nalaṉumkati nalaṉum intā-eṉat taruvārtamai irantārkaḷuk kellām kantācivaṉ maintā-eṉak kaṉanīṟaṇin tiṭilē.
translation: If one wears the glorious sacred ash chanting "O Skanda, O son of Siva", they will grant gifts to all who beg of them. They will hand over the wish-fulfilling gem, great treasures, the five celestial trees, a flourishing realm, an unfading beautiful form, great prosperity, and the highest state, saying "Here, take this."
commentary: True devotion turns the worshipper into a boundless giver. Empowered by the grace of Skanda (Murugan), the devotee gains the ability to hand out infinite blessings, granting mythical treasures like the wish-fulfilling gem and the highest spiritual state to anyone who asks for help.

translit: eṇṇārpuram erittāraruḷ eytumtiru neṭumāl naṇṇātatōr aṭinīḻalil naṇṇumpaṭi paṇṇum paṇṇārmoḻi malaiyāḷaruḷ pālāpaṉi raṇṭu kaṇṇā-ema taṇṇā-eṉak kaṉanīṟaṇin tiṭilē.
translation: If one wears the glorious sacred ash chanting "O son graced by the mountain goddess of musical speech, O Lord with twelve eyes, O our elder brother", it will cause them to rest in the shadow of the divine feet. Those feet remain unreached even by the great Vishnu, who received the grace of the Lord who burned the cities of the foes.
commentary: Murugan is the direct path to the ultimate refuge. By appealing to him lovingly as an elder brother, the seeker finds rest at the divine feet of his father, Siva. According to sacred lore, these are the very same supreme feet that even the great god Vishnu could not reach.

translit: mañcēr piṇimaṭi yātiyai nōkki varuntuṟumeṉ neñcē taṇikaiyaṉ āṟeḻut tuṇṭuveṇṇīṟuṇṭunī eñcēl iravum pakalum tuticey tiṭutikaṇṭāy añcēl itucat tiyamāmeṉ collai aṟintukoṇṭē.
translation: O my heart, you suffer as you look at the diseases and lethargy that gather like clouds. There is the six-lettered mantra of the Lord of Thanigai, and there is the sacred white ash. Do not falter. Praise him night and day. Do not fear. Understand my word, for this is the truth.
commentary: The poet comforts his own anxious mind. He tells his heart to stop worrying about disease and lethargy. The remedy is simple and constant devotion: chanting the six-syllable mantra of the Lord of Thanigai (the deity Murugan) and wearing sacred white ash.

translit: aṟiyāta nampiṇi ātiyai nīkkum aruḷmaruntiṉ neṟiyām taṇikaiyaṉ āṟeḻut tuṇṭuveṇṇīṟuṇṭunī eṟiyā tiravum pakalum tuticey tiṭutikaṇṭāy kuṟiyā tirukkalai eṉāṇai eṉṟaṉ kuṇaneñcamē.
translation: There is the six-lettered mantra of the Lord of Thanigai, and there is the sacred white ash. They form the path of the medicine of grace that removes our unknowable diseases and root afflictions. Do not cast them aside. Praise him night and day. Do not fail to hold this as your aim. This is my command, O my good heart.
commentary: This devotion acts as a medicine of grace. It cures the deepest roots of human suffering, far beyond ordinary physical illness. The poet commands his heart to hold firmly to this practice day and night.

translit: eṉṟē piṇikaḷ oḻiyumeṉ ṟētuyar eytiyiṭēl niṉṟē taṇikaiyaṉ āṟeḻut tuṇṭuveṇṇīṟuṇṭunī iṉṟē iravum pakalum tuticey tiṭutikaṇṭāy naṉṟē-ek kālamum vāḻiya vāḻiya naṉṉeñcamē.
translation: Do not suffer in sorrow asking when these diseases will end. Stand firm. There is the six-lettered mantra of the Lord of Thanigai, and there is the sacred white ash. Praise him night and day starting this very day. May you live well in all times, O my good heart, may you live well.
commentary: Despair only causes more sorrow. Instead of asking when the pain will end, the heart must begin its practice of devotion today. The verse closes with a gentle blessing for the mind to live well forever in this state of remembrance.

translit: pōtukoṇ ṭavaṉum mālumniṉ ṟēttum puṇṇiya niṉtiru aṭikkē yātukoṇ ṭaṭaikēṉ yātumēṟ ceykēṉ yātuniṉ tiru-uḷam aṟiyēṉ tītukoṇ ṭavaṉeṉ ṟeṉakkaruḷ ciṟitum ceytiṭā tiruppaiyō ciṟiyōṉ ētivaṉ ceyaloṉ ṟilai-eṉak karuti īvaiyō taṇikaivāḻ iṟaiyē.
translation: O Holy One whose sacred feet Brahma holding the lotus and Vishnu stand and praise! With what offering shall I reach them? What more shall I do? I do not know your divine will. Will you deny me even a fraction of your grace, judging me full of evil? Or will you grant it, deciding this lowly one is incapable of any action? O Lord who lives in Thanigai!
commentary: The poet feels completely helpless before the divine. He wonders if God will turn away from his faults or take pity on his total inability to help himself. He asks for grace not as a reward for his own effort, but as a pure gift to someone who has nothing else to offer.

translit: vāḻvaṉō niṉpoṉ aṭiniḻal kiṭaittē vayaṅkumā ṉantaveḷ ḷattuḷ āḻvaṉō eḷiyēṉ allativ vulakil aṟañceyāk koṭiyarpāṟ ceṉṟē tāḻvaṉō tāḻnta paṇipurin tavamē cañcarit tuḻaṉṟuven narakil vīḻvaṉō iḵteṉ ṟaṟikilēṉ taṇikai veṟpiṉuḷ oḷiraruḷ viḷakkē.
translation: Will I find life by attaining the shelter of your golden feet? Will this poor soul immerse himself in the shining flood of bliss? Or will I stoop low, approaching cruel men in this world who perform no righteous deeds? Will I wander in vain performing menial service for them, only to fall into the blazing hell? I do not know my fate. O shining lamp of grace in the hills of Thanigai!
commentary: This verse contrasts the pure joy of divine grace with the misery of worldly dependence. The poet fears being forced to serve cruel and selfish people just to survive in the physical world. He calls out to God, unsure if his destiny is the freedom of spiritual bliss or the trap of degrading worldly labor.

translit: kārpūtta kaṇṭat toṭumēvu mukkaṭ kaṉikaṉintu cīrpūt toḻukucen tēṉē taṇikaiyil teḷamutē pērpūtta oṟṟiyil niṉmuṉṉar ēṟṟiṭap pētaiyaṉēṉ ērpūtta oṇpaḷi tamkāṇ kilaṉataṟ keṉceyvaṉē.
translation: O red honey flowing from the ripened fruit of the three-eyed Lord whose neck bears the dark hue of clouds! O clear nectar in Thanigai! In renowned Otriyur, to light an offering before you, I, an ignorant person, cannot find any beautiful bright camphor. What shall I do?
commentary: The speaker addresses Lord Murugan as the sweet essence of his father, Lord Siva. Siva is described here with three eyes and a dark neck, a reference to the ancient story of him swallowing the world's poison to save all beings. The devotee stands in the temple town of Otriyur, yearning to perform the traditional ritual of waving a burning camphor flame before the deity. Finding himself without this simple physical offering, he feels entirely helpless.

translit: karumarun tāya maṇikaṇṭa nāyakaṉ kaṇmaṇiyām arumarun tētaṇi kācalam mēvumeṉ āruyirē tirumaruṅ kāroṟṟi yūrmē viyaniṉ tirumuṉṉarāy orumaruṅ kēṟṟa-eṉ ceykēṉ kaṟpūra oḷiyiṉukkē.
translation: O rare medicine, the very eye of the jewel-necked Lord who is the cure for the cycle of birth! O my precious life residing in Thanigachalam! What shall I do to light the radiant camphor on one side before your divine presence as you rest in holy Otriyur?
commentary: God is praised here as the rare medicine that cures the soul's endless cycle of birth and death. The speaker continues to grieve his inability to offer the radiant light of burning camphor. The traditional flame represents the light of awareness, and lacking it highlights the devotee's deep feeling of spiritual unworthiness.

translit: pāleṭut tēttumnaṟ pāmpoṭu vēṅkaiyum pārttiṭa-ōr kāleṭut tampalat tāṭum pirāṉtiruk kaṇmaṇiyē vēleṭut tōyteṉ taṇikā calattamar vittakaniṉ pāleṭut tēṟṟak kiṭaikkuṅ kolōveṇ paḷitameṟkē.
translation: O holy eye of the Lord who lifts one foot and dances in the Hall while the good serpent and the tiger watch and offer praise! O wielder of the spear! O wise one residing in southern Thanigachalam! Will I ever get white camphor to take and light before you?
commentary: This verse describes Lord Siva performing his cosmic dance with one raised foot, watched by legendary sages who took the forms of a serpent and a tiger. Addressing Murugan as the wielder of the sacred spear and the son of this dancing Lord, the speaker wonders if he will ever obtain the pure white camphor needed for his worship. The question reveals a deep, aching thirst to connect with the divine.

translit: kaṇṇappaṉ eṉṉum tiruppeya rālula kampukaḻum tiṇṇappaṉ ēttum civaṉār makaṉukkut teṇṭaṉiṭṭa viṇṇappam oṉṟinta mētiṉi māyaiyil vīḻvataṟut teṇṇap paṭumniṉ tiruvaruḷ īka-iv vēḻaiyaṟkē.
translation: To the son of Lord Siva praised by Thinnappan, who is celebrated by the world by the holy name Kannappan! I bow to you and make one request: sever my fall into the illusion of this earth and grant your esteemed divine grace to this poor soul.
commentary: The poem closes with a reminder of Kannappan, a legendary hunter who showed such fierce devotion that he plucked out his own eyes to offer to Lord Siva. By recalling this ultimate sacrifice, the devotee leaves behind his worry over the missing camphor and makes a much greater request. He simply asks God to cut away the illusions of worldly life and grant him permanent grace.

sections.title: Praying for the Grace to Serve Devotees

translit: eppā lavarum iṟaiñcum taṇikai iruntaruḷeṉ appā-uṉ poṉṉaṭik keṉneñ cakamiṭa mākkimikka veppāṉa nañcaṉa vañcakar pāṟcelum ventuyarnīt tippāril niṉaṭi yārkkēval ceyya eṉakkaruḷē.
translation: My Father, you graciously reside in Thanigai, worshipped by people from all directions. Make my heart the abode for your golden feet. Remove the cruel sorrow of seeking out deceitful people who are like burning poison. Grant me the grace to serve your devotees in this world.
commentary: The true purpose of life is serving those who love God. The poet asks the Lord of Thanigai to protect him from the misery of seeking favors from deceitful, worldly people. By making his heart a temple for God's feet, he hopes to spend his life serving only God's devotees.

translit: eyyā taruḷtaṇi kācalam mēviya eṉarumai aiyā niṉatu tiruvaṭi ētti-aṉ ṟō-ayaṉum ceyyāḷ maruvum puyaṉuṭait tēvaṉum cēṇavaṉum naiyāta āyuḷum celvamum vaṇmaiyum naṇṇiṉarē.
translation: My precious Lord, you reside in Thanigachalam and grant unfailing grace. Was it not by praising your holy feet that Brahma, Vishnu whose shoulders are embraced by Lakshmi, and Indra of the heavens attained an imperishable life, wealth, and power?
commentary: True lasting wealth and power come only from divine grace. The poet points out that even the supreme creator Brahma, the protector Vishnu, and the heavenly king Indra achieved their immortal status and prosperity solely by bowing to the holy feet of the Lord.

translit: vāḷāruṅ kaṇṇiyar māyaiyai nīkki malikaraṇak kōḷākum vātaṉai nīttumeyñ ñāṉak kuṟikoṭuniṉ tāḷākum nīḻal atucārntu niṟkat takuntatiru nāḷākum nāḷenta nāḷaṟi yēṉtaṇi kācalaṉē.
translation: When is the auspicious day I become fit to stand in the shade of your feet, dispelling the illusion of women with sword-like eyes, abandoning the afflictions caused by the unruly senses, and bearing the mark of true wisdom? I do not know, O Lord of Thanigachalam.
commentary: Worldly desires and the restless senses pull the mind away from spiritual peace. The poet longs for the exact day when he will finally shed the illusion of physical attraction and the turmoil of his own mind. He seeks to replace these distractions with true wisdom and find permanent shelter in the shade of God's feet.

translit: ūṉpārkkum ivvuṭaṟ poymaiyait tērtal oḻintavamē māṉpārkkum kaṇṇiyar maiyalil vīḻum mayakkamaṟṟē tēṉpārkkum cōlait taṇikā calattuṉ tiru-aḻakai nāṉpārkkum nāḷenta nāḷmayil ēṟiya nāyakaṉē.
translation: When is the day I will free myself from the delusion of lusting after women with deer-like eyes, stop wasting time failing to realize the falsity of this fleshy body, and behold your divine beauty in Thanigachalam with its honey-filled groves, O Lord who rides the peacock?
commentary: The physical body is temporary, and chasing after sensual pleasures is a deep waste of a human lifetime. The poet questions when he will finally wake up from these physical delusions and fix his vision entirely on the divine beauty of the Lord who rides the peacock.

translit: eṉṉē kuṟainamak kēḻaineñ cēmayil ēṟivarum maṉṉē eṉaneṭu mālum piramaṉum vāḻttiniṟkum taṉṉēr taṇikait taṭamalai vāḻumnaṟ ṟantai-aruḷ poṉṉēr tiruvaṭip pōtukaṇ ṭāynam pukaliṭamē.
translation: What do we lack, O poor heart? The great Vishnu and Brahma stand and praise him, crying out, "O King who comes riding on a peacock!" Our good Father resides on the incomparable, broad mountain of Thanigai. His golden, flower-like holy feet are truly our refuge.
commentary: The human heart has no reason to feel poor or lacking when it holds onto God. Addressing his own mind, the poet offers comfort by reminding himself that the very same Lord whom the greatest gods praise is his loving Father. Those golden feet offer the ultimate and perfect refuge.

translit: pētaineñ cē-eṉṟaṉ piṉpōn tiṭuti-ip pēyulaka vātai-añ cēlpoṟi vāykkalaṅ kēliṟai yummayaṅkēl pōtaiyeñ cēltaṇi kācalam pōyap poruppamarnta tātai-añ cēvaṭik kīḻkkuṭi yākat tayaṅkuvamē.
translation: O foolish heart, follow me. Do not fear the torments of this devilish world. Do not be disturbed by the senses. Do not be confused even slightly. Do not waste time. Let us go to Mount Thanigai and shine as subjects beneath the beautiful red feet of the Father who resides on that mountain.
commentary: The poet speaks directly to his own mind, urging it to turn away from worldly anxieties and sensory distractions. Instead of being pulled by fear or confusion, he tells his heart to follow his spiritual resolve and seek out Mount Thanigai, a sacred hill in Tamil Nadu dedicated to Lord Murugan. By taking refuge there as subjects of the divine Father, he promises his mind a life of lasting peace, far removed from the exhaustion of the material world.

sections.title: Praying That Days Are not Spent in Vain

translit: kuṉṟamot tilaṅku paṇaimulai neṭuṅkaṇ kōtaiyar pālvirain tōṭic ceṉṟa-ip pulaiyēṉ maṉattiṉai mīṭṭuṉ tiruvaṭik kākkumnāḷ uḷatō eṉtaṉi uyirē eṉṉuṭaip poruḷē eṉuḷat tiṇiteḻum iṉpē maṉṟalam poḻilcūḻ taṇikaiyam poruppil vantamarn taruḷceyum maṇiyē.
translation: Is there a day when I will rescue the mind of this lowly one who ran swiftly toward women with long eyes and large breasts shining like mountains, and offer it to Your holy feet? My matchless life! My true wealth! The sweet bliss that rises firmly in my heart! O Gem who came and sat to bestow grace upon the Thanigai mountain surrounded by fragrant groves.
commentary: Physical attraction acts as a powerful trap that draws the mind away from spiritual life. Vallalar asks when he will finally be able to reel his wandering mind back from these sensory distractions. For him, the divine presence at Thanigai is no distant deity: it is his own breath, his real wealth, and his only lasting source of joy.

translit: maṇikkuḻai aṭarttu matarttavēṟ kaṇṇār vañcaka mayakkiṉil āḻntu kaṇikkarum tuyarkoḷ maṉattiṉai mīṭṭuṉ kaḻalaṭik kākkumnāḷ uḷatō kuṇikkarum poruḷē kuṇapperuṅ kuṉṟē kuṟikuṇaṅ kaṭantatōr neṟiyē eṇikkarum mālum ayaṉumniṉ ṟēttum entaiyē taṇikai-em iṟaiyē.
translation: Is there a day when I will rescue my mind, which took on incalculable sorrow by sinking into the deceitful illusion of women whose large spear-like eyes crowd their gem-set earrings, and offer it to Your ankleted feet? O Reality beyond measure! O great mountain of virtues! O unique path beyond attributes and signs! My father, praised by Vishnu and Brahma, our Lord of Thanigai!
commentary: Chasing physical desires leads directly to incalculable sorrow. Vallalar contrasts the deceptive, fleeting beauty of the physical world with the eternal reality of God. He addresses the divine as a path that exists completely beyond human signs and attributes, yet still stands as a vast mountain of pure goodness.

translit: iṟaikkuḷē ulakam aṭaṅkalum maruṭṭum ilaineṭu vēṟkaṇār aḷakac ciṟaikkuḷē varuntum maṉattiṉai mīṭṭuṉ tiruvaṭik kākkumnāḷ uḷatō maṟaikkuḷē maṟaintam maṟaikkari tāya vaḷḷalē uḷḷakap poruḷē aṟaikkuḷē maṭavārk kaṉanaṭai payiṟṟum aṇitirut taṇikaivāḻ araicē.
translation: Is there a day when I will rescue my mind, which suffers inside the prison of the dark tresses of women whose long, leaf-shaped, spear-like eyes bewitch all the worlds in an instant, and offer it to Your holy feet? O generous Lord hidden within the Vedas and rare even for those Vedas to find! The supreme reality within the heart! The King living in beautiful holy Thanigai where swans teach their graceful walk to young women within their mansions.
commentary: The mind feels imprisoned by sensory desires, caught like a captive in a cell. Vallalar contrasts this immediate, physical capture with the deeply hidden nature of the divine. He says that God is concealed even from the most sacred ancient scriptures, the Vedas, yet can always be found quietly dwelling within the human heart.

translit: araimatik kuṟaḻum oṇṇutal vāṭkaṇ alarmulai aṇaṅkaṉār alkul puraimatit tuḻalum maṉattiṉai mīṭṭuṉ poṉṉaṭik kākkumnāḷ uḷatō paraimatit tiṭañcēr parāparaṟ karumaip pālaṉē vēluṭai yavaṉē viraimatit tōṅkum malarppoḻil taṇikai veṟpiṉil oḷirummey viḷakkē.
translation: Is there a day when I will rescue my mind, which wanders esteeming the loins of goddess-like women with bright foreheads like the half-moon, sword-like eyes, and blossoming breasts, and offer it to Your golden feet? O precious child of the Supreme Lord who shares his space with the esteemed Supreme Goddess! O wielder of the spear! O true lamp shining on the Thanigai mountain with its flower groves towering with esteemed fragrance!
commentary: The wandering mind places false value on the physical body, mistaking passing beauty for something permanent. Vallalar prays for the strength to redirect this misplaced devotion toward God instead. He looks to the divine as a beacon of absolute truth shining on the temple hill, capable of guiding him out of illusion.

translit: viḷakkuṟaḻ maṇippūṇ mēlaṇin tōṅki vimmuṟum iḷamulai maṭavār kaḷakkiṉil āḻnta maṉattiṉai mīṭṭuṉ kaḻalaṭik kākkumnāḷ uḷatō aḷakkaruṅ karuṇai vāriyē ñāṉa amutamē āṉantap perukkē kiḷakkarum pukaḻkoḷ taṇikaiyam poruppil kiḷarntaruḷ puriyumeṉ kiḷaiyē.
translation: Is there a day when I will rescue my mind, sunk in the turmoil caused by young women with swelling young breasts highly adorned with gem-set ornaments shining like lamps, and offer it to Your ankleted feet? O ocean of immeasurable compassion! O nectar of wisdom! O flood of bliss! My true kin who joyously bestows grace on the Thanigai mountain of indescribable fame!
commentary: Pursuing worldly lust does not bring peace, but only leaves the mind sunk in deep turmoil. Vallalar looks to divine grace as the only way to rescue himself from this agitation. He calls God his true family, describing the divine as an ocean of limitless compassion and a flood of wisdom that washes away all confusion.

translit: kiḷaikkuṟum piṇikkōr uṟaiyuḷām maṭavār kīḻuṟum alkuleṉ kuḻivīḻn tiḷaikkumvaṉ koṭiya maṉattiṉai mīṭṭuṉ iṇai-aṭik kākkumnāḷ uḷatō viḷaikkumā ṉanta viyaṉtaṉi vittē meyaṭi yavaruḷa viruppē tiḷaikkummā tavattōrk karuḷceyun taṇikait teyvamē aruṭceḻun tēṉē.
translation: O Deity of Thanigai who grants grace to those immersed in great penance! O rich honey of grace! O vast, peerless seed that yields bliss! O desire within the hearts of true devotees! Is there a day You will rescue my cruel, harsh mind that falls into the pit of the loins of women, an abode of multiplying diseases, and grows weary there, and instead fix it upon Your twin feet?
commentary: The physical body is prone to weariness and disease. Vallalar contrasts this stark mortal reality with the eternal bliss of the divine, asking when his mind will turn away from the trap of lust. He calls out to the divine, the seed of joy and the honey of grace, to anchor his wandering thoughts in spiritual truth.

translit: tēṉvaḻi malarppūṅ kuḻaltuṭi iṭaivēl tiṟalviḻi mātarār puṇarppām kāṉvaḻi naṭakkum maṉattiṉai mīṭṭuṉ kaḻalvaḻi naṭattumnāḷ uḷatō māṉvaḻi varumeṉ ammaiyai vēṇṭi vaṇpuṉat taṭaintiṭṭa maṇiyē vāṉvaḻi aṭaikkum cikaricūḻ taṇikai māmalai amarntaruḷ maruntē.
translation: O medicine seated gracefully upon the great mountain of Thanigai, surrounded by peaks that block the path of the sky! O jewel who reached the fertile millet field out of desire for my Mother Valli born of a deer! Is there a day You will rescue my mind that walks the forest path of union with women who have honey-dripping floral hair, slender drum-like waists, and piercing spear-like eyes, and make it walk the path of Your ankleted feet?
commentary: The mind chasing physical beauty is like someone wandering lost on a wild forest path. Vallalar asks when his awareness will finally walk the clear, safe path of the divine instead. He calls the Lord the medicine for this distracted condition, recalling the traditional story of Murugan coming down to a humble millet field out of love for his consort Valli.

translit: marunteṉa mayakkum kutalai-an tīñcol vāṇutal maṅkaiyar iṭattil porunteṉa valikkum maṉattiṉai mīṭṭuṉ poṉṉaṭik kākkumnāḷ uḷatō aruntiṭā tarunta aṭiyaruḷ ōṅkum āṉantat tēṟalē amutē iruntaru muṉivar pukaḻceyum taṇikai iṉitamarn taruḷiya iṉpē.
translation: O joy seated sweetly in Thanigai praised by great sages! O nectar of bliss, O ambrosia that swells in the hearts of devotees who drink it ceaselessly! Is there a day You will rescue my mind that compels me to unite with bright-foreheaded women whose sweet lisping words intoxicate like a potion, and fix it upon Your golden feet?
commentary: Physical attraction acts like a potion, where sweet words cloud the mind with temporary illusions. Vallalar contrasts this intoxication with the divine presence, calling God the true nectar of bliss that constantly fills the hearts of those who seek it. He prays for his mind to be rescued from this worldly spell and fixed firmly on the eternal.

translit: iṉpamaṟ ṟuṟukaṇ viḷaiviḻi nilamām ēntiḻai yavarpuḻuk kuḻiyil tuṉpamuṟ ṟuḻalum maṉattiṉai mīṭṭuṉ tuṇaiyaṭik kākkumnāḷ uḷatō aṉparmuṟ ṟuṇara aruḷceyum tēvē ari-ayaṉ paṇiperi yavaṉē vaṉpatai akaṟṟi maṉpataik karuḷvāṉ makiḻntuṟum taṇikaiyiṉ vāḻvē.
translation: O life of Thanigai, rejoicing to banish cruelty and bestow grace upon humanity! O Great One served by Vishnu and Brahma! O God who grants grace so devotees may know all things completely! Is there a day You will rescue my suffering mind that wanders in the worm-filled pit of jeweled women, a place devoid of joy that yields only affliction, and fix it upon Your protecting pair of feet?
commentary: Physical attraction promises joy but in the end delivers only suffering. Stripping away romantic illusions, Vallalar points to the raw, mortal reality of the human body to break the mind's attachment to it. He asks the Lord, who is described as being served even by the great gods Vishnu and Brahma, to lift his mind out of this misery and give it the protection of true grace.

translit: vāḻumiv vulaka vāḻkkaiyai mikavum valittiṭum maṅkaiyar tampāl tāḻumeṉ koṭiya maṉattiṉai mīṭṭuṉ tāḷmalark kākkumnāḷ uḷatō cūḻumneñ ciruḷaip pōḻummey oḷiyē tōṟṟamī ṟaṟṟaciṟ cukamē ūḻumuṟ pavamōr ēḻumviṭ ṭakala utavucīr aruṭperuṅ kuṉṟē.
translation: O great mountain of magnificent grace that helps dispel past karma and the seven kinds of birth! O supreme bliss without beginning or end! O true light that pierces the surrounding darkness of the heart! Is there a day You will rescue my cruel mind that sinks toward women who fiercely bind one to this worldly life, and fix it upon Your lotus feet?
commentary: Lust tightly binds a person to the endless cycles of worldly life. Vallalar asks to be saved from this trap by the supreme light of grace. He prays for the divine to pierce the darkness of his heart, wipe away his past karma (the accumulated burden of his actions), and free him from all future rebirths.

translit: mūṭarkaḷ tamakkuḷ muṟpaṭuṅ koṭiya muṟiyaṉēṉ taṉakkuniṉ aṭiyām ēṭaviḻ kamalat tirunaṟa varunta eṉṟukol aruḷpurin tiṭuvāy āṭara vaṇintē ampalat tāṭum aiyaruk korutavap pēṟē kōṭaṇi tarukkaḷ kulavumnaṟ ṟaṇikaik kuṉṟamarn tiṭukuṇak kuṉṟē
translation: O mountain of virtue seated on the hill of good Thanigai where branching trees abound! O unique reward of penance for the Lord who dances in the Hall wearing a dancing snake! When will you grant me, a cruel wretch who stands foremost among fools, the grace to drink the divine nectar from the blossoming lotus of your feet?
commentary: True spiritual longing often begins with a deep sense of unworthiness. The poet feels lost among fools, asking when he will finally be allowed to taste the pure nectar of divine grace. He praises Murugan as the ultimate reward of Lord Siva's own spiritual practice, showing the immense preciousness of this grace.

translit: kaṟṟavar pukaḻniṉ tiruvaṭi malaraik kaṭaiyaṉēṉ muṭimicai amartti uṟṟa-iv vulaka mayakkaṟa meymai uṇarttumnāḷ entanāḷ aṟiyēṉ naṟṟavar uṇarum paracivat teḻunta nalaruṭ cōtiyē navaitīr koṟṟavēl ukanta kumaraṉē taṇikaik kuṉṟamarn tiṭukuṇak kuṉṟē.
translation: O mountain of virtue seated on the hill of Thanigai! O Kumara who delights in the faultless, victorious spear! O good Jothi of grace arising from the supreme Siva known by true ascetics! I do not know when you will plant your lotus feet, praised by the wise, upon the head of this lowly one and reveal the truth to dispel this worldly delusion.
commentary: The touch of the divine is the only cure for worldly confusion. The poet longs for the moment the Lord's feet will rest upon his head to wipe away all delusion and reveal the ultimate truth. He recognizes the divine youth, Murugan, as the very Light of Grace that rises from the supreme reality.

translit: ñālavāḻ veṉumpuṉ malamicain tuḻalum nāyiṉum kaṭaiya-in nāykkuṉ cīlavāḻ vaḷikkum tiruvaṭik kamalat tēṉtaru nāḷumoṉ ṟuṇṭō ālavāy ukanta oruciva taruvil aruḷpaḻut taḷintaceṅ kaṉiyē kōlavā ṉavarkaḷ pukaḻtirut taṇikaik kuṉṟamarn tiṭukuṇak kuṉṟē.
translation: O mountain of virtue seated on the hill of holy Thanigai praised by the radiant celestials! O red fruit of grace fully ripened on the peerless tree of Siva who delights in Alavay! I roam like a dog feeding on the foul filth called worldly life. Is there a day when you will give this dog, lower than a dog, the honey from the lotus of your feet that bestows a life of virtue?
commentary: Worldly existence, driven by selfish desires, feels like feeding on filth to the awakened soul. Feeling lower than a stray dog, the poet begs for the sweet honey of divine grace to transform his life into one of true virtue. He sees the Lord as a perfectly ripened fruit growing on the tree of ultimate reality.

translit: pavameṉuṅ kaṭaṟkuḷ vīḻntuḻaṉ ṟēṅkum pāviyēṉ taṉmukam pārttiṅ kevaiyumnā ṭāmal eṉṉaṭi niḻaṟkīḻ iruntiṭeṉ ṟuraippaten nāḷō civameṉum tarumak kaṭalakat teḻunta teḷḷiya amutamē tēṉē kuvimulai vallik koṭiyoṭun taṇikaik kuṉṟamarn tiṭukuṇak kuṉṟē.
translation: O mountain of virtue seated on the hill of Thanigai alongside the vine-like Valli with swelling breasts! O clear nectar and honey arisen within the ocean of dharma called Sivam! I am a sinner floundering in despair in the ocean of birth. When will you look at my face and say, "Seek nothing else; remain beneath the shade of my feet"?
commentary: The cycle of birth and suffering is like a vast, terrifying ocean. The poet longs for the ultimate reassurance, waiting for the day the divine presence will look directly at him and tell him to stop searching. He wants nothing more than the perfect safety and rest found only at the Lord's feet.

translit: mulaimukaṅ kāṭṭi mayakkiṭum koṭiyār muṉpuḻaṉ ṟēṅkumiv eḷiyēṉ nilaimukaṅ kāṭṭum niṉtirup pāta nīḻalvan taṭaiyumnāḷ eṉṟō malaimukam kuḻaiya vaḷaittiṭum teyva maṇimakiḻ kaṇṇiṉuḷ maṇiyē kolaimukam cellārk karuḷtarun taṇikaik kuṉṟamarn tiṭukuṇak kuṉṟē.
translation: O mountain of virtue seated on the hill of Thanigai, bestowing grace upon those who do not tread the path of murder! O pupil in the eye of the divine jewel who bent the mountain so it yielded! I am a poor wretch who wanders in despair before cruel women who bewitch me by showing their breasts. When is the day I will reach the shade of your holy feet that reveals the eternal state?
commentary: Vallalar says plainly that divine grace is only granted to those who refuse to murder any living being. This is Jeevakarunyam, the absolute compassion for all life that forms the foundation of his teaching. Trapped by physical desires and worldly temptations, he pleads for the shelter of divine grace to bring him to an eternal, unchanging state of peace.

translit: varupayaṉ aṟiyā tuḻaṉṟiṭum ēḻai matiyiṉēṉ uyntiṭum vaṇṇam oruvarum niṉatu tiruvaṭip pukaḻai uṉṉumnāḷ entanāḷ aṟiyēṉ aruvuru ākum civapirāṉ aḷitta arumpeṟal celvamē amutē kuruvuru āki aruḷtarum taṇikaik kuṉṟamarn tiṭukuṇak kuṉṟē.
translation: I wander blindly without knowing the consequences to come. To save my poor mind, I do not know the day I will meditate on the glory of your peerless holy feet. O rare wealth granted by Lord Siva, who is both form and formless! O nectar! O mountain of virtue seated on the hill of Thanigai, who takes the form of the Guru to bestow grace!
commentary: The poet feels lost in his own ignorance, unsure when he will ever focus his mind on the divine. He calls upon the deity of Thanigai hill as a spiritual teacher (Guru) who can guide him out of this blind wandering. He describes this deity as a precious gift from Lord Siva, the supreme God who exists both with and without physical form.

translit: aḻitarum ulaka vāḻviṉai meyyeṉ ṟalaintiṭum pāviyēṉ iyaṟṟum paḻitarum piḻaiyai eṇṇuṟēl iṉṟu pātukāt taḷippatuṉ paramē moḻitarum mukkaṭ ceṅkarum pīṉṟa muttamē muktiyiṉ mutalē koḻitarum aruvi poḻitarun taṇikaik kuṉṟamarn tiṭukuṇak kuṉṟē.
translation: I am a sinner who wanders, believing this perishable worldly life is true. Do not tally the blameworthy faults I commit. It is your supreme duty to protect and save me today. O pearl produced by the celebrated, three-eyed red sugarcane of Lord Siva! O source of liberation! O mountain of virtue seated on the hill of Thanigai, where cascading waterfalls pour down!
commentary: He admits that he has wasted his life chasing temporary worldly things as if they were permanent. Instead of asking for a fair judgment of his mistakes, he appeals directly to God's duty to protect and save him. To show his devotion, he praises the deity as a pearl born from Lord Siva, describing Siva playfully as a sweet, red sugarcane.

translit: niṉnilai aṟiyā vañcakar iṭattil niṉṟuniṉ ṟalaitarum eḷiyēṉ taṉnilai aṟintum aiyakō iṉṉum tayai-ilā tiruntaṉai eṉṉē poṉnilaip potuvil naṭañceyum pavaḷap poruppiṉuḷ malarntiṭum pūvē kolnilai vēlkaik koḷumtirut taṇikaik kuṉṟamarn tiṭukuṇak kuṉṟē.
translation: Even knowing the state of this poor person who constantly wanders among deceivers blind to your true nature, alas, why do you still remain without compassion? O flower blossoming within the coral mountain that dances in the golden hall! O mountain of virtue seated on the hill of holy Thanigai, holding a deadly spear in your hand!
commentary: The poet asks God a direct, painful question: why withhold compassion when you see me suffering? He feels trapped among deceitful people who do not understand the divine truth. He appeals to the deity as a radiant flower blooming from a dancing coral mountain, picturing the vibrant presence of the divine.

translit: pāṭiniṉ tiruccīr pukaḻntiṭāk koṭiya patakarpāl nāḷtoṟum ceṉṟē vāṭiniṉ ṟēṅkum ēḻaiyēṉ neñca vāṭṭamiṅ kaṟintilai eṉṉē āṭinī ṟāṭi aruḷceyum paramaṉ akammakiḻ arumpeṟal maruntē kōṭilaṅ kuyarvāṉ aṇitirut taṇikaik kuṉṟamarn tiṭukuṇak kuṉṟē.
translation: Every day I go to cruel, sinful people who do not sing and praise your holy glory, and I stand there withering and longing. Do you not know the sorrow of my poor heart here? Why? O rare medicine who brings joy to the heart of the Supreme Lord who dances smeared with holy ash and grants grace! O mountain of virtue seated on the hill of holy Thanigai, adorned with soaring peaks touching the sky!
commentary: Seeking help from cruel and unspiritual people only drains the poet's spirit. He asks how God can see this daily sorrow and still do nothing. He calls out to the deity as a rare, healing medicine, one who brings joy even to the Supreme Lord covered in sacred ash.

translit: vaṉpoṭu cerukkum vañcarpāl alaiyā vaṇṇamiṉ ṟaruḷceyāy eṉṉil tuṉpoṭu melivēṉ niṉtiru malarttāḷ tuṇai-aṉṟit tuṇai-oṉṟum kāṇēṉ aṉpoṭum paramaṉ umaikaiyil koṭukka akamakiḻn taṇaikkumār amutē koṉpeṟum ilaivēl karattoṭum taṇikaik kuṉṟamarn tiṭukuṇak kuṉṟē.
translation: If you do not grant your grace today so that I stop wandering among cruel and arrogant deceivers, I will waste away in sorrow. I see no refuge other than your holy lotus feet. O rare nectar whom the Supreme Lord lovingly placed into the hands of Goddess Uma, who embraced you with a joyful heart! O mountain of virtue seated on the hill of Thanigai, wielding a fearsome, leaf-shaped spear!
commentary: The poet warns that without immediate divine grace, he will simply waste away from the pain of worldly life. He declares that he has absolutely no other safe shelter to turn to. He appeals to the deity as a sweet nectar, recalling the loving moment when the Supreme Lord placed the divine child into the joyful arms of the Goddess Uma.

translit: cakamā ṟuṭaiyār aṭaiyā neṟiyār caṭaiyār viṭaiyār taṉi-āṉār ukamā ruṭaiyār umai-ōr puṭaiyār utavum urimait tirumakaṉār mukamā ṟuṭaiyār mukammā ṟuṭaiyār eṉavē eṉatu muṉvantār akamā ruṭaiyēṉ patiyā teṉṟēṉ alaivāy eṉṟār aḵteṉṉē.
translation: The rightful holy son of the Lord, who is unreachable by the six religions, wears matted hair, rides a bull, stands alone, spans the eons, and keeps Uma on one side, came before me. He has six faces, but he came disguised as a stranger. With a melting heart, I asked, "What is your town?" He replied, "Alaivay." What does this mean?
commentary: The young woman meets Murugan, but he appears in disguise as an ordinary man. When she asks where he is from, he gives the name of his famous temple town, Alaivay. However, the word also means "wandering" or "the edge of the waves," leaving her completely bewildered by his playful and elusive answer.

translit: vituvāḻ caṭaiyār viṭaimēl varuvār vitimāl aṟiyā vimalaṉār matuvāḻ kuḻalāḷ puṭaivāḻ uṭaiyār makaṉār kukaṉār mayilūrvār mutuvāḻ vaṭaiyā tavamē alaivēṉ muṉvan tiṭayāṉ aṟiyātē putuvāḻ vuṭaiyār eṉavē matipōy niṉṟēṉ antō pollēṉē.
translation: He is Guhan, the son of the pure Lord who wears the moon in his matted hair, comes on a bull, remains unknown to Brahma and Vishnu, and keeps the goddess with honey-fragrant hair by his side. He rides a peacock. When he came before me, who wanders in vain without attaining the ancient life of grace, I did not recognize him. Thinking he was just a newly rich stranger, I lost my senses and stood there. Alas, I am wicked.
commentary: The young woman realizes she missed her chance to recognize the divine when he stood right in front of her. Deceived by his ordinary appearance, she mistook him for a wealthy stranger and simply froze in confusion. This captures the regret of a soul that fails to see God's presence when it is hidden in everyday life.

translit: kāyō ṭuṭaṉāy kaṉalkai ēntik kāṭē iṭamāk kaṇaṅkoṇṭa pēyō ṭāṭip palitēr tarumōr pittap perumāṉ tirumakaṉār tāyō ṭuṟaḻum taṇikā calaṉār takaicēr mayilār taṉivēlār vēyō ṭuṟaḻtōḷ pāvaiyar muṉeṉ veḷvaḷai koṇṭār viṉavāmē.
translation: He is the holy son of the mad Lord who holds a skull and blazing fire in his hands, dwells in the cremation ground, dances with hordes of ghosts, and wanders for alms. He is the Lord of Thanigai hill who loves like a mother, rides a beautiful peacock, and wields the peerless spear. Right in front of my friends whose shoulders resemble bamboo, he took away my white bangles without even asking.
commentary: In classical Tamil poetry, a young woman suffering from lovesickness grows so thin that her bangles slip from her wrists.
