Here, she accuses the Lord of Thanigai, a sacred hill of Murugan, of stealing her white bangles right in front of her friends. She marvels at how he possesses a tender, motherly love, even though he is the son of Siva, the fierce ascetic who dances in the cremation grounds.

translit: poṉṉār puyaṉār pukaḻum pukaḻār puliyiṉ ataḷār puyamnālār teṉṉār caṭaiyār koṭimēl viṭaiyār civaṉār arumait tirumakaṉār eṉnā yakaṉār eṉṉuyir pōlvār eḻiṉmā mayilār imaiyōrkaḷ tannā yakaṉār taṇikā calaṉār taṉivan tivaṇmāl tantārē.
translation: He is the precious holy son of Lord Siva, who is praised by the golden-shouldered god, wears a tiger skin, has four arms, possesses beautiful matted hair, and bears a bull on his banner. He is my Lord, the one who is like my very life. He rides a beautiful great peacock and is the Lord of the celestials. The Lord of Thanigai hill came here all alone and caused this infatuation in me.
commentary: The divine initiates the soul's longing. The young woman recognizes her beloved as the supreme Lord who rules the celestials and rides a magnificent peacock. Yet she marvels that this great being came to her completely alone, simply to awaken this deep, consuming love in her heart.

translit: kallāl aṭiyār kallaṭi uṇṭār kaṇṭār ulakaṅ kaḷaivētam cellā neṟiyār celluṟum muṭiyār civaṉār arumait tirumakaṉār ellām uṭaiyār taṇikā calaṉār eṉnā yakaṉār iyalvēlār nallār iṭai-eṉ veḷvaḷai koṭupiṉ naṇṇār mayilmēl naṭantārē.
translation: He is the precious holy son of Lord Siva, who sat beneath the banyan tree, who gladly accepted the blow of a stone, who perceives all the worlds, whose path the Vedas cannot reach, and whose crown soars high. He is the Lord of Thanigai hill who possesses everything, my Lord who wields the true spear. Right in the midst of my good friends, he took my white bangles, and without ever coming back, he departed on his peacock.
commentary: The poem concludes with the pain of separation. After capturing her heart and causing her bangles to slip away in lovesickness, the Lord departs on his peacock without looking back. The verse recalls Siva's history of accepting a thrown stone from a devoted follower as an act of pure worship, hinting that Murugan too will eventually answer the raw devotion he has awakened in her.

translit: kārūr caṭaiyār kaṉalār maḻuvār kalavār puramūṉ ṟericeytār ārūr uṭaiyār palitērn tiṭumem araṉār arumait tirumakaṉār pōrūr uṟaivār taṇikā calaṉār putiyār eṉa-eṉ muṉamvantār ērūr ematū riṉilvā eṉṟār eḷiyēṉ ēmān tiruntēṉē.
translation: He is the precious divine son of our Lord Aran, who possesses dark cloud-like hair, holds fire and a battle-axe, burned the three cities of his foes, rules Tiruvarur, and wanders seeking alms. He, the Lord of Thanigachalam who resides in Porur, came before me like a stranger. He said, "Come to our beautiful town." I, a simpleton, just stood there bewildered.
commentary: The sudden appearance of divine grace leaves the soul entirely bewildered. The Lord arrives like a stranger and extends a sudden invitation to his divine realm. Instead of responding with joy, the speaker is paralyzed by shock. This captures how overwhelming a direct encounter with God can be.

translit: kaṇṇār nutalār viṭamār kaḷaṉār karamār maḻuvār kaḷaikaṇṇār peṇṇār puyaṉār ayaṉmāṟ kariyār periyār kailaip perumāṉār taṇṇār caṭaiyār tarumā makaṉār taṇikā calaṉār taṉivēlār eṇṇār eḷiyāḷ ivaḷeṉ ṟeṉaiyāṉ eṉcey kēṉō iṭarkoṇṭē.
translation: He is the great son given by the Lord of Kailash, who has an eye on his forehead, poison in his throat, a battle-axe in his hand, shares his shoulder with a woman, acts as our refuge, possesses cool matted hair, and remains unattainable by Brahma and Vishnu. This Lord of Thanigachalam, wielding the peerless spear, does not consider me at all, nor does he think, "She is a simple, helpless woman." Gripped by sorrow, what shall I do?
commentary: The soul agonizes over feeling ignored by God. The speaker recounts the immense power and compassion of Lord Siva, contrasting that legacy of mercy with his son's apparent indifference. The divine seems entirely out of reach, leaving the lonely soul feeling helpless and abandoned in its spiritual longing.

translit: maḻuvār tarukaip perumāṉ makaṉār mayilvā kaṉaṉār ayilvēlār taḻuvār viṉaiyait taṇiyār aṇiyār taṇikā calaṉār tampātam toḻuvār aḻuvār viḻuvār eḻuvār tutiyā niṟpār avarniṟkap puḻuvār uṭalōm piṭumeṉ muṉarvan taruḷtan taruḷip pōṉārē.
translation: He is the son of the great Lord whose hand wields the battle-axe. He rides a peacock and holds a sharp spear. The beautiful Lord of Thanigachalam dispels the karma of those who embrace him. While devotees stand worshiping his feet, weeping, falling, rising, and singing his praises, he came directly before me, a mere nurturer of this worm-filled body. He bestowed his grace upon me and departed.
commentary: Grace is a free gift that defies human logic. While dedicated saints exhaust themselves with weeping and intense worship, the Lord bypasses them to visit a completely ordinary, flawed person. By calling her physical form a worm-filled body, the speaker emphasizes her total lack of merit. God bestows his grace on the humble, then vanishes again.

translit: niruttam payiṉṟār kaṭalnañ cayiṉṟār niṉaivār taṅkaḷ neṟikkēṟka aruttam pakarvār arumaip putalvar aṟumā mukaṉār ayilvēlār tiruttam peṟuvār pukaḻum taṇikait tirumā malaiyār orumātiṉ varuttam pārār vaḷaiyum tārār vārār avartam maṉameṉṉē.
translation: He is the precious son of the Lord who performs the cosmic dance, consumed the ocean's poison, and imparts truth according to the paths of those who meditate on him. He is the six-faced Lord with the sharp spear. This Lord of the great, sacred Thanigai hill, praised by the perfected ones, does not see this woman's suffering. He does not return my bangles, and he does not come to me. What kind of heart does he have?
commentary: The pain of separation from God takes a severe physical toll. In classical Tamil love poetry, a woman losing her bangles means she has grown so thin from grief that her jewelry simply slips off her wrists. The speaker wonders how the Lord can be so coldhearted as to ignore this agonizing decline.

translit: piramaṉ talaiyil palikoṇ ṭerutil peyarum piccaip perumāṉār tiramaṉ ṟiṉilē naṭaṉam purivār civaṉār makaṉār tiṟalvēlār taramaṉ ṟalaivāṉ poḻilcār eḻilcēr taṇikā calaṉār tamiyēṉmuṉ varamaṉ ṟavummāl koḷaniṉ ṟaṉaṉāl maṭavār alarāl maṉanontē.
translation: The great mendicant Lord receives alms in Brahma's skull and rides a bull. He is Lord Siva, who dances in the enduring cosmic hall. His son wields the mighty spear. He is the Lord of Thanigachalam, full of beauty and surrounded by tall, heavenly groves. He stood before this lonely woman and made me fall madly in love with him. Now, my heart aches from the gossip of the local women.
commentary: Intense spiritual devotion often brings worldly mockery. The Lord captures the soul's heart completely, then leaves her to face the judgment of society alone. The gossip of the local women represents the everyday world, which simply cannot understand the consuming, maddening love a soul feels for God.

translit: vēlkoḷum kamalak kaiyaṉai eṉaiyāḷ meyyaṉai aiyaṉai ulaka mālkoḷum maṉattar aṟivarum maruntai māṇikka maṇiyiṉai mayilmēl kālkoḷum kukaṉai entaiyai eṉatu karuttaṉai ayaṉari aṟiyāc cālkoḷum kaṭavuḷ taṉi-aruḷ makaṉait taṇikaiyil kaṇṭiṟaiñ cuvaṉē.
translation: The One whose lotus hands hold the spear, the true Lord who rules me, the medicine difficult to know for minds deluded by the world, the ruby gem, Guhan who places his feet on the peacock, my father, the Lord of my thoughts, the peerless son of grace of the supreme God whom Brahma and Vishnu cannot comprehend: I will behold and worship Him in Thanigai.
commentary: The poet vows to see and worship the divine in Thanigai, the sacred hill town of Thanigai. He calls God by the name Guhan (the one who dwells deep within the cave of the heart), describing him as the true medicine for the confusion of worldly life.

translit: kaṇṇaṉai ayaṉai viṇṇavar kōṉaik kākkavait tiṭṭavēṟ karaṉaip paṇṇaṉai aṭiyar pāṭaluk karuḷum patiyiṉai matikoḷtaṇ aruḷām vaṇṇaṉai ellā vaṇṇamum uṭaiya varataṉīṉ ṟeṭuttaruḷ makaṉait taṇṇaṉai eṉatu kaṇṇaṉai yavaṉait taṇikaiyil kaṇṭiṟaiñ cuvaṉē.
translation: The spear-handed One who appointed Vishnu, Brahma, and the king of the celestials to their protective duties, the Lord of music who bestows grace upon the songs of devotees, the One whose form is cooling grace like the moon, the gracious son born to the supreme bestower who holds all forms, the refreshing One who is my very eyes: I will behold and worship Him in Thanigai.
commentary: The divine is presented as the supreme authority who assigns the great deities of creation and protection their tasks. At the same time, this immense power is intimately personal, responding to the simple songs of devotees with cooling and refreshing grace.

translit: eṉṉuṭai uyirai yāṉpeṟum pēṟṟai eṉṉuṭaip poruḷiṉai eḷiyēṉ maṉṉuṭaik kuruviṉ vaṭiviṉai eṉkaṇ maṇiyiṉai aṇiyiṉai varattai miṉṉuṭaip pavaḷa veṟpiṉil utitta miḷiraruḷ taruviṉai aṭiyēṉ taṉṉuṭait tēvait tantaiyait tāyait taṇikaiyil kaṇṭiṟaiñ cuvaṉē.
translation: My life, the great blessing I received, my treasure, the eternal Guru's form for this poor soul, the pupil of my eye, my adornment, my boon, the radiant tree of grace that sprouted on the gleaming coral mountain, this servant's God, my father and my mother: I will behold and worship Him in Thanigai.
commentary: God is described as the poet's entire world, filling every role from mother and father to the very pupil of his eye. The verse captures the feeling of total reliance on the divine, picturing grace as a radiant tree offering shelter and eternal nourishment.

translit: paraṅkiri amaruṅ kaṟpakat taruvaip parāparañ cuṭariṉai eḷiyēṟ kiraṅkivan taruḷum ērakat tiṟaiyai eṇṇutaṟ kariyapēr iṉpai uraṅkiḷar vāṉōrk korutaṉi mutalai oppilā tōṅkiya oṉṟait taraṅkiḷar aruṇa kirikkaruḷ pavaṉait taṇikaiyil kaṇṭiṟaiñ cuvaṉē.
translation: The wish-fulfilling tree seated on Parangiri, the supreme light, the Lord of Erakam who comes down in pity to bestow grace on this poor soul, the great bliss difficult to fathom, the single unique source for the mighty celestials, the peerless exalted One, the One who graced Arunagiri of surging fame: I will behold and worship Him in Thanigai.
commentary: The poet connects his own spiritual longing to a long lineage of devotion by recalling how grace was given to Arunagiri, a famous historical saint. He names other sacred temples like Parangiri and Erakam, showing that the same singular divine light shines through all these holy places to bless those who seek it.

translit: arumpeṟal maṇiyai amutiṉai aṉpar aṉpiṉuk keḷivarum aracai virumpumā tavattōr uḷḷakat toḷirum viḷakkiṉai aḷakkarum poruḷaik karumpiṉai eṉṉuṭ kaṉintiṭum kaṉiyai muṉintiṭā taruḷaruṭ kaṭalait tarumpara civattuḷ kiḷarntoḷir oḷiyait taṇikaiyil kaṇṭiṟaiñ cuvaṉē.
translation: The rare and precious gem, the ambrosia, the king who comes easily to the love of devotees, the lamp shining within the hearts of great ascetics who long for Him, the immeasurable reality, the sugarcane, the fruit ripening within me, the ocean of grace that blesses without anger, the light that surges and shines within the supreme bestowing Siva: I will behold and worship Him in Thanigai.
commentary: Love is the simplest path to the divine. The supreme reality is immeasurable and beyond ordinary reach, yet it comes effortlessly to those who approach with devotion, ripening inside them like sweet fruit.

translit: māraṉai erittōṉ makiḻtiru makaṉai vākaiyam puyattaṉai vaṭivēl tīraṉai aḻiyāc cīraṉai ñāṉac celvaṉai valviṉai neñcac cūraṉait taṭinta vīraṉai aḻiyāc cukattaṉait tēṉtuḷi kaṭappan tāraṉaik kukaṉeṉ pēruṭai yavaṉait taṇikaiyil kaṇṭiṟaiñ cuvaṉē.
translation: I will behold and worship Him in Thanigai: the joyful divine son of the one who burned the god of love; the one with victorious shoulders; the brave one holding the sharp spear; the one of imperishable glory; the wealth of wisdom; the hero who struck down Surapadman of the cruel heart and fierce karma; the one of imperishable bliss; the one wearing a Kadamba garland dripping with honey; the one who bears the name Guhan.
commentary: Murugan is celebrated here as both a fierce protector and a source of sweet, unending joy. He carries a sharp spear to destroy cruelty, represented by the demon Surapadman, yet he also wears a fragrant flower garland dripping with honey. This contrast shows that divine power acts as a fierce force that shatters inner darkness and as a gentle presence offering ultimate bliss.

translit: vētaṉaic ciṟaikkuḷ vētaṉai paṭaccey vimalaṉai amalaṉai aṟpar pōtaṉaik kaṭaṅkāp pōtaṉai aintām pūtaṉai mātavar pukaḻum pātaṉai umaiyāḷ pālaṉai eṅkaḷ paramaṉai makiḻvikkum paraṉait tātaṉai uyirkkuḷ uyiraṉai yavaṉait taṇikaiyil kaṇṭiṟaiñ cuvaṉē.
translation: I will behold and worship Him in Thanigai: the one who imprisoned the creator god and made him suffer; the pure one; the flawless one; the teacher who transcends the teachings of the petty; the fifth element of space; the one whose feet are praised by great ascetics; the son of Uma; the supreme being who delights our Lord; the generous giver; the life within all life.
commentary: The opening lines refer to a classic story where Murugan imprisoned the creator god for failing to understand the most sacred syllable. This reminds the reader that true spiritual wisdom transcends ordinary authority and petty teachings. Ultimately, he is not just a deity in a story but the actual life within all life, filling the vastness of space.

translit: kuḻakaṉai aḻiyāk kumaraṉai aṭṭa kuṇattaṉaik kuṟittiṭal aṟitām aḻakaṉaic centil appaṉai malaitō ṟāṭalvāḻ aṇṇalait tēvar kaḻakaṉait taṇṭaik kālaṉaip piṇikkōr kālaṉai vēlaṉai maṉatil caḻakilārk karuḷum cāminā taṉaitteṉ taṇikaiyil kaṇṭiṟaiñ cuvaṉē.
translation: I will behold and worship Him in southern Thanigai: the beautiful youth; the immortal Kumaran; the one with eight attributes; the beautiful one who is hard to comprehend; the father of Tiruchendur; the Lord who delights in dwelling on every hill; the leader of the celestial assembly; the one whose feet wear anklets; the god of death to all diseases; the wielder of the spear; Lord Swaminatha who bestows grace upon those with flawless minds.
commentary: This passage praises the divine youth as a universal healer. By calling him the god of death to all diseases, the poem emphasizes that his grace cures human suffering at its root. He is a master who makes his home on every hill and grants his protection to those who approach him with a clear, flawless mind.

translit: muttaṉai muttik korutaṉi vittai mutalvaṉai murukaṉai mukkaṇ pittaṉai attaṉ eṉakkoḷum celvap piḷḷaiyaip periyavar uḷañcēr cuttaṉaip patti valaippaṭum avaṉait turiyaṉait turiyamum kaṭanta cattaṉai nitta niṉmalac cuṭarait taṇikaiyil kaṇṭiṟaiñ cuvaṉē.
translation: I will behold and worship Him in Thanigai: the liberated one; the unique seed for liberation; the primal Lord; Murugan; the blessed child whom the three-eyed madman accepts as his father; the pure one who dwells in the hearts of great beings; the one who is caught in the net of devotion; the Lord of the Turiya state; the true being who transcends Turiya; the eternal and flawless flame.
commentary: Even though the divine reality is infinite, pure love can capture it. Murugan is described as the supreme teacher who instructs even his own father, Siva, playfully called the three-eyed madman. He is the lord of Turiya (the fourth state of spiritual consciousness beyond waking, dreaming, and deep sleep) and exists even beyond it. Yet, this boundless, eternal flame willingly lets himself be caught in the simple net of his devotees' love.

translit: vaḷayil karaṅkoḷ vaḷḷalai iravil vaḷḷinā yakitaṉaik kavarnta kaḷḷaṉai aṭiyar uḷḷakat tavaṉaik karuttaṉaik karutumā ṉanta veḷḷamniṉ ṟāṭa aruḷkuru paraṉai viruppuṟu poruppaṉai viṉaiyait taḷḷavan taruḷcey tiṭuntayā nitiyait taṇikaiyil kaṇṭiṟaiñ cuvaṉē.
translation: I will behold and worship Him in Thanigai: the generous Lord holding the sharp spear in his hand; the thief who abducted lady Valli in the night; the one who dwells in the inner hearts of devotees; the true meaning; the supreme Guru whose grace lets devotees bathe in a flood of bliss as they meditate upon him; the beloved Lord of the hill; the treasure of compassion who comes to bestow grace and cast away karma.
commentary: The divine is pictured here as a thief of hearts, recalling the beloved myth where Murugan sneaks away in the night with the hunter girl Valli. Just as he stole her away, he captures the inner minds of his devotees. He acts as a supreme teacher and a treasure of compassion, washing away the burden of past actions (karma) in a sudden flood of joy.

tamil: இன்னும் எத்தனை நாள்செலும் ஏழையேன் இடர்க்கடல் விடுத்தேற
மின்னும் வேற்படை மிளிர்தரும் கைத்தல வித்தகப் பெருமானே
துன்னும் நற்றணி காசலத் தமர்ந்தருள் தோன்றலே மயில்ஏறி
மன்னும் உத்தம வள்ளலே நின்திரு மனக்கருத் தறியேனே.
translit: iṉṉum ettaṉai nāḷcelum ēḻaiyēṉ iṭarkkaṭal viṭuttēṟa miṉṉum vēṟpaṭai miḷirtarum kaittala vittakap perumāṉē tuṉṉum naṟṟaṇi kācalat tamarntaruḷ tōṉṟalē mayilēṟi maṉṉum uttama vaḷḷalē niṉtiru maṉakkarut taṟiyēṉē.
translation: O wise Lord whose hand holds the gleaming spear! O Prince who gracefully abides on the goodly hill of Thanigai! O supreme, eternal and generous Lord riding the peacock, I do not know the intention of your divine mind. How many more days will it take for this poor wretch to leave this ocean of sorrow and climb ashore?
commentary: The poet cries out to Murugan, the spear-wielding deity of the Thanigai hill, asking when his worldly struggles will finally end. He compares worldly life to an ocean of sorrow. Unable to know the divine will, he waits impatiently to be pulled safely ashore.

tamil: ஈறி லாதநின் அருள்பெற எனக்கினும் எத்தனை நாட்செல்லும்
மாறி லாதவர் மனத்தொளிர் சோதியே மயில்மிசை வரும்வாழ்வே
தூறி லாவளச் சோலைசூழ் தணிகைவாழ் சுத்தசின் மயத்தேவே
ஊறி லாப்பெரு நிலையஆ னந்தமே ஒப்பிலான் அருட்பேறே.
translit: īṟi lātaniṉ aruḷpeṟa eṉakkiṉum ettaṉai nāṭcellum māṟi lātavar maṉattoḷir cōtiyē mayilmicai varumvāḻvē tūṟi lāvaḷac cōlaicūḻ taṇikaivāḻ cuttaciṉ mayattēvē ūṟi lāpperu nilaiya-ā ṉantamē oppilāṉ aruṭpēṟē.
translation: O Jothi shining in the minds of the steadfast! O Life coming upon a peacock! O God of pure consciousness abiding in Thanigai, which is surrounded by flawless, fertile groves! O Bliss of the great and faultless state! O gift of grace from the Peerless One! How many more days will it take for me to receive your endless grace?
commentary: God is described here as Jothi, the divine light of pure consciousness that burns brightly in the minds of the devoted. The poet longs for this unending grace and wonders how many more days he must wait to receive it.

tamil: கூழை மாமுகில் அனையவர் முலைத்தலைக் குளித்துழன் றலைகின்ற
ஏழை நெஞ்சினேன் எத்தனை நாள்செல்லும் இடர்க்கடல் விடுத்தேற
மாழை மேனியன் வழுத்துமா ணிக்கமே வாழ்த்துவா ரவர்பொல்லா
ஊழை நீக்கிநல் அருள்தருந் தெய்வமே உத்தமச் சுகவாழ்வே.
translit: kūḻai māmukil aṉaiyavar mulaittalaik kuḷittuḻaṉ ṟalaikiṉṟa ēḻai neñciṉēṉ ettaṉai nāḷcellum iṭarkkaṭal viṭuttēṟa māḻai mēṉiyaṉ vaḻuttumā ṇikkamē vāḻttuvā ravarpollā ūḻai nīkkinal aruḷtarun teyvamē uttamac cukavāḻvē.
translation: O Ruby praised by the golden-hued Brahma! O God who removes the evil karma of those who praise you and grants them good grace! O supreme life of bliss! Wandering and wallowing in the breasts of women whose hair is like dark clouds, I am a man with an impoverished mind. How many more days will it take for me to escape and cross over this ocean of sorrow?
commentary: The poet confesses that sensual desires and worldly distractions have impoverished his mind. He praises the divine as the only force capable of removing the heavy burden of past karma (the accumulated results of past actions). He begs for a swift escape from this cycle of longing and sorrow.

tamil: ஐய இன்னும்நான் எத்தனை நாள்செலும் அல்லல்விட் டருள்மேவத்
துய்ய நன்னெறி மன்னிய அடியர்தம் துயர்தவிர்த் தருள்வோனே
வெய்ய நெஞ்சினர் எட்டொணா மெய்யனே வேல்கொளும் கரத்தோனே
செய்ய மேனிஎஞ் சிவபிரான் பெற்றநற் செல்வனே திறலோனே.
translit: aiya iṉṉumnāṉ ettaṉai nāḷcelum allalviṭ ṭaruḷmēvat tuyya naṉṉeṟi maṉṉiya aṭiyartam tuyartavirt taruḷvōṉē veyya neñciṉar eṭṭoṇā meyyaṉē vēlkoḷum karattōṉē ceyya mēṉi-eñ civapirāṉ peṟṟanaṟ celvaṉē tiṟalōṉē.
translation: O You who dispel the sorrow of devotees steadfast in the pure and good path, granting them your grace! O Truth unreachable by the cruel-hearted! O Lord holding a spear in hand! O good wealth begotten by our red-hued Lord Siva! O mighty one! Lord, how many more days will it take for me to leave this sorrow behind and reach your grace?
commentary: The divine truth remains entirely hidden from those who carry cruelty in their hearts. The poet asks to be lifted from his sorrow, trusting that God always protects those who walk a pure and compassionate path.

tamil: பாவி யேன் இன்னும் எத்தனை நாள்செலும் பருவரல் விடுத்துய்யக்
கூவி யேஅன்பர்க் கருள்தரும் வள்ளலே குணப்பெருங் குன்றேஎன்
ஆவி யேஎனை ஆள்குரு வடிவமே ஆனந்தப் பெருவாழ்வே
வாவி ஏர்தரும் தணிகைமா மலைமிசை மன்னிய அருள்தேனே.
translit: pāvi yēṉ iṉṉum ettaṉai nāḷcelum paruvaral viṭuttuyyak kūvi yē-aṉpark karuḷtarum vaḷḷalē kuṇapperuṅ kuṉṟē-eṉ āvi yē-eṉai āḷkuru vaṭivamē āṉantap peruvāḻvē vāvi ērtarum taṇikaimā malaimicai maṉṉiya aruḷtēṉē.
translation: O generous Lord who calls out to devotees and grants them grace! O great mountain of virtue! O my very life! O form of the Guru who rules me! O great life of bliss! O honey of grace abiding on the great Thanigai hill adorned with beautiful ponds! How many more days will it take for this sinner to leave this suffering and be saved?
commentary: God is not a distant figure, but an intimately close Guru (spiritual teacher) who actively calls out to devotees to grant them grace. Surrendering completely, the poet asks how much longer he must endure his suffering before being saved by this generous love.

tamil: எளிய னேன்இன்னும் எத்தனை நாள்செலும் இடர்க்கடல் விடுத்தேற
ஒளிஅ னேகமாய்த் திரண்டிடும் சிற்பர உருவமே உருவில்லா
வெளிய தாகிய வத்துவே முத்தியின் மெய்ப்பயன் தருவித்தே
அளிய தாகிய நெஞ்சினர்க் கருள்தரும் ஆறுமா முகத்தேவே.
translit: eḷiya ṉēṉiṉṉum ettaṉai nāḷcelum iṭarkkaṭal viṭuttēṟa oḷi-a ṉēkamāyt tiraṇṭiṭum ciṟpara uruvamē uruvillā veḷiya tākiya vattuvē muttiyiṉ meyppayaṉ taruvittē aḷiya tākiya neñciṉark karuḷtarum āṟumā mukattēvē.
translation: How many more days will it take for poor me to escape and cross this ocean of hardship? Oh God with six great faces, you bestow grace upon those with tender hearts and grant them the true fruit of liberation. You are the form of Supreme Intelligence gathered as countless lights. You are the Reality that is the formless space.
commentary: The pain of worldly life is an ocean that can only be crossed with divine help. Vallalar describes this divine presence in three ways: as a personal deity with six faces (the god Murugan), as a supreme intelligence made of countless lights, and as an ultimate reality that is formless space. True liberation, he adds, is a gift granted to those who have tender, compassionate hearts.

tamil: தொண்ட னேன்இன்னும் எத்தனை நாள்செலும் துயர்க்கடல் விடுத்தேற
அண்ட னேஅண்டர்க் கருள்தரும் பரசிவன் அருளிய பெருவாழ்வே
கண்ட னேகர்வந் தனைசெய அசுரனைக் களைந்தருள் களைகண்ணே
விண்ட னேர்புகுஞ் சிகரிசூழ் தணிகையில் விளங்கிய வேலோனே.
translit: toṇṭa ṉēṉiṉṉum ettaṉai nāḷcelum tuyarkkaṭal viṭuttēṟa aṇṭa ṉē-aṇṭark karuḷtarum paracivaṉ aruḷiya peruvāḻvē kaṇṭa ṉēkarvan taṉaiceya acuraṉaik kaḷaintaruḷ kaḷaikaṇṇē viṇṭa ṉērpukuñ cikaricūḻ taṇikaiyil viḷaṅkiya vēlōṉē.
translation: How many more days will it take for me, your servant, to escape and cross this ocean of sorrow? Oh Lord of the universe, you are the great life bestowed by Supreme Siva who grants grace to the celestials. You are the refuge who destroyed the demon and bestowed grace as countless witnesses offered worship. Oh Lord of the spear, you shine in Thanigai surrounded by peaks that reach the sky.
commentary: God is the ultimate refuge who actively destroys the evils that cause human sorrow. Vallalar calls upon the Lord of the spear, a traditional warrior form of Murugan residing on the sacred hill of Thanigai. By praising this deity as a destroyer of demons, he paints a picture of divine grace cutting away the ignorance that keeps the soul trapped in pain.

tamil: வீண னேன்இன்னும் எத்தனை நாள்செல்லும் வெந்துயர்க் கடல்நீந்தக்
காண வானவர்க் கரும்பெருந் தலைவனே கருணையங் கண்ணானே
தூண நேர்புயச் சுந்தர வடிவனே துளக்கிலார்க் கருள்ஈயும்
ஏண னேஎனை ஏன்றுகொள் தேசிக இறைவனே இயலோனே.
translit: vīṇa ṉēṉiṉṉum ettaṉai nāḷcellum ventuyark kaṭalnīntak kāṇa vāṉavark karumperun talaivaṉē karuṇaiyaṅ kaṇṇāṉē tūṇa nērpuyac cuntara vaṭivaṉē tuḷakkilārk karuḷīyum ēṇa ṉē-eṉai ēṉṟukoḷ tēcika iṟaivaṉē iyalōṉē.
translation: How many more days will it take for worthless me to swim across this ocean of cruel sorrow? Oh rare and great Lord to the celestials who long to see you, you possess compassionate eyes. You have a beautiful form with shoulders like pillars. Oh capable Lord, you grant grace to the unwavering. Oh God, my Guru who accepts me, you are the perfect one.
commentary: The divine acts as a personal Guru, a spiritual teacher who accepts and guides the struggling soul. Vallalar contrasts his own feelings of worthlessness with the perfect, beautiful, and compassionate nature of God. Grace, he notes, is given to those whose devotion remains steady and steady.

tamil: கடைய னேன்இன்னும் எத்தனை நாள்செலும் கடுந்துயர்க் கடல்நீந்த
விடையின் ஏறிய சிவபிரான் பெற்றருள் வியன்திரு மகப்பேறே
உடைய நாயகிக் கொருபெருஞ் செல்வமே உலகெலாம் அளிப்போனே
அடைய நின்றவர்க் கருள்செயுந் தணிகைவாழ் ஆனந்தத் தெளிதேனே.
translit: kaṭaiya ṉēṉiṉṉum ettaṉai nāḷcelum kaṭuntuyark kaṭalnīnta viṭaiyiṉ ēṟiya civapirāṉ peṟṟaruḷ viyaṉtiru makappēṟē uṭaiya nāyakik koruperuñ celvamē ulakelām aḷippōṉē aṭaiya niṉṟavark karuḷceyun taṇikaivāḻ āṉantat teḷitēṉē.
translation: How many more days will it take for the lowest one like me to swim across this ocean of severe sorrow? Oh wondrous divine son begotten by Lord Siva who rides the bull, you are the great wealth of the supreme Goddess. Oh protector of all the worlds, you grant grace to those who seek refuge. You are the clear honey of bliss dwelling in Thanigai.
commentary: God is the sweet, blissful protector of all who seek shelter. The poet draws on traditional imagery of Lord Siva and the supreme Goddess to describe a divine family that governs the universe. To those who take refuge in this protection, God is experienced directly as the pure honey of absolute bliss.

tamil: பேய னேன்இன்னும் எத்தனை நாள்செலும் பெருந்துயர்க் கடல்நீந்த
மாய னேமுதல் வானவர் தமக்கருள் மணிமிடற் றிறையோர்க்குச்
சேய னேஅகந் தெளிந்தவர்க் கினியனே செல்வனே எனைக்காக்குந்
தாய னேஎன்றன் சற்குரு நாதனே தணிகைமா மலையானே.
translit: pēya ṉēṉiṉṉum ettaṉai nāḷcelum peruntuyark kaṭalnīnta māya ṉēmutal vāṉavar tamakkaruḷ maṇimiṭaṟ ṟiṟaiyōrkkuc cēya ṉē-akan teḷintavark kiṉiyaṉē celvaṉē eṉaikkākkun tāya ṉē-eṉṟaṉ caṟkuru nātaṉē taṇikaimā malaiyāṉē.
translation: How many more days will it take for this ignorant one to swim across the ocean of great sorrow? Oh son of the blue-throated Lord who grants grace to Vishnu and the primal celestials, you are sweet to those with clear hearts. Oh precious one, you are the mother who protects me. You are my true Guru and the Lord of the great mountain of Thanigai.
commentary: The ultimate reality can be approached in the most intimate and personal terms: as a protective mother and a guiding teacher. Vallalar mentions the blue-throated Lord, referring to the traditional story of Siva drinking poison to save the world, to highlight this deeply protective nature. He says that this vast, universal God feels incredibly sweet to anyone whose heart is pure and clear.

sections.title: The Disgrace of a Birth That Does not Praise

translit: kallai otta-eṉ neñciṉai urukkēṉ kaṭavuḷ niṉaṭi kaṇṭiṭa viḻaiyēṉ allai ottakō taiyarkkuḷaṅ kuḻaivēṉ aṉpi lāroṭum amarntavam uḻalvēṉ tillai appaṉeṉ ṟulakeṭut tēttum civapi rāṉtaruñ celvaniṉ taṇikai ellai uṟṟuṉai ēttiniṉ ṟāṭēṉ eṉcey vāṉpiṟan tēṉeḷi yēṉē.
translation: I do not melt my stone-like heart. O God, I do not desire to see your feet. I soften my heart for women with hair dark as the night. I linger and wander in vain among those devoid of love. O wealth given by Lord Siva whom the world praises as the Father of Tillai, I do not reach the borders of your Thanigai to praise you and dance. Why was I, this poor wretch, born?
commentary: The verse contrasts a heart that remains stubborn and cold toward God with one that easily melts for worldly lust and trivial attachments. The speaker addresses Lord Murugan at Thanigai, calling him the treasure of Lord Siva. The painful closing question asks what point there is in being born at all if a human life is not used to seek grace.

translit: maiyal neñciṉēṉ maticiṟi tillēṉ māta rārmulai malai-ivarn turuḷvēṉ aiya niṉtiru aṭittuṇai maṟavā aṉpar taṅkaḷai aṭuttuḷam makiḻēṉ uyya niṉtirut taṇikaiyai aṭaiyēṉ uṭaiya nāyakaṉ utaviya pēṟē eyya ivveṟum vāḻkkaiyil uḻalvēṉ eṉcey vāṉpiṟan tēṉeḷi yēṉē.
translation: I have a deluded heart. I have no intelligence. I climb and roll upon the mountain-like breasts of women. O Lord, I do not draw near to the devotees who never forget your holy pair of feet and rejoice in my heart. I do not reach your holy Thanigai to be saved. O great boon granted by the Supreme Master, I wander toiling in this empty life. Why was I, this poor wretch, born?
commentary: The speaker mourns the loss of vital energy and time spent chasing sexual desire rather than seeking the company of true devotees. Without spiritual community and the pursuit of grace, human life becomes nothing more than empty toil. A life lived only for the physical body entirely misses its true purpose.

translit: pulaiya mātartam pōkattai viḻaintēṉ puṉmai yāvaikkum pukaliṭam āṉēṉ nilaiya māmtirut taṇikaiyai aṭaiyēṉ niruttaṉ īṉṟaruḷ niṉmalak koḻuntē vilaiyi lātaniṉ tiruvaruḷ viḻaiyēṉ vīṇar taṅkaḷai virumpiniṉ ṟalaintēṉ ilai-e ṉātaṇu vaḷavum oṉṟīyēṉ eṉcey vāṉpiṟan tēṉeḷi yēṉē.
translation: I desired the carnal pleasure of base women. I became a refuge for all kinds of evils. I do not reach the enduring holy Thanigai. O pure tender shoot gracefully begotten by the Divine Dancer, I do not desire your priceless holy grace. I desired worthless people and wandered after them. I do not give even an atom's worth to those who say they have nothing. Why was I, this poor wretch, born?
commentary: A life driven purely by physical lust is shown here as a breeding ground for broader moral failure, turning the mind into a home for all kinds of evils. Crucially, the speaker points out a complete failure to practice jīvakāruṇyam (compassion for all living beings): he regrets never giving even a tiny amount of help to those who are suffering and destitute. Vallalar teaches that failing to show compassion makes a human birth entirely worthless.

translit: maruṭṭu maṅkaiyar puḻukkuḻi āḻntu varunti nāḷtoṟum maṉamiḷaik kiṉṟēṉ teruṭṭum niṉtirut taṇikaiyai aṭaiyēṉ civapi rāṉpeṟṟa celvamē niṉatu aruṭṭi ṟattiṉai niṉaintunek kuruki aḻutu kaṇkaḷnīr ārntiṭa nillēṉ iruṭṭu vāḻkkaiyil iṭaṟivīḻ kiṉṟēṉ eṉcey vāṉpiṟan tēṉeḷi yēṉē.
translation: Plunging into the worm-filled pits of deluding women, I suffer and my mind grows weary every day. I do not reach your enlightening holy Thanigai. O wealth begotten by Lord Siva, I do not stand weeping with eyes brimming with tears, melting within as I think of the nature of your grace. I stumble and fall in this dark life. Why was I, this poor wretch, born?
commentary: The physical body is described bluntly as a decaying, temporary vessel, stripping away the romantic illusions of lust. The daily exhaustion of chasing physical pleasure stands in stark contrast to the spiritual relief of weeping for divine grace. True spiritual longing is an experience that physically melts the heart and brings genuine light to an otherwise dark life.

translit: nacci lēpaḻa kiyakaruṅ kaṇṇār nalattai vēṭṭunaṟ pulattiṉai iḻantēṉ picci lēmika mayaṅkiya maṉattēṉ pētai yēṉkoṭum pēyaṉēṉ poyyēṉ cacci lēcivaṉ aḷittiṭum maṇiyē taṅkamē uṉṟaṉ taṇikaiyai viḻaiyēṉ ecci lēviḻain tiṭaruṟu kiṉṟēṉ eṉcey vāṉpiṟan tēṉeḷi yēṉē.
translation: Desiring the pleasure of dark-eyed women accustomed to poison, I lost all good sense. I possess a mind deeply deluded by madness. I am an ignoramus, a cruel demon, and a liar. O gem bestowed by Siva in truth, O gold, I do not desire your Thanigai. Desiring impure things, I suffer affliction. Why was I, this poor wretch, born?
commentary: The pursuit of pure physical gratification is described here as a madness that destroys good sense and turns a person into a cruel liar. The voice is that of someone looking back in harsh self-judgment. Trading the pure, enduring gold of divine grace for temporary, impure pleasures only guarantees a life of suffering.

translit: miṉṉai aṉṉanuṇ iṭai-iḷa maṭavār veyya nīrkkuḻi viḻuntiḷait tuḻaṉṟēṉ puṉṉai yañcaṭai muṉṉavaṉ aḷitta poṉṉai aṉṉaniṉ pūṅkaḻal pukaḻēṉ aṉṉai eṉṉanal aruḷtarum taṇikai aṭaintu niṉṟuneñ cakammakiḻn tāṭēṉ eṉṉai eṉṉai-iṅ keṉceyal antō eṉcey vāṉpiṟan tēṉeḷi yēṉē.
translation: I fell into the hot pit of young women with waists thin as lightning and wandered in exhaustion. I do not praise your golden flower-like feet given by the ancient Lord whose matted hair bears punnai flowers. I do not reach Thanigai, which grants good grace like a mother, to stand there and dance with a joyful heart. Alas, what am I, and what are my actions here? Why was I, this poor wretch, born?
commentary: Sexual desire exhausts the spirit and distracts from divine grace. The destructive heat of physical lust stands in stark contrast to the motherly, comforting grace found at the holy hill of Thanigai. Vallalar asks what purpose his life serves if he fails to seek this divine comfort.

translit: paṭṭi māṭeṉat tiritarum maṭavār pāḻṅku ḻikkuḷvīḻn tāḻntiḷaik kiṉṟēṉ taṭṭi lārpukaḻ taṇikaiyai aṭaiyēṉ campu eṉṉumōr taru-oḷir kaṉiyē oṭṭi lēṉniṉai uḷattiṭai niṉaiyēṉ utavu ṟātunac cuṟumaram āṉēṉ eṭṭi eṉmuṉam iṉippuṟum antō eṉcey vāṉpiṟan tēṉeḷi yēṉē.
translation: I fall deep into the ruinous pit of women who wander like stray cattle and grow weary. I do not reach Thanigai praised by faultless people. O shining fruit of the tree called Sambu! I do not unite with you, nor do I think of you in my heart. I became a poisonous tree offering no help to anyone. Alas, even the bitter strychnine tree is sweeter than me. Why was I, this poor wretch, born?
commentary: A life lived without devotion or usefulness to others is like a poisonous tree. Even a notoriously bitter strychnine tree has more value than a human heart completely closed to the divine. Reaching out to Murugan as the shining fruit of Sambu (a name for Lord Siva), Vallalar mourns the spiritual sweetness he has missed by wasting his days.

translit: ōṅki nīṇṭavāḷ uṟaḻkaruṅ kaṇṇār uvarppuk kēṇiyil uḻaittakam iḷaittēṉ vīṅki nīṇṭatōr ōti-eṉa niṉṟēṉ viḻaluk kē-iṟait talaintaṉaṉ vīṇē tāṅki ṉēṉuṭaṟ cumaitaṉaic civaṉār taṉaya niṉtirut taṇikaiyai aṭaiyēṉ ēṅki ṉēṉcuḻaṟ paṭuturum peṉavē eṉcey vāṉpiṟan tēṉeḷi yēṉē.
translation: Laboring in the salty well of women with dark eyes like long raised swords, I grew exhausted in my heart. I stood like an overgrown long reed and wandered in vain watering barren weeds. I carried the burden of this body. O son of Lord Siva! I do not reach your holy Thanigai. I languished like a piece of straw caught in a whirlpool. Why was I, this poor wretch, born?
commentary: Pouring life's energy into hollow worldly desires is like watering barren weeds. Without spiritual direction, a person becomes like a piece of straw trapped in a whirlpool, exhausted by the sheer burden of carrying a physical body through life.

translit: paṇa ḷāviya moḻiyiṉāl mayakkum paṭiṟṟu maṅkaiyar pālviḻai vuṟṟēṉ taṇa ḷāviya cōlaicūḻ taṇikait taṭatta ḷāviya tarumanal tēvē peṇa ḷāviya puṭaiyuṭaip perumāṉ peṟṟa celvamē aṟṟavark kamutē eṇa ḷāviya vañcaka neñcō ṭeṉcey vāṉpiṟan tēṉeḷi yēṉē.
translation: I desired deceitful women who bewilder others with words mixed with melodies. O good Lord of virtue residing by the vast ponds of Thanigai surrounded by cool groves! O wealth obtained by the great Lord who shares his form with the Goddess! O nectar to those who have severed attachments! With a deceitful heart full of calculating thoughts, why was I, this poor wretch, born?
commentary: Worldly entanglements breed a deceitful, calculating mind, shutting out the pure grace of God. Divine presence is sweet nectar to those who finally cut their earthly attachments. Vallalar mourns his own mind's inability to break free from its desires to taste that nectar.

translit: kāṉa ṟā-aḷa kattiyar aḷakkar kāmat tāḻntakaṅ kalaṅkuṟa niṉṟēṉ vāṉa mēvuṟum poḻiltirut taṇikai malaiyai nāṭiniṉ malarppatam pukaḻēṉ ñāṉa nāyaki orupuṭai amarnta nampa ṉārkkoru naltavap pēṟē īṉaṉ āki-iṅ kiṭarppaṭu kiṉṟēṉ eṉcey vāṉpiṟan tēṉeḷi yēṉē.
translation: I stood with a troubled heart, sinking into the ocean of lust for women whose tresses never lack fragrance. I do not seek the mountain of holy Thanigai with sky-reaching groves, nor do I praise your flower-like feet. O great fruit of penance for the trustworthy Lord who holds the Goddess of wisdom on one side! I became a base man and suffer here. Why was I, this poor wretch, born?
commentary: The pull of the senses acts like a heavy ocean dragging the soul downward. The sinking weight of physical lust directly opposes the sky-reaching spiritual heights of Thanigai. Taking on the voice of a flawed and suffering person, Vallalar speaks for anyone struggling to turn away from bodily desires toward divine wisdom.

translit: pūvuṇṭaveḷ viṭai-ēṟiya puṉitaṉtaru makaṉār pāvuṇṭator amutaṉṉavar pacumāmayil mēlvan tāvuṇṭaṉar eṉatiṉṉalam aṟiyāreṉa iruntāl nāvuṇṭavar tirumuṉpitu nalam aṉṟumak keṉavē.
translation: He is the son of the pure Lord who mounts the white bull. He is like the sweet nectar found in poetry. He came upon the great green peacock and consumed my sweet beauty. If you stand there as if you do not know this, those who have tongues to speak will tell you in your holy presence, "This is not right of you."
commentary: The young woman speaks boldly, insisting that the Lord cannot steal her heart and then simply ignore her. In the traditions of Tamil love poetry, it is considered unjust for a lover to abandon the one who has surrendered entirely to him. She warns him that if he plays innocent, the townspeople will rightfully call him out for his cruelty.

translit: oṉṟārpuram ericeytavar oṟṟittiru nakarār maṉṟārnaṭam uṭaiyārtaru makaṉārpacu mayilmēl niṉṟāratu kaṇṭēṉkalai nillātu kaḻaṉṟa teṉṟāroṭu colvēṉeṉai yāṉēmaṟan tēṉē.
translation: I saw the son of the Lord, the one who burned the cities of foes, who dwells in holy Otriyur, and who dances in the hall. He stood upon the green peacock. Seeing that, my garments slipped and fell away. To whom can I tell this? I completely forgot myself.
commentary: The sight of the Lord on his peacock shatters the young woman's self-control. In this poetic tradition, garments slipping away represents the complete loss of worldly ego and social conditioning. Overwhelmed by divine beauty, she forgets her own identity and has no one left to confide in.

translit: vārārmulai umaiyāḷtiru maṇavāḷartam makaṉār ārā-amu taṉaiyāruyir aṉaiyārayil avaṉār nērārpaṇi mayiliṉmicai niṉṟāratu kaṇṭēṉ nīrārviḻi imainīṅkiṉa niṟainīṅkiya taṉṟē.
translation: He is the son of the holy groom of Uma with her beautiful, bound breasts. He is like insatiable nectar. He is like my very life. He wields the spear. I saw him standing upon the peacock that subdues the serpent. The eyelids of my tear-filled eyes stopped blinking, and my feminine reserve entirely left me.
commentary: Uma is a name for the goddess Parvati, the consort of Siva. Total absorption in the divine vision of their son strips away all conventional social boundaries. Her unblinking, tear-filled gaze shows a mind entirely fixed on God, leaving no room for ordinary caution or feminine reserve.

translit: oṉṟōṭiraṇ ṭeṉuṅkaṇṇiṉar utavuntiru makaṉār eṉṟōṭikal eḻilārmayil ēṟi-aṅ kuṟṟār naṉṟōṭiṉaṉ makiḻkūrntavar nakaimāmukaṅ kaṇṭēṉ kaṉṟōṭiṉa pacuvāṭiṉa kalai-ūṭiṉa aṉṟē.
translation: He is the holy son given by the Lord with three eyes. He mounted the exceedingly beautiful and valorous peacock. Eagerly I ran to him, and with great joy I saw his magnificent, smiling face. The calves ran, the cows languished, and my garments slipped away.
commentary: The radiant presence of the divine disrupts the ordinary world entirely. The animals forget their natural bonds, with calves scattering and cows growing faint, while the young woman sheds the last physical symbols of her worldly identity.

translit: malaivāṅkuvil araṉārtiru makaṉārpacu mayiliṉ nilaitāṅkuṟa niṉṟāravar niṟkumnilai kaṇṭēṉ alaitīṅkiṉa kuḻaltūṅkiṉa akamēṅkiṉa araimēl kalainīṅkiṉa mulaivīṅkiṉa kaḷi-ōṅkiṉa aṉṟē.
translation: He is the holy son of Hara, who bent the mountain into a bow. I saw the posture he struck as he stood upon the green peacock. My wavy hair fell loose. My heart yearned. The garments slipped from my waist. My breasts swelled, and my ecstatic joy surged.
commentary: Hara is a name for Siva, who in mythology used the cosmic mountain Meru as a mighty bow. Here, the young woman's deep spiritual longing transforms her body as well as her mind. Her loosening hair, yearning heart, and surging joy are classic poetic signs of ecstatic devotion, where worldly shame dissolves completely into pure bliss.

translit: māṉkaṇṭakai uṭaiyārtaru makaṉārtamai mayilmēl nāṉkaṇṭaṉaṉ avarkaṇṭaṉar nakaikoṇṭaṉam uṭaṉē mīṉkaṇṭaṉa viḻiyāratu paḻiyāka viḷaittār ēṉkaṇṭaṉai eṉṟāḷaṉai eṉeṉṟuraik kēṉē.
translation: I saw the son of the Lord who holds a deer in His hand, mounted on a peacock. I looked at Him, He looked at me, and at once we smiled at each other. The women with fish-like eyes made a scandal out of this. My mother asked why I looked at Him. What can I say?
commentary: The sudden, joyful connection between the soul and God often looks like madness to the rest of the world. Speaking in the voice of a lovesick young woman, the poet describes sharing a secret smile with Murugan (the son of Lord Siva) that sparks immediate neighborhood gossip. Caught between spiritual ecstasy and her mother's scolding, she has no words left to explain her awakening.

translit: ceṅkaṇviṭai taṉilēṟiya civaṉārtiru makaṉār eṅkaṇmaṇi aṉaiyārmayi liṉmītuvan tiṭṭār aṅkaṇmika makiḻvōṭuceṉ ṟavarniṉṟatu kaṇṭēṉ iṅkaṇvaḷai iḻantēṉmayal uḻantēṉkalai eṉavē.
translation: The divine son of Lord Siva who rides the red-eyed bull came mounted on a peacock. He is like the very pupil of my eye. I went there with great joy and saw Him standing. Right there I lost my bangles, I languished in infatuation, and my garments slipped away.
commentary: Physical signs of lovesickness in ancient poetry describe the soul's total surrender to God. When the young woman sees her Lord, her wrists grow so thin from longing that her bangles slip off, and she loses her usual composure. This shows a spiritual love so overwhelming that it sweeps away all worldly self-consciousness.

translit: taṇtēṉpoḻi itaḻippoli caṭaiyārtaru makaṉār paṇtēṉpuri toṭaiyārtamaip pacumāmayil mītil kaṇṭēṉvaḷai kāṇēṉkalai kāṇēṉmiku kāmam koṇṭēṉtuyil viṇṭēṉoṉṟum kūṟēṉvaru māṟē.
translation: I saw the son of the Lord whose matted hair shines with cassia flowers showering cool honey. He wore a sweet garland and came upon a great green peacock. I saw Him. Now I cannot find my bangles. I cannot find my garments. Overcome by intense passion, I lost my sleep. I will say nothing of how this happened.
commentary: The longing for divine grace consumes every part of a person's life. The young woman loses her sleep and her modesty, completely overwhelmed by her desire for the divine. This intense passion represents the soul abandoning all earthly attachments and physical comforts to seek God alone.

translit: māvīḻntiṭu viṭaiyārtiru makaṉārpacu mayilmēl nīvīḻntiṭa niṉṟāratu kaṇṭēṉeṉṟaṉ neñcē pūvīḻntatu vaṇṭēmati pōyvīḻntatu vaṇṭē nāvīḻntatu malarēkaḻai nāṇvīḻntatu malarē.
translation: I saw the divine son of the bull-riding Lord standing upon a green peacock, drawing you in, O my heart. The bees descended on the flowers, and my reason slipped away. My speech failed against the flower arrows, and the string of the sugarcane bow struck.
commentary: The sweetness of God's presence strikes the soul like a sudden force. The imagery of flower arrows and a sugarcane bow belongs to the traditional Indian god of love, representing an infatuation that defeats ordinary logic. When the heart is entirely captured by divine grace, the everyday mind simply gives way and speech fails.

translit: veṟṟārpuram erittārtarum mēlārmayil mēlē uṟṟāravar eḻilmāmukat tuḷḷēnakai kaṇṭēṉ poṟṟārpuyaṅ kaṇṭēṉtuyar viṇṭēṉeṉaip pōla maṟṟārpeṟu vārō-iṉi vāḻvēṉmaṉam makiḻntē.
translation: The exalted son of the Lord who burned the cities of foes arrived upon a peacock. I saw the smile on His beautiful face. I saw His shoulders adorned with a golden garland and shed my sorrow. Who else could attain a blessing like mine? Now I will live with a joyful heart.
commentary: The agony of separation finally ends in the deep joy of the divine presence. Seeing the Lord's smile washes away all the soul's grief, replacing fear and longing with absolute confidence. Feeling uniquely blessed by this vision, the soul realizes that true and lasting happiness has finally arrived.

sections.title: The Ten Verses on the Expanse of Divine Grace

translit: āṟumukap peruṅkaruṇaik kaṭalē teyva yāṉaimakiḻ maṇikkuṉṟē aracē mukkaṭ pēṟumukap peruñcuṭarkkuṭ cuṭarē cevvēl piṭittaruḷum peruntakaiyē pirama ñāṉam vīṟumukap peruṅkuṇattōr itayat tōṅkum viḷakkamē āṉanta veḷḷa mēmuṉ tēṟumukap periya-aruṭ kuruvāy eṉṉaic ciṟukālai āṭkoṇṭa tēva tēvē.
translation: O great ocean of compassion with six faces! O mountain of gems that delights Devasena! O King! O flame within the great flame of the three-eyed Lord's supreme state! O noble one who graciously holds the red spear! O lamp that shines in the hearts of the great-natured ones whose faces glow with supreme wisdom! O flood of bliss! O God of gods who appeared in the past as the great Guru of Grace to impart clarity and claimed me in my early youth.
commentary: Vallalar addresses the divine in the traditional form of Murugan, the six-faced god holding a red spear. He describes God as an ocean of compassion and a light shining within the ultimate light of the three-eyed Lord, Siva. He recalls how this divine presence came to him as a teacher (Guru) to claim and guide him while he was still a young boy.

translit: kaṇṇimati puṉaintacaṭaik kaṉiyē mukkaṭ karumpē-eṉ kaṇṇēmeyk karuṇai vāḻvē puṇṇiyanal nilai-uṭaiyōr uḷattil vāykkum puttamutē āṉanta pōka mē-uḷ eṇṇiyameyt tavarkkellām eḷitil īnta eṉaracē āṟumukat tiṟaiyām vittē tiṇṇiya-eṉ maṉamurukkik kuruvāy eṉṉaic ciṟukālai āṭkoṇṭa tēva tēva.
translation: O fruit of the matted hair adorned with the crescent moon! O three-eyed sugarcane! O my eye! O life of true compassion! O fresh nectar welling up in the hearts of those established in a state of true merit! O experience of bliss! O my King who easily grants the desires of all true ascetics who contemplate within! O seed that is the six-faced Lord! O God of gods who melted my hardened mind, came as the Guru, and claimed me in my early youth.
commentary: Here the divine is described using the beloved symbols of Siva, wearing the crescent moon in his matted hair. Vallalar praises this divine presence as the source of true compassion and the seed of Murugan. He gives thanks to this God for melting his stubborn mind and taking him as a disciple early in life.

translit: niṉṉirutāḷ tuṇaipiṭittē vāḻkiṉ ṟēṉnāṉ niṉṉai-alāl piṉṉai-oru nēyam kāṇēṉ eṉṉai-iṉit tiruvuḷattil niṉaiti yōnāṉ ēḻaiyiṉum ēḻaikaṇṭāy entāy entāy poṉṉai-aṉṟi virumpāta pullar tampāl pōkaloḻin tuṉpatamē pōṟṟum vaṇṇam ciṉṉamaḷit taruṭkuruvāy eṉṉai muṉṉē ciṟukālai āṭkoṇṭa tēva tēvē.
translation: I live holding firmly to the support of your two feet. I see no love other than you. Will you think of me sweetly in your divine heart? Behold, I am the poorest of the poor! O my father, my father! You freed me from going to base people who desire nothing but gold. You gave me the mark so that I praise only your feet. O God of gods who came as the Guru of Grace and claimed me long ago in my early youth.
commentary: Vallalar says his only support and his only love is the divine. He expresses deep gratitude that God saved him from having to seek help from greedy people who care only for gold. Instead, the divine teacher marked him out for a spiritual life from a very young age, ensuring he would only ever depend on grace.

translit: kalvi-elām kaṟpittāy niṉpāl nēyam kāṇavaittāy ivvulakam kāṉal eṉṟē ollumvakai aṟivittāy uḷḷē niṉṟeṉ uṭaiyāṉē niṉaruḷum utavu kiṉṟāy illai-eṉap piṟarpālceṉ ṟiravā vaṇṇam ēṟṟamaḷit tāyirakkam eṉṉē eṉṉē celva-aruṭ kuruvāki nāyi ṉēṉaic ciṟukālai āṭkoṇṭa tēva tēvē.
translation: You taught me all learning. You made me discover love for you. You made me understand by all possible means that this world is a mirage. Standing within me, O my Master, you grant your grace. You uplifted me so that I do not go to others and beg in poverty. What great compassion this is! O God of gods who became the wealthy Guru of Grace and claimed me, though I am lower than a dog, in my early youth.
commentary: True knowledge and true love come directly from the divine. Vallalar credits God with teaching him everything he knows and showing him that worldly life is only a temporary illusion. He marvels at the compassion that uplifted him, a grace that lives inside him and keeps him from ever having to beg for worldly favors.

translit: entaipirāṉ eṉiṟaivaṉ irukka iṅkē eṉṉakuṟai namakkeṉṟē iṟumāp puṟṟē manta-ula kiṉilpiṟarai orukā cukkum matiyāmal niṉaṭiyē matikkiṉ ṟēṉyāṉ inta-aṭi yēṉiṭattuṉ tiruvu ḷantāṉ evvāṟō aṟikilēṉ ēḻai yēṉāl cintaimakiḻn taruṭkuruvāy eṉṉai muṉṉē ciṟukālai āṭkoṇṭa tēva tēvē.
translation: "While my Father and Lord is here, what do I lack?" I swell with such pride. I do not value others in this dull world even for a single coin. I value only your feet. I do not know how your divine heart feels toward this poor servant. O God of gods who rejoiced in your heart, became the Guru of Grace, and claimed me long ago in my early youth.
commentary: Having the divine as a father and master brings complete fearlessness. Vallalar says he feels a deep spiritual pride because he lacks nothing, and he refuses to value worldly people or their wealth. He rests entirely on his devotion, trusting the teacher who claimed his heart long ago.

translit: māṟāta peruñcelva yōkar pōṟṟum māmaṇiyē āṟumuka maṇiyē niṉcīr kūṟāta pulaivāymai uṭaiyār tammaik kūṭāta vaṇṇamaruṭ kuruvāy vantu tēṟāta nilai-ellām tēṟṟi ōṅkum civañāṉac ciṟappaṭaintu tikaippu nīṅkic cīṟāta vāḻviṭaināṉ vāḻa eṉṉaic ciṟukālai āṭkoṇṭa tēva tēvē.
translation: O great gem praised by yogis of unfailing spiritual wealth. O six-faced gem. You came as the guru of grace to prevent me from associating with those of base speech who do not praise your glory. You clarified all my confused states. O God of gods who claimed me in my early youth so that I could attain the excellence of supreme divine wisdom, dispel my bewilderment, and live a peaceful life.
commentary: God acts as a protective teacher to guide the soul away from harmful company. By stepping into this life early on, the divine prevented a fall into the society of people who speak basely and ignore spiritual truth. This early intervention cleared away mental confusion and secured a peaceful, grounded life of wisdom.

translit: kaṟṟaṟinta meyuṇarcci uṭaiyōr uḷḷak kamalattē ōṅkuperuṅ kaṭavu ḷēniṉ poṟṟakaimā malaraṭiccīr vaḻuttu kiṉṟa puṇṇiyartaṅ kuḻuvileṉaip pukutti eṉṟum uṟṟavaruḷ cintaṉaitan tiṉpa mēvi uṭaiyāyuṉ aṭiyavaṉeṉ ṟōṅkum vaṇṇam ciṟaṟaṟivai akaṟṟi-aruṭ kuruvāy eṉṉaic ciṟukālai āṭkoṇṭa tēva tēvē.
translation: O great God who flourishes in the heart-lotus of those who have learned and realized the truth. You placed me in the assembly of meritorious ones who praise the glory of your great, beautiful, golden lotus feet. You always granted me thoughts of your grace and filled me with bliss. O Master, you dispelled my petty knowledge so I could rise as your true devotee. O God of gods who came as the guru of grace and claimed me in my early youth.
commentary: Just as the divine keeps the seeker away from worldly influences, it actively places them among true devotees. This assembly of spiritually minded people provides the perfect environment where petty, limited human knowledge naturally falls away. Filled instead with thoughts of grace, the mind finds lasting bliss.

translit: ñālamelām paṭaittavaṉaip paṭaitta mukkaṇ nāyakaṉē vaṭivēṟkai nāta ṉēnāṉ kōlamelām koyēṉnaṟ kuṇamoṉ ṟillēṉ kuṟṟamē viḻaintēṉik kōtu ḷēṉaic cālamelām ceyummaṭavār mayakkiṉ nīkkic caṉmārkkam aṭaiya-aruḷ taruvāy ñāṉac cīlamelām uṭaiya-aruṭ kuruvāy vantu ciṟukālai āṭkoṇṭa tēva tēvē.
translation: O three-eyed Lord who created the creator of all worlds. O Lord holding the sharp spear in your hand. I possess no good traits. I lack even a single virtue. I desired only faults. You freed me, this flawed one, from the delusion of deceptive women and granted your grace so I could attain Sanmarkkam. O God of gods who came as the guru of grace possessing all virtues of wisdom and claimed me in my early youth.
commentary: The spiritual path often begins with a stark admission of personal flaws and the strong pull of worldly desires. God's grace cuts through these powerful distractions, freeing the mind from deception and material attachments. This rescue allows the soul to attain Sanmarkkam, the pure path of truth, light, and compassion.

translit: kaṟpaṉaiyē eṉumulakac caḻakkil antō kālūṉṟi mayaṅkukiṉṟa kaṭaiya ṉēṉaic coṟpaṉamiv vulakiyaṟkai eṉṟu neñcam tuṇivukoḷac ceyvittuṉ tuṇaippoṟ ṟāḷai aṟpakalum niṉaintukaṉin turuki ñāṉa āṉanta pōkamuṟa aruḷal vēṇṭum ciṟparacaṟ kuruvāyvan teṉṉai muṉṉē ciṟukālai āṭkoṇṭa tēva tēvē.
translation: Alas, I am the lowest one, planting my feet and wallowing in the illusions of this worldly life which is mere imagination. You made my heart firmly realize that the nature of this world is but a dream. You must grant your grace so I can think of your saving golden feet day and night, melting in devotion to experience the bliss of wisdom. O God of gods who came before me as the supreme, true guru of wisdom and claimed me in my early youth.
commentary: Everyday worldly life feels incredibly solid, yet it is in the end a fleeting dream. The divine teacher makes the heart see through this illusion and let go of its tight grip on material things. Once the mind stops clinging to worldly imagination, it can pour its energy entirely into deep, melting devotion and the joy of divine wisdom.

translit: paṉṉirukaṇ malarmalarnta kaṭalē ñāṉap parañcuṭarē āṟumukam paṭaitta kōvē eṉṉirukaṇ maṇiyē-en tāyē eṉṉai īṉṟāṉē eṉaracē eṉṟaṉ vāḻvē miṉṉiruvar puṭaiviḷaṅka mayilmī tēṟi virumpumaṭi yārkāṇa mēvun tēvē ceṉṉiyilniṉ aṭimalarvait teṉṉai muṉṉē ciṟukālai āṭkoṇṭa tēva tēvē.
translation: O ocean blooming with twelve lotus eyes. O supreme light of wisdom. O King with six faces. O pupil of my two eyes. O my mother. O father who gave birth to me. O my King. O my very life. O God who rides the peacock, shining with two lightning-like consorts at your sides, appearing for your loving devotees to behold. O God of gods who placed your lotus feet on my head and claimed me in my early youth.
commentary: God is intimately close, acting as mother, father, master, and the very breath of life itself. The vivid imagery of a six-faced Lord with twelve eyes riding a peacock represents the supreme light of wisdom appearing in a beloved, personal form. Placing the divine feet on the seeker's head is a traditional and absolute act of blessing, marking a total claim over the soul.

sections.title: Desire for the Attainment of Divine Grace

tamil: உலகம் பரவும் பரஞ்சோதி உருவாம் குருவே உம்பரிடைக்
கலகம் தருசூர்க் கிளைகளைந்த கதிர்வேல் அரசே கவின்தருசீர்த்
திலகம் திகழ்வாள் நுதற்பரையின் செல்வப் புதல்வா திறல்அதனால்
இலகும் கலப மயிற்பரிமேல் ஏறும் பரிசென் இயம்புகவே.
translit: ulakam paravum parañcōti uruvām kuruvē umpariṭaik kalakam tarucūrk kiḷaikaḷainta katirvēl aracē kaviṉtarucīrt tilakam tikaḻvāḷ nutaṟparaiyiṉ celvap putalvā tiṟalataṉāl ilakum kalapa mayiṟparimēl ēṟum pariceṉ iyampukavē.
translation: O Guru whose form is the Supreme Jothi praised by the world! O King with the radiant spear who destroyed the clan of Suran that caused conflict among the celestials! O precious son of Goddess Parai, whose bright forehead shines with a beautiful and auspicious tilak! Tell me how you mount and ride your resplendent peacock steed with such might.
commentary: The devotee addresses the divine form of Murugan, calling him the supreme Jothi (divine light) and the ultimate teacher. The verse refers to the traditional story where Murugan uses his spear to defeat the demon Suran, an act that represents destroying the forces of conflict and ignorance. By asking how the Lord rides his majestic peacock, the devotee is expressing absolute awe at the divine power.

tamil: புகுவா னவர்தம் இடர்முழுதும் போக்கும் கதிர்வேல் புண்ணியனே
மிகுவான் முதலாம் பூதம்எலாம் விதித்தே நடத்தும் விளைவனைத்தும்
தகுவான் பொருளாம் உனதருளே என்றால் அடியேன் தனைஇங்கே
நகுவான் வருவித் திருள்நெறிக்கே நடத்தல் அழகோ நவிலாயே.
translit: pukuvā ṉavartam iṭarmuḻutum pōkkum katirvēl puṇṇiyaṉē mikuvāṉ mutalām pūtamelām vitittē naṭattum viḷaivaṉaittum takuvāṉ poruḷām uṉataruḷē eṉṟāl aṭiyēṉ taṉai-iṅkē nakuvāṉ varuvit tiruḷneṟikkē naṭattal aḻakō navilāyē.
translation: O virtuous one with the radiant spear who removes all the afflictions of those who seek refuge! If creating and directing the vast sky and all the elements, and all such outcomes, are truly the work of your Grace, which is the supreme reality, tell me: is it fair to bring your servant here to be mocked and to make me walk the path of darkness?
commentary: If divine grace creates and governs the entire universe, it must also be responsible for the individual soul. The devotee asks God a direct, intimate question: if you control everything, is it right to leave me in darkness where the world mocks my struggles? This shows an absolute reliance on grace as the only real power in the world.

tamil: அழகா அமலா அருளாளா அறிவா அறிவார் அகம்மேவும்
குழகா குமரா எனைஆண்ட கோவே நின்சீர் குறியாரைப்
பழகா வண்ணம் எனக்கருளிப் பரனே நின்னைப் பணிகின்றோர்க்
கழகா தரவாம் பணிபுரிவார் அடியார்க் கடிமை ஆக்குகவே.
translit: aḻakā amalā aruḷāḷā aṟivā aṟivār akammēvum kuḻakā kumarā eṉai-āṇṭa kōvē niṉcīr kuṟiyāraip paḻakā vaṇṇam eṉakkaruḷip paraṉē niṉṉaip paṇikiṉṟōrk kaḻakā taravām paṇipurivār aṭiyārk kaṭimai ākkukavē.
translation: O beautiful one! O pure one! O bestower of grace! O embodiment of knowledge! O Kumara who dwells in the hearts of the wise! O King who rules me! O Supreme Lord, grant me the grace to avoid associating with those who do not cherish your glories. Make me a servant to the devotees who lovingly serve those who bow to you.
commentary: The true spiritual path requires the right company. The devotee begs to be kept far away from people who do not value divine grace. Instead, the ultimate wish is to become a servant to those who serve God's devotees, showing that true spiritual rank is found in deep, humble service to others.

tamil: ஆக்கும் தொழிலால் களித்தானை அடக்குந் தொழிலால் அடக்கிப்பின்
காக்கும் தொழிலால் அருள்புரிந்த கருணைக் கடலே கடைநோக்கால்
நோக்கும் தொழில்ஓர் சிறிதுன்பால் உளதேல் மாயா நொடிப்பெல்லாம்
போக்கும் தொழில்என் பால்உண்டாம் இதற்கென் புரிவேன் புண்ணியனே.
translit: ākkum toḻilāl kaḷittāṉai aṭakkun toḻilāl aṭakkippiṉ kākkum toḻilāl aruḷpurinta karuṇaik kaṭalē kaṭainōkkāl nōkkum toḻilōr ciṟituṉpāl uḷatēl māyā noṭippellām pōkkum toḻileṉ pāluṇṭām itaṟkeṉ purivēṉ puṇṇiyaṉē.
translation: You subdued the one who grew proud of his power of creation, and then bestowed grace upon him through your power of protection. O ocean of mercy! If you cast even a slight side-glance upon me, I will gain the power to dispel all illusions in an instant. What must I do to earn this, O virtuous one?
commentary: The opening refers to a myth where the creator deity grew arrogant and was humbled by the supreme Lord. Even a brief sideways glance of divine mercy contains enough power to shatter all worldly illusions instantly. The devotee feels entirely helpless against these illusions and asks exactly what must be done to earn a single look of true grace.

tamil: புரிவேன் விரதம் தவந்தானம் புரியா தொழிவேன் புண்ணியமே
பரிவேன் பாவம் பரிவேன்இப் பரிசால் ஒன்றும் பயன்காணேன்
திரிவேன் நினது புகழ்பாடிச் சிறியேன் இதனைத் தீர்வேனேல்
எரிவேன் எரிவாய் நரகத்தே இருப்பேன் இளைப்பேன் விளைப்பேனே.
translit: purivēṉ viratam tavantāṉam puriyā toḻivēṉ puṇṇiyamē parivēṉ pāvam parivēṉip paricāl oṉṟum payaṉkāṇēṉ tirivēṉ niṉatu pukaḻpāṭic ciṟiyēṉ itaṉait tīrvēṉēl erivēṉ erivāy narakattē iruppēṉ iḷaippēṉ viḷaippēṉē.
translation: I may perform vows, penance, and charity, or I may fail to do them, O embodiment of virtue. I suffer, I commit sins, and I find no benefit in this state. I wander about singing your praises. If I, a lowly one, cease doing this, I will burn. I will dwell in the fiery hell. I will grow weary and reap endless suffering.
commentary: Traditional religious practices like vows, harsh penance, and charity do not guarantee spiritual success. The devotee admits to failing at these and falling into worldly suffering. The only reliable lifeline is constant devotion and singing the Lord's praise. If that single thread breaks, the result is total spiritual ruin and endless pain.

tamil: விளைப்பேன் பவமே அடிச்சிறியேன் வினையால் விளையும் வினைப்போகம்
திளைப்பேன் எனினும் கதிர்வடிவேல் தேவே என்னும் திருமொழியால்
இளைப்பேன் அலன்இங் கியம்புகிற்பேன் எனக்கென் குறையுண் டெமதூதன்
வளைப்பேன் எனவந் திடில்அவனை மடிப்பேன் கருணை வலத்தாலே.
translit: viḷaippēṉ pavamē aṭicciṟiyēṉ viṉaiyāl viḷaiyum viṉaippōkam tiḷaippēṉ eṉiṉum katirvaṭivēl tēvē eṉṉum tirumoḻiyāl iḷaippēṉ alaṉiṅ kiyampukiṟpēṉ eṉakkeṉ kuṟaiyuṇ ṭematūtaṉ vaḷaippēṉ eṉavan tiṭilavaṉai maṭippēṉ karuṇai valattālē.
translation: I, a lowly servant, generate only rebirths. Even if I wallow in the experiences born of my past karma, I will not grow weary, for I chant the sacred words calling upon the Lord of the radiant sharp spear. What do I lack? If the messenger of death comes to capture me, I will destroy him with the strength of your grace.
commentary: Chanting the Lord's name brings absolute fearlessness, even to someone heavily burdened by the consequences of their past actions (karma). The speaker feels trapped in the endless cycle of rebirth, yet he knows that God's grace overrides all worldly laws. Wrapped in this divine strength, he declares that he can effortlessly defeat the terrifying messenger of death.

tamil: வலத்தால் வடிவேல் கரத்தேந்தும் மணியே நின்னை வழுத்துகின்ற
தலத்தால் உயர்ந்த வானவரும் தமியேற் கிணையோ சடமான
மலத்தால் வருந்தாப் பெருவாழ்வால் மகிழ்வேன் இன்பம் வளர்வேனே.
translit: valattāl vaṭivēl karattēntum maṇiyē niṉṉai vaḻuttukiṉṟa nalattāluyarnta peruntavarpāl naṇṇum paricu nalkiṉaiyēl talattāl uyarnta vāṉavarum tamiyēṟ kiṇaiyō caṭamāṉa malattāl varuntāp peruvāḻvāl makiḻvēṉ iṉpam vaḷarvēṉē.
translation: O jewel wielding the sharp spear in your right hand, if you grant me the gift of gathering with the great ascetics elevated by the virtue of praising you, are even the celestial beings of the high heavens equal to me? I will rejoice in a great life unburdened by inert impurities, and my bliss will grow.
commentary: The supreme gift is the company of true devotees. Vallalar explains that being near those who genuinely praise God elevates a person far above the highest gods of heaven. This sacred fellowship strips away the heavy impurities of the physical body and opens the door to an ever-growing, joyful life.

tamil: இன்பப் பெருக்கே அருட்கடலே இறையே அழியா இரும்பொருளே
அன்பர்க் கருளும் பெருங்கருணை அரசே உணர்வால் ஆம்பயனே
வன்பர்க் கரிதாம் பரஞ்சோதி வடிவேல் மணியே அணியேஎன்
துன்பத் திடரைப் பொடியாக்கிச் சுகந்தந் தருளத் துணியாயே.
translit: iṉpap perukkē aruṭkaṭalē iṟaiyē aḻiyā irumporuḷē aṉpark karuḷum peruṅkaruṇai aracē uṇarvāl āmpayaṉē vaṉpark karitām parañcōti vaṭivēl maṇiyē aṇiyē-eṉ tuṉpat tiṭaraip poṭiyākkic cukantan taruḷat tuṇiyāyē.
translation: O flood of bliss, ocean of grace, Lord, imperishable great reality. O king of immense compassion who graces your devotees, fruit realized through awareness. O supreme Jothi rare to the hard-hearted, jewel wielding the sharp spear, beautiful ornament. Please resolve to turn the obstacle of my sorrow to dust and graciously grant me joy.
commentary: God is an endless ocean of grace and a supreme light, but he remains completely hidden from those with hard, unfeeling hearts. The path to this divine presence requires deep love and deep awareness. The speaker calls upon this compassionate Lord to grind all worldly sorrows into dust and replace them with pure joy.

tamil: சுகமே அடியர் உளத்தோங்கும் சுடரே அழியாத் துணையேஎன்
அகமே புகுந்த அருள்தேவே அருமா மணியே ஆரமுதே
இகமே பரத்தும் உனக்கன்றி எத்தே வருக்கும் எமக்கருள
முகமே திலைஎம் பெருமானே நினக்குண் டாறு முகமலரே.
translit: cukamē aṭiyar uḷattōṅkum cuṭarē aḻiyāt tuṇaiyē-eṉ akamē pukunta aruḷtēvē arumā maṇiyē āramutē ikamē parattum uṉakkaṉṟi ettē varukkum emakkaruḷa mukamē tilai-em perumāṉē niṉakkuṇ ṭāṟu mukamalarē.
translation: O joy, flame rising in the hearts of devotees, imperishable companion. O God of grace who entered my inmost heart, rare great jewel, perfect nectar. In this world and the next, no god but you has a face to bestow grace upon us. O our Lord, you possess six blooming faces.
commentary: The divine presence is a living flame that rises directly within the human heart. The speaker contrasts the limits of other deities with the absolute mercy of his Lord. While ordinary gods lack a single face capable of granting true liberation, this Lord possesses six blooming faces, multiplying his power to bestow grace upon the world.

tamil: ஆறு முகமும் திணிதோள்ஈ ராறும் கருணை அடித்துணையும்
வீறு மயிலும் தனிக்கடவுள் வேலும் துணைஉண் டெமக்கிங்கே
சீறும் பிணியும் கொடுங்கோளும் தீய வினையும் செறியாவே
நாறும் பகட்டான் அதிகாரம் நடவா துலகம் பரவுறுமே.
translit: āṟu mukamum tiṇitōḷī rāṟum karuṇai aṭittuṇaiyum vīṟu mayilum taṉikkaṭavuḷ vēlum tuṇai-uṇ ṭemakkiṅkē cīṟum piṇiyum koṭuṅkōḷum tīya viṉaiyum ceṟiyāvē nāṟum pakaṭṭāṉ atikāram naṭavā tulakam paravuṟumē.
translation: The six faces, the twelve strong shoulders, the pair of compassionate feet, the majestic peacock, and the matchless divine spear stand here as my companions. Raging diseases, cruel planetary alignments, and evil karma will not approach me. The authority of the foul-smelling rider of the buffalo holds no sway over me. The world will praise this.
commentary: Worldly threats lose all their power when God stands by your side as a living companion. The speaker finds complete safety in the Lord's divine forms, from his twelve strong shoulders to his matching spear and majestic peacock. Protected by this presence, he has absolutely no fear of disease, cruel astrological alignments, or the god of death who traditionally rides a buffalo.

tamil: அடியார்க் கெளியர் எனும்முக்கன் ஐயர் தமக்கும் உலகீன்ற
அம்மை தனக்கும் திருவாய்முத் தளித்துக் களிக்கும் அருமருந்தே
கடியார் கடப்ப மலர்மலர்ந்த கருணைப் பொருப்பே கற்பகமே
கண்ணுள் மணியே அன்பர்மனக் கமலம் விரிக்கும் கதிரொளியே
படியார் வளிவான் தீமுதல்ஐம் பகுதி யாய பரம்பொருளே
பகர்தற் கரிய மெய்ஞ்ஞானப் பாகே அசுரப் படைமுழுதும்
தடிவாய் என்னச் சுரர்வேண்டத் தடிந்த வேற்கைத் தனிமுதலே
தணிகா சலமாம் தலத்தமர்ந்த சைவ மணியே சண்முகனே.
translit: aṭiyārk keḷiyar eṉummukkaṉ aiyar tamakkum ulakīṉṟa ammai taṉakkum tiruvāymut taḷittuk kaḷikkum arumaruntē kaṭiyār kaṭappa malarmalarnta karuṇaip poruppē kaṟpakamē kaṇṇuḷ maṇiyē aṉparmaṉak kamalam virikkum katiroḷiyē paṭiyār vaḷivāṉ tīmutalaim pakuti yāya paramporuḷē pakartaṟ kariya meyññāṉap pākē acurap paṭaimuḻutum taṭivāy eṉṉac curarvēṇṭat taṭinta vēṟkait taṉimutalē taṇikā calamām talattamarnta caiva maṇiyē caṇmukaṉē.
translation: O rare medicine who delights in giving a kiss from your sacred mouth to the three-eyed Lord who is accessible to devotees and to the Mother who bore the world! O mountain of compassion blooming with fragrant kadamba flowers! O wish-fulfilling tree! O pupil of the eye! O brilliant light blossoming the lotus hearts of devotees! O Supreme Reality manifesting as the five elements of earth, wind, sky, fire, and water! O syrup of true wisdom hard to describe! O peerless source holding the spear in your hand, who struck down the entire Asura army when the Devas pleaded for their destruction! O Saiva gem abiding in the shrine of Thanigachalam! O Shanmuga!
commentary: The supreme divine is addressed here as an adored child who delights his parents, the god Siva and the Mother goddess, with his affection. At the same time, this child is the vast cosmic reality that makes up the five elements of earth, wind, sky, fire, and water. He is also the fierce protector wielding a spear, ready to strike down the destructive forces known as Asuras whenever the celestial beings ask for help.

tamil: காயா தளியக் கனிந்தன்பால் கல்லால் அடிநின் றருள்ஒழுகும்
கனியுட் சுவையே அடியர்மனக் கவலை அகற்றும் கற்பகமே
ஓயா துயிர்க்குள் ஒளித்தெவையும் உணர்த்தி அருளும் ஒன்றேஎன்
உள்ளக் களிப்பே ஐம்பொறியும் ஒடுக்கும் பெரியோர்க் கோர்உறவே
தேயாக் கருணைப் பாற்கடலே தெளியா அசுரப் போர்க்கடலே
தெய்வப் பதியே முதற்கதியே திருச்செந் தூரில் திகழ்மதியே
தாயாய் என்னைக் காக்கவரும் தனியே பரம சற்குருவே
தணிகா சலமாம் தலத்தமர்ந்த சைவ மணியே சண்முகனே.
translit: kāyā taḷiyak kaṉintaṉpāl kallāl aṭiniṉ ṟaruḷoḻukum kaṉiyuṭ cuvaiyē aṭiyarmaṉak kavalai akaṟṟum kaṟpakamē ōyā tuyirkkuḷ oḷittevaiyum uṇartti aruḷum oṉṟē-eṉ uḷḷak kaḷippē aimpoṟiyum oṭukkum periyōrk kōruṟavē tēyāk karuṇaip pāṟkaṭalē teḷiyā acurap pōrkkaṭalē teyvap patiyē mutaṟkatiyē tiruccen tūril tikaḻmatiyē tāyāy eṉṉaik kākkavarum taṉiyē parama caṟkuruvē taṇikā calamām talattamarnta caiva maṇiyē caṇmukaṉē.
translation: O taste within the fruit dripping with grace beneath the banyan tree, ripening with love without passing through an unripe stage! O wish-fulfilling tree removing the anxieties from devotees' minds! O One who ceaselessly hides within souls, revealing everything and granting grace! O joy of my heart! O true relation to the great ones who conquer their five senses! O unwaning milky ocean of compassion! O churning ocean of war for the bewildered Asuras! O divine Lord! O primal refuge! O radiant moon in Tiruchendur! O peerless supreme Satguru who comes to protect me like a mother! O Saiva gem abiding in the shrine of Thanigachalam! O Shanmuga!
commentary: The divine acts as the ultimate spiritual teacher (Satguru), guiding the soul from within while offering the tender, fierce protection of a mother. This grace is described as a fruit that ripens through pure love, skipping the bitter unripe stage entirely. While this presence is a soothing ocean of compassion for those who conquer their senses, it remains a turbulent ocean of war for the inner demons of bewilderment and ignorance.

tamil: நாணும் அயன்மால் இந்திரன்பொன் நாட்டுப் புலவர் மணம்வேட்ட
நங்கை மார்கள் மங்கலப்பொன் நாண்காத் தளித்த நாயகமே
சேணும் புவியும் பாதலமும் தித்தித் தொழுகும் செந்தேனே
செஞ்சொற் சுவையே பொருட்சுவையே சிவன்கைப் பொருளே செங்கழுநீர்ப்
பூணும் தடந்தோட்பெருந் தகையே பொய்யர் அறியாப் புண்ணியமே
போகங் கடந்த யோகியர்முப் போகம் விளைக்கும் பொற்புலமே
தாணு என்ன உலகமெலாம் தாங்கும் தலைமைத் தயாநிதியே
தணிகா சலமாம் தலத்தமர்ந்த சைவ மணியே சண்முகனே.
translit: nāṇum ayaṉmāl intiraṉpoṉ nāṭṭup pulavar maṇamvēṭṭa naṅkai mārkaḷ maṅkalappoṉ nāṇkāt taḷitta nāyakamē cēṇum puviyum pātalamum tittit toḻukum centēṉē ceñcoṟ cuvaiyē poruṭcuvaiyē civaṉkaip poruḷē ceṅkaḻunīrp pūṇum taṭantōṭperun takaiyē poyyar aṟiyāp puṇṇiyamē pōkaṅ kaṭanta yōkiyarmup pōkam viḷaikkum poṟpulamē tāṇu eṉṉa ulakamelām tāṅkum talaimait tayānitiyē taṇikā calamām talattamarnta caiva maṇiyē caṇmukaṉē.
translation: O Lord who protected the auspicious golden marriage threads of the women wedded to Brahma, Vishnu, Indra, and the devas of the golden world when they cowered in shame! O pure honey flowing sweetly through the heavens, earth, and the netherworld! O sweetness of refined words! O sweetness of meaning! O treasure in Siva's hand! O great Lord with broad shoulders adorned with red lilies! O merit unknown to the deceitful! O golden field yielding three harvests of bliss for the yogis who have transcended worldly pleasures! O supreme treasure of compassion supporting all the worlds like a fixed pillar! O Saiva gem abiding in the shrine of Thanigachalam! O Shanmuga!
commentary: Lord Murugan is celebrated as the ultimate protector who safeguards the universe and its divine beings when they are terrified and defenseless. His presence flows like sweet honey through all the worlds, offering deep meaning and joy to those who seek him. For yogis who have left behind ordinary worldly pleasures, he is the fertile ground that yields the highest spiritual harvest.

tamil: முன்னைப் பொருட்கு முதற்பொருளே முடியா தோங்கும் முதுமறையே
முக்கட் கரும்பீன் றெடுத்தமுழு முத்தே முதிர்ந்த முக்கனியே
பொன்னைப் புயங்கொண் டவன்போற்றும் பொன்னே புனித பூரணமே
போத மணக்கும் புதுமலரே புலவர் எவரும் புகும்பதியே
மின்னைப் பொருவும் உலகமயல் வெறுத்தோர் உள்ள விளக்கொளியே
மேலும் கீழும் நடுவும்என விளங்கி நிறைந்த மெய்த்தேவே
தன்னைப் பொருவும் சிவயோகம் தன்னை உடையோர் தம்பயனே
தணிகா சலமாம் தலத்தமர்ந்த சைவ மணியே சண்முகனே.
translit: muṉṉaip poruṭku mutaṟporuḷē muṭiyā tōṅkum mutumaṟaiyē mukkaṭ karumpīṉ ṟeṭuttamuḻu muttē mutirnta mukkaṉiyē poṉṉaip puyaṅkoṇ ṭavaṉpōṟṟum poṉṉē puṉita pūraṇamē pōta maṇakkum putumalarē pulavar evarum pukumpatiyē miṉṉaip poruvum ulakamayal veṟuttōr uḷḷa viḷakkoḷiyē mēlum kīḻum naṭuvumeṉa viḷaṅki niṟainta meyttēvē taṉṉaip poruvum civayōkam taṉṉai uṭaiyōr tampayaṉē taṇikā calamām talattamarnta caiva maṇiyē caṇmukaṉē.
translation: O Primal Reality to the most ancient reality! O ancient Veda towering without end! O perfect pearl brought forth by the three-eyed sugarcane! O fully ripened triple fruit! O gold praised by the Lord who bears the golden goddess on his chest! O pure perfection! O fresh flower fragrant with wisdom! O ultimate refuge entered by all the wise! O lamp lighting the hearts of those who reject worldly illusions that vanish like lightning! O true God shining perfectly full above, below, and in the middle! O reward for those possessing the peerless Siva-yoga! O Saiva gem abiding in the shrine of Thanigachalam! O Shanmuga!
commentary: The divine child is the original source of all existence and the living essence of the oldest sacred teachings. Vallalar pictures him as a perfect pearl formed from the sweetness of his father, the three-eyed god Siva. For those who recognize that worldly attachments vanish as quickly as lightning, this divine presence becomes a steady, perfect light burning within the heart.

tamil: பித்தப் பெருமான் சிவபெருமான் பெரிய பெருமான் தனக்கருமைப்
பிள்ளைப் பெருமான் எனப்புலவர் பேசிக் களிக்கும் பெருவாழ்வே
மத்தப் பெருமால் நீக்கும்ஒரு மருந்தே எல்லாம் வல்லோனே
வஞ்சச் சமண வல்இருளை மாய்க்கும் ஞான மணிச்சுடரே
அத்தக் கமலத் தயிற்படைகொள் அரசே மூவர்க் கருள்செய்தே
ஆக்கல் அளித்தல் அழித்தல்எனும் அம்முத் தொழிலும் தருவோனே
சத்த உலக சராசரமும் தாளில் ஒடுக்கும் தனிப்பொருளே
தணிகா சலமாம் தலத்தமர்ந்த சைவ மணியே சண்முகனே.
translit: pittap perumāṉ civaperumāṉ periya perumāṉ taṉakkarumaip piḷḷaip perumāṉ eṉappulavar pēcik kaḷikkum peruvāḻvē mattap perumāl nīkkumoru maruntē ellām vallōṉē vañcac camaṇa valiruḷai māykkum ñāṉa maṇiccuṭarē attak kamalat tayiṟpaṭaikoḷ aracē mūvark karuḷceytē ākkal aḷittal aḻittaleṉum ammut toḻilum taruvōṉē catta ulaka carācaramum tāḷil oṭukkum taṉipporuḷē taṇikā calamām talattamarnta caiva maṇiyē caṇmukaṉē.
translation: O great life whom poets joyously praise as the precious child-lord of Lord Siva, the great Lord of divine madness! O unique medicine curing the great delusion of madness! O all-powerful One! O brilliant gem of wisdom destroying the dense darkness of deceitful Jains! O King holding a spear in your lotus hand! O One who graces the Trinity, entrusting them with the three tasks of creation, preservation, and destruction! O peerless Reality absorbing all the moving and unmoving beings of the seven worlds into your feet! O Saiva gem abiding in the shrine of Thanigachalam! O Shanmuga!
commentary: Poets love to sing of Murugan as the precious son of Siva, the great god of divine madness. Here, the son is the unique medicine that cures the deep madness of human delusion. Vallalar plainly states that this brilliant gem of wisdom destroys the dense darkness of deceitful Jains. As the supreme power, he is the one who delegates the cosmic tasks of creation, preservation, and destruction to the Trinity, eventually gathering all moving and unmoving life back to his own feet.

tamil: ஏதம் அகற்றும் என்அரசே என்ஆ ருயிரே என்அறிவே
என்கண் ஒளியே என்பொருளே என்சற் குருவே என்தாயே
காத மணக்கும் மலர்கடப்பங் கண்ணிப் புயனே காங்கெயனே
கருணைக் கடலே பன்னிருகண் கரும்பே இருவர் காதலனே
சீத மதியை முடித்தசடைச் சிவனார் செல்வத் திருமகனே
திருமா லுடன்நான் முகன்மகவான் தேடிப் பணியும் சீமானே
சாதல் பிறத்தல் தவிர்த்தருளும் சரணாம் புயனே சத்தியனே
தணிகா சலமாம் தலத்தமர்ந்த சைவ மணியே சண்முகனே.
translit: ētam akaṟṟum eṉaracē eṉā ruyirē eṉaṟivē eṉkaṇ oḷiyē eṉporuḷē eṉcaṟ kuruvē eṉtāyē kāta maṇakkum malarkaṭappaṅ kaṇṇip puyaṉē kāṅkeyaṉē karuṇaik kaṭalē paṉṉirukaṇ karumpē iruvar kātalaṉē cīta matiyai muṭittacaṭaic civaṉār celvat tirumakaṉē tirumā luṭaṉnāṉ mukaṉmakavāṉ tēṭip paṇiyum cīmāṉē cātal piṟattal tavirttaruḷum caraṇām puyaṉē cattiyaṉē taṇikā calamām talattamarnta caiva maṇiyē caṇmukaṉē.
translation: My King who removes affliction, my precious life, my knowledge, the light of my eyes, my true wealth, my true Guru, my mother. You wear on your shoulders garlands of kadamba flowers fragrant for leagues, O Kangeyan. Ocean of compassion, sugarcane with twelve eyes, lover of two consorts, you are the precious son of Lord Siva whose matted hair holds the cool moon. You are the sovereign sought and worshipped by Vishnu, Brahma, and Indra. O truthful one whose lotus feet graciously abolish birth and death. O Saiva gem abiding in the shrine of Thanigachalam! O Shanmuga!
commentary: In this passage, the divine is every intimate relationship a soul can have: mother, true wealth, and the very light in the eyes. Vallalar calls upon Murugan, the son of Lord Siva, using traditional imagery of fragrant flowers and sweet sugarcane to describe his boundless compassion. This deep personal bond is what allows the soul to receive the grace that breaks the endless cycle of birth and death.

tamil: வன்பிற் பொதிந்த மனத்தினர்பால் வருந்தி உழல்வேன் அல்லால்உன்
மலர்த்தாள் நினையேன் என்னேஇம் மதியி லேனும் உய்வேனோ
அன்பிற் கிரங்கி விடமுண்டோன் அருமை மகனே ஆரமுதே
அகிலம் படைத்தோன் காத்தோன்நின் றழித்தோன் ஏத்த அளித்தோனே
துன்பிற் கிடனாம் வன்பிறப்பைத் தொலைக்கும் துணையே சுகோதயமே
தன்பிற் படும்அச் சுரர்ஆவி தரிக்க வேலைத் தரித்தோனே
தணிகா சலமாம் தலத்தமர்ந்த சைவ மணியே சண்முகனே.
translit: vaṉpiṟ potinta maṉattiṉarpāl varunti uḻalvēṉ allāluṉ malarttāḷ niṉaiyēṉ eṉṉē-im matiyi lēṉum uyvēṉō aṉpiṟ kiraṅki viṭamuṇṭōṉ arumai makaṉē āramutē akilam paṭaittōṉ kāttōṉniṉ ṟaḻittōṉ ētta aḷittōṉē tuṉpiṟ kiṭaṉām vaṉpiṟappait tolaikkum tuṇaiyē cukōtayamē tōkai mayilmēl tōṉṟuperuñcuṭarē iṭarāṟ cōrvuṟṟē taṉpiṟ paṭumac curarāvi tarikka vēlait tarittōṉē taṇikā calamām talattamarnta caiva maṇiyē caṇmukaṉē.
translation: I suffer and wander among those whose hearts are packed with cruelty, and I do not think of your lotus feet. Alas, will I, utterly lacking sense, ever be saved?
