The very first reward mentioned here is the ability to look at a starving person and feel deep pity, which is the absolute foundation of all spiritual progress. Praising sincere devotees also brings a full lifespan, inner peace, and lasting freedom from disease.

translit: vaṉperu neruppiṉaip puṉpuḻup paṟṟumō vāṉai-oru māṉtāvumō valiyuḷḷa puliyai-ōr elicīṟu mōperiya malaiyai-ōr īcciṟakiṉāl tuṉpuṟa acaikkumō vaccirat tūṇoru turumpiṉāl tuṇṭamāmō cūriyaṉai iruḷvantu cūḻumō kāṟṟilmaḻai tōyumō illai-atupōl aṉpuṭaiya niṉaṭiyar poṉaṭiyai uṉṉumavar aṭimalar muṭikkaṇintōrk kavalamuṟu mōkāmam vekuḷi-uṟu mōmaṉat taṟpamumvi kaṟpamuṟumō taṉpukaḻcey ceṉṉaiyil kantakōṭ ṭattuḷvaḷar talamōṅku kantavēḷē taṉmukat tuyyamaṇi uṉmukac caivamaṇi caṇmukat teyvamaṇiyē.
translation: Can a wretched worm grasp a fierce great fire? Can a deer leap over the sky? Can a mouse roar at a mighty tiger? Can a fly's wing violently shake a huge mountain? Can a diamond pillar be broken into pieces by a piece of straw? Can darkness come and surround the sun? Can rain soak the wind? No. In the exact same way, will misery strike those who wear upon their heads the lotus feet of those who meditate upon the golden feet of your loving devotees? Will lust or anger afflict them? Will they suffer mental pettiness or delusion? O Lord Skanda whose eminent shrine flourishes in Kandakottam in Chennai renowned for its glory. O pure gem with a cool face, O Saiva gem of the inner face, O divine gem with six faces.
commentary: It is a law of nature that a tiny fly cannot move a mountain and darkness cannot swallow the sun. In the exact same way, it is utterly impossible for misery, anger, or delusion to overcome someone who sincerely honors the devotees of God. Humbling oneself before those who live in grace acts as an absolute shield against mental suffering.

translit: kāṇaliṭai nīrumoru kaṭṭaiyil kaḷvaṉum kāṇuṟu kayiṟṟil aṟavum kaṭitaru kiḷiñciliṭai veḷḷiyum poṉṉaik katittapit taḷaiyiṉiṭaiyum māṉalil kaṇṭuḷa mayaṅkalpōl kaṟpaṉaiyai māyaiyil kaṇṭuviṇē maṉai-eṉṟum makaveṉṟum uṟaveṉṟum niti-eṉṟum vāḷveṉṟum māṉameṉṟum ūṉaliṉ uṭampeṉṟum uyireṉṟum uḷameṉṟum uḷeṉṟum veḷi-eṉṟumvāṉ ulakeṉṟum aḷavuṟuvi kāramuṟa niṉṟa-eṉai uṇmai-aṟi vittakuruvē tāṉamiku ceṉṉaiyil kantakōṭ ṭattuḷvaḷar talamōṅku kantavēḷē taṉmukat tuyyamaṇi uṉmukac caivamaṇi caṇmukat teyvamaṇiyē.
translation: Just as the deluded mind sees water in a mirage, a thief in a wooden post, a snake in a rope, silver in an oyster shell, and gold in gleaming brass, I saw mere mental constructs in illusion and vainly suffered endless modifications, constantly thinking of 'wife', 'child', 'relatives', 'wealth', 'livelihood', 'honor', 'body of flesh', 'life-breath', 'mind', 'inner', 'outer', and 'heavenly world'. O Guru who taught the truth to me as I stood in such immense confusion! O Lord Skanda whose eminent shrine flourishes in Kandakottam in highly charitable Chennai. O pure gem with a cool face, O Saiva gem of the inner face, O divine gem with six faces.
commentary: Human beings suffer deeply because they mistake passing worldly connections for permanent reality. Just as a thirsty person might see a shimmering mirage and think it is real water, the mind projects absolute value onto temporary things like family, wealth, social honor, and the physical body. Vallalar praises the divine teacher who shatters these mental illusions and reveals the enduring truth.

translit: kaṟṟoḷikoḷ uṇarviṉōr vēṇṭāta ipperuṅ kaṉmavuṭa lilparuvamnēr kaṇṭaḻiyum iḷamaitāṉ pakalvēṭa mōpuraik kaṭalnīrko lōkapaṭamō uṟṟoḷiyiṉ veyiliṭṭa mañcaḷō vāṉiṭṭa oruvilō nīrkkumiḻiyō urai-aṉal peṟakkāṟṟuḷ ūtum turattiyō uṉṟumaṟi yēṉ itaṉaināṉ paṟṟuṟuti yākkoṇṭu vaṉitayairkaṇ valaiyiṉil paṭṭumati keṭṭuḻaṉṟē pāvamē payilkiṉṟa tallātu niṉaṭip paṟṟaṇuvum uṟṟaṟikilēṉ caṟṟai-akal ceṉṉaiyil kantakōṭ ṭattuḷvaḷar talamōṅku kantavēḷē taṉmukat tuyyamaṇi uṉmukac caivamaṇi caṇmukat teyvamaṇiyē.
translation: Learned people of luminous awareness reject this gross karmic body. Is the youthfulness that appears in its season and quickly perishes merely a daytime disguise? Is it illusory sea water? Is it a deception? Is it the fading color of turmeric exposed to bright sunlight? Is it a rainbow in the sky? Is it a water bubble? Is it a bellows blowing air to kindle a roaring fire? I understand none of this. Taking this fleeting youth as permanent, I fell into the net of women's eyes, lost my mind, and wandered aimlessly. I practice nothing but sin, and I have not known even an atom of attachment to your feet. O Lord Skanda whose eminent shrine flourishes in Kandakottam in Chennai where baseness vanishes. O pure gem with a cool face, O Saiva gem of the inner face, O divine gem with six faces.
commentary: Physical youth is a passing show that wise people do not cling to. It fades as quickly as a rainbow, a water bubble, or the bright yellow of turmeric left out in the blazing sun. Believing that this temporary state will last forever traps a person in worldly desires and pulls them away from the lasting shelter of divine grace.

translit: caṭamāki iṉpam tarātāki mikuperuñ cañcalā kāramākic caṟṟāki veḷimayal paṟṟāki ōṭumit taṉmaipeṟu celvamntō viṭamāki orukapaṭa naṭamāki yāṟṟiṭai viraintucelum veḷḷamāki vēlai-alai yāki-āṅ kāravalai yākimutir vēṉiluṟu mēkamākik kaṭamāya cakaṭamuṟu kālāki nīṭuvāyk kālōṭum nīrākiyē kaṟvilā makaḷirpōl poṟpilā tuḻalumitu karutāta vakai-aruḷuvāy taṭamēvu ceṉṉaiyil kantakōṭ ṭattuḷvaḷar talamōṅku kantavēḷē taṇmukat tuyyamaṇi uṇmukac caivamaṇi caṇmukat teyvamaṇiyē.
translation: This fleeting wealth is inert and gives no joy. It takes the form of immense sorrow. It is petty and clings to external illusions as it flees. Alas, it becomes poison. It becomes a deceitful dance. It becomes a fast-rushing flood in a river. It becomes ocean waves. It becomes the net of ego. It becomes clouds in late summer. It becomes the wheel of the illusory chariot. It becomes water rushing through a long irrigation channel. Like unchaste women, it wanders devoid of beauty. Grant me the grace to not think of this wealth. O Lord Skanda whose eminent shrine flourishes in Kandakottam in Chennai surrounded by wide tanks. O pure gem with a cool face, O Saiva gem of the inner face, O divine gem with six faces.
commentary: Vallalar says that chasing material wealth is a trap that brings sorrow instead of happiness. He compares money to a rushing flood or a passing cloud, because it moves quickly and never stays in one place. Though people believe riches will give them security, he asks the divine for the grace to forget about wealth entirely.

translit: uppuṟṟa pāṇṭameṉa oṉpatu tuvārattuḷ uṟṟacum poḻukumuṭalai uyarkiṉṟa vāṉiṭai eṟintakal eṉṟummalai uṟṟiḻiyum aruvi-eṉṟum veppuṟṟa kāṟṟiṭai viḷakkeṉṟum mēkamuṟu miṉeṉṟum vīcukāṟṟiṉ mēṟpaṭṭa pañceṉṟum mañceṉṟum viṉaitanta veṟumāya vēṭameṉṟum kappuṟṟa paṟavaik kuṭampai-eṉ ṟumpoytta kaṉaveṉṟum nīrileḻutum kai-eḻut teṉṟumuṭ kaṇṭukoṇ ṭatilākai kaiviṭēṉ eṉceykuvēṉ tappaṟṟa ceṉṉaiyil kantakōṭ ṭattuḷvaḷā• talamōṅku kantavēḷē taṇmukat tuyyamaṇi uṇmukac caivamaṇi caṇmukat teyvamaṇiyē.
translation: This body leaks from nine holes like a pot of salt. I have realized inwardly that it is like a stone thrown into the high sky. It is like a waterfall rushing down a mountain. It is like a lamp caught in a hot wind. It is like lightning in a cloud. It is like cotton caught in a strong wind. It is like a passing cloud. It is an empty, illusory disguise given by karma. It is like a bird's nest on a branch. It is like a false dream. It is like letters written on water. Even though I have understood this, I do not let go of my attachment to it. What shall I do? O Lord Skanda whose eminent shrine flourishes in Kandakottam in flawless Chennai. O pure gem with a cool face, O Saiva gem of the inner face, O divine gem with six faces.
commentary: The human body is fragile and destined to end quickly. Vallalar compares it to a lamp blowing in a hot wind or a stone falling from the sky to show how little time it really has. Even though he knows perfectly well that the body is temporary, he admits the painful truth that human beings still struggle to let go of their attachment to it.

translit: entainiṉai vāḻttāta pēyarvāy kūḻukkum ēkkaṟṟi rukkumveṟuvāy eṅkaḷperu māṉuṉai vaṇaṅkāta mūṭartalai ikaḻviṟa keṭukkumtalai kantamiku niṉmēṉi kāṇāta kayavarkaṇ kalanīr corinta-aḻukaṇ kaṭavuḷniṉ pukaḻtaṉaik kēḷāta vīṇarcevi kaittiḻavu kēṭkumcevi pantamaṟa niṉai-eṇāp pāvikaḷ tamneñcam pakīreṉa naṭuṅkumneñcam paramaniṉ tirumuṉṉar kuviyāta vañcarkai pali-ēṟka nīḷkoṭuṅkai cantamiku ceṉṉaiyil kantakōṭ ṭattuḷvaḷā• talamōṅku kantavēḷē taṇmukat tuyyamaṇi uṇmukac caivamaṇi caṇmukat teyvamaṇiyē.
translation: The mouths of the fiends who do not praise You, our Father, are empty mouths yearning even for gruel. The heads of the fools who do not bow to You, our Lord, are heads that carry despised firewood. The eyes of the base men who do not behold Your fragrant form are weeping eyes pouring pots of tears. The ears of the vain men who do not listen to Your glory, O God, are ears that hear bitter news of death. The hearts of the sinners who do not think of You to sever their attachments are hearts that tremble in terror. The hands of the deceitful ones that do not join in reverence before Your divine presence, O Supreme Lord, are long, cruel hands stretched out to beg for alms. O Lord Skanda whose eminent shrine flourishes in Kandakottam in beautiful Chennai. O pure gem with a cool face, O Saiva gem of the inner face, O divine gem with six faces.
commentary: A life lived without any thought of the divine leads directly to misery and fear. Vallalar describes those who ignore God as suffering deep physical and emotional poverty, where their hands are reduced to begging and their ears hear only sorrow. He presents spiritual neglect not just as an error, but as the root cause of human suffering.

translit: aiyaniṉ cīrpēcu celvarvāy nallateḷ aḻutuṇ ṭuvantatiruvāy appaniṉ tiruvaṭi vaṇaṅkiṉōr talaimuṭi aṇintōṅki vāḻuntalai meyyaniṉ tirumēṉi kaṇṭapuṇ ṇiyarkaṇkaḷ mikka-oḷi mēvukaṇkaḷ vēlaniṉ pukaḻkēṭṭa vittakar tiruccevi viḻāccupam kēṭkumcevi tuyyaniṉ patameṇṇum mēlōrkaḷ neñcammeyc cukarūpa māṉaneñcam tōṉṟaluṉ tirumuṉ kuvittaperi yōrkaikaḷ cuvarṉṉamiṭu kiṉṟakaikaḷ caiyamuyar ceṉṉaiyil kantakōṭ ṭattuḷvaḷar talamōṅku kantavēḷē taṇmukat tuyyamaṇi uṇmukac caivamaṇi caṇmukat teyvamaṇiyē.
translation: O Master, the mouths of the blessed ones who speak Your glory are divine mouths that gladly consume clear, sweet nectar. O Father, the heads of those who bow to Your holy feet are exalted heads that wear crowns. O True One, the eyes of the virtuous who have beheld Your holy form are eyes filled with immense light. O Wielder of the Spear, the holy ears of the wise who have heard Your praise are ears that hear the auspicious sounds of festivals. The hearts of the noble ones who meditate on Your pure feet are hearts embodied in true bliss. O Chief, the hands of the great ones joined in reverence before Your holy presence are hands that give gold in charity. O Lord Skanda whose eminent shrine flourishes in Kandakottam in Chennai with mountain-like towering mansions. O pure gem with a cool face, O Saiva gem of the inner face, O divine gem with six faces.
commentary: Devotion elevates every part of a person's life. Those who turn their minds and bodies toward the divine do not just avoid suffering. Their eyes fill with light, their hearts find true joy, and their hands are empowered to give generously to others. Spiritual focus transforms ordinary human existence into a state of grace.

translit: uḻaluṟṟa uḻavumutal uṟutoḻil iyaṟṟimalam ottapala poruḷīṭṭivīṇ uṟuvayiṟu niṟaiyaveṇ cōṟaṭait tivvuṭalai otipōl vaḷarttunāḷum viḻaluṟṟa vāḻkkaiyai virumpiṉēṉ aiya-iv veyya-uṭal poyeṉkilēṉ veḷimayak kōmāya viṭamayak kō-eṉatu vitimayak kō-aṟikilēṉ kaḻaluṟṟa niṉtuṇaik kālmalar vaṇaṅkiniṉ karuṇaiyai viḻaintukoṇṭem kaḷaikaṇē īrāṟu kaṇkoṇṭa eṉṟaṉiru kaṇṇē-e ṉappukaḻkilēṉ taḻaivuṟṟa ceṉṉaiyil kantakōṭ ṭattuḷvaḷar talamōṅku kantavēḷē taṇmukat tuyyamaṇi uṇmukac caivamaṇi caṇmukat teyvamaṇiyē.
translation: I performed exhausting labors like farming and other trades. I gathered various riches that are no better than filth. I stuffed white rice to fill this vain belly and nurtured this body like a fat lizard. I desired this worthless life every single day. O Master, I do not declare that this cruel body is false. Is this the delusion of the external world, the delusion of poisonous illusion, or the delusion of my fate? I do not know. I do not bow to the pair of Your lotus feet wearing anklets. I do not yearn for Your grace and praise You, crying out that You are our Refuge and my very own two eyes who possesses twelve eyes! O Lord Skanda whose eminent shrine flourishes in Kandakottam in flourishing Chennai. O pure gem with a cool face, O Saiva gem of the inner face, O divine gem with six faces.
commentary: Most people exhaust themselves working simply to feed and maintain their physical bodies. Vallalar laments the idea of spending time gathering money and eating just to survive, comparing a well-fed body to a fat lizard. He questions why anyone would choose the delusion of this mindless worldly routine instead of crying out for divine grace.

translit: vāṉameṅ kē-amuta pāṉameṅkē amarar vāḻkkai-api māṉameṅkē māṭci-eṅ kē-avarkaḷ cūḻcci-eṅ kētēva maṉṉaṉara cāṭci-eṅkē ñāṉameṅ kēmuṉivar mōṉameṅ kē-anta nāṉmukaṉ ceykai-eṅkē nāraṇaṉ kāttalai naṭattaleṅ kēmaṟai naviṉṟiṭum oḻukkameṅkē īṉamaṅ kēceyta tārukaṉai āyira ilakkamuṟu ciṅkamukaṉai eṇariya tiṟalpeṟṟa cūraṉai maṟakkaruṇai īntupaṇi koṇṭilai-eṉil tāṉamiṅ kērceṉṉai kantakōṭ ṭattuḷvaḷar talamōṅku kantavēḷē taṇmukat tuyyamaṇi uṇmukac caivamaṇi caṇmukat teyvamaṇiyē.
translation: Where would the heaven be? Where would the drinking of nectar be? Where would the proud life of the immortals be? Where would their glory be? Where would their strategies be? Where would the rule of the king of the gods be? Where would wisdom be? Where would the silence of the sages be? Where would the creative work of Brahma with four faces be? Where would Narayana's governance of protection be? Where would the conduct prescribed by the Vedas be? All this would be lost if you had not shown fierce compassion to subdue Taruka who committed vile deeds, Singamuka with a hundred million faces, and Sura of incalculable might. O Lord Skanda whose eminent shrine flourishes in Kandakottam in charitable Chennai. O pure gem with a cool face, O Saiva gem of the inner face, O divine gem with six faces.
commentary: Sometimes divine compassion takes a fierce form to protect the world. Vallalar points to the traditional stories of Lord Skanda defeating powerful demons and sees these battles as acts of necessary mercy. Without this forceful intervention, the entire cosmic order of creation, protection, and heavenly life would have collapsed.

translit: maṉamāṉa oruciṟuvaṉ matiyāṉa kuruvaiyum matittiṭāṉ niṉ aṭiccīr makiḻkalvi kaṟṟiṭāṉ cummā-i rāṉkāma maṭuviṉiṭai vīḻntucuḻalvāṉ ciṉamāṉa veñcurat tuḻaluvaṉ ulōpamām ciṟukukaiyi ṉūṭupukuvāṉ ceṟumōka iruḷiṭaic celkuvāṉ matameṉum ceykuṉṟil ēṟiviḻuvāṉ iṉamāṉa māccariya veṅkuḻiyiṉ uḷḷē iṟaṅkuvāṉ ciṟitumantō eṉcolkē ḷāṉeṉatu kaippaṭāṉ maṟṟitaṟ kēḻaiyēṉ eṉceykuvēṉ taṉanīṭu ceṉṉaiyil kantakōṭ ṭattuḷvaḷar talamōṅku kantavēḷē taṇmukat tuyyamaṇi uṇmukac caivamaṇi caṇmukat teyvamaṇiyē.
translation: This little boy called the mind does not respect the guru of the intellect. He does not learn the joyous knowledge of the glory of your divine feet. He will not remain still. He falls into the pool of lust and swirls around. He wanders in the harsh desert of anger. He enters the small cave of miserliness. He walks into the dense darkness of delusion. He climbs the artificial hill of pride and falls down. He descends into the cruel pit of envy. Alas, he does not listen to my words even a little. He does not come under my control. What can I, a poor soul, do about this? O Lord Skanda whose eminent shrine flourishes in Kandakottam in wealthy Chennai. O pure gem with a cool face, O Saiva gem of the inner face, O divine gem with six faces.
commentary: The human mind behaves like a stubborn, unruly child who refuses to listen to the inner teacher of the intellect. Left to itself, the mind wanders away from divine joy and tumbles into destructive states like lust, anger, greed, and envy. The speaker admits total helplessness in controlling this wild inner force and turns to the divine for help.

translit: vāykoṇ ṭuraittalari teṉceykēṉ eṉceykēṉ vaḷḷaluṉ cēvaṭikkaṇ maṉṉātu poṉṉācai maṇṇācai peṇṇācai vāyntuḻalum eṉatumaṉatu pēykoṇṭu kaḷuṇṭu kōliṉāl mottuṇṭu pittuṇṭa vaṉkuraṅkō pēcuṟu kulālaṉāṟ cuḻalkiṉṟa tikiriyō pētaiviḷai yāṭupantō kāykoṇṭu pāykiṉṟa vevvilaṅ kōperuṅ kāṟṟiṉāṟ cuḻalkaṟaṅkō kālavaṭi vō-intra jālavaṭi vō-eṉatu karmavaṭi vō-aṟikilēṉ tāykoṇṭa ceṉṉaiyil kantakōṭ ṭattuḷvaḷar talamōṅku kantavēḷē taṇmukat tuyyamaṇi uṇmukac caivamaṇi caṇmukat teyvamaṇiyē.
translation: It is hard to express this with my mouth. What shall I do? What shall I do? O bountiful Lord, my mind does not remain fixed at your red feet but wanders around, caught in the desire for gold, land, and women. Is it a monkey possessed by a ghost, drunk on toddy, beaten with a stick, and driven mad? Or is it the spinning wheel of a talking potter? Or a ball played with by an innocent girl? Or a fierce beast leaping with rage? Or a top spun by a strong wind? Is it the form of time? Or the form of an illusion? Or the form of my own karma? I do not know. O Lord Skanda whose eminent shrine flourishes in Kandakottam in Chennai which has a mother's nature. O pure gem with a cool face, O Saiva gem of the inner face, O divine gem with six faces.
commentary: A mind caught in worldly desires for wealth, property, and physical pleasure is in a state of chaotic, frantic motion. It behaves like a possessed, drunken monkey or a top whipped around by a strong wind. The speaker confesses that he does not know if this inner chaos comes from past actions or simple illusion, only that he is completely powerless to stop it on his own.

translit: kaṟṟmē lavaroṭum kūṭinil lēṉkalvi kaṟkumneṟi tērntukallēṉ kaṉivukoṇ ṭuvatutiru aṭiyai-oru kaṉaviṉum karutilēṉ nallaṉallēṉ kuṟṟamē ceyvateṉ kuṇamākum apperuṅ kuṟṟamel lāmkuṇameṉak koḷḷuvatu niṉaruṭkuṇamākum eṉṉileṉ kuṟaitavirt taruḷpurikuvāy peṟṟamēl varumoru peruntakaiyiṉ aruḷurup peṟṟeḻun tōṅkucuṭarē piraṇavā kārāriṉ mayavimala corūpamē pētamil parappiramamē taṟṟakaiya ceṉṉaiyil kantakōṭ ṭattuḷvaḷar talamōṅku kantavēḷē taṇmukat tuyyamaṇi uṇmukac caivamaṇi caṇmukat teyvamaṇiyē.
translation: I do not associate with the learned and noble ones. I do not discern the path of true education and learn. I do not think with a melting heart about your divine feet even in a dream. I am not a good person. Doing wrong is my nature. If accepting all my great faults as virtues is your graceful nature, then remove my flaws and grant me your grace. O rising flame that took the graceful form of the great Lord who rides the bull! O pure form embodying the sacred syllable Om! O nondual supreme Brahman! O Lord Skanda whose eminent shrine flourishes in Kandakottam in dignified Chennai. O pure gem with a cool face, O Saiva gem of the inner face, O divine gem with six faces.
commentary: Human beings are deeply prone to error, often failing to seek out good company or remember the divine. The speaker frankly admits that doing wrong feels entirely natural to him. The plea for salvation here rests entirely on the nature of God: since the divine nature is pure grace, God can choose to accept a person's flaws as virtues and heal them completely.

translit: pāyppaṭṭa puli-aṉṉa nāyppaṭṭa kayavartam pāḻpaṭṭa maṉaiyilneṭunāḷ paṇpaṭṭa kaḻunīrum viṇpaṭṭa iṉṉamutu paṭṭapā ṭākumaṉṟip pōyppaṭṭa pullumaṇi pūppaṭṭa pāṭumnaṟ pūṇpaṭṭa pāṭutaviṭum puṉpaṭṭa umiyumuyar poṉpaṭṭa pāṭavarkaḷ pōkamoru pōkamāmō āyppaṭṭa maṟaimuṭic cēyppaṭṭa niṉaṭik kāṭpaṭṭa peruvāḻvilē aruḷpaṭṭa neṟiyummeyp poruḷpaṭṭa nilaiyumuṟa amarpōka mēpōkamām tāyppaṭṭa ceṉṉaiyil kantakōṭ ṭattuḷvaḷar talamōṅku kantavēḷē taṇmukat tuyyamaṇi uṇmukac caivamaṇi caṇmukat teyvamaṇiyē.
translation: Serving in the ruined houses of vile people, who are like leaping tigers and base dogs, for many days, is like heavenly nectar suffering the fate of discarded rice water. It is like a precious gem suffering the fate of worthless grass. It is like fine ornaments suffering the fate of fading flowers. It is like high gold suffering the fate of bran and useless husk. Is the pleasure of those vile men true pleasure? Becoming a servant to your divine feet, which are praised at the pinnacle of the thoroughly searched Vedas, and abiding in the path of grace and the state of true reality is alone the true pleasure. O Lord Skanda whose eminent shrine flourishes in Kandakottam in Chennai which has a mother's nature. O pure gem with a cool face, O Saiva gem of the inner face, O divine gem with six faces.
commentary: Chasing wealth by serving cruel and greedy people degrades the soul. It takes something precious and treats it like garbage, much like throwing away heavenly nectar or treating gold as useless husk. True joy has nothing to do with this kind of worldly success: it is found only in serving the divine and living steadily in the path of grace.

translit: cēvalam koṭikoṇṭa niṉai-aṉṟi vēṟuciṟu tēvaraic cintaiceyvōr ceṅkaṉiyai viṭṭuvēp paṅkaṉiyai uṇṇumoru ciṟukaruṅ kākkainikarvār nāvalaṅ kāramaṟa vēṟupukaḻ pēciniṉ naṟpukaḻ vaḻuttātapēr nāyppāl virumpi-āṉ tūyppālai nayavāta navaiyuṭaip pēyar āvār nīvalan taraniṉatu kuṟṟēval puriyātu niṉṟumaṟ ṟēvalpurivōr nelluk kiṟaikkātu pulluk kiṟaikkiṉṟa neṭiyaveṟu vīṇarāvār tāvalam ceṉṉaiyil kantakōṭ ṭattuḷvaḷar talamōṅku kantavēḷē taṇmukat tuyyamaṇi uṇmukac caivamaṇi caṇmukat teyvamaṇiyē.
translation: Those who think of minor deities instead of you, the Lord who holds the rooster banner, are like a small black crow that ignores a ripe, sweet fruit to eat a bitter neem fruit. Those who lose the beauty of their tongues by speaking other praises without exalting your good fame are like flawed madmen who desire a dog's milk and reject a cow's pure milk. Those who do not perform small services for you to gain strength, but instead stand performing services for others, are utterly vain fools who water weeds instead of watering the paddy crop. O Lord Skanda whose eminent shrine flourishes in Kandakottam in Chennai of enduring strength. O pure gem with a cool face, O Saiva gem of the inner face, O divine gem with six faces.
commentary: Devotion to lesser gods is a poor substitute for the supreme divine. Using stark contrasts from daily life, this verse compares choosing minor deities to eating a bitter neem fruit instead of a sweet fruit, or preferring a dog's milk to a cow's pure milk. Serving worldly ends instead of God is like wasting water on weeds instead of nourishing the actual food crop.

translit: piramaṉiṉi eṉṉaip piṟappikka vallaṉō peyciṟaiyil iṉṉumorukāl piṉpaṭṭu niṟkumō muṉpaṭṭa cūṭṭil peṟuntuyar maṟantuviṭumō iravuniṟam uṭai-ayamaṉ iṉi-eṉaik kaṉaviṉum iṟappikka eṇṇamuṟumō eṇṇuṟāṉ utai-uṇṭu citai-uṇṭa taṉuṭal iruntavaṭu eṇṇuṟāṉō karavupeṟu viṉaivantu naliyumō ataṉai-oru kācukkum matiyēṉelām kaṟṟavarkaḷ paṟṟumniṉ tiru-aruḷai yāṉum kalantiṭap peṟṟuniṉṟēṉ taramaruvu ceṉṉaiyil kantakōṭ ṭattuḷvaḷar talamōṅku kantavēḷē taṇmukat tuyyamaṇi uṇmukac caivamaṇi caṇmukat teyvamaṇiyē.
translation: Will Brahma be able to make me be born again? Will he ever stand in the prison again? Will he forget the great sorrow he suffered from the heat he previously endured? Will Yama of night-like color ever think of making me die even in a dream? He will not think of it. Does he not remember the scars on his body from being kicked and shattered? Will deceitful karma come and afflict me? I do not value it for even a single coin. I have attained and merged with your holy grace, which all learned ones hold fast. O Lord Skanda whose eminent shrine flourishes in Kandakottam in Chennai of enduring quality. O pure gem with a cool face, O Saiva gem of the inner face, O divine gem with six faces.
commentary: Merging with divine grace completely breaks the cycle of birth, death, and worldly consequence. The verse asks if Brahma (the creator god in Hindu tradition) can force another birth, or if Yama (the god of death) would dare approach. It recalls old stories where both deities were punished and scarred for overstepping their bounds. Sheltered by this ultimate grace, even the accumulated weight of past actions, known as karma, is dismissed as being worth less than a single coin.

translit: nīruṇṭu poḻikiṉṟa kāruṇṭu viḷaikiṉṟa nilaṉuṇṭu palaṉumuṇṭu niti-uṇṭu tuti-uṇṭu mati-uṇṭu katikoṇṭa neṟi-uṇṭu nilaiyum uṇṭu ūruṇṭu pēruṇṭu maṇi-uṇṭu paṇi-uṇṭu uṭai-uṇṭu koṭaiyumuṇṭu uṇṭuṇṭu makiḻavē uṇavuṇṭu cāntamuṟum uḷamuṇṭu vaḷamumuṇṭu tēruṇṭu kari-uṇṭu pari-uṇṭu maṟṟuḷḷa celvaṅkaḷ yāvumuṇṭu tēṉuṇṭu vaṇṭuṟu kaṭampaṇiyum niṉpatat tiyāṉamuṇ ṭāyilaracē tāruṇṭa ceṉṉaiyil kantakōṭ ṭattuḷvaḷar talamōṅku kantavēḷē taṇmukat tuyyamaṇi uṇmukac caivamaṇi caṇmukat teyvamaṇiyē.
translation: O King, if one gains meditation upon your feet adorned with honey-filled kadamba flowers swarming with bees, then there is water, there are rainclouds that pour down, there is yielding land, and there is a harvest. There is wealth, there is praise, there is intelligence, there is a path to liberation, and there is a steady state. There is a town, there is fame, there are jewels, there is service, there are clothes, and there is charity. There is food to eat and rejoice in, there is a peaceful heart, and there is prosperity. There are chariots, elephants, horses, and all other forms of wealth. O Lord Skanda whose eminent shrine flourishes in Kandakottam in garland-draped Chennai. O pure gem with a cool face, O Saiva gem of the inner face, O divine gem with six faces.
commentary: True meditation on the divine provides everything a person could ever need. The verse lists every kind of prosperity, from rain and fertile land to inner peace and the ultimate path to liberation. By securing a clear connection to God, both spiritual fulfillment and material abundance follow naturally.

translit: uḷameṉatu vacamniṉṟa tillai-eṉ tollaiviṉai ollaiviṭ ṭiṭavumillai uṉpatat taṉpillai eṉṟaṉak kuṟṟatuṇai uṉai-aṉṟi vēṟumillai iḷaiyaṉava ṉukkaruḷa vēṇṭumeṉ ṟuṉpāl icaikkiṉṟa pērumillai ēḻaiyava ṉukkaruḷva tēṉeṉṟuṉ etirniṉ ṟiyampukiṉ ṟōrumillai vaḷamaruvum uṉatutiru aruḷkuṟaiva tillaimēl maṟṟoru vaḻakkumillai vantirap pōrkaḷuk kilai-eṉpa tillainī vaṉmaṉat tavaṉumallai taḷarvilāc ceṉṉaiyil kantakōṭ ṭattuḷvaḷar talamōṅku kantavēḷē taṇmukat tuyyamaṇi uṇmukac caivamaṇi caṇmukat teyvamaṇiyē.
translation: My mind does not remain under my control. My ancient karma has not quickly left me. I have no love for your feet. I have no companion other than you. There is no one to speak to you on my behalf, saying that I am vulnerable and you must grant me grace. And there is no one standing before you saying that you should not grant grace to this poor fellow. Your holy grace, full of richness, never diminishes. There is no other argument beyond this. You do not say no to those who come begging. You do not have a hard heart. O Lord Skanda whose eminent shrine flourishes in Kandakottam in untiring Chennai. O pure gem with a cool face, O Saiva gem of the inner face, O divine gem with six faces.
commentary: This is a plea of total helplessness and complete trust. The speaker confesses to having a restless mind, heavy past actions, and a lack of true devotion. There is no intermediary to speak up for him, but there is also no one to stand in his way. His only hope rests entirely on the truth that God is never hard-hearted and will never turn away someone who comes begging.

translit: ettikkum eṉuḷam tittikkum iṉpamē eṉuyirk kuyirākumōr ēkamē āṉanta pōkamē yōkamē eṉperuñ celvamēnaṉ muttikku mutalāṉa mutalvaṉē meyññāṉa mūrttiyē muṭivilāta murukaṉē neṭiyamāl marukaṉē civapirāṉ muttāṭum arumaimakaṉē pattik kuvantaruḷ parintaruḷum niṉaṭip paṟṟaruḷi eṉṉai-intap paṭiyilē uḻalkiṉṟa kuṭiyilē oruvaṉāp paṇṇāmal āṇṭaruḷuvāy cattikkum nīrcceṉṉai kantakōṭ ṭattuḷvaḷar talamōṅku kantavēḷē taṇmukat tuyyamaṇi uṇmukac caivamaṇi caṇmukat teyvamaṇiyē.
translation: O bliss that tastes sweet in my heart in all directions, O One who is the life of my life, O joyous experience, O yoga, O my great wealth, O primal Lord who is the source of true liberation, O form of true knowledge, O endless Murugan, O nephew of tall Vishnu, O precious son kissed by Lord Siva. Grant me the grasp of your feet that lovingly bestow grace upon devotion, and rule me, saving me from becoming just another person wandering endlessly on this earth. O Lord Skanda whose eminent shrine flourishes in Kandakottam in Chennai bounded by resounding waters. O pure gem with a cool face, O Saiva gem of the inner face, O divine gem with six faces.
commentary: Knowing the divine means experiencing a sweet joy that becomes the very life of your own life. The verse addresses the Lord as the source of all true knowledge and liberation. The final prayer is a direct appeal for this grace, asking to be saved from wandering endlessly and aimlessly like just another person caught up in the turning wheel of worldly life.

translit: nāṉkoṇṭa viratamniṉ aṭi-alāl piṟartammai nāṭāmai ākuminta nalvirata māmkaṉiyai iṉmai-eṉum orutuṭṭa nāyvantu kavvi-antō tāṉkoṇṭu pōvatiṉi eṉceyvēṉ eṉceyvēṉ taḷarāmai eṉṉumorukait taṭikoṇ ṭaṭikkavō valiyilēṉ ciṟiyaṉēṉ taṉmukam pārttaruḷuvāy vāṉkoṇṭa teḷamuta vāriyē mikukaruṉai maḻaiyē maḻaikkoṇṭalē vaḷḷalē eṉirukaṇ maṇiyē-eṉ iṉpamē mayilēṟu māṇikkamē tāṉkoṇṭa ceṉṉaiyil kantakōṭ ṭattuḷvaḷar talamōṅku kantavēḷē taṇmukat tuyyamaṇi uṇmukac caivamaṇi caṇmukat teyvamaṇiyē.
translation: The vow I have taken is to seek no one but your feet. Alas, a wicked dog called poverty has come and snatched the great fruit of this good vow in its jaws. It carries it away. What will I do now? What will I do? I am small and weak. I lack the strength to take up the hand-stick called untiring resolve and beat that dog. Please look upon my face and bestow your grace. O ocean of clear nectar from the sky. O abundant rain of compassion. O rain cloud. O benevolent Lord. O pupil of my two eyes. O my joy. O ruby who mounts the peacock. O Lord Skanda whose eminent shrine flourishes in Kandakottam in glorious Chennai. O pure gem with a cool face, O Saiva gem of the inner face, O divine gem with six faces.
commentary: Severe poverty threatens to destroy the vow to rely completely on God. The poem compares spiritual devotion to a precious fruit and poverty to a wild dog that suddenly snatches it away. The speaker confesses a lack of inner strength, described as a sturdy stick of resolve, to fight off the desperation of being poor. Unable to drive the dog away alone, he cries out to the divine for help. This captures the raw vulnerability of a spiritual seeker facing harsh worldly survival.

sections.title: Ten Verses of Surrender to Kandan

translit: aruḷār amutē caraṇam caraṇam aḻakā amalā caraṇam caraṇam poruḷā eṉai-āḷ puṉitā caraṇam poṉṉē maṇiyē caraṇam caraṇam maruḷvārk kariyāy caraṇam caraṇam mayilvā kaṉaṉē caraṇam caraṇam karuṇā layaṉē caraṇam caraṇam kantā caraṇam caraṇam caraṇam
translation: O nectar full of grace, I surrender, I surrender. O beautiful one, O pure one, I surrender, I surrender. O holy one who values and rules me, I surrender. O gold, O jewel, I surrender, I surrender. O rare one to the deluded, I surrender, I surrender. O rider of the peacock, I surrender, I surrender. O temple of compassion, I surrender, I surrender. O Kanda, I surrender, I surrender, I surrender.
commentary: Devotion here takes the form of absolute surrender. The word caraṇam means taking refuge at the feet of the divine. The speaker addresses God as Kanda, the compassionate rider of the peacock. While worldly delusion makes God seem distant and rare, a heart full of love finds him to be a pure, guiding light.

translit: paṇṇēr maṟaiyiṉ payaṉē caraṇam patiyē paramē caraṇam caraṇam viṇṇēr oḷiyē veḷiyē caraṇam veḷiyiṉ viḷaivē caraṇam caraṇam uṇṇēr uyirē uṇarvē caraṇam uruvē aruvē uṟavē caraṇam kaṇṇē maṇiyē caraṇam caraṇam kantā caraṇam caraṇam caraṇam
translation: O fruit of the musical Vedas, I surrender. O Lord, O Supreme One, I surrender, I surrender. O light matching the sky, O vast space, I surrender. O harvest of the vast space, I surrender, I surrender. O inner life, O inner awareness, I surrender. O form, O formless one, O my kin, I surrender. O my eye, O apple of my eye, I surrender, I surrender. O Kanda, I surrender, I surrender, I surrender.
commentary: God is both the vast cosmos outside and the intimate life within. The verse describes Kanda as the essence of the sacred scriptures and the limitless space of reality itself. At the same time, this supreme Lord is the inner awareness and the very apple of the devotee's eye. Form and formlessness dissolve into a single loving presence.

translit: muṭiyā mutalē caraṇam caraṇam murukā kumarā caraṇam caraṇam vaṭivēl aracē caraṇam caraṇam mayilūr maṇiyē caraṇam caraṇam aṭiyārk keḷiyāy caraṇam caraṇam ariyāy periyāy caraṇam caraṇam kaṭiyāk katiyē caraṇam caraṇam kantā caraṇam caraṇam caraṇam
translation: O endless source, I surrender, I surrender. O Murugan, O Kumara, I surrender, I surrender. O king with the sharp spear, I surrender, I surrender. O jewel riding the peacock, I surrender, I surrender. O one easily reached by devotees, I surrender, I surrender. O rare one, O great one, I surrender, I surrender. O unfailing destination, I surrender, I surrender. O Kanda, I surrender, I surrender, I surrender.
commentary: The divine is the origin of everything, yet remains entirely within reach. The verse invokes traditional names for the youthful God: Murugan, Kumara, and Kanda. He is pictured holding the sharp spear (vel), a symbol of piercing wisdom. Though he is the supreme and endless source, he makes himself easily accessible to anyone who approaches with a sincere heart.

translit: pūvē maṇamē caraṇam caraṇam poruḷē aruḷē caraṇam caraṇam kōvē kukaṉē caraṇam caraṇam kuruvē tiruvē caraṇam caraṇam tēvē teḷivē caraṇam caraṇam civacaṇ mukaṉē caraṇam caraṇam kāvēr taruvē caraṇam caraṇam kantā caraṇam caraṇam caraṇam
translation: O flower, O fragrance, I surrender, I surrender. O substance, O grace, I surrender, I surrender. O king, O Guha, I surrender, I surrender. O Guru, O divine wealth, I surrender, I surrender. O God, O clarity, I surrender, I surrender. O Siva Shanmuga, I surrender, I surrender. O giving tree matching the divine grove, I surrender, I surrender. O Kanda, I surrender, I surrender, I surrender.
commentary: God and his grace are completely inseparable. Just as you cannot have a flower without its fragrance, you cannot have the divine reality without its overflowing grace. The verse uses familiar titles like Guha (the one dwelling deep in the heart's cave) and Shanmuga (the six-faced Lord). He is the ultimate teacher and the divine wealth that clears away all confusion.

translit: naṭavum taṉimā mayilōy caraṇam nallār pukaḻum vallōy caraṇam tiṭamum tiruvum taruvōy caraṇam tēvark kariyāy caraṇam caraṇam taṭavaṇ puyaṉē caraṇam caraṇam taṉimā mutalē caraṇam caraṇam kaṭavuḷ maṇiyē caraṇam caraṇam kantā caraṇam caraṇam caraṇam
translation: O driver of the unique great peacock, I surrender. O mighty one whom the good praise, I surrender. O giver of strength and wealth, I surrender. O rare one to the gods, I surrender, I surrender. O one with broad generous shoulders, I surrender, I surrender. O unique great source, I surrender, I surrender. O divine jewel, I surrender, I surrender. O Kanda, I surrender, I surrender, I surrender.
commentary: Total reliance on God brings both strength and spiritual wealth. The speaker praises the Lord's broad, generous shoulders, which are a traditional image of his readiness to protect and give abundantly. Even though the highest celestial beings struggle to understand him, he stands as a unique, powerful guide for those who surrender their lives to his care.

translit: kōlak kuṟamāṉ kaṇavā caraṇam kulamā maṇiyē caraṇam caraṇam cīlat tavaruk karuḷvōycaraṇam civaṉār putalvā caraṇam caraṇam ñālat tuyartīr nalaṉē caraṇam naṭuvā kiyanal oḷiyē caraṇam kālaṉ teṟuvōy caraṇam caraṇam kantā caraṇam caraṇam caraṇam
translation: Refuge, husband of the beautiful deer-like maid of the Kurava tribe! Refuge, refuge, great jewel of the lineage! Refuge, You who bestow grace upon those of virtuous conduct! Refuge, refuge, son of Lord Siva! Refuge, goodness that cures the sorrow of the earth! Refuge, good light that stands at the center! Refuge, refuge, You who destroy Death! O Kanda, I surrender, I surrender, I surrender.
commentary: Skanda is celebrated here as both the approachable husband of a hill-tribe woman and the mighty conqueror of death. The "deer-like maid of the Kurava tribe" refers to Valli, a hunter's daughter who became Skanda's beloved consort. By calling him the son of Siva (the supreme deity of grace and destruction) and the central light, this verse presents him as a cosmic force who cures the sorrows of the world.

translit: naṅkaṭ kiḷiyāy caraṇam caraṇam nantā uyarcam pantā caraṇam tiṅkaṭ caṭaiyāṉ makaṉē caraṇam civaitan taruḷum putalvā caraṇam tuṅkac cukamnaṉ ṟaruḷvōy caraṇam curarvāḻt tiṭunam turaiyē caraṇam kaṅkaik korumā matalāy caraṇam kantā caraṇam caraṇam caraṇam
translation: Refuge, refuge, You who are an endearing parrot to us! Refuge, unfailing and supreme Sambandha! Refuge, son of the Lord wearing the crescent moon in His matted hair! Refuge, son gracefully borne by Sivai! Refuge, You who graciously grant supreme bliss! Refuge, our Lord praised by the celestials! Refuge, the incomparable great child of the river Ganga! O Kanda, I surrender, I surrender, I surrender.
commentary: The divine child is described through the different ways he was nurtured. Skanda was carried by the sacred river Ganga (the Ganges) before being formed, and he is the beloved son of Sivai (the goddess Parvati) and Siva, who is recognized by the moon in his tangled hair. Calling him Sambandha connects him to the famous child-saint of South India, who is traditionally viewed as an earthly incarnation of Skanda himself.

translit: oḷiyuḷ oḷiyē caraṇam caraṇam oṉṟē palavē caraṇam caraṇam teḷiyum teruḷē caraṇam caraṇam civamē tavamē caraṇam caraṇam aḷiyum kaṉiyē caraṇam caraṇam amutē aṟivē caraṇam caraṇam kaḷiyoṉ ṟaruḷvōy caraṇam caraṇam kantā caraṇam caraṇam caraṇam
translation: Refuge, refuge, light within the light! Refuge, refuge, the one and the many! Refuge, refuge, clear wisdom! Refuge, refuge, the supreme Sivam and penance! Refuge, refuge, sweet ripening fruit! Refuge, refuge, ambrosia and intelligence! Refuge, refuge, You who grant peerless joy! O Kanda, I surrender, I surrender, I surrender.
commentary: The physical forms of the young god dissolve here into pure spiritual concepts. Skanda becomes the light within all light, representing the underlying reality that is simultaneously one single truth and the many forms of the universe. He is described as Sivam (the ultimate state of spiritual purity) and sweet ambrosia, offering the seeker both clear wisdom and absolute joy.

translit: maṉṉē eṉai-āḷ varatā caraṇam matiyē aṭiyēṉ vāḻvē caraṇam poṉṉē puṉitā caraṇam caraṇam pukaḻvār itayam pukuvāy caraṇam aṉṉē vaṭivēl aracē caraṇam aṟumā mukaṉē caraṇam caraṇam kaṉṉēr puyaṉē caraṇam caraṇam kantā caraṇam caraṇam caraṇam
translation: Refuge, O King, the benefactor who governs me! Refuge, O moon of wisdom, the life of this servant! Refuge, refuge, O gold, O pure one! Refuge, You who enter the hearts of those who praise You! Refuge, O mother, O King wielding the sharp spear! Refuge, refuge, O great six-faced Lord! Refuge, refuge, You with shoulders strong as stone! O Kanda, I surrender, I surrender, I surrender.
commentary: The poet approaches the divine with deep personal intimacy, calling the warrior god with stone-like shoulders his mother, his king, and his very life. Skanda is famously depicted with six faces and carrying a sharp spear that symbolizes piercing wisdom. Despite this martial and majestic imagery, he is a gentle presence who willingly enters the hearts of those who sing his praise.

translit: vētap poruḷē caraṇam caraṇam viṇṇōr perumāḷ caraṇam caraṇam pōtat tiṟaṉē caraṇam caraṇam puṉaimā mayilōy caraṇam caraṇam nātat toliyē caraṇam caraṇam navai-il lavaṉē caraṇam caraṇam kātuk kiṉitām pukaḻōy caraṇam kantā caraṇam caraṇam caraṇam
translation: Refuge, refuge, meaning of the Vedas! Refuge, refuge, Lord of the heavenly beings! Refuge, refuge, power of true wisdom! Refuge, refuge, You who ride the adorned great peacock! Refuge, refuge, sound of the primal vibration! Refuge, refuge, You who are free from flaws! Refuge, You whose fame is sweet to the ears! O Kanda, I surrender, I surrender, I surrender.
commentary: The hymn closes by linking Skanda to the very foundations of the cosmos. He is the true meaning hidden within the Vedas (the ancient sacred scriptures) and the source of the primal sound that vibrated at the dawn of creation. Seated on his magnificent peacock mount, he rules the heavens as the flawless embodiment of wisdom itself.

tamil: வெம்பு முயிருக் கோருறவாய் வேளை நமனும் வருவானேல்
தம்பி தமையன் துணையாமோ தனையர் மனைவி வருவாரோ
உம்பர் பரவுந் திருத்தணிகை உயர்மா மலைமே லிருப்பவர்க்குத்
தும்பைக் குடலை எடுக்காமல் துக்க வுடலை எடுத்தேனே.
translit: vempu muyiruk kōruṟavāy vēḷai namaṉum varuvāṉēl tampi tamaiyaṉ tuṇaiyāmō taṉaiyar maṉaivi varuvārō umpar paravun tiruttaṇikai uyarmā malaimē liruppavarkkut tumpaik kuṭalai eṭukkāmal tukka vuṭalai eṭuttēṉē.
translation: If Yama comes at the appointed time claiming to be the only kin to this distressed soul, will an elder or younger brother offer help? Will sons or a wife come along? Instead of carrying a basket of Thumbai flowers for the Lord who dwells on the great high mountain of holy Thanigai praised by the celestials, I have taken up this body of sorrow.
commentary: At the moment of death, no family member can step in to help or accompany the departing soul. Yama is the god of death, and when he arrives, all worldly attachments prove useless. The verse contrasts two kinds of burdens. The poet regrets carrying the heavy weight of a physical body born for sorrow, rather than carrying a simple basket of white thumbai flowers in devotion to the Lord at Thanigai.

tamil: தொல்லைக் குடும்பத் துயரதனில் தொலைத்தே னந்தோ காலமெலாம்
அல்ல லகற்றிப் பெரியோரை யடுத்து மறியேன் அரும்பாவி
செல்லத் தணிகைத் திருமலைவாழ் தேவா உன்றன் சந்நிதிக்கு
வில்வக் குடலை எடுக்காமல் வீணுக் குடலை எடுத்தேனே.
translit: tollaik kuṭumpat tuyarataṉil tolaittē ṉantō kālamelām alla lakaṟṟip periyōrai yaṭuttu maṟiyēṉ arumpāvi cellat taṇikait tirumalaivāḻ tēvā uṉṟaṉ cannitikku vilvak kuṭalai eṭukkāmal vīṇuk kuṭalai eṭuttēṉē.
translation: Alas, I wasted all my time in the miseries of family life. A great sinner, I have not learned to dispel my distress and approach the great ones. O God dwelling on the prosperous holy mountain of Thanigai, instead of carrying a basket of Vilva leaves to Your presence, I have taken up this useless body.
commentary: The demands and miseries of family life consume our time and keep us from seeking wise guides. Here, the missed opportunity for devotion is carrying a basket of sacred vilva leaves. A human body becomes a useless burden if it is entirely spent on domestic struggles rather than a spiritual connection.

tamil: அவல வயிற்றை வளர்ப்பதற்கே அல்லும் பகலும் அதினினைவாய்க்
கவலைப் படுவ தன்றிசிவ கனியைச் சேரக் கருதுகிலேன்
திவலை யொழிக்குந் திருத்தணிகைத் திருமால் மருகன் திருத்தாட்குக்
குவளைக் குடலை எடுக்காமற் கொழுத்த வுடலை எடுத்தேனே.
translit: avala vayiṟṟai vaḷarppataṟkē allum pakalum atiṉiṉaivāyk kavalaip paṭuva taṉṟiciva kaṉiyaic cērak karutukilēṉ tivalai yoḻikkun tiruttaṇikait tirumāl marukaṉ tiruttāṭkuk kuvaḷaik kuṭalai eṭukkāmaṟ koḻutta vuṭalai eṭuttēṉē.
translation: Day and night, my mind is fixed solely on feeding this miserable stomach. I worry only about that, and I never think of reaching the supreme fruit of Siva. Instead of carrying a basket of Kuvalai flowers for the holy feet of Vishnu's nephew in holy Thanigai which dispels all taint, I have taken up this fattened body.
commentary: Obsession with daily survival reduces life to a constant anxiety about feeding the stomach. This fixation blinds a person to the ultimate spiritual reward, called here the supreme fruit of Siva. Murugan is traditionally known as Vishnu's nephew. The verse repeats the central lament: building up a fattened physical body is a tragic waste compared to carrying a light basket of kuvalai (water lily) blossoms for the divine.

sections.title: The Kommi Dance for Lord Shanmuga

translit: kuṟavar kuṭicai nuḻaintāṇṭi - antak kōmāṭṭi eccil viḻaintāṇṭi tuṟavar vaṇaṅkum pukaḻāṇṭi - avaṉ tōṟṟattaip pāṭi aṭiyuṅkaṭi.
translation: He entered the hut of the Kurava tribe. He desired the half-eaten food of that noble lady. He holds the glory worshipped by renunciates. Girls, sing of his majestic appearance and clap your hands.
commentary: The song opens with a famous story of Murugan disguising himself to win the love of Valli, a young woman from a forest tribe. By eagerly eating food she had already tasted, the supreme god worshipped by strict ascetics shows that pure love matters far more than traditional rules of ritual purity.

translit: māmayil ēṟi varuvāṇṭi - aṉpar vāḻtta varaṅkaḷ taruvāṇṭi tīmaiyi lāta pukaḻāṇṭi - avaṉ cīrttiyaip pāṭi aṭiyuṅkaṭi.
translation: He comes riding a great peacock. He grants boons when devotees praise him. He holds flawless fame. Girls, sing of his renown and clap your hands.
commentary: The women sing of Murugan's grace and his readiness to bless those who approach him with love. Riding his traditional peacock mount, he acts as a faultless protector of his devotees.

translit: paṉṉiru tōḷkaḷ uṭaiyāṇṭi - koṭum pāvikaḷ tammai aṭaiyāṇṭi eṉṉiru kaṇkaḷ aṉaiyāṇṭi - avaṉ ēṟṟattaip pāṭi aṭiyuṅkaṭi.
translation: He has twelve shoulders. He does not associate with cruel sinners. He is like my own two eyes. Girls, sing of his greatness and clap your hands.
commentary: Murugan is often depicted with six faces and twelve arms, representing his vast power and his ability to act in all directions. Though he is a fierce judge who rejects the cruel, to the devoted speaker he is as dear and essential as her own eyesight.

translit: vēṅkai maramāki niṉṟāṇṭi - vanta vēṭar tamai-elām veṉṟāṇṭi tīṅkucey cūraṉaik koṉṟāṇṭi - antat tīraṉaip pāṭi aṭiyuṅkaṭi.
translation: He stood disguised as a vengai tree. He conquered all the hunters who came. He killed the evil Surapadman. Girls, sing of that brave warrior and clap your hands.
commentary: This verse recounts two of Murugan's greatest legends side by side. He turned himself into a beautiful vengai tree to playfully deceive Valli's family in the forest, and he also acted as the supreme cosmic warrior who destroyed the terrible demon Surapadman.

translit: cīrtikaḻ tōkai mayilmēlē - iḷañ ceñcuṭar tōṉṟun tiṟampōlē kūrvaṭi vēlkoṇṭu namperumāṉ - varuṅ kōlattaip pāruṅkaḷ kōtaiyarkāḷ.
translation: Holding his sharp and beautiful spear, our Lord arrives upon a glorious plumed peacock, resembling the rising of a young red sun. Look at his majestic form, O women with lovely hair.
commentary: The imagery shifts to pure radiance, comparing the arrival of the spear-wielding god to a bright red sunrise. The speaker asks her friends to pause their dance and simply witness his breathtaking beauty.

translit: āṟu mukaṅkaḷil puṉcirippum - iraṇ ṭāṟu puyantikaḻ aṟputamum vīṟu parañcuṭar vaṇṇamumōr - tiru mēṉiyum pāruṅkaḷ veḷvaḷaikāḷ.
translation: Look, O girls with white bangles, at the gentle smile on his six faces, the marvel of his twelve radiant arms, the majestic color of the supreme flame, and his incomparable sacred form.
commentary: The speaker addresses her companions, a traditional device in Tamil folk poetry, asking them to visualize the majestic form of Lord Murugan. He appears with his customary six faces and twelve arms. Yet he also shines with the colour of the supreme flame, pointing to his identity as the absolute light.

translit: āṉanta māṉa amutaṉaṭi - para māṉanta nāṭṭuk karacaṉaṭi tāṉanta millāc caturaṉaṭi - civa caṇmukaṉ naṅkuru cāmiyaṭi.
translation: Friend, he is the nectar of bliss. He is the king of the realm of supreme bliss. He is the infinitely capable one. Lord Siva Shanmuga is our Guru.
commentary: The divine appears here as the ultimate teacher and the direct source of pure joy. By calling him the king of supreme bliss, the verse shows that his realm offers complete sweetness and freedom. He serves as the infinite guide for the waking soul.

translit: vētamuṭi collum nātaṉaṭi - catur vētamu ṭitikaḻ pātaṉaṭi nāta vaṭivukoḷ nītaṉaṭi - para nātaṅ kaṭanta nalattaṉaṭi.
translation: Friend, he is the Lord proclaimed by the crown of the Vedas. His feet shine upon the peaks of the four Vedas. He is the righteous one whose form is the primal sound. He embodies the goodness that transcends the supreme sound.
commentary: The highest spiritual reality stands above even the most sacred texts. The Vedas are the ancient scriptures of India, and this Lord rests firmly above their very highest teachings. He takes the form of the first cosmic sound, and he also stretches far beyond it into absolute stillness.

translit: tattuvat tuḷḷē aṭaṅkāṇṭi - para tattuvam aṉṟit tuṭaṅkāṇṭi cattuva ñāṉa vaṭivāṇṭi - civa caṇmuka nātaṉaip pāṭuṅkaṭi.
translation: Friend, he cannot be contained within the fundamental principles of nature. He acts only from the supreme truth. His form is pure spiritual wisdom. Sing of Lord Siva Shanmuga, O friends.
commentary: The supreme being cannot be measured by the tattvas, the basic building blocks of physical and mental reality. Instead of being made of material elements, his entire form consists of pure spiritual wisdom. The speaker invites her friends to sing his praises because he acts only from this absolute truth.

translit: caccitā ṉanta uruvāṇṭi - para taṟpara pōkan taruvāṇṭi uccitāḻ aṉpark kuṟavāṇṭi - anta uttama tēvaṉaip pāṭuṅkaṭi.
translation: Friend, his form is existence, consciousness, and bliss. He grants the supreme transcendent joy. He is close kin to the devotees who bow their heads in worship. Sing of that supreme God, O friends.
commentary: The phrase 'existence, consciousness, and bliss' translates the ancient concept of satchidananda, describing the pure nature of the supreme reality. He gives this ultimate joy freely to anyone who approaches him with a bowed head and a loving heart. Far from being a distant ruler, God acts as close kin to those who surrender in love.

translit: aṟputa māṉa aḻakaṉaṭi - tuti aṉpark karuḷcey kuḻakaṉaṭi ciṟpara yōkat tiṟattaṉaṭi-antac cēvakaṉ cīrttiyaip pāṭuṅkaṭi.
translation: He is a wondrously beautiful one, O friends. He is the youthful one who bestows grace upon the devotees who praise him. He embodies the supreme yoga of consciousness. Sing the fame of that warrior, O friends!
commentary: The divine is presented as a beautiful, youthful warrior who grants grace to those who sing his praises. His very nature is the highest state of conscious union, completely open to the devotion of his friends.

translit: caivan taḻaikkat taḻaittāṇṭi -ñāṉa campantap pērkoṇ ṭaḻaittāṇṭi poyvanta uḷḷattil pōkāṇṭi - antap puṇṇiyaṉ poṉṉaṭi pōṟṟuṅkaṭi.
translation: He flourished so that the Saiva path would flourish, O friends. He is called by the name of Jnana Sambandar. He will not enter a heart filled with falsehood. Praise the golden feet of that meritorious one, O friends!
commentary: Truthfulness is the strict condition for receiving the divine. Vallalar connects God with the famous child-saint Jnana Sambandar (a seventh-century poet who revived the Saiva path of worshipping Lord Siva), showing that God will only enter a heart completely free of deceit.

translit: vāci naṭattit taruvāṇṭi - oru vāciyil iṅkē varuvāṇṭi ācil karuṇai uruvāṇṭi - avaṉ aṟputat tāḷmalar ēttuṅkaṭi.
translation: He governs the breath and bestows it, O friends. He comes here upon a unique steed, O friends. He is the embodiment of flawless compassion. Praise his wondrous lotus feet, O friends!
commentary: God is the source and controller of the very breath in our bodies. The Tamil word for breath (vāci) also means a horse, creating a poetic image of the divine riding into the worshipper upon the breath itself. Ultimately, his true form is pure, flawless compassion.

translit: irāppakal illā iṭattāṇṭi - aṉpar iṉpa uḷaṅkoḷ naṭattāṇṭi arāppaḷi īnta tiṭattāṇṭi - anta aṇṇalaip pāṭi aṭiyuṅkaṭi.
translation: He dwells in the space without night or day, O friends. He performs his dance in the joyful hearts of devotees. He is firmly established in Arappalli. Sing of that Lord and clap your hands, O friends!
commentary: The divine exists in a state completely beyond time, described here as a space with no night or day. Yet this timeless God is intimately present, dancing directly inside the joyful hearts of those who love him. He is also praised as the deity residing in Arappalli (a sacred temple in the Kolli Hills of Tamil Nadu).

translit: oṉṟiraṇ ṭāṉa uḷavāṇṭi - anta oṉṟiraṇ ṭākā aḷavāṇṭi miṉtiraṇ ṭaṉṉa vaṭivāṇṭi - anta mēlavaṉ cīrttiyaip pāṭuṅkaṭi.
translation: He is the secret that became one and two, O friends. He is the measure that becomes neither one nor two. He possesses a form like a gathered mass of lightning. Sing the fame of that supreme one, O friends!
commentary: God is the ultimate mystery of existence, appearing as both the single source and the diverse world of duality. At the same time, he is beyond all human categories of numbers and logic entirely. His true form is pure, intense light, shining like a concentrated mass of lightning.

translit: vārum vārumteyva vaṭivēl murukarē vaḷḷi maṇāḷarē vārum puḷḷi mayilōrē vārum.
translation: Come, come, Murugar with the divine sharp spear! Come, husband of Valli! Come, rider of the spotted peacock!
commentary: The poet urgently invites the deity Murugan to make himself present. He addresses him using his most famous traditional symbols: his divine spear, his earth-born wife Valli, and his chosen mount, the spotted peacock.

translit: caṅkam olittatu tāḻkaṭal vimmiṟṟu caṇmuka nātarē vārum uṇmai viṉōtarē vārum.
translation: The conch has sounded and the deep sea has swelled. Come, Lord Shanmugar! Come, performer of true wonders!
commentary: The stirring sounds of the temple and the ocean signal the time for morning worship. Vallalar calls upon the deity as Shanmugar (the six-faced Lord), asking this performer of true miracles to come forward as the temple conch blows and the sea tide swells.

translit: poḻutu viṭintatu poṟkōḻi kūviṟṟu poṉṉāṉa vēlarē vārum miṉṉārmun nūlarē vārum.
translation: Dawn has broken and the golden rooster has crowed. Come, golden Lord of the spear! Come, wearer of the shining sacred thread!
commentary: Daylight breaks with the crowing of a golden rooster, a creature that is also the traditional emblem on Murugan's battle flag. Vallalar asks the golden Lord, wearing the sacred thread of spiritual initiation across his chest, to reveal himself.

translit: kākam karaintatu kālaiyum āyiṟṟu kaṇṇutal cēyarē vārum oṇṇutal nēyarē vārum.
translation: The crow has cawed and morning has arrived. Come, child of the Lord with the forehead eye! Come, lover of the bright-foreheaded woman!
commentary: The everyday cawing of a crow announces the morning and prompts another call to the divine child. Vallalar addresses Murugan as the son of Siva, referring to Siva as the Lord with the third eye on his forehead.

translit: ceṅkatir tōṉṟiṟṟut tēvarkaḷ cūḻntaṉar ceṅkalva rāyarē vārum eṅkuru nātarē vārum.
translation: The red sun has appeared and the celestials have gathered. Come, Lord Chengalvarayar! Come, our Lord and Guru!
commentary: The rising red sun brings a gathering of heavenly beings eager to see the deity. Vallalar calls upon Murugan by the local name Chengalvarayar, addressing him directly as his supreme spiritual teacher (Guru).

translit: aruṇaṉ utittaṉaṉ aṉparkaḷ cūḻntaṉar āṟumukat tōrē vārum māṟilakat tōrē vārum.
translation: The morning sun has risen. Devotees have gathered around. O six-faced Lord, come. O Lord of the flawless heart, come.
commentary: The morning awakening of the deity continues as the sun comes up. The devotees call out to Murugan, the six-faced god. They ask him to bring his perfect, flawless presence to bless those who have gathered in the early dawn.

translit: cūriyaṉ tōṉṟiṉaṉ toṇṭarkaḷ cūḻntaṉar cūracaṅ kārarē vārum vīraciṅ kārarē vārum .
translation: The sun has appeared. Your servants have gathered around. O destroyer of Sura, come. O beautifully adorned warrior, come.
commentary: As the sun fully appears, the servants stand ready. The song addresses Murugan as the warrior who destroyed the demon Sura. The devotees praise his battle adornments and call him to come forward.

translit: vīṇai muraṉṟatu vētiyar cūḻntaṉar vēlāyutat tōrē vārum kālāyutat tōrē vārum.
translation: The veena has sounded. The Vedic scholars have gathered around. O Lord wielding the spear, come. O Lord with the rooster, come.
commentary: Sacred music from the veena fills the air as scholars gather to chant. The Lord is called by his most famous symbols: the spear he carries and the rooster on his battle flag. These symbols represent his power and his readiness to protect his devotees.

translit: cēval olittatu ciṉṉam piṭittaṉar tēvarkaḷ tēvarē vārum mūvar mutalvarē vārum.
translation: The rooster has crowed. They have taken up the trumpets. O God of gods, come. O primal Lord of the three, come.
commentary: The natural world joins the temple instruments as a rooster crows and ceremonial trumpets sound. The verse elevates Murugan above all others, calling him the supreme God. He is praised as the source even above the three main deities of Hinduism (Brahma, Vishnu, and Siva).

translit: pattarkaḷ cūḻntaṉar pāṭal payiṉṟaṉar paṉṉiru tōḷarē vārum poṉmalart tāḷarē vārum.
translation: Devotees have gathered around. They have sung their songs. O twelve-shouldered Lord, come. O Lord with golden flower-like feet, come.
commentary: The morning gathering is complete as the devotees sing their songs. They praise his twelve shoulders, which match his six faces and show his immense strength. They call upon his golden feet, asking for his grace to begin the day.

translit: mālai koṇarntaṉar mañcaṉam pōntatu māmayil vīrarē vārum tīmaiyil tīrarē vārum.
translation: They have brought the garland. The sacred bath has arrived. O warrior on the great peacock, come. O hero who conquers evil, come.
commentary: The physical preparations for worship are complete and waiting. Devotees have gathered the flower garland and the water for the sacred bath to honor the divine. The song calls out to the Lord in his traditional form as the warrior who rides a great peacock, asking him to arrive and vanquish all evil.

translit: toṇṭarkaḷ nāṭiṉar tōttiram pāṭiṉar cuppira maṇiyarē vārum vaippiṉ aṇiyarē vārum.
translation: The devotees seek you and sing hymns of praise. O Subramanya, come. O jewel of our treasure, come.
commentary: The gathered devotees pour their hearts into song as they actively seek the divine presence. They call upon Subramanya (a traditional name for the divine as a radiant, youthful Lord) to come to them. To these seekers, the presence of God is a deeply cherished jewel and their greatest treasure.

translit: vaṉmūṭṭaip pūcciyum puṉcīlaip pēṉumtam vāykkoḷḷiyāl eṉmūṭṭait tēkam cuṟukkiṭa vēcuṭ ṭirāmuḻutum toṉmūṭ ṭaiyiṉum tuṇiyiṉum pāyiṉum cūḻkiṉṟatōr poṉmūṭṭai vēṇṭi-eṉ ceykēṉ aruḷmukkaṭ puṇṇiyaṉē.
translation: Fierce bedbugs and lice in wretched rags sting my bundled body with their fiery mouths, burning me all night long. Seeking a bag of gold, I wallow amidst old bundles, rags, and mats. What shall I do, O gracious and virtuous Lord with three eyes?
commentary: The physical discomforts of poverty and the endless search for wealth deeply distract the mind from God. Vallalar describes the harsh reality of sleeping among bugs in dirty rags while still obsessing over a bag of gold. He asks the divine how he can ever escape this miserable, degrading cycle to find true grace.

translit: māṉmuṭimē lumkamalat tāṉmuṭimē lumtēvar kōṉmuṭimē lumpōyk kulāvumē - vāṉmuṭinīr ūrntuvalam ceytoḻukum oṟṟiyūrt tiyākarainām cārntuvalam ceykālkaḷ tām.
translation: The feet that approach and circumambulate Lord Thyagar of Otriyur, a city where heavenly waters flow around in reverence, will joyously step upon the crowns of Vishnu, Brahma on the lotus, and Indra the king of the gods.
commentary: Walking in reverence around the shrine of the divine brings a spiritual status higher than that of the greatest mythological gods. Vallalar states plainly that the feet of a true devotee will stand above the crowns of Vishnu, Brahma, and Indra. Earthly devotion, rooted in direct love for God, surpasses the heights of the traditional heavens.

translit: cattimāṉ eṉparniṉ taṉṉai aiyaṉē pattimāṉ taṉakkalāl pakarva teṅṅaṉē.
translation: They call you the Lord of Power, O Master. How can this be told to anyone but a true devotee?
commentary: The true power of the divine is something only a devoted heart can recognize. Intellectual study cannot grasp the supreme energy of God. Vallalar asks how anyone without deep, lived love could possibly understand this truth.

tamil: படியே அளந்த மாலவனும் பழைய மறைசொற் பண்ணவனும்
முடியீ றறியா முதற்பொருளே மொழியும் ஒற்றி நகர்க்கிறையே
அடியார் களுக்கே இரங்கிமுனம் அடுத்த சுரநோய் தடுத்ததுபோல்
படிமீ தடியேற் குறுபிணிபோம் படிநீ கடைக்கண் பார்த்தருளே.
translit: paṭiyē aḷanta mālavaṉum paḻaiya maṟaicoṟ paṇṇavaṉum muṭiyī ṟaṟiyā mutaṟporuḷē moḻiyum oṟṟi nakarkkiṟaiyē aṭiyār kaḷukkē iraṅkimuṉam aṭutta curanōy taṭuttatupōl paṭimī taṭiyēṟ kuṟupiṇipōm paṭinī kaṭaikkaṇ pārttaruḷē.
translation: O Primal Reality, whose beginning and end remain unknown to Vishnu who measured the earth and Brahma who chants the ancient Vedas! O Lord of the renowned city of Otriyur! Just as you took pity on your devotees in the past and dispelled their fever, please cast your merciful glance upon me so that the afflictions gripping your humble servant on this earth may vanish.
commentary: God is the primal reality that even the greatest deities cannot measure or comprehend. Vallalar asks the Lord of Otriyur to cure his worldly afflictions with a single glance of mercy. He reminds the divine of past miracles, asking for that same healing grace to ease his own physical and spiritual suffering.

translit: maṉṟāṭum māmaṇiyē niṉpoṟ pāta malarttuṇaiyē tuṇaiyāka vāḻkiṉ ṟōrkku oṉṟālum kuṟaivillai ēḻai yēṉyāṉ oṉṟumilēṉ ivvulakil uḻalā niṉṟēṉ iṉṟāka nāṭkaḻiyil eṉṉē ceykēṉ iṇaimulaiyār maiyaliṉāl iḷaittu niṉṟēṉ eṉṟālum ciṟiteḷiyēṟ kiraṅkal vēṇṭum eḻilārum oṟṟiyūr iṉpa vāḻvē.
translation: O great Gem dancing in the hall! Those who live with your pair of golden lotus feet as their refuge lack absolutely nothing. I am a poor wretch who has nothing. I keep wandering aimlessly in this world. If my days pass away in vain like this, what shall I do? I stand exhausted by my infatuation with women. Even so, you must show a little compassion to this humble one, O blissful life of beautiful Otriyur!
commentary: Taking refuge in God brings complete fulfillment, leaving a person wanting nothing. Vallalar contrasts this perfect peace with his own exhaustion, confessing that he has wasted his days chasing worldly lusts and wandering without purpose. He throws himself entirely on the compassion of the Lord, asking for grace despite all his human flaws.

translit: cōṟu vēṇṭiṉum tukilaṇi mutalām cukaṅkaḷ vēṇṭiṉum cukamalāc cukamām vēṟu vēṇṭiṉum niṉai-aṭain taṉṟi mēvo ṇāteṉum mēlavar uraikkōr māṟu vēṇṭilēṉ vantuniṟ kiṉṟēṉ vaḷḷalē uṉṟaṉ maṉakkuṟip paṟiyēṉ cēṟu vēṇṭiya kayappaṇaik kaṭaṟcār tikaḻum oṟṟiyūrc civaparañ cuṭarē.
translation: Whether one desires food, comforts like clothes and ornaments, or that supreme joy beyond worldly pleasures, the exalted ones declare that none of these can be attained except by reaching You. I do not contradict their words. I have come and stand before You, O Bountiful Lord. I do not know Your mind's intent, O Supreme Light of Siva in radiant Otriyur, situated by the sea with deep and muddy fertile fields.
commentary: Every human desire, from the basic need for food to the highest spiritual joy, is fulfilled only through divine grace. Wise elders teach that no true comfort or lasting peace is possible without reaching God. The poet accepts this truth completely and stands before the Supreme Light of Siva waiting for direction. By admitting he does not know the Lord's intent, he shows total surrender, leaving his fate entirely in divine hands.

tamil: பொதுநின் றருள்வீ ரொற்றியுளீர் பூவுந் தியதென் முலையென்றேன்
இதுவென் றறிநா மேறுகின்ற தென்றா ரேறு கின்றதுதான்
எதுவென் றுரைத்தே னெதுநடுவோ ரெழுத்திட் டறிநீ யென்றுரைத்தார்
அதுவின் றணங்கே யென்னடியவ் வையர் மொழிந்த வருண்மொழியே.
translit: potuniṉ ṟaruḷvī roṟṟiyuḷīr pūvun tiyateṉ mulaiyeṉṟēṉ ituveṉ ṟaṟinā mēṟukiṉṟa teṉṟā rēṟu kiṉṟatutāṉ etuveṉ ṟuraittē ṉetunaṭuvō reḻuttiṭ ṭaṟinī yeṉṟuraittār atuviṉ ṟaṇaṅkē yeṉṉaṭiyav vaiyar moḻinta varuṇmoḻiyē.
translation: "O Lord of Otriyur who stands in the public hall and bestows grace, my breasts are blooming like flowers," I said. He replied, "Know that this is what we mount." I asked, "What is it that you mount?" He said, "Place a letter in the middle of the word 'what' and know." O beautiful friend, what are these gracious words spoken by the Lord?
commentary: The Lord plays a word game with the young woman. When she speaks of her physical beauty, he turns her words into a riddle about his divine mount. The Tamil word for 'what' is etu: adding the letter 'ru' in the middle makes erutu, which means bull. This is the traditional animal mount of Siva, allowing the Lord to answer her romantic advance with a spiritual tease.

tamil: மருகா வொற்றி வாணர்பலி வாங்க வகையுண் டேயென்றேன்
ஒருகா லெடுத்தேன் காணென்றா ரொருகா லெடுத்துக் காட்டுமென்றேன்
வருகா விரிப்பொன் னம்பலத்துள் வந்தாற் காட்டு வேமென்றார்
அருகா வியப்பா மென்னடியவ் வையர் மொழிந்த வருண்மொழியே.
translit: marukā voṟṟi vāṇarpali vāṅka vakaiyuṇ ṭēyeṉṟēṉ orukā leṭuttēṉ kāṇeṉṟā rorukā leṭuttuk kāṭṭumeṉṟēṉ varukā virippoṉ ṉampalattuḷ vantāṟ kāṭṭu vēmeṉṟār arukā viyappā meṉṉaṭiyav vaiyar moḻinta varuṇmoḻiyē.
translation: "O dwellers of Otriyur, do you have the means to collect alms?" I asked. He replied, "See, I have lifted one leg." I said, "Lift that one leg and show me." He said, "If you come to the Golden Hall where the Kaveri flows, we will show you." O friend by my side, this is a wonder! What are these gracious words spoken by the Lord?
commentary: The young woman asks how a wandering beggar collects alms, and the Lord replies by identifying himself as the supreme dancer. The Lord with one raised leg is Nataraja, the cosmic dancer whose famous temple is the Golden Hall in Chidambaram. The divine shifts effortlessly from the humble image of a beggar to the majesty of the creator.

tamil: விட்டொற் றியில்வாழ் வீரெவனிவ் வேளை யருள நின்றதென்றேன்
சுட்டுஞ் சுதனே யென்றார்நான் சுட்டி யறியச் சொல்லுமென்றேன்
பட்டுண் மருங்கே நீகுழந்தைப் பருவ மதனின் முடித்ததென்றார்
அட்டுண் டறியா ரென்னடியவ் வையர் மொழிந்த வருண்மொழியே.
translit: viṭṭoṟ ṟiyilvāḻ vīrevaṉiv vēḷai yaruḷa niṉṟateṉṟēṉ cuṭṭuñ cutaṉē yeṉṟārnāṉ cuṭṭi yaṟiyac collumeṉṟēṉ paṭṭuṇ maruṅkē nīkuḻantaip paruva mataṉiṉ muṭittateṉṟār aṭṭuṇ ṭaṟiyā reṉṉaṭiyav vaiyar moḻinta varuṇmoḻiyē.
translation: "O Lord living in Otriyur, who is it that stands here to bestow grace at this hour?" I asked. He replied, "It is the pointing son." I said, "Tell me clearly so I may know." He said, "O woman with a silk-clad waist, you accomplished it in your childhood." They do not know how to cook and eat. O friend, what are these gracious words spoken by the Lord?
commentary: The Lord playfully evades her questions by bringing up stories of ancient devotion. He refers to the pointing son, a classic reference to the child saint Thirugnanasambandar, who as a toddler pointed up at the divine couple when asked who had miraculously fed him milk. He then tells the young woman that she too accomplished her great spiritual work in her own childhood.

tamil: வேலை ஞாலம் புகழொற்றி விளங்குந் தேவர் நீரணியும்
மாலை யாதென் றேனயன்மால் மாலை யகற்று மாலையென்றார்
சோலை மலரன் றேயென்றேன் சோலை யேநாந் தொடுத்ததென்றார்
ஆலு மிடையா யென்னடியவ் வையர் மொழிந்த வருண்மொழியே.
translit: vēlai ñālam pukaḻoṟṟi viḷaṅkun tēvar nīraṇiyum mālai yāteṉ ṟēṉayaṉmāl mālai yakaṟṟu mālaiyeṉṟār cōlai malaraṉ ṟēyeṉṟēṉ cōlai yēnān toṭuttateṉṟār ālu miṭaiyā yeṉṉaṭiyav vaiyar moḻinta varuṇmoḻiyē.
translation: "O shining God of Otriyur praised by the sea-girt earth, what is the garland you wear?" I asked. He replied, "It is the garland that dispels the delusion of Brahma and Vishnu." I said, "Is it not made of flowers from the grove?" He replied, "It is the grove itself that we wove." O friend with a swaying waist, what are these gracious words spoken by the Lord?
commentary: A single Tamil word, mālai, means both a flower garland and a state of deep delusion. The young woman asks about his physical garland, and the Lord replies that his presence destroys the spiritual ignorance of even the greatest gods. When she presses him about flowers from the grove, he claims mastery over all of nature by saying he wove the forest itself.

tamil: உயிரு ளுறைவீர் திருவொற்றி யுள்ளீர் நீரென் மேற்பிடித்த
வயிர மதனை விடுமென்றேன் மாற்றா ளலநீ மாதேயாஞ்
செயிர தகற்றுன் முலைப்பதிவாழ் தேவ னலவே டெளியென்றார்
அயிர மொழியா யென்னடியவ் வையர் மொழிந்த வருண்மொழியே.
translit: uyiru ḷuṟaivīr tiruvoṟṟi yuḷḷīr nīreṉ mēṟpiṭitta vayira mataṉai viṭumeṉṟēṉ māṟṟā ḷalanī mātēyāñ ceyira takaṟṟuṉ mulaippativāḻ tēva ṉalavē ṭeḷiyeṉṟār ayira moḻiyā yeṉṉaṭiyav vaiyar moḻinta varuṇmoḻiyē.
translation: "O Lord who dwells in the soul, O Lord of Thiru Otriyur, let go of the stubborn anger you hold against me," I said. He replied, "O lady, you are not a rival. Am I not the God who lives upon your blemish-dispelling breasts? Understand this." O friend of fine words, what are these gracious words spoken by the Lord?
commentary: The young woman begs the Lord to drop his anger, but he reveals there is no anger at all. He assures her she has no rivals for his affection. By claiming to dwell directly upon her physical form, he affirms the total, inseparable intimacy between the divine and the devoted soul.

tamil: தண்கா வளஞ்சூழ் திருவொற்றித் தலத்தி லமர்ந்த சாமிநுங்கை
யெண்கார் முகமாப் பொன்னென்றே னிடையிட் டறித லரிதென்றார்
மண்கா தலிக்கு மாடென்றேன் மதிக்குங் கணைவில் லன்றென்றார்
அண்கார்க் குழலா யென்னடியவ் வையர் மொழிந்த வருண்மொழியே.
translit: taṇkā vaḷañcūḻ tiruvoṟṟit talatti lamarnta cāminuṅkai yeṇkār mukamāp poṉṉeṉṟē ṉiṭaiyiṭ ṭaṟita lariteṉṟār maṇkā talikku māṭeṉṟēṉ matikkuṅ kaṇaivil laṉṟeṉṟār aṇkārk kuḻalā yeṉṉaṭiyav vaiyar moḻinta varuṇmoḻiyē.
translation: I said, "O Lord dwelling in Otriyur surrounded by cool groves, is your hand beautiful gold?" He said, "It is difficult to know if you interject." I said, "It is the wealth that the earth loves." He said, "It is not the esteemed bow and arrow." O friend with thick dark hair, what are these gracious words spoken by the Lord?
commentary: The heroine shares a riddling conversation she had with Lord Siva. Their dialogue relies on Tamil wordplay, where terms for gold and wealth double as secret references to the bull he rides and the weapons he carries.

tamil: அலங்கும் புனற்செய் யொற்றியுளீ ரயன்மா லாதி யாவர்கட்கும்
துலங்கு மதுதா னென்னென்றேன் சுட்டென் றுரைத்தா ராகெட்டேன்
அலங்கற் குழலா யென்னடியவ் வையர் மொழிந்த வருண்மொழியே.
translit: alaṅkum puṉaṟcey yoṟṟiyuḷī rayaṉmā lāti yāvarkaṭkum ilaṅku maikāṇīreṉṟē ṉitaṉmuṉ ṉēḻnī koṇṭateṉṟār tulaṅku matutā ṉeṉṉeṉṟēṉ cuṭṭeṉ ṟuraittā rākeṭṭēṉ alaṅkaṟ kuḻalā yeṉṉaṭiyav vaiyar moḻinta varuṇmoḻiyē.
translation: I said, "O Lord of Otriyur of waving watery fields, you do not see the darkness that shines for Brahma, Vishnu, and all the rest." He said, "Before this, you took the number seven." I asked, "What is that which shines clearly?" He replied, "A demonstrative letter." I am undone. O friend with garland-adorned hair, what are these gracious words spoken by the Lord?
commentary: The playful riddle continues using the rules of Tamil grammar. The heroine and the Lord trade double meanings about numbers and demonstrative letters, turning the strict rules of language into a poetry of divine flirtation.

tamil: விண்டு வணங்கு மொற்றியுளீர் மென்பூ விருந்தும் வன்பூவில்
வண்டு விழுந்த தென்றேனெம் மலர்க்கை வண்டும் விழுந்ததென்றார்
தொண்டர்க் கருள்வீர் நீரென்றேன் றோகாய் நாமே தொண்டரென்றார்
அண்டர்க் கரியா ரென்னடியவ் வையர் மொழிந்த வருண்மொழியே.
translit: viṇṭu vaṇaṅku moṟṟiyuḷīr meṉpū viruntum vaṉpūvil vaṇṭu viḻunta teṉṟēṉem malarkkai vaṇṭum viḻuntateṉṟār toṇṭark karuḷvīr nīreṉṟēṉ ṟōkāy nāmē toṇṭareṉṟār aṇṭark kariyā reṉṉaṭiyav vaiyar moḻinta varuṇmoḻiyē.
translation: I said, "O Lord of Otriyur worshipped by Vishnu, while soft flowers were available, the bee fell on a hard flower." He replied, "The bangle fell from our flower-like hand too." I said, "You bestow grace on your devotees." He said, "O beautiful one, we ourselves are devotees." He is difficult for the celestials to reach. O friend, what are these gracious words spoken by the Lord?
commentary: The heroine speaks of lovesickness, a traditional poetic state where a devotee pines so deeply for God that she grows thin and her bangles slip from her wrists. When she praises the Lord for showering grace on his followers, he answers with absolute humility, declaring that he himself is a servant to those who love him.

tamil: மட்டார் மலர்க்கா வொற்றியுளீர் மதிக்குங் கலைமேல் விழுமென்றேன்
எட்டா மெழுத்தை யெடுக்குமென்றா ரெட்டா மெழுத்திங் கெதுவென்றேன்
உட்டா வகற்று மந்தணர்க ளுறையூர் மாதே யுணரென்றார்
அட்டார் புரங்க ளென்னடியவ் வையர் மொழிந்த வருண்மொழியே.
translit: maṭṭār malarkkā voṟṟiyuḷīr matikkuṅ kalaimēl viḻumeṉṟēṉ eṭṭā meḻuttai yeṭukkumeṉṟā reṭṭā meḻuttiṅ ketuveṉṟēṉ uṭṭā vakaṟṟu mantaṇarka ḷuṟaiyūr mātē yuṇareṉṟār aṭṭār puraṅka ḷeṉṉaṭiyav vaiyar moḻinta varuṇmoḻiyē.
translation: I said, "O Lord of Otriyur of fragrant flower groves, it will fall upon the esteemed garment." He replied, "It will take the eighth letter." I asked, "What is the eighth letter here?" He said, "Realize it, O woman of the town where pure ones who dispel inner flaws dwell." He burnt the three cities. O friend, what are these gracious words spoken by the Lord?
commentary: The riddle turns to the sacred sounds of the Tamil alphabet. The "eighth letter" refers to the Tamil vowel a (அ), which stands both for the number eight and for the divine source of all things.

tamil: ஒற்றி நகரீர் மனவாசி யுடையார்க் கருள்வீர் நீரென்றேன்
பற்றி யிறுதி தொடங்கியது பயிலு மவர்க்கே யருள்வதென்றார்
மற்றி துணர்கி லேனென்றேன் வருந்தே லுணரும் வகைநான்கும்
அற்றி டென்றா ரென்னடியவ் வையர் மொழிந்த வருண்மொழியே.
translit: oṟṟi nakarīr maṉavāci yuṭaiyārk karuḷvīr nīreṉṟēṉ paṟṟi yiṟuti toṭaṅkiyatu payilu mavarkkē yaruḷvateṉṟār maṟṟi tuṇarki lēṉeṉṟēṉ varuntē luṇarum vakaināṉkum aṟṟi ṭeṉṟā reṉṉaṭiyav vaiyar moḻinta varuṇmoḻiyē.
translation: I said, "O Lord of Otriyur city, you grant grace to those who master the breath of the mind." He said, "We bestow grace only on those who practice that which begins with the final sound of attachment." I said, "I do not understand this." He said, "Do not worry, sever the four ways of perceiving." O friend, what are these gracious words spoken by the Lord?
commentary: The dialogue moves from clever wordplay to direct spiritual instruction. To receive divine grace, the Lord tells the heroine she must cut away the four inner instruments of ordinary perception: the thinking mind, the intellect, memory, and the ego. True understanding dawns only when these everyday ways of knowing are silenced.

tamil: வான்றோய் பொழிற்சூ ழொற்றியுளீர் வருந்தா தணைவே னோவென்றேன்
ஊன்றோ யுடற்கென் றார்தெரிய வுரைப்பீ ரென்றே னோவிதுதான்
சான்றோ ருங்கண் மரபோர்ந்து தரித்த பெயர்க்குத் தகாதென்றார்
ஆன்றோய் விடங்க ரென்னடியவ் வையர் மொழிந்த வருண்மொழியே.
translit: vāṉṟōy poḻiṟcū ḻoṟṟiyuḷīr varuntā taṇaivē ṉōveṉṟēṉ ūṉṟō yuṭaṟkeṉ ṟārteriya vuraippī reṉṟē ṉōvitutāṉ cāṉṟō ruṅkaṇ marapōrntu taritta peyarkkut takāteṉṟār āṉṟōy viṭaṅka reṉṉaṭiyav vaiyar moḻinta varuṇmoḻiyē.
translation: Lord of Otriyur surrounded by sky-reaching groves! I asked, "Will I embrace you without suffering?" He replied, "That belongs to a body soaked in flesh." I said, "Speak clearly." He said, "It does not befit the name given by the wise who understood your lineage." He is the great Vidankar. O friend, what are these gracious words spoken by the Lord?
commentary: The devotee yearns for a painless, direct embrace with the divine. The Lord playfully deflects her request, reminding her that physical embracing and its related suffering belong to bodies made of flesh, not to the spirit. When she asks for a straight answer, he teases her further, saying her bold request does not suit the modesty expected of her noble lineage. This exchange highlights the tension between human longing and divine reality.

tamil: தீது தவிர்க்கு மொற்றியுளீர் செல்ல லறுப்ப தென்றென்றேன்
ஈது நமக்குந் தெரியுமென்றா ரிறையா மோவிங் கிதுவென்றேன்
ஓது மடியர் மனக்கங்கு லோட்டு மியாமே யுணரென்றார்
ஆது தெரியே னென்னடியவ் வையர் மொழிந்த வருண்மொழியே.
translit: tītu tavirkku moṟṟiyuḷīr cella laṟuppa teṉṟeṉṟēṉ ītu namakkun teriyumeṉṟā riṟaiyā mōviṅ kituveṉṟēṉ ōtu maṭiyar maṉakkaṅku lōṭṭu miyāmē yuṇareṉṟār ātu teriyē ṉeṉṉaṭiyav vaiyar moḻinta varuṇmoḻiyē.
translation: Lord of Otriyur who eradicates evil! I asked, "When will you sever my sorrow?" He replied, "We know this too." I asked, "Is this a proper response here?" He said, "Realize that we ourselves drive away the dark night in the minds of chanting devotees." I do not understand this at all. O friend, what are these gracious words spoken by the Lord?
commentary: The devotee asks when God will finally put an end to her worldly sorrows. He reassures her that he is fully aware of her struggles and hears her plea. The Lord explains that his true work is to drive away the dark night of ignorance from the minds of those who sincerely chant his name. He promises that true relief comes when divine light replaces inner darkness.

tamil: ஒண்கை மழுவோ டனலுடையீ ரொற்றி நகர்வா ழுத்தமர்நீர்
வண்கை யொருமை நாதரென்றேன் வண்கைப் பன்மை நாதரென்றார்
எண்க ணடங்கா வதிசயங்கா ணென்றேன் பொருளன் றிதற்கென்றார்
அண்கொ ளணங்கே யென்னடியவ் வையர் மொழிந்த வருண்மொழியே.
translit: oṇkai maḻuvō ṭaṉaluṭaiyī roṟṟi nakarvā ḻuttamarnīr vaṇkai yorumai nātareṉṟēṉ vaṇkaip paṉmai nātareṉṟār eṇka ṇaṭaṅkā vaticayaṅkā ṇeṉṟēṉ poruḷaṉ ṟitaṟkeṉṟār aṇko ḷaṇaṅkē yeṉṉaṭiyav vaiyar moḻinta varuṇmoḻiyē.
translation: You hold a battle-axe and fire in your bright hands. You are the noble one living in Otriyur city. I said, "You are the singular Lord of generous hands." He replied, "We are the plural Lord of generous hands." I said, "This is a wonder beyond calculation." He said, "That is not the meaning of this." O beautiful friend! what are these gracious words spoken by the Lord?
commentary: The devotee praises God as the unique, peerless Lord of endless generosity. The Lord playfully contradicts her, claiming instead to be a Lord of multiplicity or plural forms. When she marvels at this mysterious answer, he dismisses her literal understanding. The exchange uses lighthearted wordplay to show that God is both the absolute one and the source of the countless many.

tamil: ஒருவ ரெனவா ழொற்றியுளீ ருமக்கம் மனையுண் டேயென்றேன்
இருவ ரொருபே ருடையவர்காண் என்றா ரென்னென் றேனென்பேர்
மருவு மீறற் றயலகரம் வயங்கு மிகர மானதென்றார்
அருவு மிடையா யென்னடியவ் வையர் மொழிந்த வருண்மொழியே.
