translit: oruva reṉavā ḻoṟṟiyuḷī rumakkam maṉaiyuṇ ṭēyeṉṟēṉ iruva rorupē ruṭaiyavarkāṇ eṉṟā reṉṉeṉ ṟēṉeṉpēr maruvu mīṟaṟ ṟayalakaram vayaṅku mikara māṉateṉṟār aruvu miṭaiyā yeṉṉaṭiyav vaiyar moḻinta varuṇmoḻiyē.
translation: Lord of Otriyur living as the peerless One! I asked, "Do you have a mother?" He replied, "See, two people share one name." I asked, "What does that mean?" He said, "In my name, if you remove the final letter, the adjacent 'a' becomes a shining 'i'." O friend with an imperceptible waist! what are these gracious words spoken by the Lord?
commentary: The devotee asks if the peerless Lord has a mother, seeking to understand his origins. The Lord answers with a grammatical riddle about his own name, hinting that he and his feminine counterpart share a single identity. By changing the letters of his name, the masculine form becomes feminine. He playfully reveals that the divine encompasses both male and female principles perfectly.

tamil: பேரா ரொற்றி யீரும்மைப் பெற்றா ரெவரென் றேனவர்தம்
ஏரார் பெயரின் முன்பினிரண் டிரண்ட கத்தா ரென்றாரென்
நேரா வுரைப்பீ ரென்றேனீ நெஞ்ச நெகிழ்ந்தா லாமென்றார்
ஆரார் சடைய ரென்னடியவ் வையர் மொழிந்த வருண்மொழியே.
translit: pērā roṟṟi yīrummaip peṟṟā revareṉ ṟēṉavartam ērār peyariṉ muṉpiṉiraṇ ṭiraṇṭa kattā reṉṟāreṉ nērā vuraippī reṉṟēṉī neñca nekiḻntā lāmeṉṟār ārār caṭaiya reṉṉaṭiyav vaiyar moḻinta varuṇmoḻiyē.
translation: Lord of Otriyur of great fame! I asked, "Who begot you?" He replied, "They are the ones placed inside two and two, before and after their beautiful name." I said, "Speak to me directly." He said, "You will know if your heart melts." He wears the Aathi flower on his matted hair. O friend, what are these gracious words spoken by the Lord?
commentary: The devotee tries to uncover God's origins by asking who his parents are. The Lord offers a dizzying mathematical riddle about letters and numbers instead of a real lineage. When she begs for a straight answer, he drops the wordplay entirely and gives her a deep spiritual truth. He tells her that the divine reality cannot be understood through clever logic, but reveals itself naturally when the heart melts in pure love.

tamil: தளிநான் மறையீ ரொற்றிநகர் தழைத்து வாழ்வீர் தனிஞான
வொளிநா வரைசை யைந்தெழுத்தா லுவரி கடத்தி னீரென்றேன்
களிநா வலனை யீரெழுத்தாற் கடலில் வீழ்த்தி னேமென்றார்
அளிநாண் குழலா யென்னடியவ் வையர் மொழிந்த வருண்மொழியே.
translit: taḷināṉ maṟaiyī roṟṟinakar taḻaittu vāḻvīr taṉiñāṉa voḷinā varaicai yainteḻuttā luvari kaṭatti ṉīreṉṟēṉ kaḷinā valaṉai yīreḻuttāṟ kaṭalil vīḻtti ṉēmeṉṟār aḷināṇ kuḻalā yeṉṉaṭiyav vaiyar moḻinta varuṇmoḻiyē.
translation: I said, "O Lord of the sacred four Vedas, dwelling and prospering in Otriyur, You helped the peerless light of wisdom, the king of speech, cross the ocean with five letters." He replied, "We plunged the joyful poet into the ocean with two letters." O friend with hair swarming with bees, what are these gracious words spoken by the Lord?
commentary: The heroine praises the Lord for saving a famous saint who was thrown into the ocean tied to a heavy stone. She notes that the saint floated to safety by chanting the Lord's sacred five-lettered name (Na-ma-si-va-ya). The Lord playfully replies with a riddle, claiming he plunged another poet into the sea using only two letters. He is teasing her with clever wordplay to draw out their conversation and test her devotion.

tamil: ஓமூன் றெழிலீ ரொற்றியுளீ ருற்றோர்க் களிப்பீ ரோவென்றேன்
தாமூன் றென்பார்க் கயன்மூன்றுந் தருவே மென்றா ரம்மமிகத்
தேமூன் றினநும் மொழியென்றேன் செவ்வா யுறுமுன் முறுவலென்றார்
ஆமூன் றறுப்பா ரென்னடியவ் வையர் மொழிந்த வருண்மொழியே.
translit: ōmūṉ ṟeḻilī roṟṟiyuḷī ruṟṟōrk kaḷippī rōveṉṟēṉ tāmūṉ ṟeṉpārk kayaṉmūṉṟun taruvē meṉṟā rammamikat tēmūṉ ṟiṉanum moḻiyeṉṟēṉ cevvā yuṟumuṉ muṟuvaleṉṟār āmūṉ ṟaṟuppā reṉṉaṭiyav vaiyar moḻinta varuṇmoḻiyē.
translation: I asked, "O Lord dwelling in Otriyur holding the beauty of the three-lettered Om, will You grant Your grace to those who reach You?" He said, "To those who speak of the three, we will give the three of Brahma." I said, "Ah, Your words are steeped in honey." He replied, "That is the smile appearing on the red lips." He cuts away the three impurities. O friend, what are these gracious words spoken by the Lord?
commentary: This verse is a playful exchange built entirely on the number three. The heroine asks if the Lord, who holds the three-lettered sacred sound Om, will grant his grace to his devotees. The Lord answers with a riddle, offering the three creative powers of Brahma, the creator god. When she calls his words as sweet as honey, he twists her phrase to describe a smile on his red lips, drawing the human soul closer through gentle humor.

tamil: மன்னி வளரு மொற்றியுளீர் மடவா ரிரக்கும் வகையதுதான்
முன்னி லொருதா வாமென்றேன் முத்தா வெனலே முறையென்றார்
என்னி லிதுதா னையமென்றே னெவர்க்குந் தெரியு மென்றுரைத்தார்
அன்னி லோதி யென்னடியவ் வையர் மொழிந்த வருண்மொழியே .
translit: maṉṉi vaḷaru moṟṟiyuḷīr maṭavā rirakkum vakaiyatutāṉ muṉṉi lorutā vāmeṉṟēṉ muttā veṉalē muṟaiyeṉṟār eṉṉi litutā ṉaiyameṉṟē ṉevarkkun teriyu meṉṟuraittār aṉṉi lōti yeṉṉaṭiyav vaiyar moḻinta varuṇmoḻiyē .
translation: I said, "O Lord dwelling permanently in flourishing Otriyur, the way women entreat before You is to simply say 'give'." He replied, "The proper way is to say 'give three'." I said, "To me, this is a doubt." He said, "Everyone knows this." O swan-like friend with lovely hair, what are these gracious words spoken by the Lord?
commentary: The Lord and the heroine continue their romantic wordplay. She points out that women who beg for his grace simply use the single Tamil word "tha" (give). He cheekily corrects her, saying the proper request is "mutha" (a word sounding like a request for three things, though it actually translates to a kiss). The Lord responds to her deep spiritual yearning with the intimate, teasing affection of a lover.

tamil: வளஞ்சே ரொற்றி யீருமது மாலை கொடுப்பீ ரோவென்றேன்
குளஞ்சேர் மொழியா யுனக்கதுமுன் கொடுத்தே மென்றா ரிலையென்றேன்
உளஞ்சேர்ந் ததுகா ணிலையன்றோ ருருவு மன்றங் கருவென்றார்
அளஞ்சேர் வடிவா யென்னடியவ் வையர் மொழிந்த வருண்மொழியே.
translit: vaḷañcē roṟṟi yīrumatu mālai koṭuppī rōveṉṟēṉ kuḷañcēr moḻiyā yuṉakkatumuṉ koṭuttē meṉṟā rilaiyeṉṟēṉ uḷañcērn tatukā ṇilaiyaṉṟō ruruvu maṉṟaṅ karuveṉṟār aḷañcēr vaṭivā yeṉṉaṭiyav vaiyar moḻinta varuṇmoḻiyē.
translation: I asked, "O Lord of prosperous Otriyur, will You give me Your garland?" He said, "O woman with cooling words, We gave it to you before." I said, "No." He replied, "Look, it has reached your heart. It is not a leaf, nor is it a form, but remains formless there." O friend of beautiful form, what are these gracious words spoken by the Lord?
commentary: The heroine asks the Lord for his flower garland as a sign of his favor. He replies that he has already given it to her, revealing it to be a formless presence hidden inside her heart. This is a poetic pun on the Tamil word "malai" (which means both a physical flower garland and the evening time). He has given her no physical flowers. Instead, he has filled her heart with the deep longing that awakens in the evening.

tamil: வீற்றா ரொற்றி யூரமர்ந்தீர் விளங்கு மதனன் மென்மலரே
மாற்றா ரென்றே னிலைகாணெம் மாலை முடிமேற் காணென்றார்
சாற்றாச் சலமே யீதென்றேன் சடையின் முடிமே லன்றென்றார்
ஆற்றா விடையா யென்னடியவ் வையர் மொழிந்த வருண்மொழியே.
translit: vīṟṟā roṟṟi yūramarntīr viḷaṅku mataṉaṉ meṉmalarē māṟṟā reṉṟē ṉilaikāṇem mālai muṭimēṟ kāṇeṉṟār cāṟṟāc calamē yīteṉṟēṉ caṭaiyiṉ muṭimē laṉṟeṉṟār āṟṟā viṭaiyā yeṉṉaṭiyav vaiyar moḻinta varuṇmoḻiyē.
translation: I said, "O Lord seated in majestic Otriyur, the soft flowers of the illustrious god of love are my enemies." He said, "They are not. Look upon the garland on Our crown." I said, "This is utter deceit." He replied, "Is it not water on the crown of Our matted hair?" O friend with a slender waist, what are these gracious words spoken by the Lord?
commentary: The heroine complains that she is tormented by the flower arrows of Kama, the god of love. The Lord tells her to look at the crown of his head for comfort, prompting her to accuse him of trickery and deceit (salam). He playfully misinterprets her accusation, pretending she meant the identical-sounding word for water (salam) and confirming that he does indeed carry a river on his matted hair. This constant bantering reflects a deep, intimate bond between the human soul and the divine.

tamil: புயப்பா லொற்றி யீரச்சம் போமோ வென்றே னாமென்றார்
வயப்பா வலருக் கிறையானீர் வஞ்சிப் பாவிங் குரைப்பதென்றேன்
வியப்பா நகையப் பாவெனும்பா வெண்பா கலிப்பா வுடனென்றார்
அயப்பா லிடையா யென்னடியவ் வையர் மொழிந்த வருண்மொழியே.
translit: puyappā loṟṟi yīraccam pōmō veṉṟē ṉāmeṉṟār vayappā valaruk kiṟaiyāṉīr vañcip pāviṅ kuraippateṉṟēṉ viyappā nakaiyap pāveṉumpā veṇpā kalippā vuṭaṉeṉṟār ayappā liṭaiyā yeṉṉaṭiyav vaiyar moḻinta varuṇmoḻiyē.
translation: "O Lord of Otriyur with strong shoulders, will my fear depart?" I asked. "Yes," he said. "You are the master of mighty poets; why do you speak deceitful verse here?" I asked. "Along with the astonishing smiling verse, clear verse, and joyous verse," he said. O friend with a delicate waist, what are these gracious words spoken by the Lord?
commentary: The heroine asks if her fear will fade, and the Lord assures her it will. When she playfully accuses him of using deceitful words, he answers with a clever pun. He uses the names of traditional Tamil poetic meters to claim his words are instead full of smiles, clarity, and joy.

tamil: தண்ணம் பொழிற்சூ ழொற்றியுளீர் சங்கங் கையிற்சேர்த் திடுமென்றேன்
திண்ணம் பலமேல் வருங்கையிற் சேர்த்தோ முன்னர் தெரியென்றார்
வண்ணம் பலவிம் மொழிக்கென்றேன் வாய்ந்தொன் றெனக்குக் காட்டென்றார்
அண்ணஞ் சுகமே யென்னடியவ் வையர் மொழிந்த வருண்மொழியே.
translit: taṇṇam poḻiṟcū ḻoṟṟiyuḷīr caṅkaṅ kaiyiṟcērt tiṭumeṉṟēṉ tiṇṇam palamēl varuṅkaiyiṟ cērttō muṉṉar teriyeṉṟār vaṇṇam palavim moḻikkeṉṟēṉ vāyntoṉ ṟeṉakkuk kāṭṭeṉṟār aṇṇañ cukamē yeṉṉaṭiyav vaiyar moḻinta varuṇmoḻiyē.
translation: "O Lord of Otriyur surrounded by cool groves, place conch bangles on my hand," I said. "We surely placed them on your arriving hand before; look," he said. "There are many meanings to these words," I said. "Show me one that fits," he said. O friend like a swan and a parrot, what are these gracious words spoken by the Lord?
commentary: The heroine asks the Lord to put conch bangles on her wrists, a traditional sign in Tamil poetry that a lovesick woman is wasting away and needs her lover. The Lord gives a teasing reply, claiming he already adorned her hands long ago. When she notes his words carry hidden meanings, he challenges her to explain even one.

tamil: உகஞ்சே ரொற்றி யூருடையீ ரொருமா தவரோ நீரென்றேன்
முகஞ்சேர் வடிவே லிரண்டுடையாய் மும்மா தவர்நா மென்றுரைத்தார்
சுகஞ்சேர்ந் தனவும் மொழிக்கென்றேன் றோகா யுனது மொழிக்கென்றார்
அகஞ்சேர் விழியா யென்னடியவ் வையர் மொழிந்த வருண்மொழியே.
translit: ukañcē roṟṟi yūruṭaiyī rorumā tavarō nīreṉṟēṉ mukañcēr vaṭivē liraṇṭuṭaiyāy mummā tavarnā meṉṟuraittār cukañcērn taṉavum moḻikkeṉṟēṉ ṟōkā yuṉatu moḻikkeṉṟār akañcēr viḻiyā yeṉṉaṭiyav vaiyar moḻinta varuṇmoḻiyē.
translation: "O Lord of Otriyur which endures through the ages, are you a singular great ascetic?" I asked. "O girl with two sharp spears on your face, we are the three great ascetics," he said. "Joy gathers in your words," I said. "O peacock, it is in your words," he said. O friend with beautiful eyes, what are these gracious words spoken by the Lord?
commentary: The heroine asks the Lord if he is the single supreme ascetic. He replies that he actually embodies the three great gods of creation, preservation, and destruction. He then playfully changes the subject by comparing her beautiful eyes to sharp spears, turning a theological statement into a lover's compliment.

tamil: ஊரா மொற்றி யீராசை யுடையே னென்றே னெமக்கலது
நேரா வழக்குத் தொடுக்கின்றாய் நினக்கே தென்றார் நீரெனக்குச்
சேரா வணமீ தென்றேன்முன் சேர்த்தீ தெழுதித் தந்தவர்தாம்
ஆரா ரென்றா ரென்னடியவ் வையர் மொழிந்த வருண்மொழியே.
translit: ūrā moṟṟi yīrācai yuṭaiyē ṉeṉṟē ṉemakkalatu nērā vaḻakkut toṭukkiṉṟāy niṉakkē teṉṟār nīreṉakkuc cērā vaṇamī teṉṟēṉmuṉ cērttī teḻutit tantavartām ārā reṉṟā reṉṉaṭiyav vaiyar moḻinta varuṇmoḻiyē.
translation: "O Lord of Otriyur, I possess desire," I said. "You file an improper claim against us; what do you possess?" he asked. "This is the condition that keeps you from joining me," I said. "Who drew up and gave you this deed?" he asked. O friend, what are these gracious words spoken by the Lord?
commentary: The heroine confesses her deep longing for the Lord. He treats her confession like a legal dispute, joking that she has filed an improper claim and possesses nothing. They banter back and forth using the language of property deeds and court cases to describe their divine romance.

tamil: வருத்தந் தவரீ ரொற்றியுளீர் மனத்த காத முண்டென்றேன்
நிருத்தந் தருநம் மடியாரை நினைக்கின் றோரைக் கண்டதுதன்
றிருத்தந் தருமுன் னெழுத்திலக்கஞ் சேருந் தூர மோடுமென்றார்
அருத்தந் தெரியே னென்னடியவ் வையர் மொழிந்த வருண்மொழியே.
translit: varuttan tavarī roṟṟiyuḷīr maṉatta kāta muṇṭeṉṟēṉ niruttan tarunam maṭiyārai niṉaikkiṉ ṟōraik kaṇṭatutaṉ ṟiruttan tarumuṉ ṉeḻuttilakkañ cērun tūra mōṭumeṉṟār aruttan teriyē ṉeṉṉaṭiyav vaiyar moḻinta varuṇmoḻiyē.
translation: "O Lord of Otriyur who removes suffering, there is a great depth of desire in my mind," I said. "When it sees those who think of our dancing devotees, it runs away to a distance named by joining that first letter with a measure of miles," he said. I do not understand the meaning. O friend, what are these gracious words spoken by the Lord?
commentary: The heroine tells the Lord that her mind is filled with deep desire. The Lord answers with a clever pun on the Tamil word for desire, which also means a physical distance of about ten miles. He tells her that worldly desire runs ten miles away the moment it sees true devotees of the dancing Lord.

tamil: மைய லகற்றீ ரொற்றியுளீர் வாவென் றுரைப்பீ ரோவென்றேன்
துய்ய வதன்மேற் றலைவைத்துச் சொன்னாற் சொல்வே மிரண்டென்றார்
உய்ய வுரைத்தீ ரெனக்கென்றே னுலகி லெவர்க்கு மாமென்றார்
ஐய விடையா யென்னடியவ் வையர் மொழிந்த வருண்மொழியே.
translit: maiya lakaṟṟī roṟṟiyuḷīr vāveṉ ṟuraippī rōveṉṟēṉ tuyya vataṉmēṟ ṟalaivaittuc coṉṉāṟ colvē miraṇṭeṉṟār uyya vuraittī reṉakkeṉṟē ṉulaki levarkku māmeṉṟār aiya viṭaiyā yeṉṉaṭiyav vaiyar moḻinta varuṇmoḻiyē.
translation: I said, "You of Otriyur who do not dispel my delusion, will You tell me to come?" He said, "If you place a head on that pure thing, we will say both." I said, "You have spoken this for my salvation." He said, "It applies to everyone in the world." Oh friend with a beautiful waist, what are these gracious words spoken by the Lord?
commentary: The heroine asks the Lord for a personal invitation to join him. He answers with a playful riddle, telling her that his message of grace is meant for more than just her alone. He makes it clear that the path to salvation applies to everyone in the world equally.

tamil: தாவென் றருளு மொற்றியுளீர் தமியேன் மோக தாகமற
வாவென் றுரைப்பீ ரென்றேன்பின் வருமவ் வெழுத்திங் கிலையென்றார்
ஓவென் றுயர்தீர்த் தருளுவதீ தோவென் றேன்பொய் யுரைக்கின்றாய்
ஆவென் றுரைத்தா ரென்னடியவ் வையர் மொழிந்த வருண்மொழியே.
translit: tāveṉ ṟaruḷu moṟṟiyuḷīr tamiyēṉ mōka tākamaṟa vāveṉ ṟuraippī reṉṟēṉpiṉ varumav veḻuttiṅ kilaiyeṉṟār ōveṉ ṟuyartīrt taruḷuvatī tōveṉ ṟēṉpoy yuraikkiṉṟāy āveṉ ṟuraittā reṉṉaṭiyav vaiyar moḻinta varuṇmoḻiyē.
translation: I said, "You of Otriyur who graciously grant what is asked, will You tell me to come so my lonely thirst of passion is quenched?" He said, "The letter that follows that is not here." Crying "Oh," I said, "Is this how You graciously cure my suffering?" He said, "You speak lies, ah!" Oh friend, what are these gracious words spoken by the Lord?
commentary: The Lord playfully deflects the heroine's romantic longing with a pun about missing letters. When she cries out that he is ignoring her suffering, he lightly accuses her of exaggerating her pain. This teasing dialogue shows the deep, informal intimacy that exists between the soul and God.

tamil: வயலா ரொற்றி மேவுபிடி வாதர் நும்பே ரியாதென்றேன்
இயலா யிட்ட நாமமதற் கிளைய நாம மேயென்றார்
செயலார் கால மறிந்தென்னைச் சேர்வீ ரென்றேன் சிரித்துனக்கிங்
கயலா ரென்றா ரென்னடியவ் வையர் மொழிந்த வருண்மொழியே.
translit: vayalā roṟṟi mēvupiṭi vātar numpē riyāteṉṟēṉ iyalā yiṭṭa nāmamataṟ kiḷaiya nāma mēyeṉṟār ceyalār kāla maṟinteṉṉaic cērvī reṉṟēṉ cirittuṉakkiṅ kayalā reṉṟā reṉṉaṭiyav vaiyar moḻinta varuṇmoḻiyē.
translation: I said, "You stubborn Lord dwelling in Otriyur surrounded by fields, what is Your name?" He said, "It is the younger name to the naturally given name." I said, "You will know the proper time for action and unite with me." He laughed and said, "We are strangers to you here." Oh friend, what are these gracious words spoken by the Lord?
commentary: The heroine tries to pin down the Lord's exact name and secure a promise that he will unite with her at the right time. He laughs and calls himself a stranger to her, intentionally keeping her in a state of longing. The soul constantly reaches for the divine, finding that God loves to remain mysterious and slightly out of grasp.

tamil: என்மே லருள்கூர்ந் தொற்றியுளீ ரென்னை யணைய நினைவீரேற்
பொன்மேல் வெள்ளி யாமென்றேன் பொன்மேற் பச்சை யறியென்றார்
மின்மேற் சடையீ ரீதெல்லாம் விளையாட் டென்றே னன்றென்றார்
அன்மேற் குழலா யென்னடியவ் வையர் மொழிந்த வருண்மொழியே.
translit: eṉmē laruḷkūrn toṟṟiyuḷī reṉṉai yaṇaiya niṉaivīrēṟ poṉmēl veḷḷi yāmeṉṟēṉ poṉmēṟ paccai yaṟiyeṉṟār miṉmēṟ caṭaiyī rītellām viḷaiyāṭ ṭeṉṟē ṉaṉṟeṉṟār aṉmēṟ kuḻalā yeṉṉaṭiyav vaiyar moḻinta varuṇmoḻiyē.
translation: I said, "You of Otriyur, if You show grace and resolve to embrace me, it will be gold upon silver." He said, "Know that green is upon gold." I said, "You with matted hair shining like lightning, this is all just a game." He said, "It is not." Oh friend with beautiful hair, what are these gracious words spoken by the Lord?
commentary: The heroine imagines their union as gold resting upon silver, painting a poetic picture of her soul merging with the Lord. He counters with an image of green upon gold, referring to the goddess who already shares his divine form. She calls this exchange a game, but he gently insists that this divine relationship is absolute reality.

tamil: நாலா ரணஞ்சூ ழொற்றியுளீர் நாகம் வாங்கி யென்னென்றேன்
காலாங் கிரண்டிற் கட்டவென்றார் கலைத்தோல் வல்லீர் நீரென்றேன்
வேலார் விழிமாத் தோலோடு வியாளத் தோலு முண்டென்றார்
ஆலார் களத்த ரென்னடியவ் வையர் மொழிந்த வருண்மொழியே.
translit: nālā raṇañcū ḻoṟṟiyuḷīr nākam vāṅki yeṉṉeṉṟēṉ kālāṅ kiraṇṭiṟ kaṭṭaveṉṟār kalaittōl vallīr nīreṉṟēṉ vēlār viḻimāt tōlōṭu viyāḷat tōlu muṇṭeṉṟār ālār kaḷatta reṉṉaṭiyav vaiyar moḻinta varuṇmoḻiyē.
translation: I said, "You of Otriyur surrounded by the four Vedas, why do You carry a snake?" He said, "To bind the two feet there." I said, "You are an expert with the deer skin." He said, "Oh you with spear-like eyes, I also have the elephant skin and the tiger skin." He has a poison-stained throat. Oh friend, what are these gracious words spoken by the Lord?
commentary: The heroine questions the fearsome symbols the Lord wears, asking why he carries a wild snake and animal skins. He replies that the snake is used to bind feet, hinting at his power to tie down wandering worldly attachments. The soul realizes that God's frightening aspects are actually tools of grace used to conquer illusion and pride.

tamil: முடியா வளஞ்சூ ழொற்றியுளீர் முடிமே லிருந்த தென்னென்றேன்
கடியா வுள்ளங் கையின்முதலைக் கடிந்த தென்றார் கமலமென
வடிவார் கரத்தி லென்னென்றேன் வரைந்த வதனீ றற்றதென்றார்
அடியார்க் கெளியா ரென்னடியவ் வையர் மொழிந்த வருண்மொழியே.
translit: muṭiyā vaḷañcū ḻoṟṟiyuḷīr muṭimē lirunta teṉṉeṉṟēṉ kaṭiyā vuḷḷaṅ kaiyiṉmutalaik kaṭinta teṉṟār kamalameṉa vaṭivār karatti leṉṉeṉṟēṉ varainta vataṉī ṟaṟṟateṉṟār aṭiyārk keḷiyā reṉṉaṭiyav vaiyar moḻinta varuṇmoḻiyē.
translation: I asked, "O Lord of Otriyur surrounded by endless wealth, what is that sitting upon your head?" He said, "It is that which bit the beginning of the unbiting palm." I asked, "What is in your beautifully shaped lotus hand?" He replied, "It is that which has its drawn end removed." He makes himself so accessible to his devotees. O friend, what are these gracious words spoken by the Lord?
commentary: The heroine engages the Lord of Otriyur in a playful exchange of riddles. She asks him to identify the traditional symbols resting on his head and held in his hand, which typically include a snake and a small deer. Instead of giving a direct answer, the Lord replies with cryptic wordplay to tease her. This lighthearted conversation highlights a deeply intimate relationship with the divine. The Lord emerges as a warm presence who makes himself completely accessible to those who love him.

tamil: ஒன்றும் பெருஞ்சீ ரொற்றிநக ருள்ளா ருவந்தின் றுற்றனர்யான்
என்றும் பெரியீர் நீர்வருதற் கென்ன நிமித்த மென்றுரைத்தேன்
துன்றும் விசும்பே யென்றனர்நான் சூதா முமது சொல்லென்றேன்
குன்றுங் குடமு மிடையுனது கொங்கை யெனவே கூறினரே.
translit: oṉṟum peruñcī roṟṟinaka ruḷḷā ruvantiṉ ṟuṟṟaṉaryāṉ eṉṟum periyīr nīrvarutaṟ keṉṉa nimitta meṉṟuraittēṉ tuṉṟum vicumpē yeṉṟaṉarnāṉ cūtā mumatu colleṉṟēṉ kuṉṟuṅ kuṭamu miṭaiyuṉatu koṅkai yeṉavē kūṟiṉarē.
translation: He who dwells in deeply glorious Otri city came happily today. I asked, "O eternally great one, what is the reason for your coming?" He replied, "The dense sky." I told him, "Your words are tricky." He then declared, "Your breasts are mountains and pots, and your waist is the sky."
commentary: In this traditional poetic form, the song unfolds in the voice of a young woman playfully arguing with the Lord. When she asks why he has come, he gives a riddling answer about the sky, which in ancient love poetry is a teasing compliment about a woman's famously slender waist. It shows the intimate, deeply personal affection the soul feels for God.

tamil: கானார் சடையீ ரென்னிருக்கைக் கன்றும் பசுப்போற் கற்றதென்றேன்
மானார் விழியாய் கற்றதுநின் மருங்குற் கலையு மென்றார் நீர்
தானா ரென்றே னனிப்பள்ளித் தலைவ ரெனவே சாற்றினர்நான்
ஆனா லொற்றி யிருமென்றே னங்கு மிருந்தே னென்றாரே.
translit: kāṉār caṭaiyī reṉṉirukkaik kaṉṟum pacuppōṟ kaṟṟateṉṟēṉ māṉār viḻiyāy kaṟṟatuniṉ maruṅkuṟ kalaiyu meṉṟār nīr tāṉā reṉṟē ṉaṉippaḷḷit talaiva reṉavē cāṟṟiṉarnāṉ āṉā loṟṟi yirumeṉṟē ṉaṅku miruntē ṉeṉṟārē.
translation: I said, "O Lord with forest-like matted hair, coming to my house has become a habit for you, like a calf following a cow." He replied, "O woman with deer-like eyes, the garment on your waist has also formed a habit of slipping away." I asked, "Who are you?" He proclaimed, "I am the Lord of Nanippalli." I told him, "If so, stay in Otri." He answered, "I live there too."
commentary: The banter continues with classic signs of spiritual lovesickness. The woman accuses God of following her around, and he counters by pointing out that she is already melting with love, shown by the traditional trope of her slipping garments. Their quick exchange of jokes about where he lives reminds us that God dwells both everywhere and right beside the devoted soul.

tamil: வானங் கொடுப்பீர் திருவொற்றி வாழ்வீ ரன்று வந்தீரென்
மானங் கெடுத்தீ ரென்றேன்முன் வனத்தார் விடுத்தா ரென்றார்நீர்
ஊனந் தடுக்கு மிறையென்றே னுலவா தடுக்கு மென்றார்மால்
ஏனம் புடைத்தீ ரணையென்பீ ரென்றே னகலா ரென்றாரே.
translit: vāṉaṅ koṭuppīr tiruvoṟṟi vāḻvī raṉṟu vantīreṉ māṉaṅ keṭuttī reṉṟēṉmuṉ vaṉattār viṭuttā reṉṟārnīr ūṉan taṭukku miṟaiyeṉṟē ṉulavā taṭukku meṉṟārmāl ēṉam puṭaittī raṇaiyeṉpī reṉṟē ṉakalā reṉṟārē.
translation: I said, "You who grant the heavens and live in Thiru Otri, you came that day and ruined my honor." He replied, "The forest sages unleashed that deer long ago." I said, "You are the Lord who blocks all flaws." He replied, "There is also an imperishable mat." I said, "You struck the great boar, yet you ask me to embrace you." He replied, "Those who do will never depart."
commentary: This exchange is built entirely on clever wordplay, where the woman's complaints are instantly turned into divine assurances. When she teases him about his fierce mythical deeds, he responds with a plain spiritual truth: anyone who truly embraces him will never be separated from him again.

tamil: இருமை யளவும் பொழிலொற்றி யிடத்தீர் முனிவ ரிடரறநீர்
பெருமை நடத்தீ ரென்றேனென் பிள்ளை நடத்தி னானென்றார்
தரும மலவிவ் விடையென்றேன் றரும விடையு முண்டென்றார்
கரும மெவன்யான் செயவென்றேன் கருதாண் பாலன் றென்றாரே.
translit: irumai yaḷavum poḻiloṟṟi yiṭattīr muṉiva riṭaraṟanīr perumai naṭattī reṉṟēṉeṉ piḷḷai naṭatti ṉāṉeṉṟār taruma malaviv viṭaiyeṉṟēṉ ṟaruma viṭaiyu muṇṭeṉṟār karuma mevaṉyāṉ ceyaveṉṟēṉ karutāṇ pālaṉ ṟeṉṟārē.
translation: I said, "O Lord of Otri, filled with groves extending across both worlds, you acted with greatness to end the sorrow of the sages." He replied, "My son conducted it." I said, "This answer is not fair." He replied, "I also ride the bull of fairness." I asked, "What duty must I perform?" He replied, "That is not your concern."
commentary: The playful argument reaches a moment of deep surrender. When the soul finally stops teasing and asks what duty she must actually perform, God replies that it is not her concern. Once a person is fully absorbed in divine love, grace takes over completely, leaving no more religious burdens or rituals to carry out.

tamil: ஒசிய விடுகு மிடையாரை யொற்றி யிருந்தே வுருக்குகின்ற
வசியர் மிகநீ ரென்றேனென் மகனே யென்றார் வளர்காமப்
பசிய துடையே னென்றேனுட் பணியல் குலுமப் படியென்றார்
நிசிய மிடற்றீ ராமென்றேன் நீகண் டதுவே யென்றாரே.
translit: ociya viṭuku miṭaiyārai yoṟṟi yiruntē vurukkukiṉṟa vaciyar mikanī reṉṟēṉeṉ makaṉē yeṉṟār vaḷarkāmap paciya tuṭaiyē ṉeṉṟēṉuṭ paṇiyal kulumap paṭiyeṉṟār niciya miṭaṟṟī rāmeṉṟēṉ nīkaṇ ṭatuvē yeṉṟārē.
translation: I said, "Staying here in Otri, you melt women with slender, swaying waists. You are a great charmer." He replied, "That is my son." I said, "I have a growing hunger of desire." He replied, "Your inner serpent feels the same." I said, "You possess a dark, night-like throat." He replied, "It is exactly as you have seen."
commentary: The woman admits her immense hunger for him, and he confirms that he sees her deepest inner longing. She then gently mentions his dark throat, stained by the poison he drank to save the universe in ancient lore. Beneath the romance of the dialogue is a clear reminder of God's supreme compassion in protecting all living beings.

tamil: கலையா ளுடையீ ரொற்றிநின்றீர் காம மளித்தீர் களித்தணையீர்
மலையா ளுமது மனைவியென்றேன் மலைவா ளுனைநான் மருவினென்றார்
அலையாண் மற்றை யவளென்றே னலைவா ளவளு மறியென்றார்
நிலையாண் மையினீ ராவென்றே னீயா வென்று நின்றாரே.
translit: kalaiyā ḷuṭaiyī roṟṟiniṉṟīr kāma maḷittīr kaḷittaṇaiyīr malaiyā ḷumatu maṉaiviyeṉṟēṉ malaivā ḷuṉaināṉ maruviṉeṉṟār alaiyāṇ maṟṟai yavaḷeṉṟē ṉalaivā ḷavaḷu maṟiyeṉṟār nilaiyāṇ maiyiṉī rāveṉṟē ṉīyā veṉṟu niṉṟārē.
translation: I said, "You possess all arts and stand in Otriyur. You gave me this desire, yet you do not embrace me in joy. The daughter of the mountain is your wife." He replied, "She will be bewildered if I embrace you." I asked, "What about the other one, the lady of the waves?" He said, "She too will be agitated, you should know." I asked, "Are you truly of steadfast manhood?" He stood there and asked, "Are you?"
commentary: The devotee speaks as a woman longing for God's embrace. She teases the Lord about his two mythological wives: Parvati, the daughter of the mountain, and Ganga, the river goddess of the waves in his hair. He plays along, claiming they would be jealous. When she questions his manhood for refusing her, he turns the question back on her own steadfastness. This banter shows a deeply intimate relationship with the divine where playful teasing replaces formal distance.

tamil: சீலம் படைத்தீர் திருவொற்றித் தியாக ரேநீர் திண்மைமிகுஞ்
சூலம் படைத்தீ ரென்னென்றேன் றொல்லை யுலக முணவென்றார்
ஆலம் படுத்த களத்தீரென் றறைந்தே னவளிவ் வானென்றார்
சாலம் பெடுத்தீ ருமையென்றேன் றார மிரண்டா மென்றாரே.
translit: cīlam paṭaittīr tiruvoṟṟit tiyāka rēnīr tiṇmaimikuñ cūlam paṭaittī reṉṉeṉṟēṉ ṟollai yulaka muṇaveṉṟār ālam paṭutta kaḷattīreṉ ṟaṟaintē ṉavaḷiv vāṉeṉṟār cālam peṭuttī rumaiyeṉṟēṉ ṟāra miraṇṭā meṉṟārē.
translation: I said, "O Lord Thyagar of Thiru Otriyur possessing great virtue! Why do you wield this exceedingly firm trident?" He said, "To spear the ancient world for food." I said, "You have a throat that contained the poison." He replied, "She became this sky." I said, "You act with deception towards Uma." He said, "I have two wives."
commentary: The conversation turns to the traditional symbols of the Lord. When asked why he carries a firm trident, he jokes that it is a spear for catching his food. The devotee mentions the poison he swallowed to save the world, which stained his throat, and he deflects again with a pun. The dialogue turns God's fearsome attributes into subjects of affectionate humor.

tamil: ஞால ராதி வணங்குமொற்றி நாதர் நீரே நாட்டமுறும்
பால ராமென் றுரைத்தேனாம் பால ரலநீ பாரென்றார்
மேல ராவந் திடுமென்றேன் விளம்பேல் மகவு மறியுமென்றார்
கோல ராமென் றுரைத்தேன்யாங் கொண்டோ முக்க ணென்றாரே.
translit: ñāla rāti vaṇaṅkumoṟṟi nātar nīrē nāṭṭamuṟum pāla rāmeṉ ṟuraittēṉām pāla ralanī pāreṉṟār mēla rāvan tiṭumeṉṟēṉ viḷampēl makavu maṟiyumeṉṟār kōla rāmeṉ ṟuraittēṉyāṅ koṇṭō mukka ṇeṉṟārē.
translation: I said, "You are the Lord of Otriyur worshipped by the people of the world. You are a sought-after child." He said, "We are not a child, look closely." I said, "The snake upon you will come." He said, "Do not speak of it, the child knows it too." I said, "You are of beautiful form." He said, "We possess three eyes."
commentary: The devotee affectionately calls the Lord a child, but he tells her to look closer. She playfully warns him about the dangerous snake he wears as an ornament, and he answers that his mythological child already knows how to handle it. When she praises his beautiful form, he bluntly reminds her of his strange, fearsome third eye. He constantly counters her romantic praises with stark reminders of his wild nature.

tamil: வண்மை தருவீ ரொற்றிநின்று வருவீ ரென்னை மருவீர்நீர்
உண்மை யுடையீ ரென்றேனா முடைப்பேம் வணங்கி னோர்க்கென்றார்
கண்மை யுடையீ ரென்றேனீ களமை யுடையேம் யாமென்றார்
தண்மை யருளீ ரென்றேனாந் தகையே யருள்வ தென்றாரே.
translit: vaṇmai taruvī roṟṟiniṉṟu varuvī reṉṉai maruvīrnīr uṇmai yuṭaiyī reṉṟēṉā muṭaippēm vaṇaṅki ṉōrkkeṉṟār kaṇmai yuṭaiyī reṉṟēṉī kaḷamai yuṭaiyēm yāmeṉṟār taṇmai yaruḷī reṉṟēṉān takaiyē yaruḷva teṉṟārē.
translation: I said, "You bestow bounty. Coming from Otriyur, you do not embrace me. You possess truth." He replied, "Yes, we become the possession of those who bow to us." I said, "You have blackness in your eyes." He said, "We have blackness in our throat." I said, "Grant me your cool grace." He said, "We grant only what is fitting."
commentary: The devotee praises the Lord's truth, and he replies with a pun, saying he becomes the true possession of those who bow to him. She points out the dark beauty of his eyes, and he redirects her attention to the dark poison in his throat. When she begs for his comforting grace, he promises only to give what is fitting. The exchange blends spiritual longing with sharp replies that keep the devotee entirely focused on the divine.

tamil: ஒன்னார் புரமூன் றெரிசெய்தீ ரொற்றி யுடையீ ருவப்புடனே
யென்னா குலத்தை யோட்டுமென்றே னிடைய ரலநா மென்றுரைத்தார்
பொன்னாற் சடையீ ரென்றேனென் புதிய தேவி மனைவியென்றார்
சொன்னாற் கேள்வி வியப்பென்றேன் சுத்த வியப்பொன் றென்றாரே.
translit: oṉṉār puramūṉ ṟericeytī roṟṟi yuṭaiyī ruvappuṭaṉē yeṉṉā kulattai yōṭṭumeṉṟē ṉiṭaiya ralanā meṉṟuraittār poṉṉāṟ caṭaiyī reṉṟēṉeṉ putiya tēvi maṉaiviyeṉṟār coṉṉāṟ kēḷvi viyappeṉṟēṉ cutta viyappoṉ ṟeṉṟārē.
translation: I said, "You burned the three cities of your foes. O Lord of Otriyur, joyously drive away my sorrow." He replied, "We are not cowherds to drive away a herd of cows." I said, "You have matted hair shining like gold." He said, "My new goddess is my wife." I said, "Listening to your words is a wonder." He said, "It is one pure wonder."
commentary: The devotee asks the Lord to drive away her sorrow, using the Tamil word ākulam. He replies with a pun by splitting the word into ā (cow) and kulam (herd), joking that he is no cowherd to drive cattle. Surprised by his constant wordplay, she calls his speech a wonder. He agrees, calling it a pure wonder. This poetic game uses the charm of language to express the absolute joy of intimacy with God.

tamil: கனிமா னிதழி முலைச்சுவடு களித்தீ ரொற்றிக் கடிநகரீர்
தனிமா னேந்தி யென்றேனென் றலைமே லொருமா னேந்தியென்றார்
துனிமாற் றுகிலீ ரென்றேனற் றுகில்கோ வணங்கா ணென்றாரென்
பனிமால் வரையீ ரென்றேனென் பனிமால் வரைகா ணென்றாரே.
translit: kaṉimā ṉitaḻi mulaiccuvaṭu kaḷittī roṟṟik kaṭinakarīr taṉimā ṉēnti yeṉṟēṉeṉ ṟalaimē lorumā ṉēntiyeṉṟār tuṉimāṟ ṟukilī reṉṟēṉaṟ ṟukilkō vaṇaṅkā ṇeṉṟāreṉ paṉimāl varaiyī reṉṟēṉeṉ paṉimāl varaikā ṇeṉṟārē.
translation: O Lord of the secure city of Otri, you delight in the cassia garland and the breast-marks of the sweet lady! I said, "You hold a solitary deer." He replied, "I bear an unparalleled lady upon my head." I said, "You lack a garment to ward off distress." He replied, "See, the loincloth is a fine garment." I said, "You belong to the great snowy mountain." He replied, "Behold my great snowy mountain."
commentary: The heroine playfully questions the Lord of Otriyur about his ascetic appearance. She asks why he holds a solitary deer in his hand. He replies with a pun on the Tamil word for deer (mān), which also means a beautiful woman, joking that he carries a lady, the river goddess Ganga, on his head. She then teases him for wearing only a simple loincloth and living on a freezing mountain. He answers that his ascetic cloth is a perfectly fine garment and proudly claims the snowy peak of Mount Kailash as his true home.

sections.title: The Husband Who Fills the Eyes

tamil: மைய லழகீ ரூரொற்றி வைத்தீ ருளவோ மனையென்றேன்
கையி னிறைந்த தனத்தினுந்தங் கண்ணி னிறைந்த கணவனையே
மெய்யின் விழைவா ரொருமனையோ விளம்பின் மனையும் மிகப்பலவாம்
எய்யி லிடையா யென்கின்றா ரிதுதான் சேடி யென்னேடி.
translit: maiya laḻakī rūroṟṟi vaittī ruḷavō maṉaiyeṉṟēṉ kaiyi ṉiṟainta taṉattiṉuntaṅ kaṇṇi ṉiṟainta kaṇavaṉaiyē meyyiṉ viḻaivā rorumaṉaiyō viḷampiṉ maṉaiyum mikappalavām eyyi liṭaiyā yeṉkiṉṟā ritutāṉ cēṭi yeṉṉēṭi.
translation: I asked, "O Lord of enchanting beauty residing in Otriyur, do you have a wife?" He says, "O you with a slender waist, women truly desire a husband who fills their eyes more than wealth that fills their hands. Do I have just one wife? If I tell the truth, my wives are very many." What is this, my friend?
commentary: The heroine asks the Lord a simple question about whether he is married, and he answers with a spiritual riddle. He tells her that he has countless wives, meaning the many devoted souls who love him more than they love worldly wealth. The Lord uses the language of romance to describe the deep devotion between God and humanity. The heroine is left entirely confused by his playful answer, turning to her friend for an explanation.

tamil: காராய வண்ண மணிவண்ண கண்ண கனசங்கு சக்ர தரநீள்
சீராய தூய மலர்வாய நேய ஸ்ரீராம ராம வெனவே
தாராய வாழ்வு தருநெஞ்சு சூழ்க தாமோத ராய நமவோம்
நாராய ணாய நமவாம னாய நமகேச வாய நமவே.
translit: kārāya vaṇṇa maṇivaṇṇa kaṇṇa kaṉacaṅku cakra taranīḷ cīrāya tūya malarvāya nēya śrīrāma rāma veṉavē tārāya vāḻvu taruneñcu cūḻka tāmōta rāya namavōm nārāya ṇāya namavāma ṉāya namakēca vāya namavē.
translation: O one colored like the dark rainclouds! O gem-hued one! O Krishna! O bearer of the mighty conch and discus! O one of immense glory! O one with a pure lotus mouth! O beloved one! May my heart immerse itself in chanting "Sri Rama, Rama" to grant me a life of deliverance. Om, salutations to Damodara. Salutations to Narayana. Salutations to Vamana. Salutations to Keshava.
commentary: The speaker addresses the divine using the traditional imagery of Krishna and Vishnu, praising his dark raincloud complexion and his holding of the sacred conch and discus. The core of this devotion is the constant repetition of the name Rama within the heart to achieve spiritual freedom. The verse concludes by bowing to various names of the divine: Damodara, Narayana, Vamana, and Keshava.

sections.title: The Decad on the Name of Rama

translit: tirumakaḷem perumāṭṭi makiḻum vaṇṇac ceḻuṅkaṉiyē koḻumpākē tēṉē teyvat tarumakaṉaik kāttaruḷak karattē veṉṟit taṉu-eṭutta orumutalē tarumap pēṟē irumaiyumeṉ ṉuḷattamarnta rāma nāmat teṉaracē eṉamutē eṉtā yēniṉ marumalarppoṉ aṭivaḻuttum ciṟiyēṉ antō maṉantaḷarntēṉ aṟintumaruḷ vaḻaṅki lāyē.
translation: O rich fruit, thick syrup, and honey who delights our Lady, the Goddess of Wealth! O Supreme One who took up the victorious bow in Your hand to protect the divine son of Dharma! O reward of righteousness! O my King bearing the name Rama, who abides in my heart in this world and the next! O my nectar! O my mother! Alas, I am a lowly one who praises Your fragrant, golden, flower-like feet, and my heart has grown weary. Even knowing this, You have not granted Your grace.
commentary: The verse approaches Rama as both the fierce protector of righteousness and the gentle beloved of the Goddess of Wealth. The speaker claims an intimate bond with God but suffers from deep exhaustion, wondering why divine relief is continually withheld.

translit: kalaikkaṭalē karuṇaineṭuṅ kaṭalē kāṉaṅ kaṭantataṭaṅ kaṭalē-eṉ karuttē ñāṉa malaikkaṇeḻuñ cuṭarēvāṉ cuṭarē aṉpar maṉattoḷirum cuyañcuṭarē maṇiyē vāṉōr talaikkaṇuṟu makuṭacikā maṇiyē vāymait tacarataṉtaṉ kulamaṇiyē tamiyēṉ uḷḷa nilaikkaṇuṟum śrīrāma vaḷḷa lē-eṉ nilai-aṟintum aruḷa-iṉṉum niṉainti lāyē.
translation: O ocean of arts! O vast ocean of compassion! O expansive ocean who crossed the mirage! O my very thought! O flame rising on the mountain of wisdom! O celestial flame! O self-luminous flame shining in the minds of devotees! O jewel! O crest jewel on the crowns of the celestials! O jewel of the lineage of truthful Dasaratha! O bountiful Lord Sri Rama who abides within the heart of this lonely one! Even knowing my state, You still have not thought to grant Your grace.
commentary: Praising Rama through images of endless oceans and brilliant flames, the text recalls his earthly birth as the son of King Dasaratha. The plea deepens as the speaker asks why a God who dwells so intimately in the devotee's own heart chooses to ignore their suffering.

translit: maṇṇāḷā niṉṟavartam vāḻvu vēṇṭēṉ maṟṟavarpōl paṟṟaṭaintu māḷa vēṇṭēṉ viṇṇāḷā niṉṟa-oru mēṉmai vēṇṭēṉ vittakaniṉ tiruvaruḷē vēṇṭi niṉṟēṉ puṇṇāḷā niṉṟamaṉa muṭaiyēṉ ceyta poyaṉaittum tiruvuḷattē poṟuppāy aṉṟik kaṇṇāḷā cuṭarkkamalak kaṇṇā eṉṉaik kaiviṭileṉ ceyvēṉē kaṭaiya ṉēṉē.
translation: I do not desire the life of those who rule the earth. I do not desire to perish, caught in attachments like the rest. I do not desire the singular greatness of ruling the heavens. O wise Lord, I stand desiring only Your divine grace. You must forgive in Your divine heart all the falsehoods committed by me, whose mind is afflicted like an open wound. O beloved Lord with radiant lotus eyes, if You abandon me, what will I, the lowest of the low, do?
commentary: True spiritual yearning seeks neither earthly wealth nor the power to rule the heavens. The speaker asks only for divine grace, pleading with God to forgive human falsehoods and heal a mind that feels like an open wound.

translit: tevviṉaiyār arakkarkulam ceṟṟa veṟṟic ciṅkamē eṅkaḷkula teyva mēyō vevviṉaitīrt taruḷkiṉṟa rāma nāma viyaṉcuṭarē ivvulaka viṭayak kāṭṭil ivviṉaiyēṉ akappaṭṭēṉ pulaṉām kaḷvark kilakkāṉēṉ tuṇai-oṉṟum illēṉ antō ceyviṉai-oṉ ṟaṟiyēṉiṅ keṉṉai entāy tiruvuḷattil cērttilaiyēl ceyva teṉṉē.
translation: O victorious lion who destroyed the lineage of hostile demons! O deity of our lineage! O majestic flame of the name Rama, who dispels cruel karma and grants grace! I am caught in this worldly forest of sensory objects. I have become a target for the thieves called the senses. Alas, I have no support at all. I do not know what to do here. O my father, if You do not gather me into Your divine heart, what am I to do?
commentary: The human mind is easily captured by the physical senses, which act like thieves in a dark forest. Just as Rama defeated literal demons in the sacred stories, the speaker begs him to defeat these inner enemies and rescue the soul from the dangers of worldly distraction.

translit: vāṉvaṇṇak karumukilē maḻaiyē nīla maṇivaṇṇak koḻuñcuṭarē maruntē vāṉat tēṉvaṇṇac ceḻuñcuvaiyē rāma nāmat teyvamē niṉpukaḻait teḷintē ōtā ūṉvaṇṇap pulaivāyār iṭattē ceṉṟāṅ kuḻaikkiṉṟēṉ ceyvakai-oṉ ṟuṇarēṉ antō kāṉvaṇṇak kuṭumpattiṟ kilakkā eṉṉaik kāṭṭiṉaiyē eṉṉēniṉ karuṇai ītō.
translation: O dark raincloud sharing the color of the sky! O rain! O rich flame sharing the color of a blue sapphire! O medicine! O rich sweetness like celestial honey! O deity bearing the name Rama! I go and toil among those foul-mouthed people of flesh who do not clearly chant Your praise. Alas, I do not know what to do. You have made me a target for family life, which is like a wild forest. What is this? Is this Your compassion?
commentary: The verse captures the deep isolation of trying to live a spiritual life among people who only care for physical survival and material things. Trapped in the wild forest of family obligations, the devotee openly challenges God, asking how leaving a soul in such a painful struggle can ever be called compassion.

translit: poṉṉuṭaiyār vāyililpōy vīṇē kālam pōkkukiṉṟēṉ ivvulakap puṇarppai vēṇṭi eṉṉuṭaiyāy niṉṉaṭiyai maṟantēṉ antō eṉceykēṉ eṉceykēṉ ēḻai yēṉnāṉ piṉṉuṭaiyēṉ piḻai-uṭaiyēṉ allāl uṉṟaṉ pēraruḷum uṭaiyēṉō piṟantēṉ vāḷā uṉṉuṭaiya tiruvuḷatteṉ niṉaiti yō-eṉ orumutalvā śrīrāmā uṇarki lēṉē.
translation: I go to the doors of the wealthy and waste my time in vain, seeking worldly connections. My Lord who possesses me, I forgot your feet. Alas, what will I do, what will I do, poor wretch that I am. I possess only faults and shortcomings. Do I possess your great grace? I was born for nothing. My singular Lord, Sri Rama, I do not know what you hold in your sacred heart.
commentary: Vallalar describes the trap of chasing worldly success and begging from the wealthy. He says this search only wastes time and makes a person forget God. Looking to Sri Rama, he asks if there is still room for grace in his flawed life.

translit: aṟampaḻukkum taruvē-eṉ kuruvē eṉṟaṉ āruyiruk korutuṇaiyē aracē pūvai niṟampaḻukka aḻakoḻukum vaṭivak kuṉṟē neṭuṅkaṭaluk kaṇaiyaḷitta nilaiyē veyya maṟampaḻukkum ilaṅkai-irā vaṇaṉaip paṇṭōr vāḷiṉāṟ paṇikoṇṭa maṇiyē vāymait tiṟampaḻukkum śrīrāma vaḷḷa lēniṉ tiruvaruḷē aṉṟimaṟṟōr ceyali lēṉē.
translation: O tree that yields the fruit of righteousness! O my guru! The singular companion to my precious life! O King! O mountain of form dripping with beauty, blooming with the hue of the kaya flower! O steadfast one who built a bridge across the vast ocean! O gem who once subdued Ravana of Lanka, a man ripe with cruel sins, using your weapon! O benevolent Sri Rama, ripe with the power of truth! I have no refuge other than your sacred grace.
commentary: The focus shifts entirely to the greatness of the divine. Addressing God as Sri Rama, Vallalar recalls familiar stories of Rama building a bridge across the ocean and defeating the cruel king Ravana. He says that trusting in God's grace is the only true refuge.

translit: kallāya vaṉmaṉattar tampāl ceṉṟē kaṇkalakkaṅ koḷkiṉṟēṉ kavalai vāḻvai ellāmuḷ iruntaṟintāy aṉṟō caṟṟum iraṅkilai-em perumāṉē eṉṉē eṉṉē pollāta vevviṉaiyēṉ eṉiṉum eṉṉaip puṇṇiyaṉē purappataruṭ pukaḻcci aṉṟō alārnta tuyarkkaṭalniṉ ṟeṭutti ṭāyēl āṟṟēṉnāṉ paḻiniṉpāl ākku vēṉē.
translation: I go to those with stony, hard hearts and stand with tear-filled eyes. You dwell within me and know all my sorrowful life, do you not? You show me no pity at all, my Lord. What is this, what is this! Even though I carry evil and cruel deeds, O virtuous one, protecting me brings glory to your grace. If you do not lift me from this dark ocean of sorrow, I cannot bear it. I will place the blame on you.
commentary: Vallalar speaks to God with the fierce intimacy of a child demanding attention from a parent. He asks how God, who lives within his heart and knows his suffering, can watch him beg from cold-hearted people without intervening. He even warns that if God does not save him, the blame will fall on God himself.

translit: maiyāṉa neñcakattōr vāyil cārntē maṉamtaḷarntēṉ varuntukiṉṟa varuttam ellām aiyā-eṉ uḷattamarntāy nītāṉ caṟṟum aṟiyāyō aṟiyāyēl aṟivā ryārē poyyāṉa taṉmaiyiṉēṉ eṉiṉum eṉṉaip puṟamviṭuttal aḻakēyō poruḷā eṇṇi meyyā-eṉ ṟaṉai-annāḷ āṇṭāy innāḷ veṟuttaṉaiyēl eṅkēyāṉ mēvu vēṉē.
translation: I approach the doors of those with dark hearts and lose my spirit. O Lord seated in my heart, do you not know all the sorrow I suffer? If you do not know, who else will know? Even though I possess a false nature, is it right for you to cast me aside? Considering me worthy, O Truth, you took me as your own in the past. If you reject me today, where will I go?
commentary: The pain of seeking help from worldly people continues to break his spirit. Because God dwells inside him as an inner witness, Vallalar says God must already know his sorrow intimately. He pleads that since God claimed him in the past, he cannot abandon him now, because there is nowhere else to turn.

translit: kūṟuvatōr kuṇamillāk koṭitām celvak kuruṭṭaṟivōr iṭaippaṭumeṉ kuṟaikaḷ ellām āṟuvatōr vaḻikāṇēṉ antō antō avalameṉum karuṅkaṭalil aḻuntu kiṉṟēṉ ēṟuvatōr vakai-aṟiyēṉ entāy entāy ēṟṟukiṉṟōr niṉṉai-aṉṟi illēṉ eṉṉaic cīṟuvatō iraṅkuvatō yātō uṉṟaṉ tiruvuḷattait teriyēṉē ciṟiya ṉēṉē.
translation: I am caught among men of blind intellect, corrupted by cruel wealth devoid of any worthy quality. I see no way to relieve my many grievances. Alas, alas! I am sinking in the dark ocean of despair. I know no way to climb out, my Father, my Father. I have no one to lift me but you. Will you be angry with me, or will you show me pity? Being so lowly, I do not know what lies in your sacred heart.
commentary: Wealth without goodness blinds people to the suffering of others, and Vallalar feels trapped among such individuals. Sinking in despair, he admits total helplessness. He tells God that he has no other rescuer, leaving his fate entirely to whatever pity or anger lies in the divine heart.

sections.title: Five Verses of Praise to Veeraraghava

note: Editor's note: composed at the request of Kondamur Sri Srinivasa Varadachariar Swamigal.
tamil: தண்ணமர் மதிபோல் சாந்தந் தழைத்தசத் துவனே போற்றி
வண்ணமா மணியே போற்றி மணிவண்ணத் தேவா போற்றி
அண்ணலே எவ்வு ளூரில் அமர்ந்தருள் ஆதி போற்றி
விண்ணவர் முதல்வா போற்றி வீரரா கவனே போற்றி.
translit: taṇṇamar matipōl cāntan taḻaittacat tuvaṉē pōṟṟi vaṇṇamā maṇiyē pōṟṟi maṇivaṇṇat tēvā pōṟṟi aṇṇalē evvu ḷūril amarntaruḷ āti pōṟṟi viṇṇavar mutalvā pōṟṟi vīrarā kavaṉē pōṟṟi.
translation: Praise to the pure one flourishing with peace like the cool moon. Praise to the great, vibrant gem. Praise to the jewel-colored God. Praise to the Lord, the primal one who sits and bestows grace in Evvulur. Praise to the foremost of heavenly beings. Praise to Veeraraghava.
commentary: The poem begins by envisioning the divine presence as deeply peaceful and visually radiant. Evvulur is the historical name for Thiruvallur, a town near Chennai famous for its ancient temple to Lord Vishnu, who is worshipped there as Veeraraghava.

tamil: பாண்டவர் தூத னாகப் பலித்தருள் பரனே போற்றி
நீண்டவன் என்ன வேதம் நிகழ்த்துமா நிதியே போற்றி
தூண்டலில் லாமல் ஓங்குஞ் ஜோதிநல் விளக்கே போற்றி
வேண்டவர் எவ்வு ளூர்வாழ் வீரரா கவனே போற்றி.
translit: pāṇṭavar tūta ṉākap palittaruḷ paraṉē pōṟṟi nīṇṭavaṉ eṉṉa vētam nikaḻttumā nitiyē pōṟṟi tūṇṭalil lāmal ōṅkuñ jōtinal viḷakkē pōṟṟi vēṇṭavar evvu ḷūrvāḻ vīrarā kavaṉē pōṟṟi.
translation: Praise to the supreme one who graciously acted as the messenger for the Pandavas. Praise to the great treasure described by the Vedas as the exalted one. Praise to the good lamp of Jothi that shines high without needing to be kindled. Praise to Veeraraghava who lives in Evvulur, sought by all who pray.
commentary: God is praised here for stepping into human history to help those in need, specifically by acting as a messenger for the Pandava princes in the ancient Mahabharata epic. The verse also describes the divine as a self-sustaining lamp of Jothi (spiritual light), shining entirely on its own without needing anyone to kindle it.

tamil: மேதினி புரக்கும் வேந்தர் வீறெலாம் நினதே போற்றி
கோதிலா மனத்தே நின்று குலாவிய கோவே போற்றி
ஓதிய எவ்வு ளூரில் உறைந்தருள் புரிவாய் போற்றி
வேதியன் தன்னை ஈன்ற வீரரா கவனே போற்றி.
translit: mētiṉi purakkum vēntar vīṟelām niṉatē pōṟṟi kōtilā maṉattē niṉṟu kulāviya kōvē pōṟṟi ōtiya evvu ḷūril uṟaintaruḷ purivāy pōṟṟi vētiyaṉ taṉṉai īṉṟa vīrarā kavaṉē pōṟṟi.
translation: Praise to you, for all the majesty of kings who protect the earth is truly yours. Praise to the king who stands and rejoices in flawless minds. Praise to you who reside and grant grace in renowned Evvulur. Praise to Veeraraghava who gave birth to the creator.
commentary: All worldly power and majesty in the end belong to the divine. The verse praises Veeraraghava as the supreme origin of everything, noting the traditional scriptural belief that he gave birth to the creator of the universe itself.

tamil: இளங்கொடி தனைக்கொண் டேகும் இராவணன் தனைய ழித்தே
களங்கமில் விபீட ணர்க்குக் கனவர சளித்தாய் போற்றி
துளங்குமா தவத்தோர் உற்ற துயரெலாம் தவிர்த்தாய் போற்றி
விளங்குநல் எவ்வு ளூர்வாழ் வீரரா கவனே போற்றி.
translit: iḷaṅkoṭi taṉaikkoṇ ṭēkum irāvaṇaṉ taṉaiya ḻittē kaḷaṅkamil vipīṭa ṇarkkuk kaṉavara caḷittāy pōṟṟi tuḷaṅkumā tavattōr uṟṟa tuyarelām tavirttāy pōṟṟi viḷaṅkunal evvu ḷūrvāḻ vīrarā kavaṉē pōṟṟi.
translation: Praise to you who destroyed Ravana when he carried away the tender vine-like woman. Praise to you who gave the great kingdom to the blemishless Vibhishana. Praise to you who dispelled all the sorrows of those performing radiant great penance. Praise to Veeraraghava who lives in good, illustrious Evvulur.
commentary: This verse recalls the epic story of the Ramayana. It honors the deity in his form as Lord Rama, who rescued his abducted wife Sita, defeated the demon king Ravana, and rewarded the righteous Vibhishana with a great kingdom.

tamil: அற்புதத் திருவை மார்பில் அணைத்தபே ரழகா போற்றி
பொற்புறு திகிரி சங்கு பொருந்துகைப் புனிதா போற்றி
வற்புறு பிணிதீர்த் தென்னை மகிழ்வித்த வரதா போற்றி
வெற்புயர் எவ்வு ளூர்வாழ் வீரரா கவனே போற்றி.
translit: aṟputat tiruvai mārpil aṇaittapē raḻakā pōṟṟi poṟpuṟu tikiri caṅku poruntukaip puṉitā pōṟṟi vaṟpuṟu piṇitīrt teṉṉai makiḻvitta varatā pōṟṟi veṟpuyar evvu ḷūrvāḻ vīrarā kavaṉē pōṟṟi.
translation: Praise to the great, beautiful one who holds the wondrous goddess of wealth upon your chest. Praise to the pure one whose hands hold the beautiful discus and conch. Praise to the granter of boons who cured my severe disease and brought me joy. Praise to Veeraraghava who lives in Evvulur with its high mountains.
commentary: The imagery here matches the traditional form of Lord Vishnu, carrying a conch shell and a discus with the goddess of wealth resting upon his chest. The poem concludes with a deeply personal note of gratitude, thanking the deity for curing a terrible disease and restoring the poet to joy.

note: Editor's note: composed at the request of a devotee.
tamil: சீர்வளர் மதியும் திருவளர் வாழ்க்கைச் செல்வமும் கல்வியும் பொறையும்
பார்வளர் திறனும் பயன்வளர் பரிசும் பத்தியும் எனக்கருள் பரிந்தே
வார்வளர் தனத்தாய் மருவளர் குழலாய் மணிவளர் அணிமலர் முகத்தாய்
ஏர்வளர் குணத்தாய் இசைதுலுக் காணத் திரேணுகை எனும்ஒரு திருவே.
translit: cīrvaḷar matiyum tiruvaḷar vāḻkkaic celvamum kalviyum poṟaiyum pārvaḷar tiṟaṉum payaṉvaḷar paricum pattiyum eṉakkaruḷ parintē vārvaḷar taṉattāy maruvaḷar kuḻalāy maṇivaḷar aṇimalar mukattāy ērvaḷar kuṇattāy icaituluk kāṇat tirēṇukai eṉumoru tiruvē.
translation: Compassionately grant me excellent wisdom, the wealth of a blessed life, education, patience, great abilities praised by the world, fruitful gifts, and devotion. O Mother with beautiful breasts bound by a bodice, fragrant hair, and a radiant flower-like face adorned with gems. O Mother of beautiful qualities. O incomparable Goddess known as Renuka of renowned Thulukkanam.
commentary: The opening verse asks for a complete foundation for a good life, blending worldly success with spiritual depth. The prayer lists wisdom, wealth, education, and patience alongside devotion to the divine. The Goddess Renuka is addressed using classical imagery of physical beauty and radiant grace, establishing her as the source of all these gifts.

tamil: உவந்தொரு காசும் உதவிடாக் கொடிய உலுத்தர்தம் கடைதொறும்ஓடி
அவந்தனில் அலையா வகைஎனக் குன்தன் அகமலர்ந் தருளுதல் வேண்டும்
நவந்தரு மதிய நிவந்தபூங் கொடியே நலந்தரு நசைமணிக் கோவை
இவந்தொளிர் பசுந்தோள் இசைதுலுக் காணத் திரேணுகை எனும்ஒரு திருவே.
translit: uvantoru kācum utaviṭāk koṭiya uluttartam kaṭaitoṟumōṭi avantaṉil alaiyā vakai-eṉak kuṉtaṉ akamalarn taruḷutal vēṇṭum navantaru matiya nivantapūṅ koṭiyē nalantaru nacaimaṇik kōvai ivantoḷir pacuntōḷ icaituluk kāṇat tirēṇukai eṉumoru tiruvē.
translation: You must grant me your grace with a joyful heart so that I do not wander in vain, running to the doorsteps of cruel misers who will not gladly give even a single coin. O blooming creeper rising to the new moon. O garland of desirable gems granting goodness. O Mother with beautifully shining tender shoulders. O incomparable Goddess known as Renuka of renowned Thulukkanam.
commentary: Poverty forces people to surrender their dignity and beg from those who lack compassion. The prayer asks the Goddess for enough material stability to avoid wandering to the doors of cruel misers who refuse to help others. Securing one's daily needs is presented as a necessary part of a dignified life.

tamil: விருந்தினர் தம்மை உபசரித் திடவும் விரவுறும் உறவினர் மகிழத்
திருந்திய மனத்தால் நன்றிசெய் திடவும் சிறியனேற் கருளுதல் வேண்டும்
வருந்திவந் தடைந்தோர்க் கருள்செயும் கருணை வாரியே வடிவுறு மயிலே
இருந்திசை புகழும் இசைதுலுக் காணத் திரேணுகை எனும்ஒரு திருவே.
translit: viruntiṉar tammai upacarit tiṭavum viravuṟum uṟaviṉar makiḻat tiruntiya maṉattāl naṉṟicey tiṭavum ciṟiyaṉēṟ karuḷutal vēṇṭum varuntivan taṭaintōrk karuḷceyum karuṇai vāriyē vaṭivuṟu mayilē irunticai pukaḻum icaituluk kāṇat tirēṇukai eṉumoru tiruvē.
translation: You must bestow your grace upon this lowly one so that I may host guests, bring joy to my gathered relatives, and do good deeds with a perfected mind. O ocean of compassion who grants grace to those who approach in distress. O beautiful peacock. O incomparable Goddess known as Renuka of renowned Thulukkanam, whose fame is sung by all.
commentary: Material stability is requested here specifically to serve others. The verse asks for resources to feed guests, care for relatives, and perform good deeds with a pure heart. A prosperous life is meant to provide the capacity to be generous and compassionate.

tamil: புண்ணியம் புரியும் புனிதர்தம் சார்பும் புத்திரர் மனைவியே முதலாய்
நண்ணிய குடும்ப நலம்பெறப் புரியும் நன்கும் எனக்கருள் புரிவாய்
விண்ணிய கதிரின் ஒளிசெயும் இழையாய் விளங்கருள் ஒழுகிய விழியாய்
எண்ணிய அடியர்க் கிசைதுலுக் காணத் திரேணுகை எனும்ஒரு திருவே.
translit: puṇṇiyam puriyum puṉitartam cārpum puttirar maṉaiviyē mutalāy naṇṇiya kuṭumpa nalampeṟap puriyum naṉkum eṉakkaruḷ purivāy viṇṇiya katiriṉ oḷiceyum iḻaiyāy viḷaṅkaruḷ oḻukiya viḻiyāy eṇṇiya aṭiyark kicaituluk kāṇat tirēṇukai eṉumoru tiruvē.
translation: Grant me the association of pure people who perform virtuous deeds. Bestow upon me the goodness that brings prosperity to my gathered family, starting with my children and wife. O Mother wearing jewels that shine like the sun in the sky. O Mother whose eyes overflow with manifest grace. O incomparable Goddess known as Renuka of renowned Thulukkanam, who favors the devotees who meditate upon you.
commentary: A wholesome family life and the company of pure people are central to this prayer. It envisions a prosperous household where children and family members thrive together in harmony. The Goddess is praised as a radiant mother whose eyes overflow with grace for those who meditate on her.

tamil: மனமெலி யாமல் பிணியடை யாமல் வஞ்சகர் தமைமரு வாமல்
சினநிலை யாமல் உடல்சலி யாமல் சிறியனேன் உறமகிழ்ந் தருள்வாய்
அனமகிழ் நடையாய் அணிதுடி இடையாய் அழகுசெய் காஞ்சன உடையாய்
இனமகிழ் சென்னை இசைதுலுக் காணத் திரேணுகை எனும்ஒரு திருவே.
translit: maṉameli yāmal piṇiyaṭai yāmal vañcakar tamaimaru vāmal ciṉanilai yāmal uṭalcali yāmal ciṟiyaṉēṉ uṟamakiḻn taruḷvāy aṉamakiḻ naṭaiyāy aṇituṭi iṭaiyāy aḻakucey kāñcaṉa uṭaiyāy iṉamakiḻ ceṉṉai icaituluk kāṇat tirēṇukai eṉumoru tiruvē.
translation: Grant your grace joyfully to this lowly one so that my mind does not weaken, disease does not afflict me, I do not associate with deceitful people, anger does not take root in me, and my body does not grow weary. O Mother with the joyful gait of a swan. O Mother with a beautiful waist like a hand-drum. O Mother wearing a beautiful golden garment. O incomparable Goddess known as Renuka of renowned Thulukkanam in Chennai, where communities rejoice.
commentary: The final verse focuses on mental and physical endurance. It asks for a steady mind, freedom from disease, protection from deceitful people, and a life without anger or bodily weariness. A strong, healthy body and a calm mind are treated as essential tools for living a peaceful and virtuous life in the world.

translit: ōkaimaṭa vāralku lēpirama patamavarkaḷ untiyē vaikuntammēl ōṅkumulai yēkailai avarkumuta vāyiṉitaḻ ūṟalē amutamavartam pākaṉaiya moḻiyēnal vētavāk kiyamavarkaḷ pārvaiyē karuṇainōkkam pāṅkiṉava rōṭuviḷai yāṭavaru cukamatē paramacuka mākuminta yūkamaṟi yāmalē tēkammika vāṭiṉīr uṟucuvaip paḻameṟintē uṟṟaveṟu vāymellum vīṇarnīr eṉṟunal lōrainin tipparavartam vākaivāy matamaṟa maruntaruḷka tavacikā maṇi-ulaka nātavaḷḷal makiḻavaru vēḷūril aṉparpava rōkamaṟa vaḷarvait tiyanātaṉē.
translation: "The pelvic region of beautiful young women is the realm of Brahma. Their navel is Vaikuntam. Their high breasts are Kailash. The moisture from their red lotus lips is divine nectar. Their sweet words, soft as syrup, are the true Vedic scriptures. Their glance is the look of supreme grace. The pleasure of playing with them is the ultimate bliss. You let your bodies wither because you do not understand this logic. You are fools who throw away a highly delicious fruit to chew on thin air." Saying this, men insult the virtuous. O Vaithiyanathar, you flourish in Velur to the joy of the benevolent Ulaganathan, the crown jewel among ascetics, and you cure the disease of earthly birth for your devotees. Please give a medicine to destroy the arrogance in the mouths of these men.
commentary: People obsessed with physical pleasure mock spiritual seekers for wasting their lives. They take the sacred worlds of the Hindu gods, like Vaikuntam and Kailash, and reduce them to nothing more than the bodies of women. Believing physical gratification is the ultimate bliss, they accuse those who seek divine truth of throwing away a delicious fruit to chew on empty air. The poet asks the divine healer to cure this arrogant ignorance.

translit: uṇṭatē uṇavutāṉ kaṇṭatē kāṭci-itai uṟṟaṟiya māṭṭārkaḷāy uyiruṇṭu pāvapuṇ ṇiyamuṇṭu viṉaikaḷuṇ ṭuṟupiṟavi uṇṭutuṉpat toṇṭatē ceyunaraka vātai-uṇ ṭiṉpamuṟu corkkamuṇ ṭivaiyumaṉṟit toḻukaṭavuḷ uṇṭukati uṇṭeṉṟu cilarcolum turpputti yālulakilē koṇṭatē cātakam veṟuttumaṭa mātartam koṅkaiyum veṟuttukkaiyil koṇṭatīṅ kaṉiyaiviṭ ṭantarat torupaḻam koḷḷuvīr eṉparanta vaṇṭarvā yaṟa-oru maruntaruḷka tavacikā maṇi-ulaka nātavaḷḷal makiḻavaru vēḷūril aṉparpava rōkamaṟa vaḷarvait tiyanātaṉē.
translation: "What we eat is the only food. What we see is the only reality. Failing to grasp this, some foolishly claim in this world that a soul exists, that sin and merit exist, that karma exists, and that future births exist. They claim a hell exists that gives suffering for bad deeds, and a heaven exists that gives pleasure. Beyond these things, they say there is a God to worship and a state of liberation. Out of this conditioning, you reject the breasts of young women. You drop the sweet fruit in your hands, hoping to catch a fruit in the sky." Saying this, men mock the virtuous. O Vaithiyanathar, you flourish in Velur to the joy of the benevolent Ulaganathan, the crown jewel among ascetics, and you cure the disease of earthly birth for your devotees. Please give a medicine to destroy the mouths of these base men.
commentary: Materialists believe that only what they can see and consume is real. They completely reject the existence of the soul, karma (the spiritual law of cause and effect), future births, and divine liberation. Trapped in this narrow mindset, they laugh at those who give up worldly pleasures, accusing them of dropping real sweetness from their hands to chase an imaginary reward in the sky.

translit: umparvāṉ amutaṉaiya coṟkaḷāṟ periyōr uraittavāy maikaḷaināṭi ōtukiṉ ṟārtamaik kaṇṭava matittetiril otipōla niṟpatumalāl kamparvāy ivarvāyk kataippeṉpar ciṟukaruṅ kākkaivāyk kattalivarvāyk kattalil ciṟiteṉpar cūṭēṟu neyoru kalaṅkoḷḷa vēṇṭumeṉpar imparnām kēṭṭakatai ituveṇpar aṉṟiyum ivarkkētu teriyumeṉpar ivai-elām evaṉō-ōr vampaṉām vīṇaṉmuṉ iṭṭakaṭ ṭeṉparanta vamparvā yaṟa-oru maruntaruḷka tavacikā maṇi-ulaka nātavaḷḷal makiḻavaru vēḷūril aṉparpava rōkamaṟa vaḷarvait tiyanātaṉē.
translation: Seeing those who seek and chant the true words spoken by the great ones, words sweet as heavenly nectar, these men disrespect them. They stand before them like lifeless blocks of wood. They say: "Their talk is just a fairy tale. The cawing of a small black crow is nothing compared to their shouting. We need a whole pot of hot ghee to cure their madness. This is the story we hear in this world. Furthermore, what do these people actually know? All these teachings are just lies spun long ago by some useless vagabond." O Vaithiyanathar, you flourish in Velur to the joy of the benevolent Ulaganathan, the crown jewel among ascetics, and you cure the disease of earthly birth for your devotees. Please give a medicine to destroy the mouths of these malicious men.
commentary: Cynical people dismiss sacred teachings as ancient lies invented by vagabonds. When they see devoted people chanting words of truth, they stand stubbornly against them and mock their devotion as a mental illness. They compare the chanting of holy texts to the meaningless cawing of crows, entirely blind to the sweetness and depth of the teachings.

translit: kallaiyum urukkalām nārurit tiṭalām kaṉintakaṉi yācceyyalām kaṭuviṭamum uṇṇalām amutākka lāmkoṭuṅ karaṭipuli ciṅkamutalā vellumiru kaṅkaḷaiyum vacamākka lāmaṉṟi vittaiyum kaṟpikkalām mikkavā ḻaittaṇṭai viṟakākka lāmmaṇalai mēvutēr vaṭamākkalām illaiyoru teyvamvē ṟillai-em pāliṉpam īkiṉṟa peṇkaḷkuṟiyē eṅkaḷkula teyvameṉum mūṭarait tēṟṟa-eṉil ettuṇaiyum aritaritukāṇ vallaiyavar uṇarvaṟa maruntaruḷka tavacikā maṇi-ulaka nātavaḷḷal makiḻavaru vēḷūril aṉparpava rōkamaṟa vaḷarvait tiyanātaṉē.
translation: You can melt a stone. You can peel fiber from a stone and turn it into a ripe fruit. You can drink deadly poison and turn it into nectar. You can tame fierce bears, tigers, lions, and other wild beasts and teach them tricks. You can turn a soft banana stem into dry firewood. You can twist sand into a thick chariot rope. However, it is impossible to bring clarity to the fools who declare: "There is no other God. The sex organs of women who give us pleasure are our only family deity." O Vaithiyanathar, you flourish in Velur to the joy of the benevolent Ulaganathan, the crown jewel among ascetics, and you cure the disease of earthly birth for your devotees. Please give a medicine to swiftly destroy the perverted understanding of these men.
commentary: It is entirely impossible to bring spiritual clarity to those who worship only sexual pleasure. A person might perform impossible feats, like melting solid rock, turning poison into nectar, or taming wild tigers and bears. Yet bringing wisdom to fools who deny God and live only for lust is a far more difficult task.

translit: paṭi-aḷavu cāmpalaip pūciyē caivam paḻuttapaḻa mōpūcuṇaip paḻamō eṉakkaruṅ kalpōlum acaiyātu pāḻāku kiṉṟārkaḷōr piṭi-aḷavu cātamum koḷḷārkaḷ allatoru peṇṇai-eṉi ṉuṅkoḷkilār pēykoṇṭa tō-aṉṟi nōykoṇṭa tōperum pittēṟṟa tō-aṟikilēṉ ceṭi-aḷavu ūttaivāyp pallaḻuk kellām terintiṭak kāṭṭinakaitāṉ ceytuvaḷai yāpperum cemmarat tuṇṭupōl cemmāppar avarvāymatam maṭi-aḷava tā-oru maruntaruḷka tavacikā maṇi-ulaka nātavaḷḷal makiḻavaru vēḷūril aṉparpava rōkamaṟa vaḷarvait tiyanātaṉē.
translation: Men look at the virtuous and mock them: "They smear bowls of ash on their bodies. Are they the ripe fruits of Saivism or just ash gourds? They sit motionless like black stones and waste away. They do not eat even a handful of rice. They refuse to take a woman. I do not know if they are possessed by a ghost, struck by a disease, or driven by sheer madness." They flash their foul, dirty teeth in a mocking laugh. They strut with arrogance like a massive, unbending log of red wood. O Vaithiyanathar, you flourish in Velur to the joy of the benevolent Ulaganathan, the crown jewel among ascetics, and you cure the disease of earthly birth for your devotees. Please give a medicine to completely destroy the arrogance in the mouths of these men.
commentary: Worldly people look at devout ascetics and see only madness. When they see seekers smeared with holy ash, fasting, and living without women, they compare them to lifeless stones or overgrown vegetables. Standing stiff with arrogance, they laugh at the devout, unable to understand the deep spiritual discipline unfolding right in front of them.

translit: peṇkoṇṭa cukamatē kaṇkaṇṭa palaṉitu piṭikka-aṟi yātucilartām pērūr ilāta-oru veṟuveḷiyi lēcukam peṟavē virumpivīṇil paṇkoṇṭa uṭalveḷut tuḷḷē narampelām pacai-aṟṟu mēleḻumpap paṭṭiṉi kiṭantucā kiṉṟārkaḷ īteṉṉa pāvamivar uṇmai-aṟiyār kaṇkoṇṭa kuruṭarē eṉṟuvāyp palelāṅ kāṭṭic cirittunīṇṭa kaḻumarak kaṭṭaipōl niṟpārkaḷ aiya-ik kayavarvāy matamuḻutumē maṇkoṇṭu pōka-ōr maruntaruḷka tavacikā maṇi-ulaka nātavaḷḷal makiḻavaru vēḷūril aṉparpava rōkamaṟa vaḷarvait tiyanātaṉē.
translation: "The pleasure found with a woman is the only visible fruit. Failing to grasp this, some people vainly desire to attain bliss in an empty void that has no name or town. Their once-harmonious bodies turn pale, their nerves lose all vitality and protrude. They starve and die. What a pity! They do not know the truth; they are blind despite having eyes." Saying this, they bare all their teeth in laughter and stand rigid like tall impaling stakes. O Lord, grant a medicine to turn to dust the utter arrogance in the mouths of these base people! O Vaithiyanathar, you flourish in Velur to the joy of the benevolent Ulaganathan, the crown jewel among ascetics, and you cure the disease of earthly birth for your devotees.
commentary: Worldly people often mock those who dedicate their lives to spiritual truth. To these cynics, physical pleasure is the only reality, and they laugh at seekers who discipline their bodies to find an invisible divine presence. Vallalar asks God, the divine healer, for a cure for this arrogant spiritual blindness.

translit: tiruttamuṭai yōrkaruṇai yālinta ulakil tiyaṅkuvīr aḻiyāccukam cērulaka māmparama patamataṉai aṭaiyumneṟi cēravā ruṅkaḷeṉṟāl iruttiṉiya cuvai-uṇavu vēṇṭumaṇi āṭaitarum iṭamvēṇṭum ivaikaḷ ellām illaiyā yiṉumiravu pakaleṉpa taṟiyāmal iṟukappi ṭittaṇaikkap peruttamulai yōṭiḷam paruvamuṭaṉ aḻakuṭaiya peṇṇakap paṭumākilō pēciṭīr apparama patanāṭṭi ṉukkunum piṟakitō varuvameṉpār varuttumavar uṟavaṟa maruntaruḷka tavacikā maṇi-ulaka nātavaḷḷal makiḻavaru vēḷūri aṉparpava rōkamaṟa vaḷarvait tiyanātaṉē.
translation: When compassionate and reformed people say, "O you who languish in this world! Come, walk the path to reach the supreme abode of imperishable bliss," they reply, "We need intensely sweet food. We need a place that gives fine clothes. Even if all these are absent, if we can secure a beautiful young woman with full breasts to embrace tightly without noticing day or night, just say the word. Then we will follow right behind you to that land of the supreme abode." Grant a medicine to sever all ties with such tormenting people! O Vaithiyanathar, you flourish in Velur to the joy of the benevolent Ulaganathan, the crown jewel among ascetics, and you cure the disease of earthly birth for your devotees.
commentary: When compassionate people invite others to seek eternal bliss, materialistic minds demand physical comforts and sensual pleasures instead. Vallalar asks for the grace to be cut off entirely from the influence of people who value only the body's desires.

translit: pētai-ula kīrviratam ētutavam ētuvīṇ pēccivai elāmvētaṉām pittaṉvāyp pittēṟu kattunūl kattiya perumpuraṭ ṭākumallāl ōtai-uṟum ulakā yatattiṉuḷa uṇmaipōl oruciṟitum illai-illai uḷḷataṟi yātilavu kāttakiḷi pōluṭal ularntīrkaḷ iṉiyākiṉum mētai-uṇa vātivēṇ ṭuva-elām uṇṭunīr viraimalart toṭai-ātiyā vēṇṭuva elāṅkoṇṭu mēṭaimēl peṇkaḷoṭu viḷaiyāṭu vīrkaḷeṉpār vātai-avar cārpaṟa maruntaruḷka tavacikā maṇi-ulaka nātavaḷḷal makiḻavaru vēḷūril aṉparpava rōkamaṟa vaḷarvait tiyanātaṉē.
translation: "O foolish people of the world! What is fasting? What is penance? This is all empty talk. It is nothing but a great deception shouted by the mad babbling scriptures called the Vedas. Besides the truth found in the loud philosophy of materialism, there is absolutely no truth anywhere else. Unaware of reality, you have withered your bodies like the parrot waiting for the silk-cotton fruit to ripen! At least from now on, eat all the excellent food you desire, adorn yourselves with fragrant flower garlands, take whatever you want, and play with women on the upper terraces," they say. Grant a medicine to cut off all association with these tormenting people! O Vaithiyanathar, you flourish in Velur to the joy of the benevolent Ulaganathan, the crown jewel among ascetics, and you cure the disease of earthly birth for your devotees.
commentary: Hardline materialists actively try to persuade others that spiritual texts are lies and that physical indulgence is the only truth. They compare spiritual seekers to a parrot foolishly waiting for an inedible fruit to ripen. Vallalar prays to be kept completely apart from their damaging influence.

translit: īṉam paḻuttamaṉa vātai-aṟa niṉṉaruḷai eṇṇinal lōrkaḷorupāl iṟaivaniṉ tōttiram iyampi-iru kaṇṇīr iṟaippa-atu kaṇṭuniṉṟu ñāṉam paḻuttuviḻi yāloḻuku kiṉṟanīr namulakil oruvaralavē ñāṉi-ivar yōṉivaḻi tōṉṟiyava rō-eṉa nakaipparcum mā-aḻukilō ūṉam kuḻuttakaṇ ṇāmeṉpar ulakattil uyarpeṇṭu cākkoṭutta oruvaṉmukam eṉṉa-ivar mukamvāṭu kiṉṟateṉa uḷaṟuvār vāyaṭaṅka māṉam paḻuttiṭu maruntaruḷka tavacikā maṇi-ulaka nātavaḷḷal makiḻavaru vēḷūril aṉparpava rōkamaṟa vaḷarvait tiyanātaṉē.
translation: On one side, the virtuous contemplate Your grace to cure their base mental agony. When they sing Your praises and shed tears from both eyes, these people stand watching and laugh, saying, "This water flows from eyes ripe with wisdom! He does not belong to our world. He is a sage! Was he even born of a womb?" If a devotee simply weeps, they say, "His eyes are diseased." They blabber, "Why does his face wither like a man who has lost his noble wife to death?" Grant a medicine to instill honor and silence their mouths! O Vaithiyanathar, you flourish in Velur to the joy of the benevolent Ulaganathan, the crown jewel among ascetics, and you cure the disease of earthly birth for your devotees.
commentary: Cynics sneer at genuine tears of devotion, viewing deep spiritual emotion as a weakness or a joke. When devotees weep out of love for God, worldly people mock them as diseased or foolish. Vallalar asks the divine healer to silence their cruelty and restore true spiritual dignity.

translit: kaṟpavai elāmkaṟ ṟuṇarntaperi yōrtamaik kāṇpatē arumai-arumai kaṟpataru miṭiyaṉivaṉ iṭai-aṭain tāleṉak karuṇaiyāl avarvaliyavan tiṟpuṟaṉ iruppa-atu kaṇṭuman tōkaṭi teḻuntupōyt toḻututaṅkaṭ kiyaluṟuti vēṇṭātu kaṇkeṭṭa kuruṭarpōl ēmānti rupparivartām poṟpiṉaṟu cuvai-aṟiyum aṟivuṭaiyar aṉṟumēṟ pullāti uṇumuyirkaḷum pōṉṟiṭār ivarkaḷaik kūraipōyp pāḻām puṟaccuvar eṉappukalalām vaṟpuṟum paṭitaruma vaḻi-ōṅku tavacikā maṇi-ulaka nātavaḷḷal makiḻavaru vēḷūril aṉparpava rōkamaṟa vaḷarvait tiyanātaṉē.
translation: It is exceedingly rare to see great souls who have learned all that is to be learned. Out of compassion, they might come voluntarily to a destitute man's door, like a wish-fulfilling tree arriving on its own. Seeing them stand outside, these people do not immediately rise, go out, worship them, and seek spiritual certainty for themselves. Alas, they sit utterly deluded like the sightless blind! They lack the wisdom to know true excellence. They are not even equal to grazing animals. They can only be called ruined outer walls stripped of their roof. O Vaithiyanathar, you flourish in Velur to the joy of the benevolent Ulaganathan, the crown jewel among ascetics who makes the firmly established path of dharma flourish, and you cure the disease of earthly birth for your devotees.
commentary: Ignorant people fail to recognize true spiritual masters even when grace arrives directly at their doorstep. Vallalar says that if a great sage approaches them to offer wisdom, they sit completely blind to the rare opportunity. He compares them to hollow, ruined walls and says they have less awareness than a grazing animal.

translit: meyyōr tiṉaittaṉaiyum aṟikilār poykkatai viḷampa-eṉil ivvulakilō mēlulakil ēṟukiṉum añcātu moḻivarteru mēvumaṇ ṇeṉiṉumutavak kaiyō maṉattaiyum viṭukka-icai yārkaḷkolai kaḷavukaṭ kāmammutalāk kaṇṭatī maikaḷaṉṟi naṉmai-eṉ pataṉai-oru kaṉavilum kaṇṭaṟikilār aiyō muṉivartamai vitippaṭi paṭaittaviti aṅkaitāṅ kaṅkai-eṉṉum āṟṟil kuḷikkiṉum tīmūḻki eḻiṉumav vacuttanīṅ kātukaṇṭāy maiyōr aṇuttuṇaiyum mēvuṟāt tavacikā maṇi-ulaka nātavaḷḷal makiḻavaru vēḷūril aṉparpava rōkamaṟa vaḷarvait tiyanātaṉē.
translation: They do not know even a millet seed of truth. If asked to spin false tales, they will speak them fearlessly in this world or even if they ascend to the heavens. They will not allow their hands or minds to offer even the dust on the street to help another. They know only evils such as murder, theft, liquor, and lust. They have never seen or known anything called goodness, even in a dream. Alas, even if Brahma who created such hateful people according to fate bathes in the river Ganges or plunges into fire and rises, his impurity will never leave. O Vaithiyanathar, you flourish in Velur to the joy of the benevolent Ulaganathan, the crown jewel among ascetics who holds not even an atom of darkness, and you cure the disease of earthly birth for your devotees.
commentary: People who live entirely without compassion carry a spiritual stain that nothing can wash away. Vallalar describes individuals who spin endless lies, commit crimes, and refuse to offer even the dust on the street to help someone in need. Because Jeevakarunyam (compassion for all living beings) is the absolute foundation of spiritual life, its total absence is a deep evil. He says the impurity of this selfishness is so deep that even the creator god Brahma, who formed such beings, could never cleanse himself of it by bathing in the sacred river Ganges or stepping into holy fire.

translit: iḷavēṉil mālaiyāyk kuḷircōlai yāymalar ilañcipūm poykai-arukāy ēṟṟacan tirakānta mēṭaiyāy ataṉmēl ilaṅkumara miya-aṇaiyumāyt taḷavēyum mallikaip pantarāyp pālpōl taḻaittiṭu nilākkālamāyt taṉi-iḷan teṉṟalāy niṟainaram puḷavīṇai taṉṉicaip pāṭaliṭamāy kaḷavēka lantakaṟ puṭaiyamaṭa varalpuṭai kalantanaya vārttai-uṭaṉāyk kaḷikoḷa iruntavarkaḷ kaṇṭacuka niṉṉaṭik kaḻalniḻaṟ cukanikarumē vaḷavēlai cūḻulaku pukaḻkiṉṟa tavacikā maṇi-ulaka nātavaḷḷal makiḻavaru vēḷūril aṉparpava rōkamaṟa vaḷarvait tiyanātaṉē.
translation: Consider a spring evening in a cool grove near a pond blooming with flowers. Picture a fine moonstone terrace holding a shining beautiful bed under a canopy of blooming jasmine. Imagine a time of moonlight glowing like milk, an unmatched gentle southern breeze, and a place filled with the musical song of a fully stringed vina. Think of the joy experienced by those sitting in such delight, sharing sweet words and secret intimacy with a chaste young woman. Can that joy ever equal the bliss found in the shade of your ankleted feet? O Vaithiyanathar, you flourish in Velur to the joy of the benevolent Ulaganathan, the crown jewel among ascetics praised by the world surrounded by the fertile ocean, and you cure the disease of earthly birth for your devotees.
commentary: The deepest worldly pleasures cannot compare to the bliss of divine grace. Vallalar builds an image of ultimate earthly romance, combining spring breezes, moonlight, fragrant jasmine, sweet music, and intimate company. He asks whether all this sensory delight put together could ever equal the peace found at the feet of God. Earthly joys are fleeting and bound to the physical senses. The experience of the divine offers a lasting happiness that cures the very disease of worldly birth.

sections.title: Praise to the Mother of Kannamangai

tamil: உலகம் புரக்கும் பெருமான்தன் உளத்தும் புயத்தும் அமர்ந்தருளி
உவகை அளிக்கும் பேரின்ப உருவே எல்லாம் உடையாளே
திலகம் செறிவாள் நுதற்கரும்பே தேனே கனிந்த செழுங்கனியே
தெவிட்டா தன்பர் உளத்துள்ளே தித்தித் தெழும்ஓர் தெள்ளமுதே
மலகஞ் சுகத்தேற் கருளளித்த வாழ்வே என்கண் மணியேஎன்
வருத்தந் தவிர்க்க வரும்குருவாம் வடிவே ஞான மணிவிளக்கே
சலகந் தரம்போற் கருணைபொழி தடங்கண் திருவே கணமங்கைத்
தாயே சரணம் சரணம் இது தருணம் கருணை தருவாயே.
translit: ulakam purakkum perumāṉtaṉ uḷattum puyattum amarntaruḷi uvakai aḷikkum pēriṉpa uruvē ellām uṭaiyāḷē tilakam ceṟivāḷ nutaṟkarumpē tēṉē kaṉinta ceḻuṅkaṉiyē teviṭṭā taṉpar uḷattuḷḷē tittit teḻumōr teḷḷamutē malakañ cukattēṟ karuḷaḷitta vāḻvē eṉkaṇ maṇiyē-eṉ varuttan tavirkka varumkuruvām vaṭivē ñāṉa maṇiviḷakkē calakan tarampōṟ karuṇaipoḻi taṭaṅkaṇ tiruvē kaṇamaṅkait tāyē caraṇam caraṇam itu taruṇam karuṇai taruvāyē.
translation: Seated gracefully in the heart and on the shoulders of the Great Lord who protects the world, you grant joy. O form of supreme bliss, you possess everything. O sugarcane with a radiant forehead wearing a glowing mark, O honey, O luscious ripe fruit, you are the clear nectar that rises sweetly in the hearts of devotees without ever cloying. O life that granted grace to me who wears an armor of impurities, O pupil of my eye, you are the form of the Guru who comes to dispel my sorrow. O jeweled lamp of wisdom, O Goddess with broad eyes pouring compassion like a raincloud, O Mother of Kannamangai, I surrender, I surrender. This is the moment. Grant me your grace.
commentary: The divine mother is the active, compassionate power of God, inseparable from the supreme being she accompanies. She is described here residing directly on the heart and shoulders of the Lord who protects the world. The poet addresses her as a spiritual teacher (guru) who clears away sorrow and as a jeweled lamp of wisdom. Even though he feels weighed down by inner impurities, he trusts entirely in her eyes that pour out mercy like a raincloud. He surrenders completely, asking for her grace in this very moment.

sections.title: The Decad on the Ancient Mountain

tamil: திருமால் கமலத் திருக்கண்மலர் திகழு மலர்த்தாட் சிவக்கொழுந்தைக்
கருமா லகற்றுந் தனிமருந்தைக் கனக சபையிற் கலந்தஒன்றை
அருமா மணியை ஆரமுதை அன்பை அறிவை அருட்பெருக்கைக்
குருமா மலையைப் பழமலையிற் குலவி யோங்கக் கண்டேனே.
translit: tirumāl kamalat tirukkaṇmalar tikaḻu malarttāṭ civakkoḻuntaik karumā lakaṟṟun taṉimaruntaik kaṉaka capaiyiṟ kalanta-oṉṟai arumā maṇiyai āramutai aṉpai aṟivai aruṭperukkaik kurumā malaiyaip paḻamalaiyiṟ kulavi yōṅkak kaṇṭēṉē.
translation: I saw Him rejoicing and rising high on the Ancient Mountain. He is the tender shoot of Siva whose flower-like feet shine with the lotus eye offered by Vishnu. He is the peerless medicine that removes dark delusion. He is the One who has merged in the Golden Hall. He is the rare great gem, the exquisite nectar, love, knowledge, the flood of grace, and the great mountain of the Guru.
