commentary: Inner realization becomes complete when divine grace and the supreme Lord unite within the seeker's own heart. In this state of union, the divine mother sits deep within and speaks the ultimate truths directly to him.

translit: urutti raṉtiru mālayaṉ oppamuk kuṇamāy iruttal iṉṟi-ak kuṇaṅkaḷai eṉṟumāṇ ṭaruḷuṅ karuttaṉ ākaiyiṟ kuṇēcaṉak kuṇavikā rattiṟ porutta miṉmaiyaṉ ākaiyāl pukalkuṇa rakitaṉ.
translation: Unlike Rudra, Vishnu, and Brahma, he does not exist as the three qualities. Because he is the Lord who forever rules over those qualities, he is the lord of qualities. Because he has no connection to the modifications of those qualities, he is called the one devoid of qualities.
commentary: The supreme divine reality is completely free from the basic qualities of material nature. While traditional gods of creation, preservation, and destruction (Brahma, Vishnu, and Rudra) are bound by these natural traits, Vallalar says the supreme Lord rules over them without ever being affected by their changes.

translit: kaḷaṅka akkuṇam kaṭantirut talilkuṇā tītaṉ vaḷaṅko ḷattakum ulakelām maruviniṟ ṟaliṉāl viḷaṅku viccuva viyāpi-iv vicuvattai yāṇṭu tuḷaṅku ṟānalan tōṟṟaliṉ viccuva karuttaṉ.
translation: Because he transcends those tainted qualities, he is the one beyond qualities. Because he pervades all the flourishing worlds, he is the radiant cosmic pervader. Because he rules this universe and manifests unwavering goodness, he is the cosmic lord.
commentary: The supreme Lord exists entirely beyond the flaws of the material world. This divine presence fills all of creation, guiding the entire universe with a steady and perfect goodness.

translit: veyya ṉāyula kaḻittaliṉ vicuvacaṅ kāri paiya mēleṉap paṭuvaṉa palavaṟṟiṉ mēlām aiyaṉ ātaliṟ parāpara ṉāmeṉap paṭṭa ceyya ṉākiya civapirāṉ oruvaṉuṇ ṭamarīr.
translation: Because he fiercely dissolves the world, he is the cosmic destroyer. Because he is the Lord who stands above all the many things considered to be supreme, he is called the highest beyond the highest. O immortals, there is one such perfect Lord Siva.
commentary: There is one perfect reality that stands above everything else worshipped as supreme. Vallalar calls this ultimate truth Siva, the single highest Lord who holds the power to dissolve the entire cosmos.

translit: uyva tāmitu namkuru vāṇaiyoṉ ṟuraippēṉ caiva māticit tāntattu maṟaimuṭit talattum naiva tiṉṟi-āṅ katuvatu vāyatu namatu teyva mākiya civaparam poruḷeṉat teḷivīr.
translation: This brings salvation. I will declare one truth upon the command of our Guru. Understand clearly that the reality which exists undiminished as the ultimate truth in Saivism, in the ancient Siddhanta, and at the summit of the Vedas, becoming the respective truth in each path, is our deity: Siva, the supreme reality.
commentary: This single supreme reality is the actual truth hidden at the core of all major spiritual traditions. Whether seekers follow the ancient paths of Saivism, Siddhanta, or the culmination of the Vedas (the oldest Indian scriptures), Vallalar says it is this one same Lord they are reaching for.

tamil: இரண்டே காற்கை முகந்தந்தீர் இன்ப நடஞ்செய் பெருமானீர்
இரண்டே காற்கை முகங்கொண்டீர் என்னே அடிகள் என்றுரைத்தேன்
இரண்டே காற்கை முகம்புடைக்க இருந்தாய் எனைக்கென் றிங்கேநீ
இரண்டே காற்கை முகங்கொண்டாய் என்றார் மன்றில் நின்றாரே.
translit: iraṇṭē kāṟkai mukantantīr iṉpa naṭañcey perumāṉīr iraṇṭē kāṟkai mukaṅkoṇṭīr eṉṉē aṭikaḷ eṉṟuraittēṉ iraṇṭē kāṟkai mukampuṭaikka iruntāy eṉaikkeṉ ṟiṅkēnī iraṇṭē kāṟkai mukaṅkoṇṭāy eṉṟār maṉṟil niṉṟārē.
translation: "O Lord who performs the dance of bliss, you gave me two legs, hands, and a face. You took for yourself two legs, hands, and a face. What is this, O Lord?" I asked. He who stood in the hall replied, "Why do you remain here, striking your two legs, hands, and face for my sake? You have assumed two legs, hands, and a face."
commentary: The speaker points out a beautiful mystery: God gave humans a physical body, yet He Himself takes on a human-like form to meet them. When she asks the Lord why He appears with arms, legs, and a face just like hers, He answers playfully. He asks why she is suffering and striking her own body in her longing for Him, suggesting that the human form is meant for divine union rather than distress.

tamil: இரண்டே காற்கை முகங்கொண்டீர் என்னை உடையீர் அம்பலத்தீர்
இரண்டே காற்கை முகந்தந்தீர் என்னை இதுதான் என்றுரைத்தேன்
இரண்டே காற்கை முகங்கொண்டிங் கிருந்த நீயும் எனைக்கண்டே
இரண்டே காற்கை முகங்கொண்டாய் என்றார் தோழி இவர்வாழி.
translit: iraṇṭē kāṟkai mukaṅkoṇṭīr eṉṉai uṭaiyīr ampalattīr iraṇṭē kāṟkai mukantantīr eṉṉai itutāṉ eṉṟuraittēṉ iraṇṭē kāṟkai mukaṅkoṇṭiṅ kirunta nīyum eṉaikkaṇṭē iraṇṭē kāṟkai mukaṅkoṇṭāy eṉṟār tōḻi ivarvāḻi.
translation: "O Lord of the hall who rules me, you took on two legs, hands, and a face. You gave me two legs, hands, and a face. What is this?" I asked. He replied, "You, who sat here with two legs, hands, and a face, saw me and assumed two legs, hands, and a face." O friend, long may He live.
commentary: The dialogue reveals a deep spiritual law about how the soul relates to God. The Lord tells the young woman that by fixing her gaze on Him, she has actually taken on His likeness. The soul is transformed by what it worships. By constantly looking to the Divine, the human being slowly becomes a living reflection of God's own nature.

tamil: ஆடுங் கருணைத் திருநடத்தீர் ஆடும் இடந்தான் யாதென்றேன்
பாடுந் திருவுஞ் சவுந்தரமும் பழமுங் காட்டும் இடமென்றார்
நாடும் படிநன் கருளுமென்றேன் நங்காய் முன்பின் ஒன்றேயாய்
ஈடுந் தியபன் னடுவுளதால் என்றார் தோழி இவர்வாழி.
translit: āṭuṅ karuṇait tirunaṭattīr āṭum iṭantāṉ yāteṉṟēṉ pāṭun tiruvuñ cavuntaramum paḻamuṅ kāṭṭum iṭameṉṟār nāṭum paṭinaṉ karuḷumeṉṟēṉ naṅkāy muṉpiṉ oṉṟēyāy īṭun tiyapaṉ ṉaṭuvuḷatāl eṉṟār tōḻi ivarvāḻi.
translation: "O Lord of the sacred dance of grace, what is the place where you dance?" I asked. He said, "It is the place that reveals singing, wealth, beauty, and fruit." I said, "Grace me well so that I may seek it." He replied, "O young woman, it is the one thing before and after, possessing greatness and existing in the center of the twelve." O friend, long may He live.
commentary: The young woman asks where the Lord's dance of grace actually happens. He answers with a riddle, describing a mystical space at the "center of the twelve." In Tamil yogic tradition, this refers to a subtle spiritual center located twelve finger-breadths beyond the physical body, usually above the crown of the head. God's grand cosmic dance takes place right there, in the highest reaches of human awareness.

translit: paṟṟu niṉaitteḻumip pāvimaṉat tīmaiyelām uṟṟu niṉaikkileṉak kūṭuruvip pōkutaṭā.
translation: When I deeply consider all the evils of this sinful mind that swells with worldly attachments, it pierces right through my body.
commentary: The pain of recognizing one's own mental flaws is experienced as a physical wound. Remorse over worldly desires is so intense that the speaker feels physically impaled by it.

translit: eḷḷēta niṉṉiṭattē eṇṇukiṉṟa tōṟumatai uḷḷē niṉaikkileṉak kūṭuruvip pōkutaṭā.
translation: Whenever I recount my despicable faults before You and reflect upon them within, it pierces right through my body.
commentary: Bringing these flaws into the open before the Divine makes the guilt unbearable. The act of honest confession brings a sharp and physical sting of shame.

translit: tuṉṉukiṉṟa tīmainiṉpāṟ cūḻnturaikkun tōṟumatai uṉṉukiṉṟa pōtileṉak kūṭuruvip pōkutaṭā.
translation: Whenever I recount the gathering evils before You and ponder them, it pierces right through my body.
commentary: Seeing how these wrongs have accumulated over time brings renewed agony. Facing the sheer volume of past misdeeds turns quiet reflection into physical torment.

translit: eḷḷukiṉṟa tīmainiṉpā leṇṇukiṉṟa tōṟumatai uḷḷukiṉṟa pōtileṉak kūṭuruvip pōkutaṭā.
translation: Whenever I enumerate my despicable evils before You and reflect upon them, it pierces right through my body.
commentary: The repetition of this refrain mirrors the continuous loop of a guilty conscience. Naming each fault aloud to the Divine only deepens the sensation of being pierced through.

translit: mikka nilainiṟka virumpēṉ piḻaikaḷelām okka niṉaikkileṉak kūṭuruvip pōkutaṭā.
translation: I have no desire to stand in the exalted state. When I think of all my faults together, it pierces right through my body.
commentary: True remorse strips away spiritual pride. The combined weight of past mistakes crushes any ambition for higher spiritual states, leaving the speaker in a state of raw humility.

translit: kōkō veṉuṅkoṭiyēṉ kūṟiyakuṟ ṟaṅkaḷelām ōkō niṉaikkileṉak kūṭuruvip pōkutaṭā.
translation: I am a cruel person who wails aloud. Alas, when I think of all the faults I have voiced, it pierces right through me, O friend.
commentary: The realization of past mistakes brings a sharp and piercing pain. Vallalar confesses that remembering the wrong things he has said in the past cuts him to the core. This intense sorrow is a natural step toward spiritual purity.

translit: pittu maṉakkoṭiyēṉ pēciyavaṉ collaiyelām ottu niṉaikkileṉak kūṭuruvip pōkutaṭā.
translation: I am a cruel person with a mad mind. When I bring together and think of all the harsh words I spoke, it pierces right through me, O friend.
commentary: A restless and unchecked mind often leads to unkind speech. Vallalar feels pierced by guilt when he gathers the memory of every harsh word he has ever spoken. He views his own lack of mental control as a deep cruelty.

translit: tērntu teḷiyāc ciṟiyavaṉēṉ tīmaiyelām ōrntu niṉaikkileṉak kūṭuruvip pōkutaṭā.
translation: I am a petty person who lacks clear understanding. When I examine and think of all my evil deeds, it pierces right through me, O friend.
commentary: Harmful actions often grow from a lack of clear understanding. Vallalar takes full responsibility for his past ignorance and examines his misdeeds closely. Facing the reality of his own errors brings him a painful but necessary clarity.

translit: niṟutti yaṟiyē nikaḻttiyavaṉ collai uṟutti niṉaikkileṉak kūṭuruvip pōkutaṭā.
translation: I do not know how to pause and reflect. When I intently think of the harsh words I uttered, it pierces right through me, O friend.
commentary: Spiritual awareness requires the discipline to pause and reflect. Vallalar expresses deep remorse for his past inability to think before speaking. The memory of the harsh words that escaped during those thoughtless moments now cuts right through him.

translit: tōṉṟi viriyumaṉat tuṭṭaṉēṉ vaṉpiḻaiyai ūṉṟi niṉaikkileṉak kūṭuruvip pōkutaṭā.
translation: I am a wicked person with a mind that constantly wanders and expands. When I deeply think of my grievous wrongs, it pierces right through me, O friend.
commentary: The ordinary human mind constantly wanders and chases new distractions. Vallalar sees this restless mental activity as the root of his worst mistakes. Focusing deeply on these errors brings a sharp remorse that helps clear away pride and ego.

translit: eṇṇiṉaippa tiṉṟiniṉai yeḷḷi yuraittataṉai uṇṇiṉaikkun tōṟumeṉak kuḷḷa murukutaṭā.
translation: Whenever I inwardly remember how I spoke of you with contempt, without any thought or consideration, my heart melts.
commentary: True repentance brings a painful, purifying sorrow. The poet remembers a time when he spoke of the divine with thoughtless contempt. Looking back on that ignorance now causes his heart to melt with regret.

translit: kaṭaiyavaṉēṉ vaitakaṭuñ coṉṉiṉaikkun tōṟum uṭaiyavaṉē yeṉṉuṭaiya vuḷḷa murukutaṭā.
translation: O Master, whenever I recall the harsh words this lowest wretch used to abuse you, my heart melts.
commentary: The memory of past arrogance brings a deep sense of unworthiness. The poet calls himself the lowest of the low for ever using harsh words against the Master of all things. The stark contrast between God's greatness and his own past insults breaks his heart.

translit: pittaṉeṉat tīmai pitaṟṟiyateṇ ṇuntōṟum uttamaṉē yeṉṉuṭaiya vuḷḷa murukutaṭā.
translation: O Supreme One, whenever I reflect on how I babbled wicked things and called you a madman, my heart melts.
commentary: The sorrow deepens as the poet recalls calling God a madman. He views his past words as wicked babble born of sheer ignorance. Recognizing the supreme goodness of the divine makes that past disrespect deeply painful to remember.

translit: maṉṟuṭaiyāy niṉṉaruḷai vaitakoṭuñ coṟporuḷil oṉṟai niṉaikkileṉak kuḷḷa murukutaṭā.
translation: O Lord of the Hall, if I consider the meaning of even a single cruel word I used to abuse your grace, my heart melts.
commentary: To insult divine grace is a heavy burden on the conscience. The Lord of the Hall refers to the divine presence in the central space of light and awareness. Realizing that he once met that pure grace with cruel words causes the poet deep grief.

translit: veruvāma laiyō viḷampiyacol lellām oruvā niṉaikkileṉak kuḷḷa murukutaṭā.
translation: Alas, if I reflect on all the words I uttered without any fear, my heart melts.
commentary: A past lack of reverence is terrifying in hindsight. The poet grieves that he once spoke carelessly, with no fear or awe of the divine. The realization of that thoughtless bravery now turns into overwhelming remorse.

translit: pulaikkoṭiyēṉ puṉcoṟ pukaṉṟateṇ ṇuntōṟum ulaikkaṇmeḻu kākaveṉṟa ṉuḷḷa murukutaṭā.
translation: Whenever I think of the base words spoken by cruel, vile me, my heart melts like wax in a forge, O friend.
commentary: The intensity of regret is so strong that it feels physical. The speaker remembers speaking from a place of ignorance and describes this deep remorse as wax melting in the intense heat of a blacksmith's forge.

translit: īṭilperun tāyi liṉiyāyniṉ ṟaṇṇaruṭpāl ūṭiyacol luṉṉileṉak kuḷḷa murukutaṭā.
translation: You are sweeter than an incomparable great mother. When I think of the words I spoke in feigned anger against your cool grace, my heart melts, O friend.
commentary: In Tamil poetry, devotees sometimes adopt the voice of a lover who sulks or argues with God. Looking back on these moments of feigned anger, the speaker is overwhelmed by guilt because the divine is endlessly gentle and sweeter than a mother.

translit: puraittamaṉa vañcap pulaiyēṉ ṟiruvaruḷai uraittapiḻai yeṇṇileṉak kuḷḷa murukutaṭā.
translation: I am a vile person with a flawed and deceitful mind. When I think of the wrong words I spoke about the holy grace, my heart melts, O friend.
commentary: True devotion requires absolute honesty. The speaker looks inward, finds lingering deceit, and grieves over past failures to understand or speak truthfully about the holiness of divine grace.

translit: nāṭi niṉaiyā navaiyuṭaiyēṉ puṉcolelām ōṭi niṉaikkileṉak kuḷḷa murukutaṭā.
translation: I bear the flaw of not seeking and remembering you. When my mind runs back to recall all my base words, my heart melts, O friend.
commentary: Forgetfulness is treated here as a spiritual flaw. The speaker feels sorrow for all the times they lived distracted from the divine presence and spoke carelessly as a result.

translit: veppil karuṇai viḷakkaṉaiyā yeṉpiḻaiyai oppi niṉaikkileṉak kuḷḷa murukutaṭā.
translation: You are like a lamp of grace without scorching heat. When I confess and think of my mistakes, my heart melts, O friend.
commentary: Divine grace is compared to a gentle lamp that gives light without burning. Confessing mistakes to a God who offers this perfectly comforting light brings the speaker to tears of deep relief and regret.

translit: añcaleṉṟāy niṉpāl aṭātamoḻi pēciyatai añciniṉaik kileṉak kañcuṅ kalaṅkutaṭā.
translation: You told me to fear not. When I fearfully recall the unfitting words I spoke to you, I fear and tremble.
commentary: God has already offered reassurance, telling the seeker not to be afraid. Yet the memory of past disrespect still brings overwhelming guilt. The contrast between infinite divine forgiveness and the soul's own sense of unworthiness causes this deep trembling.

translit: meyyōr ciṟitumilēṉ vīṇmoḻiyā lūṭiyatai aiyō niṉaikkileṉak kañcuṅ kalaṅkutaṭā.
translation: I have not the slightest sincerity. Alas, when I think of how I sulked and spoke empty words, I fear and tremble.
commentary: The poet confesses to a complete lack of genuine devotion. Sulking and speaking carelessly are habits of an immature mind. Looking back on this behavior with newfound spiritual clarity brings a deep sense of shame.

translit: ittā raṇikkuḷeṅku millāta tīmaiceytēṉ attā niṉaikkileṉak kañcuṅ kalaṅkutaṭā.
translation: I committed evil deeds unmatched anywhere on this earth. O Father, when I think of this, I fear and tremble.
commentary: The seeker claims to have committed the worst evils on earth. This intense confession is a way of stripping away all personal pride before God. Standing in the light of perfect grace makes even ordinary human flaws feel overwhelmingly dark and terrifying.

translit: poyyāl virinta pulaimaṉattēṉ ceypiḻaiyai aiyā niṉaikkileṉak kañcuṅ kalaṅkutaṭā.
translation: My base mind swelled with lies. O Lord, when I think of the faults I committed, I fear and tremble.
commentary: The human mind is shown here as a breeding ground for lies. Recognizing that past mistakes grew out of a deeply distorted, untruthful way of thinking makes the memory of them frightening.

translit: ippāvi neñcā liḻukkuraittē ṉāṅkataṉai appāni ṉaikkileṉak kañcuṅ kalaṅkutaṭā.
translation: With this sinful heart I spoke insulting words. O Father, when I think of that, I fear and tremble.
commentary: Looking back on moments of spiritual ignorance, the poet regrets having lashed out or spoken bitterly to the divine. Realizing how deeply a hardened heart can misunderstand God's love produces this intense, lingering fear.

translit: eṇṇāk koṭumaiyelā meṇṇiyurait tēṉataṉai aṇṇā niṉaikkileṉak kañcuṅ kalaṅkutaṭā.
translation: I imagined and spoke unimaginable cruelties. Oh, when I think of that, fear and trembling grip me, my friend.
commentary: The speaker feels intense remorse for cruel words spoken in the past. Remembering these actions brings a wave of fear, showing how seriously a spiritual seeker must weigh their everyday speech.

translit: vemmāṉ maṉattu viṉaiyēṉ pukaṉṟatelām ammā niṉaikkileṉak kañcuṅ kalaṅkutaṭā.
translation: I am bound by karma and possess a fierce heart. Alas, when I think of all that I spoke, fear and trembling grip me, my friend.
commentary: The speaker traces his harsh words to a restless, unyielding heart bound by past actions, known as karma. Realizing how deeply these old patterns have shaped his speech makes him tremble.

translit: eccōṭu millā tiḻintēṉ piḻaikaḷelām accōni ṉaikkileṉak kañcuṅ kalaṅkutaṭā.
translation: I fell so low and lack even a trace of goodness. Alas, when I think of all my faults, fear and trembling grip me, my friend.
commentary: True spiritual growth requires absolute honesty about one's own failings. Confronting his own lowliness and the complete absence of goodness in his past brings on a deep spiritual dread.

translit: vantōṭi naimaṉattu vañcakaṉēṉ vañcamelām antōni ṉaikkileṉak kañcuṅ kalaṅkutaṭā.
translation: I am a deceitful person with a mind that runs about and wastes away. Alas, when I think of all my deceit, fear and trembling grip me, my friend.
commentary: A mind that constantly wanders easily falls into deception. The speaker recognizes that his own restlessness has bred dishonesty, and facing this inner deceit causes him great fear.

translit: ōvāk koṭiyē ṉuraitta piḻaikaḷelām āvā niṉaikkileṉak kañcuṅ kalaṅkutaṭā.
translation: I am ceaselessly cruel. Alas, when I think of all the wrongs I uttered, fear and trembling grip me, my friend.
commentary: The weight of continuous careless cruelty and harmful speech culminates here. This intense trembling shows the deep sensitivity the seeker has developed, where even the memory of causing harm to others brings overwhelming terror.

translit: karaicēra voṇṇāk kaṭaiyēṉ piḻaiyai araicēni ṉaikkileṉak kañcuṅ kalaṅkutaṭā.
translation: O King, if you consider the faults of this lowest wretch who cannot reach the shore, I tremble in fear, O friend.
commentary: The speaker feels overwhelmed by his own flaws and dreads facing divine judgment. He describes himself as a wretch unable to cross the dangerous ocean of worldly life. If the supreme King were to actually weigh these failings, the thought alone brings a trembling fear.

translit: maruḷuṭaiyēṉ vañca maṉattīmai yellām aruḷuṭaiyā yeṇṇileṉak kañcuṅ kalaṅkutaṭā.
translation: O Lord of Grace, if you consider all the evils of the deceitful mind of this deluded one, I tremble in fear, O friend.
commentary: The contrast here lies between human delusion and pure divine grace. A confused mind easily harbors deceit and dark thoughts. Knowing that God sees all of this hidden mental evil causes a deep, shaking terror.

translit: īṇṭavaṉēṉ vaṉcol iyampiyatai yeṉṉuṭaiya āṇṭavaṉē yeṇṇileṉak kañcuṅ kalaṅkutaṭā.
translation: O my Master, if you consider the harsh words spoken by this lowly one, I tremble in fear, O friend.
commentary: The fear of judgment shifts from inner thoughts to outward speech. Harsh language hurts others and degrades the one who speaks it. When facing the ultimate Master, there is nowhere to hide the cruelty of those everyday words.

translit: vaṟputaṉēṉ vañca maṉappiḻaiyai maṉṟāṭum aṟputaṉē yeṇṇileṉak kañcuṅ kalaṅkutaṭā.
translation: O wondrous Lord who dances in the hall, if you consider the faults of the deceitful mind of this hard-hearted one, I tremble in fear, O friend.
commentary: God is invoked as the wondrous dancer in the sacred hall. The speaker feels a sharp gap between this beautiful, dynamic divine presence and his own stiff, deceitful mind. Bringing a hard heart before a dancing God feels absolutely terrifying.

translit: tuṉpuṭaiyēṉ puṉmoḻikaḷ tūṟṟiyatai yevvuyirkkum aṉpuṭaiyā yeṇṇileṉak kañcuṅ kalaṅkutaṭā.
translation: O Lord who loves all living beings, if you consider the base words uttered by this miserable one, I tremble in fear, O friend.
commentary: God is defined by a deep love for every single living creature. Using vile words goes directly against this universal compassion. The speaker feels intense fear because his harmful speech violates the very love that makes up the divine nature.

translit: kotikkiṉṟa vaṉmoḻiyāṟ kūṟiyatai yaiyō matikkiṉṟa tōṟumuḷḷē vāḷiṭ ṭaṟukkutaṭā.
translation: Alas, every time I reflect on what I said with seething harsh words, a sword slices within me.
commentary: The memory of speaking out in boiling anger brings sudden and sharp pain. Vallalar describes the remorse of using harsh words as a physical agony, cutting him like a sword from the inside.

translit: ciṉaṅkoṇṭa pōtellāñ ceppiya vaṉcollai maṉaṅkoḷḷun tōṟumuḷḷē vāḷiṭ ṭaṟukkutaṭā.
translation: Every time my mind recalls the harsh words I spoke in moments of anger, a sword slices within me.
commentary: Anger blinds a person in the moment, leaving behind regret over cruel outbursts. When the mind turns back to those words spoken in rage, the guilt is agonizing.

translit: ceytanaṉṟi yeṇṇāc ciṟiyavaṉē ṉiṉṉaruḷai vaitteṇṇun tōṟumuḷḷē vāḷiṭ ṭaṟukkutaṭā.
translation: I am a lowly person who did not recognize the good you did. Every time I dwell upon your sweet grace, a sword slices within me.
commentary: Remorse grows even deeper when placed next to divine kindness. Realizing that he met God's constant grace with blind ingratitude makes the inner pain much sharper.

translit: poytta maṉattēṉ pukaṉṟakoṭuñ coṟkaḷelām vaittuniṉaik kuntōṟum vāḷiṭ ṭaṟukkutaṭā.
translation: Every time I remember all the cruel words I spoke with a deceitful heart, a sword slices within me.
commentary: Words spoken from a false or lying heart leave a deep wound in the speaker. Looking back honestly at one's own cruelty is a painful step in clearing the mind for grace.

translit: poṅkukiṉṟa tīmai pukaṉṟatelā meṇṇiyeṇṇi maṅkukiṉṟa tōṟumuḷḷē vāḷiṭ ṭaṟukkutaṭā.
translation: Every time I languish, thinking repeatedly of all the surging evil I spoke, a sword slices within me.
commentary: Dwelling endlessly on past mistakes can exhaust the spirit. The repeated memory of speaking malicious words drains his strength, bringing back the same piercing sorrow every single time.

translit: ūṭukiṉṟa collā luraittataṉai yeṇṇiyeṇṇi vāṭukiṉṟa tōṟumuḷḷē vāḷiṭ ṭaṟukkutaṭā.
translation: Thinking over and over about the words I spoke in feigned anger, whenever I wither in sorrow, a sword cuts within me, my friend.
commentary: The agony of regret is so sharp it feels like a physical wound. The speaker remembers speaking out of petty annoyance, and the memory now cuts like a sword through his conscience.

translit: uyaṅkukiṉṟēṉ vaṉcol luraittataṉai yeṇṇi mayaṅkukiṉṟa tōṟumuḷḷē vāḷiṭ ṭaṟukkutaṭā.
translation: I suffer. Remembering the harsh words I spoke, whenever I swoon in distress, a sword cuts within me, my friend.
commentary: Careless, harsh words leave deep scars on the one who speaks them. The guilt of having used such language becomes an unbearable inner torment.

translit: colviḷaivu nōkkātē coṉṉatelā meṇṇutoṟum valviṉaiyē ṉuḷḷakattē vāḷiṭ ṭaṟukkutaṭā.
translation: Whenever I think of all I said without considering the consequences of my words, a sword cuts within the heart of this person burdened by cruel karma, my friend.
commentary: Words spoken without thought for their impact carry a heavy cost. The speaker views these thoughtless moments as cruel karma (the inevitable results of past actions), tearing at his heart with sharp remorse.

translit: mēlviḷaivu nōkkātē vēṟucoṉṉa teṇṇutoṟum mālviṉaiyē ṉuḷḷakattē vāḷiṭ ṭaṟukkutaṭā.
translation: Whenever I think of the contrary things I said without considering the future consequences, a sword cuts within the heart of this person burdened by deluded karma, my friend.
commentary: Being contrary or argumentative without caring about the future comes from a place of delusion. Looking back on words spoken in this confused state brings a deep, cutting sorrow.

translit: viñcakattā lantō viḷampiyatai yeṇṇutoṟum vañcakattē ṉuḷḷakattē vāḷiṭ ṭaṟukkutaṭā.
translation: Alas, whenever I think of what I declared out of arrogance, a sword cuts within the heart of this deceitful person, my friend.
commentary: Arrogant speech is exposed here as a kind of self-deception. When pride finally drops away, remembering those boastful declarations brings a searing inner pain.

translit: vilaṅkukiṉṟa neñca viḷaivaiyeṇ ṇuntōṟum malaṅkukiṉṟē ṉuḷḷakattē vāḷiṭ ṭaṟukkutaṭā.
translation: Whenever I consider the outcomes of my wayward heart, I am bewildered. It slashes my inner being like a sword.
commentary: The pain of looking back at a distracted life feels like a physical wound. The speaker examines the consequences of letting the mind wander away from spiritual focus. This honest self-reflection brings deep remorse, cutting through the heart like a sharp blade.

translit: tūymaiyilā vaṉmoḻiyāṟ coṉṉavelā meṇṇutoṟum vāymaiyilē ṉuḷḷakattē vāḷiṭ ṭaṟukkutaṭā.
translation: Whenever I, devoid of truth, think of all the things I said using impure and harsh words, it slashes my inner being like a sword.
commentary: Words spoken in anger or without care leave lasting scars on the speaker's own conscience. Realizing that past speech lacked both purity and truth brings a crushing sense of guilt. The memory of using harsh language becomes a sharp internal torment.

translit: kalikkiṉṟa vañcakak karuttaik karuti valikkiṉṟa tōṟumuḷḷē vāḷiṭ ṭaṟukkutaṭā.
translation: Whenever I dwell on these flourishing deceitful thoughts and feel the pain, it slashes my inner being like a sword.
commentary: Dishonesty begins in the mind before it ever reaches the tongue. Recognizing how deceitful thoughts have grown and flourished inside the mind brings intense sorrow. The pain comes from knowing that holding onto such falsehood blocks the path to grace.

translit: nīṭṭukiṉṟa vañca neṭuñcolelā neñcakattē māṭṭukiṉṟa tōṟumuḷḷē vāḷiṭ ṭaṟukkutaṭā.
translation: Whenever I harbor all those lengthy deceitful words in my heart, it slashes my inner being like a sword.
commentary: Keeping dishonest intentions trapped inside the heart causes deep inner turmoil. Even the memory of telling long, drawn-out lies pollutes the spiritual life. The speaker feels this hidden falsehood as a violent pain in the soul.

translit: poruntukiṉṟa vañcap putumaiyeṇṇi yaiyō varuntukiṉṟa tōṟumuḷḷē vāḷiṭ ṭaṟukkutaṭā.
translation: Alas, whenever I think of these new forms of deceit that take hold of me and grieve over them, it slashes my inner being like a sword.
commentary: The human mind constantly invents fresh ways to deceive itself and others. Watching these new patterns of dishonesty take root brings immense grief. Every time the speaker catches himself falling into these clever new traps of the ego, the realization cuts deep.

translit: veruvikkum vañca veṟuñcolelām neñcil varuvikkun tōṟumuḷḷē vāḷiṭ ṭaṟukkutaṭā.
translation: Whenever I bring to my heart all those frightening, deceitful, and empty words, they cut me inside like a sword, my friend.
commentary: The memory of past insincere or cruel speech becomes a source of intense inner torment. The devotee feels actual physical pain, like a sword cut, whenever he remembers speaking empty words instead of the truth.

translit: ūṭumpō tuṉṉai yuraittavelā nāyaṭiyēṉ nāṭumpō tellāmeṉ ṉāṭi naṭuṅkutaṭā.
translation: Whenever I, a devotee lower than a dog, think about all that I said to you while sulking, my nerves tremble, my friend.
commentary: In traditional Tamil poetry, lovers often stage a temporary sulk or quarrel. Vallalar uses this intimate dynamic to describe his relationship with the divine. He feels a deep physical shudder of remorse for ever speaking to God in frustration.

translit: vāykkaṭaiyā vaṉcol vaḻaṅkiyaveṉ vaṉmaṉattai nāykkaṭaiyē ṉeṇṇutoṟum nāṭi naṭuṅkutaṭā.
translation: Whenever I, lower than a dog, think of my hard heart that carelessly uttered harsh words, my nerves tremble, my friend.
commentary: A central part of Vallalar's teaching is that the heart must be entirely soft and filled with compassion. He shudders at the memory of ever possessing a hardened heart that allowed careless, cruel words to escape his lips.

translit: kaṉṟi yuraitta kaṭuñcoṟ kaṭuvaiyelām naṉṟiyilē ṉeṇṇutoṟum nāṭi naṭuṅkutaṭā.
translation: Whenever I, devoid of gratitude, think of all the poisonous harsh words I spoke in fury, my nerves tremble, my friend.
commentary: Anger is deeply toxic to the spiritual life. The poet compares his past angry outbursts to poison, trembling with shame for showing a lack of gratitude toward grace.

translit: puṉmaiyiṉāl vaṉcoṟ pukaṉṟapulait taṉmaiyelām naṉmaiyilē ṉeṇṇutoṟum nāṭi naṭuṅkutaṭā.
translation: Whenever I, devoid of goodness, think of the base nature that made me speak harsh words out of meanness, my nerves tremble, my friend.
commentary: Harsh speech is seen here as a direct symptom of inner meanness and a lack of genuine goodness. As the poet prepares his soul to receive ArutPerunJothi, the mere memory of these base flaws makes his very nerves tremble.

translit: ūṉeṇṇum vañca vuḷattā luraittavelām nāṉeṇṇun tōṟumeṉṟa ṉāṭi naṭuṅkutaṭā.
translation: Whenever I think of all that was spoken by my deceitful heart obsessed with the flesh, my pulse trembles.
commentary: The regret for past mistakes is so intense that it becomes a physical reaction. The speaker trembles at the memory of words spoken when his mind was distracted by bodily desires and deceit.

translit: vañcaṉaiyā lañcātu vaṉcol pukaṉṟavelām nañcaṉaiyē ṉeṇṇutoṟum nāṭi naṭuṅkutaṭā.
translation: Whenever I, who am like poison, think of all the harsh words I fearlessly uttered through deceit, my pulse trembles.
commentary: The speaker calls his own past nature poisonous. Looking back at times when he lied and spoke harshly without any fear of the consequences causes him deep physical dread.

translit: kōṇaneṭu neñcak kuraṅkāṟ kutittavelām nāṇamilē ṉeṇṇutoṟum nāṭi naṭuṅkutaṭā.
translation: Whenever I, who lack shame, think of all the leaps made by the monkey of my crooked heart, my pulse trembles.
commentary: The restless, undisciplined heart is described as a jumping monkey. The speaker feels ashamed remembering how his own mind used to leap wildly from one crooked thought to another.

translit: ūṉamilā niṉṉai yuraittakoṭuñ collaiyelām ñāṉamilē ṉeṇṇutoṟum nāṭi naṭuṅkutaṭā.
translation: Whenever I, who lack wisdom, think of all the cruel words I spoke against you who are flawless, my pulse trembles.
commentary: The focus shifts to the perfection of the Divine. Remembering how a lack of wisdom led him to speak cruelly against flawless grace brings another wave of trembling remorse.

translit: eṟṟē matiyiliyē ṉeṇṇā turaittataṉaic caṟṟē niṉaittiṭiṉun tātu kalaṅkutaṭā.
translation: Alas! Even if I think for a mere moment of the things I spoke without thinking, lacking all sense, my vital elements are shaken.
commentary: Careless speech leaves a deep scar on the soul. Even a fleeting memory of speaking without sense is enough to shake the speaker to the very core of his physical being.

translit: iṉiyētu ceyvē ṉikaḻnturaitta collait taṉiyē niṉaittiṭiṉun tātu kalaṅkutaṭā.
translation: What shall I do now? Even when I think in solitude about the contemptuous words I spoke, my very being is shaken.
commentary: The memory of speaking with contempt is so powerful that it physically shakes his entire being. A sensitive spirit finds even the memory of past arrogance deeply painful.

translit: nāyaṉaiyē ṉeṇṇāma ṉalaṅkiyavaṉ collaiyelām tāyaṉaiyā yeṇṇutoṟun tātu kalaṅkutaṭā.
translation: O mother-like Lord, whenever I recall all the senseless words I babbled like a dog without thinking, my very being is shaken.
commentary: He contrasts his own ignorant behavior with the unconditional love of the divine. Addressing God as a mother highlights this pure grace. Comparing himself to an unthinking dog emphasizes his deep shame over speaking carelessly.

translit: niṟkurukā vañca niṉaivāl niṉaittavelāñ caṟkuruvē yeṇṇutoṟun tātu kalaṅkutaṭā.
translation: O true Guru, whenever I recall all the deceitful thoughts I harbored without melting in love for You, my very being is shaken.
commentary: True devotion requires a heart that melts with love for the divine. He feels intense guilt because his mind harbored deceit instead of sincere love for his spiritual guide.

translit: vennarakil vīḻum viḷaivāl viḷampiyatai eṉṉaracē yeṇṇutoṟu meṉṉai viḻuṅkutaṭā.
translation: O my King, whenever I recall the words I spoke that are destined to plunge me into cruel hell, the thought swallows me entirely.
commentary: The realization that his past words carry terrible spiritual consequences completely overwhelms him. He feels consumed by the dread of the suffering those past actions will bring.

translit: naṉkaṟiyēṉ vāḷā naviṉṟa navaiyaṉaittum eṉkuruvē yeṇṇutoṟu meṉṉai viḻuṅkutaṭā.
translation: O my Guru, whenever I recall all the vain and faulty words I spoke in my ignorance, the thought swallows me entirely.
commentary: Idle and useless speech is a serious error on the spiritual path. He admits his total ignorance and finds that the memory of his past vanity completely destroys his peace of mind.

translit: āva taṟiyā taṭiyē ṉikaḻntakoṭum pāva niṉaikkiṟ pakīreṉ ṟalaikkutaṭā.
translation: Without knowing the consequences, I, your servant, committed cruel sins. When I think of them, my heart shudders and tosses in fear, O friend.
commentary: Ignorance of the consequences often leads to actions that cause deep regret. The speaker expresses a visceral fear when recalling past mistakes. This shows that a growing spiritual awareness brings a sharp, painful clarity about one's past wrongs.

translit: vantip paṟiyēṉ vaḻaṅkiyavaṉ collaiyelām cintik kiluḷḷē tiṭukkiṭ ṭaḻuṅkutaṭā.
translation: I knew no reverence. When I think inwardly of all the harsh words I spoke, I am shocked and suffer deeply, O friend.
commentary: Harsh speech is recognized here as a direct failure of reverence. The shock and inward suffering the speaker feels upon remembering these words show the heavy burden that unkindness places on the soul.

translit: kuṟṟa niṉaitta koṭuñcolelā meṉṉuḷattē paṟṟa niṉaikkiṟ payamā yirukkutaṭā.
translation: When I hold in my mind all the cruel, fault-finding words I conceived, I am filled with terror, O friend.
commentary: Even the memory of having spoken cruelly brings terror to the awakened mind. The focus rests heavily on the intention behind the words. Spiritual purity requires cleansing one's thoughts of all judgment and fault-finding.

translit: eḷḷukiṉṟa tīmai yeṭutturaittē ṉāṅkataṉai viḷḷukiṉṟa tōṟu muḷḷamventu vetumputaṭā.
translation: I spoke mocking, evil words. Every time I recall them, my heart burns and suffers, O friend.
commentary: Mocking others is named here as an evil that causes lasting inner pain. The burning heart signifies the deep remorse of a conscience that realizes the harm caused by arrogant or dismissive speech.

translit: miṉṉiṭaiyāḷ kāṇa viḷaṅkumaṉṟi lāṭukiṉṟāy eṉṉuṭaiyā yuṉṟa ṉiṇaiyaṭitāṉ nōvātā.
translation: You dance in the shining hall for the goddess with a waist like lightning to see. My master, do your paired feet not ache?
commentary: The divine dance unfolds before the goddess Parvati, who watches it in the shining hall of consciousness. The devotee approaches God with a deeply personal concern, asking if his ceaseless dancing causes his feet to ache. This reverses the usual dynamic of prayer: instead of asking God for protection, the devotee worries over God's own physical well-being.

translit: vaṉṉamutē yiṉpa maliyamaṉṟi lāṭukiṉṟāy eṉṉamutē yuṉṟa ṉiṇaiyaṭitāṉ nōvātā.
translation: O beautiful nectar, you dance in the hall so that bliss overflows. My nectar, do your paired feet not ache?
commentary: The cosmic dance is an outpouring of pure joy meant to flood the universe with bliss. Calling God his personal nectar, Vallalar expresses an intimacy where awe naturally gives way to sweet affection. He wonders how feet that bring so much happiness to others can endure such constant motion.

translit: naṇṇiyamey yaṉpar nayakkamaṉṟi lāṭukiṉṟāy puṇṇiyaṉē yuṉṟaṉatu poṉṉaṭitāṉ nōvātā.
translation: You dance in the hall for the delight of true devotees who draw near. O embodiment of virtue, do your golden feet not ache?
commentary: God dances specifically to delight those who truly love him. The golden feet represent the ultimate refuge for the soul. Yet here, by focusing on the physical strain of this eternal performance, the devotee treats the almighty God with the gentle care of a loving friend.

translit: aṉpariṉpaṅ koḷḷanaṭa mampalattē yāṭukiṉṟāy iṉpuruvā muṉṟa ṉiṇaiyaṭitāṉ nōvātā.
translation: You dance in the open hall so that devotees experience bliss. O embodiment of bliss, do your paired feet not ache?
commentary: The open hall, or ambalam, signifies both the physical temple at Chidambaram and the vast, open space of the soul. God is the very embodiment of bliss, freely offering this joy to anyone who watches. The recurring question about his aching feet shows that true devotion feels like a warm, protective closeness.

translit: nūluṇarvā nuṇṇuṇarvi ṉōkkanaṭa māṭukiṉṟāy mālaṟiyā vuṉṟaṉ malarppātam nōvātā.
translation: You dance to be seen by the subtle awareness that surpasses scriptural knowledge. Do your flower-like feet, unknown to Vishnu, not ache?
commentary: No amount of book learning or scriptural study can truly grasp the reality of God. The divine dance can only be witnessed through a subtle, direct inner awareness. The verse mentions an ancient story where even the great god Vishnu could not find the bottom of Siva's feet, showing that these infinite feet are still treated by the devotee with simple human tenderness.

translit: eḷḷalaṟa vampalattē yiṉpanaṭa māṭukiṉṟāy vaḷḷalē yuṉṟaṉ malaraṭitāṉ nōvātā.
translation: You dance the dance of bliss flawlessly in the Hall. O benevolent Lord, do your flower feet not ache?
commentary: God's eternal dance in the space of divine consciousness brings pure joy to the world. A deep and tender empathy rises in the heart of the devotee, who worries that the Lord's soft, flower-like feet must be aching from this endless movement.

translit: caiva nilaittut taḻaittōṅka vāṭukiṉṟāy teyva maṇiyē tiruvaṭitāṉ nōvātā.
translation: You dance so the Saiva path stands firm and flourishes. O divine gem, do your holy feet not ache?
commentary: The dance of the divine sustains the path of devotion to Siva. In his great love for the Lord, the devotee sees God laboring tirelessly to keep spiritual truth alive and flourishing, and asks again out of pure concern if this effort causes Him pain.

translit: ellāru miṉpuṟ ṟirukkanaṭa māṭukiṉṟāy vallāriṉ vallāy malarppātam nōvātā.
translation: You dance so that everyone lives in bliss. O mightiest of the mighty, do your flower feet not ache?
commentary: The ultimate purpose of God's unceasing action is universal joy. The divine is the greatest of all powers, yet the devotee's love is so intimate that he feels protective of the Lord, asking how feet so delicate can bear the weight of working for the happiness of every living being.

translit: avamē kaḻintiṉpa maṉparkoḷa vāṭukiṉṟāy civamē niṉatu tiruvaṭitāṉ nōvātā.
translation: You dance so that futility vanishes and your devotees attain bliss. O Sivam, do your holy feet not ache?
commentary: God's active presence sweeps away all the wasted, futile efforts of human life and replaces them with lasting joy. Calling out to Sivam (the supreme reality of grace), the devotee feels the immense labor required to save souls from despair and wonders how the divine feet can endure it.

translit: taṟparamā maṉṟiṟ ṟaṉinaṭaṉa māṭukiṉṟāy ciṟparamē yuṉṟaṉ tirumēṉi nōvātā.
translation: You perform your unique dance in the supreme Hall. O supreme consciousness, does your holy body not ache?
commentary: The supreme consciousness is called Cirparam, a reality beyond ordinary human understanding. As the poem closes, the devotee's tender concern expands from God's feet to His entire being. The boundless divine takes on a form to perform this solitary dance of grace, and the watcher is left completely overcome with love, asking if the holy body itself aches from the effort.

translit: vilvavēr mālai miḷirntacaiya vāṭukiṉṟāy celvamē yuṉṟaṉ tirumēṉi nōvātā.
translation: You dance as the garland of bael roots sways and shines. O treasure, does your sacred form not ache?
commentary: This verse expresses deep, intimate devotion. Watching the divine cosmic dance, the speaker notices the swaying garland of bael roots, a plant sacred to Siva. Instead of feeling distant awe, he feels a sudden surge of loving concern for the dancer. He asks if endless dancing causes the sacred body to ache. Here the all-powerful divine becomes a treasured beloved who receives the devotee's care.

translit: kaṟṟateṉṟuñ cākāta kalviyeṉṟu kaṇṭukoṇṭuṉ aṟputacciṟ ṟampalatti laṉpuvaittēṉ aiyāvē.
translation: Realizing that true learning is the knowledge of deathlessness, I placed my love upon your wondrous little hall, O Lord.
commentary: The only learning that truly matters is the knowledge of how to overcome death. Vallalar directs his love toward the "little hall" (ciṟṟampalam, the space of divine light within), where this ultimate truth is revealed.

translit: īṭaṇaikaḷ nīkkinamak kiṉpaḷikku meṉṟumaṉṟil āṭun tiruvaṭikkē ācaivaittēṉ aiyāvē.
translation: Knowing they will remove our worldly ties and grant us bliss, I placed my desire upon your holy feet dancing in the hall, O Lord.
commentary: He fixes his heart entirely on the divine feet dancing in the hall. He trusts that this devotion is what severs all worldly attachments and brings true happiness.

translit: nāṉanta meytā nalampeṟavē yeṇṇimaṉṟil āṉanta nāṭakattuk kaṉpuvaittēṉ aiyāvē.
translation: Intending to attain the goodness of never meeting an end, I placed my love upon the blissful dance in the hall, O Lord.
commentary: The ultimate goal is absolute permanence, a state where existence never comes to an end. Vallalar sees the Lord's joyous dance as the source of this immortal goodness.

translit: vāṭalaṟac cākā varaṅkoṭukku meṉṟumaṉṟil āṭalaṭip poṉmalarkkē aṉpuvaittēṉ aiyāvē.
translation: Knowing they will grant the boon of deathlessness free from all withering, I placed my love upon your dancing, golden, flower-like feet in the hall, O Lord.
commentary: A deathless state means a body and soul free from any physical decay or withering. Vallalar places his devotion at the divine feet because they alone hold the power to grant this condition.

translit: poṟpuṟavē poṉṟāp poruḷaḷikku meṉṟumaṉṟil aṟputappoṟ cēvaṭikkē aṉpuvaittēṉ aiyāvē.
translation: Knowing they will beautifully grant the imperishable reality, I placed my love upon your wondrous, golden, reddened feet in the hall, O Lord.
commentary: True wealth is the spiritual reality that can never be destroyed. The speaker adores the Lord's feet because they beautifully offer this imperishable truth.

translit: īṉamaṟut teṉṟum iṟavāmai nalkumeṉṟē ñāṉamaṇi maṉṟiṭattē naṇpuvaittēṉ aiyāvē.
translation: Believing it will eradicate baseness and grant deathlessness forever, I placed my love upon the gem-like Hall of Wisdom, O Lord.
commentary: True spiritual knowledge removes human flaws and grants eternal life. Vallalar places his devotion entirely on the divine space of wisdom, trusting it to bring about this state of deathlessness.

translit: ōrtuṇainiṉ poṉṉaṭiyeṉ ṟuṉṉukiṉṟē ṉuṉṉaiyaṉṟi ārtuṇaiyum vēṇṭēṉeṉ aṉpuṭaiya aiyāvē.
translation: I meditate on your golden feet as my sole support. I want no one's support but yours, my loving Lord.
commentary: God is the only true refuge in life. Vallalar declares his complete reliance on the divine, rejecting all worldly or human forms of support.

translit: pūcaiceytu peṟṟavuṉṟaṉ poṉṉaṭimē laṉṟiyayal ācaiyoṉṟu millaiyeṉak kaṉpuṭaiya aiyāvē.
translation: I have no desire for anything other than your golden feet, which I attained by performing worship, my loving Lord.
commentary: Sincere worship erases all worldly desires. Having reached the presence of the divine, Vallalar finds that he wants absolutely nothing else.

translit: iccainiṉmē laṉṟiyeṉak keḷḷaḷavum vēṟumoṉṟil iccaiyilai niṉṉāṇai yeṉṉarumai aiyāvē.
translation: I have desire for you, but I do not have even a sesame seed's measure of desire for anything else. I swear this upon you, my precious Lord.
commentary: Worldly attachments have vanished completely. To prove his absolute focus on the divine, Vallalar swears an oath to God that he holds no other desires, even down to the smallest imaginable measure.

translit: eppaṭiniṉ ṉuḷḷa mirukkiṉṟa teṉṉaḷavil appaṭinī ceykaveṉak kaṉpuṭaiya aiyāvē.
translation: Whatever is in your heart concerning me, do exactly that, my loving Lord.
commentary: The ultimate expression of devotion is complete surrender. Vallalar gives up all personal requests, asking God to direct his life exactly as the divine will dictates.

translit: evvaṇṇam niṉkaruttiṅ keṉṉaḷavi leṇṇiyatō avvaṇṇañ ceykaveṉak kaṉpuṭaiya aiyāvē.
translation: Whatever you have intended for me in your mind, please do it exactly that way, my loving Master.
commentary: Total surrender to the divine will is the focus here. The speaker asks his Master to carry out whatever is planned for him, showing complete trust that God's intention is perfect. Surrendering in this way means letting go of personal demands and accepting grace exactly as it is given.

translit: tēcuṟuniṉ ṟaṇṇaruḷān teḷḷamutaṅ koḷḷavuḷḷē ācaipoṅku kiṉṟateṉak kaṉpuṭaiya aiyāvē.
translation: Desire surges within me to consume the clear ambrosia of your radiant, cool grace, my loving Master.
commentary: A deep yearning for divine grace fills this verse. Grace appears as a clear, cool ambrosia, the nectar of immortality. The surging desire described here is a deep spiritual hunger that can only be satisfied by a direct experience of the divine.

translit: mācaṟuniṉ poṉṉaruḷā māmaṇipeṟ ṟāṭavuḷḷē ācaipoṅku kiṉṟateṉak kaṉpuṭaiya aiyāvē.
translation: Desire surges within me to receive the great gem of your flawless golden grace and dance in joy, my loving Master.
commentary: Grace is pictured here as a flawless golden gem. Receiving this supreme treasure brings such overwhelming joy that the natural response is to dance. The experience of God's compassion is a vibrant and joyful celebration.

translit: nācamilā niṉṉaruḷām ñāṉamarun tuṇṇavuḷḷē ācaipoṅku kiṉṟateṉak kaṉpuṭaiya aiyāvē.
translation: Desire surges within me to consume the medicine of wisdom that is your indestructible grace, my loving Master.
commentary: Grace acts as a medicine of wisdom. This divine medicine cures the fundamental illness of ignorance and grants a state of being that cannot be destroyed. The surging desire is a deep longing for the ultimate truth that heals the soul completely.

translit: puṅkavar pukaḻumātaṅkamu kantikaḻ eṅkaḷ kaṇēcarān tuṅkaṟku - maṅkaḷam.
translation: Auspiciousness to our exalted Lord Ganesha, who shines with the elephant face praised by the celestials.
commentary: The benediction opens with Ganesha, the elephant-faced god of new beginnings. The word maṅkaḷam means auspiciousness or blessing. It is traditional to open and close major works by calling down this divine grace.

translit: pōtan tikaḻpara nātan taṉilniṉṟa nītarāñ caṇmuka nātaṟku - maṅkaḷam.
translation: Auspiciousness to Lord Shanmuga, the righteous one abiding in the supreme sound where wisdom shines.
commentary: Shanmuga is Murugan, the six-faced god of wisdom. He is described here as abiding in the supreme cosmic sound (para nātam), the sacred vibration where true spiritual understanding awakens.

translit: pūcaicey vāruḷam ācaicey vārtillai īcar ematunaṭa rājaṟku - maṅkaḷam.
translation: Auspiciousness to our Lord Nataraja, the Lord of Thillai who cherishes the hearts of those who worship him.
commentary: Nataraja is Siva as the cosmic dancer, presiding in the great temple town of Thillai (Chidambaram). The divine dancer responds intimately to the devotion flowing from the hearts of those who seek him.

translit: pūmi pukaḻkuru cāmi taṉai-īṉṟa vāmi eṉuñciva kāmikku - maṅkaḷam.
translation: Auspiciousness to Sivakami known as Vami, who gave birth to the Guru Lord praised by the world.
commentary: Sivakami is the goddess who stands beside Nataraja as his divine consort. She is celebrated here as the mother of the universal teacher, Murugan, who guides souls toward the ultimate truth.

translit: puṅkami kuñcelvan tuṅkamu ṟattarum ceṅka malattiru maṅkaikku - maṅkaḷam.
translation: Auspiciousness to the divine lady of the red lotus, who bestows abundant and exalted wealth.
commentary: The lady of the red lotus is Lakshmi, the goddess of prosperity. Invoking her brings both material abundance and deep spiritual wealth to the world.

translit: pūṇi laṅkuntaṉa vāṇi parampara vāṇi kalaiñarkoḷ vāṇikku - maṅkaḷam.
translation: Auspiciousness to Vani whose breasts shine with ornaments, the supreme Vani, the Vani held dear by scholars.
commentary: The blessing here is offered to Vani (Saraswati), the traditional goddess of speech, learning, and the arts. Scholars and seekers of truth revere her as the source of wisdom. This verse honors her supreme nature and the radiant clarity she brings to the human mind.

translit: puṇṇiya rākiya kaṇṇiya rāyttavam paṇṇiya pattarkku muttarkku - maṅkaḷam.
translation: Auspiciousness to the virtuous and esteemed devotees who perform austerities, and to the liberated souls.
commentary: This verse sends a blessing to both the active seekers and those who have already reached the ultimate goal. It wishes auspiciousness upon devoted practitioners performing spiritual disciplines, as well as the liberated souls who have found total freedom. By honoring both groups together, the poem blesses the entire spiritual path from steadfast effort to final realization.

glossary.def: Asura. Demon or malevolent force. Vallalar uses this term to symbolize the deep-seated ignorance and ego that God destroys to grant the soul liberation.

Sorrow or mental distress. Vallalar employs this word to showcase a humorous exchange, splitting its syllables into the Tamil words for 'cow' and 'herd' so the Lord can pretend he does not understand the devotee's spiritual plea.

Alaivay. The edge of the waves, wandering, or the sacred coastal town of Tiruchendur. Vallalar employs this as a divine pun in his poetry, where the disguised Lord gives a name that signifies both his famous temple and the restless bewilderment he brings to the soul.
Amaravati. The celestial capital city of the gods. Vallalar states that sincere devotion makes even the supreme rulers of this heavenly realm treat the seeker as close kin.

Ambalam. An open hall, specifically referring to the cosmic space where Siva performs his sacred dance. Vallalar teaches that this physical space represents the vast consciousness where the divine light performs its endless dance of grace.
Ambikai. A gentle motherly form of the Goddess. Vallalar invokes this name to express absolute trust in her tender care and spiritual guidance.

The physical universe or macrocosm. Vallalar views the entire cosmos as a living structure nourished and sustained by the union of divine wisdom and spiritual power, filled entirely with the radiant presence of the Divine.
Hara. A traditional name for Lord Siva. Vallalar uses this specific name to invoke God as the destroyer of illusions and the ultimate source of spiritual liberation.
Arappalli. A sacred temple located in the Kolli Hills of Tamil Nadu. Vallalar praises the divine presence established here as a timeless, dancing Lord.

Arunagiri. Arunagirinathar, a famous medieval Tamil saint who composed rhythmic hymns praising Lord Murugan. Vallalar invokes him as the supreme example of a struggling human who was in the end saved and transformed by divine mercy.
ArutPerunJothi. The Vast Grace-Light: Vallalar's name for God. The one infinite Light of grace from which everything comes and in which everything is held, open to every living being.
The eight traditional mystic powers. Vallalar warns spiritual seekers never to desire these occult abilities as a goal, because they naturally arrive to serve a fully realized soul.

Adhvas. The established spiritual paths or routes of progression in traditional philosophy. Vallalar teaches that a seeker must completely transcend these conventional religious routes to reach the ultimate divine truth.

Satchidananda. Pure existence, consciousness, and bliss. Vallalar identifies this triad as the foundational nature of the soul, though the seeker must eventually let go of even the awareness of this joy to achieve final freedom.

Saiva or Saivism. The spiritual tradition centered on the worship of Lord Siva. Vallalar honors its historical revival through the early saints while later broadening his own teaching into the universal path of Sanmarkkam.

Sakkiyanar. A legendary devotee who threw a stone at a sacred shrine every day as his chosen form of worship. Vallalar cites this story to prove that the divine gracefully accepts any action performed with absolute love.
Samarasam. Complete harmony or equality. Vallalar uses this word to describe the ultimate spiritual state where all divisions dissolve into universal brotherhood.
Religion, especially a sect set against other sects. In these verses Vallalar seeks the reality that sectarian disputes cannot grasp.

Sambandar. The great South Indian child-saint of the Saiva faith. Vallalar aligns Murugan with this beloved historical figure to show that supreme divine wisdom often manifests in a pure, childlike form.
Sambu or Shambu. A traditional name for Lord Siva meaning the source of happiness. Vallalar calls Murugan the shining fruit of the Sambu tree to highlight his direct divine lineage.
Sanmarkkam. The pure or true path. Vallalar established Sanmarkkam as a universal spiritual path based entirely on truth, divine light, and compassion for all living beings.
Shanmuga. The six-faced Lord Murugan. Vallalar invokes this fierce, protective warrior form specifically to destroy intense physical suffering and reverse the cruelty inflicted upon his devotees.

Saravanabhava. The sacred six-syllable name and mantra of Lord Murugan. Vallalar invokes this powerful name to call upon the ultimate sovereign who guarantees absolute spiritual protection and liberation.
Siddhi. Spiritual attainment or perfection. Vallalar views these accomplishments as natural outcomes of divine grace rather than worldly powers to be pursued for their own sake.
Supreme divine wisdom. Vallalar describes this as the highest knowledge of reality that is poured out as grace to devotees who melt inwardly with love.
Sivam. The ultimate state of absolute reality, auspiciousness, and spiritual perfection. For Vallalar, this is the ultimate divine principle that takes on the form of the supreme light to save souls.
Siva. The supreme Lord. Vallalar views him as the absolute supreme reality and the ultimate source of all grace.

Siva-yoga. Union with the divine. Vallalar teaches that this supreme spiritual connection arises from direct internal experience rather than scripture reading, providing a unique bliss impossible to achieve through mere intellectual learning.
Jothi. Divine light or flame. Vallalar identifies this supreme Jothi as the ultimate form of God that dispels the darkness of human ignorance.

Suran or Surapadman. A powerful mythological demon representing absolute arrogance. Vallalar refers to God's defeat of such beings to show that divine compassion sometimes requires fierce action to restore cosmic balance.

Ekambaram. The historic temple of Siva in Kanchipuram. Vallalar invokes this sacred site to represent the supreme Lord who must be experienced simultaneously within the soul and in the external world.

Erakam. The holy town of Swamimalai, another major temple site in the Tamil sacred landscape. Vallalar names this site to celebrate the historical lineage of grace flowing through places of deep devotion.

A highly poisonous and intensely bitter plant native to India. Vallalar uses its toxic fruit as a metaphor for worldly life, showing how material pursuits appear normal but in the end bring spiritual ruin.

Indra. The king of the celestial deities. Vallalar mentions him to emphasize the supreme majesty of the Lord, showing that even the highest heavenly rulers must praise and rely upon the ultimate divine reality.
Ravana. The mythological king of Lanka. Vallalar uses his defeat as proof that God has the power to subdue the most deeply rooted cruelties and sins.
Jeevakarunyam. Compassion for all living beings. Vallalar teaches that acting with this universal kindness is the absolute prerequisite for receiving divine grace.
Kailash. The sacred celestial abode of Lord Siva. Vallalar mentions this mountain to contrast the distant majesty of the supreme Lord with the intimate grace God shows to ordinary people.
Kama. The god of lust and sensual desire. Vallalar references his cruel arrows to personify the relentless physical cravings that distract the soul from spiritual devotion.
Ganapati or Ganesha. In Vallalar's opening prayers, this deity represents the accessible face of God who firmly establishes clarity in the human mind.
Kandakottam. A significant temple dedicated to Murugan in Chennai. Vallalar addresses these specific verses to the Lord of this shrine, establishing it as a focal point for experiencing divine grace.
Kanda or Skanda. Another name for the deity Murugan. Vallalar addresses him directly as the supreme spiritual guide who destroys worldly attachments to liberate the devoted soul.
Kevala. A dormant, isolated state of the soul or a condition of deep spiritual ignorance. Vallalar prays to be lifted completely out of this dark condition into a life sustained by pure grace.
Murder. Vallalar means the murder of any living being, not only of humans.
Guha or Guhan. The hidden one, an ancient name for Murugan. Vallalar uses this title to emphasize the divine presence dwelling deeply and secretly within the human heart.
Kumara or Kumaran. The eternal divine youth, a traditional name for Lord Murugan. Vallalar invokes this title to emphasize the vibrant, undying energy of the divine that heals all spiritual diseases.
Kuvalai. The blue water lily. In Vallalar's poetic imagery, this flower represents the cool, dark, and deeply compassionate eyes of God looking down upon the struggling soul.
A flower garland or a state of spiritual delusion. Vallalar relies on this dual meaning to show how the Lord accepts physical devotion while simultaneously destroying inner ignorance.
Deer. Lord Siva holds a leaping deer in His hand to symbolize His complete mastery over the restless human mind.
Maya. Illusion or the deceptive nature of the physical world. Vallalar describes this as a treacherous ocean or a painful ladder where worldly attachments trap the soul in empty struggle.
Murugan. The Tamil god of youth and beauty. Vallalar often addresses him as the supreme embodiment of divine grace and the ultimate refuge for a struggling soul.
Nada. The primal sound of creation. Vallalar teaches that the highest divine compassion stands far beyond even this foundational cosmic vibration.
Otriyur. The sacred coastal town of Otriyur. Vallalar spent his formative years walking daily to this shrine to pour out his early devotion to Siva.

Pancha patakam. The five heinous sins in classical Indian thought. Vallalar invokes this concept to demonstrate that absolute divine mercy will erase even the heaviest spiritual debts of a sincere seeker.
Pranava. The primal sound or the sacred syllable Om. Vallalar envisions this ancient sound as a radiant light awakening naturally in the pure hearts of spiritual seekers.
Rama. Vallalar invokes this divine figure as a supreme savior whose immense grace can rescue even the most flawed and helpless soul.

Thanigachalam. Mount Thanigai, a sacred hill shrine dedicated to Lord Murugan. Vallalar composed many of his earliest intense devotional poems directing his spiritual longing toward the deity residing at this specific site.
Thanigai. The sacred hill town of Thanigai dedicated to the youth deity Murugan. Vallalar uses this physical location as a symbol of the ultimate spiritual refuge where the weary soul finds rest.
Thillai. The sacred temple town of Chidambaram. Vallalar frequently references this sacred space as the ultimate cosmic stage where Lord Siva performs his dance of grace.
Sacred white ash. It serves as a symbol of absolute purity and the complete destruction of the ego in Vallalar's poetry.
Thyagar. Lord Thyagar, the presiding form of Siva at Thiru Otriyur. Vallalar frequently addresses the divine using this local name to establish an intimate, conversational tone.

Thumbai. A small white flower traditionally offered to the divine. Vallalar contrasts the simple joy of carrying a basket of these flowers with the heavy burden of maintaining a sorrowful physical body.
Turiya. The fourth state of spiritual awareness, beyond waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. Vallalar teaches that the ultimate divine reality exists even beyond this highly elevated human state.
Turiyatita. The supreme state beyond the fourth level of consciousness. Vallalar identifies this as the absolute peak of spiritual awareness where the soul unites completely with the divine.
Uma. The goddess Uma, also known as Parvati. Vallalar invokes her mythological role as Siva's wife to highlight the compassionate, maternal aspect of God that grants saving grace to struggling souls.

Rudra. The traditional Hindu deity of destruction. Vallalar views Rudra as a lesser divinity bound by the qualities of material nature, distinguishing him from the single supreme reality that transcends all natural laws.
Breath or life force, which also translates as a horse. Vallalar uses this poetic double meaning to describe God riding directly into the worshipper upon their very breath.
Vallabai. A divine consort associated with Ganesha. Vallalar's early poetry praises traditional deities and their consorts as unified expressions of a single supreme grace.

Valli. The tribal hunter girl who becomes the consort of Murugan. Vallalar uses the myth of God sneaking away with her in the night as a metaphor for how divine love secretly captures the devotee's mind.
The sacred spear wielded by the deity Murugan. Vallalar views this weapon as a symbol of supreme divine knowledge that actively cuts away the root of repeated worldly births.
Vengai. The Indian kino tree. Vallalar uses the legend of the Lord transforming into this tree to illustrate the playful lengths to which the divine will go to win over a devoted soul.
Vilva. Sacred leaves offered during worship. Presenting a basket of these leaves represents a meaningful spiritual life, making the physical body worthwhile rather than a useless burden.

Vinayakar. The elephant-headed deity who removes spiritual and material obstacles. Vallalar addresses him as a benevolent giver of grace who rescues the devotee from hypocrisy and grants the strength for constant devotion.
Primal light. Vallalar teaches that even this foundational cosmic element fails to capture the ultimate reality, as the supreme divine presence outlasts all such temporary dualities.
